pairs.tendency: Players take turns while a slow change builds one small step at a time, and whoever happens to move when it crosses the line sets off the flip.
pros: Each step is easy to follow.
The one who tipped it is clear.
cons: Turn order decides who takes the blame.
Waiting can hide the slow change.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves at the same time while a slow change builds from all their moves, so nobody can say whose move crossed the line.
pros: The build-up is shared by all.
The flip is a joint surprise.
cons: Nobody can trace the line to one move.
Quick play can hide the slow change.

pairs.tendency: Nobody waits for a turn while a slow change builds from many quick moves, and the flip comes in the middle of the rush.
pros: Fast play makes the build-up felt.
The flip arrives in a rush.
cons: Players have little time to notice the line.
The quickest player sets it off.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock while a slow change builds, so players rush their moves, and the flip comes when haste crosses the line.
pros: Time pressure makes the build-up felt.
A rushed flip feels real.
cons: Rushed players miss the slow change.
A clock can end a move mid-thought.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks while a slow change builds in the background, and the flip comes on a day when nobody was watching.
pros: Waiting makes the slow change real.
Players check back to see the flip.
cons: The change can be forgotten between turns.
A flip can arrive with players absent.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down while a slow change builds, so there is time to see it, and the flip lands in a calm and slow setting.
pros: Slowness helps players see the change.
The flip has a quiet weight.
cons: Slow play can bore some players.
A calm flip can feel small.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up while a slow change builds, so players get less time to notice, and the flip comes in a rush at the end.
pros: Speeding up makes the build-up feel urgent.
The flip arrives with the finish.
cons: Players have less time to see the line.
Early quiet turns can seem to do nothing.

pairs.tendency: Some throws give another turn while a slow change builds, and a run of extra turns can carry one player over the line before others can respond.
pros: Extra turns add to the build-up.
A run of moves can flip the game.
cons: One player can cross the line alone.
Others cannot respond in time.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages while a slow change builds across them, and the line is crossed at the point where one stage hands over to the next.
pros: Stages show when the build-up ends.
The new stage starts after the flip.
cons: Early stage choices may seem to do nothing.
The flip can make earlier stages feel pointless.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system whose slow change builds with little effect until a line is crossed, so players see the whole system flip, as a lake turns green.
pros: Shows a real flip in a system.
Players can trace causes to the line.
cons: The line may be hard to place on a model.
A flip can seem sudden if the build-up is unclear.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a real group watching a slow change, and groups see the line at different times, so some act early and others only after it is crossed.
pros: Each group sees the change differently.
Players learn who warns whom.
cons: Groups can talk past each other.
Groups that act late take the blame.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws on one limited thing while the slow change builds in how much is left, and one more draw crosses the line and the resource collapses for all.
pros: Shows how small draws add up.
Players share the warning signs.
cons: Each player feels one more draw is harmless.
Nobody feels they caused the collapse.

pairs.tendency: What players do now shows only some rounds later, so the line may be crossed long before anyone sees it, and the flip arrives with no clear cause.
pros: Shows a long gap between cause and effect.
Players learn to look ahead.
cons: Players can feel the flip was unfair.
Hard to tell which move crossed the line.

pairs.tendency: Players try a rule while a slow change builds, and the rule can hold things back, or add to the change, until the line is crossed anyway.
pros: A rule can be tested before use.
Players can see what it holds back.
cons: A rule can seem to work until the flip.
Players may blame the rule for the flip.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players look at when the line was crossed and what they could have seen earlier, so the flip becomes something they can talk about.
pros: Players find the moment it tipped.
Talk turns the flip into learning.
cons: Hindsight can make the line look obvious.
The debrief can blame players for a late flip.

pairs.tendency: Once the line is crossed, the change cannot be undone, so torn cards or stickers on the board show the flip for every later game.
pros: The flip leaves a lasting mark.
Players feel how final the line is.
cons: Players may avoid the line altogether.
The next game starts after the flip.

pairs.tendency: The rules make the point that small changes add up to a sudden shift, and players feel the argument only when the line is crossed.
pros: The rules show the point without saying it.
The flip becomes the argument.
cons: Players can miss the point until the flip.
A rule can make the flip look planned.

pairs.tendency: The line in the game stands for a real one, such as a habit or a promise that holds until one broken day, so the flip is felt beyond the table.
pros: The flip feels real.
Players think about real lines.
cons: The flip can upset players.
Needs care.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, such as trust, and a slow loss of points builds until one drop crosses the line and the whole value is gone.
pros: Slow loss of trust is easy to see.
Players see a value fall at once.
cons: Players may chase points and ignore the line.
A flip can seem harsh.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living while a slow change builds, so they can feel the point where it all shifts before anyone tries it for real.
pros: Players feel the shift ahead of time.
A rehearsed flip is easier to plan for.
cons: A rehearsal cannot show every line.
Players may think the real flip will look the same.

pairs.tendency: Stocks such as soil, debt or trust build up turn by turn while a slow change adds to them, and a stock crossing its limit flips the game at once.
pros: Stocks show the line coming.
Players watch a pile near its limit.
cons: A pile can seem fine until the flip.
Players may ignore piles that grow slowly.

pairs.tendency: Between turns the world moves by a fixed rule while a slow change builds, and the rule alone crosses the line, with nobody choosing the flip.
pros: The world sets the pace.
Players learn to watch for a flip that nobody chose.
cons: Players cannot stop a fixed rule.
The flip can seem unfair.

pairs.tendency: Sudden events hit while a slow change builds, and a shock that arrives near the line is the one that crosses it, so players cannot tell shock from slow change.
pros: Shocks show how little it can take.
Players talk about what really tipped it.
cons: Shocks can hide the slow change.
Players may blame the shock alone.

pairs.tendency: Each round is a year, so a slow change that took decades fits into an afternoon, and the flip comes after only a few turns of play.
pros: A long build-up is quick to play.
Players see decades flip in an hour.
cons: A few rounds can seem too short.
Players may not feel how slow it was.

pairs.tendency: A gauge shows the slow change creeping toward the line, and players can see it climb, while the flip shows up on it all at once.
pros: The gauge shows how near the line is.
Players can talk about the gauge.
cons: Players may trust the gauge too much.
Real lines are rarely marked this clearly.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different amounts while a slow change builds, so some feel it early and some late, and the flip falls hardest on those with least.
pros: Shows who feels the change first.
The flip feels unfair in a real way.
cons: Players with least can feel left out.
Players with most can ignore the line.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes rules while a slow change builds, and a rule that crosses the line may help the leader and cost everyone else.
pros: Shows who gains from a change.
Players talk about fairness.
cons: Rules can hide the line.
Players can feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: Each role wants something different while a slow change builds, so some push toward the line and others away, and the flip decides who wins.
pros: Roles show who wants the flip.
Players weigh their goals against the line.
cons: Players may push toward the line for gain.
A flip can end the contest at once.

pairs.tendency: The game opens on a described situation where a slow change is already under way, and players read where the line might be before the first move.
pros: Players start with a clear picture.
The line can be discussed first.
cons: The description can give the line away.
Players may only watch for the line.

pairs.tendency: Players argue why a move would work while a slow change builds, and the table decides when an argued move crosses the line.
pros: Arguments show how players read the change.
The table shares the flip.
cons: Talk can drift from the slow change.
A fluent talker can steer the line.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points while a slow change builds, so players can say what they notice, and a pause just before the line can change what they do.
pros: Pauses help players see the build-up.
Talk can change the flip.
cons: A pause can break the build-up.
A pause can give the line away.

pairs.tendency: The game is played again with one thing changed, so players compare when the line was crossed and what moved it in each round.
pros: Shows what moves the line.
Players find out what changed the flip.
cons: Players may repeat the same flip.
A second game can feel less surprising.

pairs.tendency: The game says what it left out, so players know the line is a simplified one and may sit elsewhere in the real thing.
pros: Players see where the model stops.
Players question where the line really sits.
cons: The note can pull players out of play.
Players may distrust the line in the game.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about help place the line, so players learn where those people see the change tipping and where outsiders would not.
pros: The line rests on real experience.
Players hear how it feels to cross it.
cons: Designers can lose control of where the line sits.
Players may disagree on the line.

pairs.tendency: Orders and goods move down a chain while a slow change builds, and one link crossing its limit sends a sudden shock through every other link.
pros: Shows how one link reaches all.
Players feel the shock travel.
cons: Players only see their own link.
A flip can come with long delays.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own stock while a slow change builds across the system, so nobody sees the line, and the flip arrives as a surprise to all.
pros: Shows how little one corner sees.
Players learn to share warnings.
cons: Nobody sees the line coming.
Players may blame others for what they could not see.

pairs.tendency: One slow step limits everything after it, while a slow change builds there, and the step crossing its limit makes the whole line stop at once.
pros: Shows where the line sits.
Players find the weak step.
cons: Other steps can hide the slow change.
A flip stops every player downstream.

pairs.tendency: Players either push goods forward or pull orders back while a slow change builds, and the flip comes when the push and pull meet at the line.
pros: Shows the build-up from both sides.
Players compare two ways of working.
cons: Each way can hide the slow change.
A flip can look different from each side.

pairs.tendency: Players move goods in batches while a slow change builds, and a batch that crosses the line floods one step and starves the next.
pros: Batches show how a flip piles up.
Players see a pile arrive all at once.
cons: Big batches can hide the slow change.
One batch can overrun a step.

pairs.tendency: Machines wear a little each round while a slow change builds, and the one that crosses the line breaks down and stops the work at once.
pros: Wear is easy to follow.
A breakdown is a clear flip.
cons: Players may ignore the wear.
A breakdown can stall the whole line.

pairs.tendency: Too little and too much both cost something while a slow change builds, and the line is crossed when stock moves too far either way at once.
pros: Players weigh two risks near the line.
Shows a flip in both directions.
cons: The line can be hard to place.
Players may chase one cost and miss the other.

pairs.tendency: Each roll moves a piece a few spaces, while a pile such as debt or soil grows a little on each landing, so the total outweighs any one throw.
pros: A single track shows the pile growing.
Easy for beginners to follow.
cons: Dice hide how much of the pile players caused.
The pile can seem to grow by itself.

pairs.tendency: Each pick adds a card to a growing collection or pile, and the passed hands show what others are adding, so the pile reads as everyone's work.
pros: Players see the pile rise through picks.
Each pick feels small but counts.
cons: Early picks matter more than they look.
The pile can be hard to track across hands.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for things that add to or draw down a pile, so prices climb as the pile gets bigger or scarcer.
pros: Prices show how big the pile is.
Players learn what a full stock is worth.
cons: Rich players can drain the pile first.
Bids can draw attention from the pile.

pairs.tendency: Each extra push adds to a pile that can tip into loss, and the pile keeps its size from one turn to the next, so risks carry over.
pros: Players feel a pile of risk growing.
Stopping early gives a visible reason.
cons: One bust can undo many careful turns.
Cautious players may never test the pile.

pairs.tendency: Pieces stay on the map turn after turn, so each area holds a growing stock of forces, and old holdings count for more than new moves.
pros: Long-held areas show past effort.
Slow build-up gives players time to plan.
cons: Early leaders can be hard to dislodge.
Many piles to track across the map.

pairs.tendency: Workers fill action spaces that add to stores of goods or debts, and stores keep rising or falling after each round of placing.
pros: Stores show what each job has built.
Planning ahead has a visible payoff.
cons: Busy boards make stores easy to miss.
Early jobs can lock in a lead.

pairs.tendency: A pattern is built tile by tile, and each placed tile stays, so the unfinished pattern is a growing pile of past choices.
pros: Progress stays on the table.
Calm, steady building.
cons: Mistakes stay in the pattern.
Little to show how fast the pile grows.

pairs.tendency: Cards held back build up in your hand like a store, and what you save or spend this turn shapes what you can do many turns later.
pros: Saving and spending show a stock clearly.
Players plan around a growing store.
cons: Big hands slow turns.
Hoarding can stall the game.

pairs.tendency: Won tricks pile up in front of each player over the hand, so the size of each pile matters at the end more than any one trick.
pros: Piles make the hand's progress clear.
Early tricks feel like they count.
cons: The pile is only counted at the end.
Players may not link a pile to the system.

pairs.tendency: Players trade goods and promises, and what each person holds in stock or owes grows or shrinks with every deal.
pros: Stocks give deals something to be about.
Debts and favours become visible.
cons: Talk can drift away from the stocks.
Players with big piles can dominate deals.

pairs.tendency: Each card or token is added to a growing collection, so the stock of each kind matters more than any single pick.
pros: Collections show a stock plainly.
Clear goals for each pick.
cons: Players may only count sets, not trends.
Collecting can feel like a checklist.

pairs.tendency: Each tile placed stays on the shared map, so the map itself is a stock of past choices, with fields, roads or damage building up over turns.
pros: The map records every choice.
Players see slow change in one picture.
cons: Early tiles shape everything after.
Tile luck can blur cause and effect.

pairs.tendency: Each answer in the chain leaves something behind, such as a debt of favours or a stock of phrases, and the chain keeps whatever was said before.
pros: A shared history builds round by round.
Players listen to what came before.
cons: Hard to keep a pile when play is spoken.
Players may forget what has piled up.

pairs.tendency: Without talking, players can only read the pile on the table, so what has built up becomes the main way anyone learns what others are doing.
pros: The pile does the talking.
Quiet play lets players notice slow change.
cons: Players cannot ask why the pile grew.
Misreading the pile goes uncorrected.

pairs.tendency: A rule change can set how fast a pile grows or shrinks, but the pile already built stays, so a new rule meets old stock.
pros: Players see rules act on a real pile.
Rule changes show their effect over time.
cons: Old piles can tie a rule to the past.
Players may change rules to dodge a pile.

pairs.tendency: Players act as characters whose stocks, such as savings, land or goodwill, grow or shrink, and a character's pile shapes what it can say or do.
pros: Characters gain a visible past.
Stocks give a reason for what a role wants.
cons: Players may forget to track the numbers.
Talking in character can bury the pile.

pairs.tendency: A physical pile such as a tower or stack grows with each move, and the whole stack matters more than any single stacking move.
pros: The pile is real and visible.
Players feel when a stack is too big.
cons: Skill of hands can matter more than the idea.
A collapse ends the lesson quickly.

pairs.tendency: The map players draw fills up with marks and places, and each mark stays on the page, so the map is a pile of past choices.
pros: The map holds the history of play.
Players see slow change on paper.
cons: Drawings can get crowded and unclear.
Players may skip tracking the numbers.

pairs.tendency: Each successful ask moves cards into a growing hand, and the questions asked show what each player's pile contains.
pros: Piles come from asking, not luck.
Questions give clues about stock sizes.
cons: Asking can matter more than the system.
Players with big hands get asked less.

pairs.tendency: The bank's stock of money grows when players lose and drops when they win, and the stock swings with each round of bets.
pros: The bank's pile shows who has been winning.
Players learn how stock absorbs swings.
cons: Each round is short, so the pile is hidden.
Luck can hide the bigger trend.

pairs.tendency: Bets on throws add to or take from each player's stock of money, and the total held after many throws matters more than any one result.
pros: Stocks rise and fall in plain view.
Bets give a quick feel for risk.
cons: Throws decide most of the pile.
Players cannot steer the stock by choice.

pairs.tendency: Chips go into a pot round after round, so the pot grows while players decide whether to stay in, and each bet adds to a stock others can win.
pros: A growing pot draws attention.
Staying in costs more each round.
cons: The pot can matter more than the system.
Big pots can push players to keep going.

pairs.tendency: Each side starts with its own stocks, such as troops, tools or money, and chosen builds decide how fast each pile can grow.
pros: Different sides have different piles.
Players see how a start shapes a pile.
cons: Sides can start unevenly by accident.
More to explain before play begins.

pairs.tendency: A contract names a target in advance, and the pile of tricks or points won during the hand shows how close the player is to it.
pros: The target gives the pile a meaning.
Players count a pile against a promise.
cons: The pile only matters once the hand ends.
Failing a contract can feel final.

pairs.tendency: Captured pieces join the captor's side and stay there, so each side's stock of pieces can swing sharply, and a large pile can change hands in one turn.
pros: Piles of pieces swing in plain view.
Lead and loss feel real.
cons: Big swings can make the pile seem unreliable.
Players behind may give up.

pairs.tendency: Caught players pile up in the jail, and the number waiting there grows until a rescuer frees them, so the stock of captives sets the pressure.
pros: The jail shows a pile growing.
Teammates have a clear reason to act.
cons: A full jail can end the game for some.
Players in jail wait without a task.

pairs.tendency: Captured pieces are taken off the board and kept as a stock, and each side's pile of taken pieces slowly decides who is ahead.
pros: Captured pieces count up over time.
Small gains add up.
cons: The pile of captures can hide board shape.
The system feels like a board fight, not stocks.

pairs.tendency: Help for players behind adds to their stock, so piles tend to even out, though the leader's earlier pile still gives them an edge.
pros: Players behind see a way to recover.
Piles stay closer together.
cons: The help can empty the lead of meaning.
Leaders may feel punished for building a pile.

pairs.tendency: Draws and throws add to or take from each pile with no choice from players, so the piles just show how luck has run.
pros: Players see piles move without effort.
Easy to play.
cons: Players cannot connect pile and choice.
Nothing about stocks can be learned.

pairs.tendency: A chase leaves little to pile up, so players may add a stock, such as tags taken or time spent as It, to give the pile a place.
pros: The chase gains a running total.
Fast play with a record of it.
cons: Running leaves no time to count the pile.
The stock can feel added on.

pairs.tendency: Each turn a player picks who gains or loses stock, so piles grow unevenly and the one with the largest pile tends to be picked on.
pros: Piles show who is ahead.
Targeting has a clear reason.
cons: Big piles can draw all the attention.
Players can gang up on the leader.

pairs.tendency: A chain across the board grows piece by piece, and each piece stays, so the chain is a pile of past moves that the other player tries to cut.
pros: A growing chain shows progress.
Building has a clear shape.
cons: A cut chain loses its whole pile.
Little shows stocks beyond the chain.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, so a pile of wins or losses grows unevenly even when choices are even over time.
pros: Players see piles from many rounds.
Short rounds with a running total.
cons: Pile size can look like luck.
Patterns in the choices are easy to miss.

pairs.tendency: Declared pairs and runs add points to a running total over the hand, so the score is a stock that grows with each declaration.
pros: Steady scoring shows a growing pile.
Players weigh showing a combination early.
cons: Declaring shows others what you hold.
The pile can seem only a score.

pairs.tendency: Each player's power changes how fast their own pile grows or shrinks, so one player may fill a stock quickly while another drains theirs.
pros: Players see the same system from different seats.
Unequal piles raise questions.
cons: Powers can swamp the pile.
Players may blame the power, not the system.

pairs.tendency: Doubling raises what the game is worth, so the stock at stake grows in one move and players weigh the size of the pile against their nerve.
pros: The pile jumps in plain view.
Tense choices about a big stock.
cons: Players who give up lose what they built.
One doubling can outweigh many turns.

pairs.tendency: Players are forced to take what is offered, so stocks of pieces rise and fall by force, and an opponent can plan for the pile a forced move will leave.
pros: Piles change in ways players can read.
Forced moves make cause and effect clear.
cons: Players have few free choices.
A forced move can empty a pile at once.

pairs.tendency: Each success adds to a character's power, which is itself a stock that grows turn by turn, so later challenges meet a bigger pile.
pros: Growth is easy to see.
Players care about the long run.
cons: Early gains can decide the rest.
Players behind may find it hard to catch up.

pairs.tendency: The list is a pile that grows by one item each turn, and the whole pile has to be held in mind, so its size is the challenge.
pros: The pile grows in a way everyone shares.
Players feel the weight of a growing stock.
cons: Memory decides more than any choice.
Players drop out as the pile grows.

pairs.tendency: A handicap sets the starting stock of the stronger player lower, so piles begin uneven by design and the game shows how a start matters.
pros: Unequal starts become visible.
Weaker players have a chance.
cons: Players may argue about the starting pile.
The right handicap is hard to set.

pairs.tendency: Searching adds clues, or tired legs, to a growing pile, and each failed search leaves what is known a little bigger.
pros: Clues build up over the hunt.
Players feel the search narrowing.
cons: Hiding leaves little to pile up.
Players may not see a stock at all.

pairs.tendency: Each jump moves a piece forward and may take others, so stocks of pieces and positions change with every hop and cannot easily be rebuilt.
pros: Piles change clearly with each jump.
Short turns keep play moving.
cons: A chain of jumps can wipe out a pile.
Hopping matters more than the system.

pairs.tendency: Kept dice form a pile that grows over the rolls, and each reroll adds to what is held, so the hand at the end is a stock of earlier choices.
pros: The held dice show a pile building.
Keeping or rerolling is a clear choice.
cons: Rolls are short, so the pile never lasts.
Luck can outweigh the piling.

pairs.tendency: A piece sent back loses all the progress it had piled up, so a large stock can vanish in one landing.
pros: Losing a big pile is memorable.
Players see what a pile is worth.
cons: One landing can erase many turns.
Players may feel the loss is only chance.

pairs.tendency: Rows built earlier lead to taking pieces later, so a stock of built rows turns into captures, and the pile of pieces taken decides the game.
pros: Rows show past effort.
Players plan rows with a payoff in mind.
cons: Breaking a row can wipe out a pile.
Takes can hide how rows grew.

pairs.tendency: Letters accumulate in a growing pool, and words built from the pool use some of it up, so the stock of letters shapes each choice.
pros: Letters show a stock being used.
Players see what the pile makes possible.
cons: Vocabulary matters more than the pile.
Players may only look at the word.

pairs.tendency: Each tile placed lengthens the line, and the open ends show what can still be played, so the line is a growing pile of past matches.
pros: The line shows past moves.
Players read what is left to play.
cons: Players with no match miss turns.
The pile only shows two ends at a time.

pairs.tendency: Melded sets stay on the table and grow as others add cards, so the table holds a shared stock that rises across the hand.
pros: The shared melds keep growing.
Players add to a pile together.
cons: Melds can show too much about hands.
Big melds can feel like they decide the game.

pairs.tendency: Each one-use power sits in a store until spent, so the unused powers are a stock that shrinks as the game goes on and cannot be refilled.
pros: Players see a stock running down.
Saving or spending becomes a clear choice.
cons: Powers can be spent early and forgotten.
The stock only shrinks, never grows.

pairs.tendency: The other player can turn a move down, so a pile grows or shrinks only with agreement, and refusals leave the stock where it was.
pros: Piles change by shared consent.
Players read each other's aims.
cons: Refusals can stall the pile.
Slow turns.

pairs.tendency: A message passes along and any change builds up as it travels, so the final version is a pile of small shifts nobody can trace.
pros: Small errors add up in plain view.
Players laugh at how far it drifts.
cons: Nobody can see the pile growing.
Players tend to blame the last person.

pairs.tendency: Passed cards change each player's stock before play, so everyone starts with a pile shaped partly by others, and the exchange sets the first pile.
pros: Each start reflects other players' choices.
Players see stocks shift hands.
cons: The pile is set before any play begins.
Players may not see how the pass mattered.

pairs.tendency: The first player sets up starting piles knowing the other will choose a side, so stocks are set as evenly as the setter can guess.
pros: Setting piles has a clear reason.
Starting stocks tend to be close.
cons: The setter can only guess the piles.
Players may not see how piles will grow.

pairs.tendency: Pieces advance across the board and turn into stronger ones, so a stock of advanced pieces builds up and decides the late game.
pros: Advanced pieces make a visible pile.
Pushing forward has a clear payoff.
cons: Late promotion can swing the whole game.
Waiting for promotion can slow play.

pairs.tendency: Each leg adds to team time or distance, so the team's total builds leg by leg and a slow leg stays in the total.
pros: Team time is a visible total.
Everyone adds a part to the pile.
cons: One slow leg can sink a team.
A short race leaves little room for piling.

pairs.tendency: Stones in a safe shape stay on the board and cannot be taken, so safe shapes slowly make up a stock the other player cannot reduce.
pros: Safe stones build a lasting pile.
Players aim at a clear target.
cons: A safe pile can end the contest early.
Little shows how the stock grew.

pairs.tendency: Named prize cards are collected over the hand, so each player's pile of prizes grows trick by trick and one card can change the total.
pros: Prizes build up in sight.
Players aim at particular cards.
cons: One card can swing the whole pile.
The pile can be counted only at the end.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle stay available to all and change as they are used, so the shared stock rises and falls in front of everyone.
pros: All players see one stock.
Shared piles give a common picture.
cons: Players with strong hands use it first.
The middle can matter less than hands.

pairs.tendency: The pot grows each round nobody wins, so a shared stock of counters rises and makes the next round worth more.
pros: The growing pot is easy to read.
Players feel the pile build.
cons: A big pot can push players to take risks.
Rounds with no winner feel flat.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are scooped and dropped pit by pit, so stocks move around the board and each pit's pile changes with every sowing.
pros: Piles shift in plain view.
Each move shows where stock goes.
cons: Counting seeds takes care.
A big pit can be emptied in one move.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand is a stock set aside before play, and taking or swapping it changes what a player starts with, so the pile is part of the opening.
pros: The extra hand is a visible pile.
Players weigh taking it.
cons: The spare pile only matters at the start.
The system plays little part afterwards.

pairs.tendency: Squares along the track add or remove stock, so a player's pile of goods, health or time builds up as they land on each one.
pros: The track gives each square a purpose.
Players see why a pile changed.
cons: Dice can decide which squares are hit.
The pile may seem only the board's doing.

pairs.tendency: Each use costs from a stock, so players watch money or points fall as they buy and rise as they earn, and the balance limits what they can do.
pros: Spending shows a stock plainly.
Players weigh each purchase.
cons: Running dry can stop a player acting.
Counting costs can slow turns.

pairs.tendency: A fixed pool is shared between places, so the stock in each place builds up or drains by the shares chosen, and the pool can only be spread so far.
pros: Players see a limited pile divided.
Splitting shows what is left out.
cons: One lost place can drain the pile.
Many piles to track at once.

pairs.tendency: Play runs until a signal, and what each player holds, such as seats or points, is counted only when it sounds, so the pile stays hidden until the stop.
pros: Fast, loud and easy to join.
The count at the stop is a surprise.
cons: Players have no time to watch a pile.
The system can disappear under the noise.

pairs.tendency: Swapped cards change the stock in each hand before play, so the hand is a pile built by many small exchanges.
pros: Players see a hand being built.
Each swap is a small choice.
cons: Many small swaps slow the game.
The pile is only used once, at the end.

pairs.tendency: The discard pile grows with each turn and one player may take all of it, so a large stock can change hands in a single move.
pros: The pile is easy to see.
Waiting makes the pile worth more.
cons: A big pile can feel like luck's prize.
Players may hold back to let it grow.

pairs.tendency: The named suit decides which cards count most, so stocks of trump cards in a hand can outweigh larger piles of other suits.
pros: A trump pile has a clear weight.
Players count one kind of stock above all.
cons: Strong trump hands can decide the game.
The other piles can seem to matter less.

pairs.tendency: Two boards each hold their own stock of pieces, so a pile built on one board can be spent or lost on the other.
pros: Players watch two piles at once.
Trade-offs between boards are plain.
cons: Hard to track two piles together.
Attention goes to one board over the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can fill any gap in a pile, so it is a store of flexibility that players save or spend, changing what other piles can reach.
pros: Players weigh keeping a wild.
Wilds show how flexible a stock can be.
cons: A wild can finish a pile with no growth.
Players who hold many wilds can seem lucky.

pairs.tendency: Pieces and piles pass off one edge and appear on the other, so a stock cannot be left in a corner and forgotten.
pros: Stocks cannot be cornered.
Players see the board as joined.
cons: Players may not expect where a pile reappears.
Counting piles across the edge takes care.

pairs.tendency: Each answer adds a little to what the group knows, so knowledge itself is a pile that grows with every question and narrows what the secret can be.
pros: Knowledge builds up round by round.
Questions show how a pile of clues grows.
cons: One wasted question adds little to the pile.
Players can lose track of what is known.

pairs.tendency: Players race to the end while stocks such as fuel, time or debt build up on the way, so the fastest runner may carry the heaviest pile.
pros: The race shows a pile that slows players.
Racing gives piles a quick reason to matter.
cons: Players may race and ignore the pile.
A leader can pull away before the pile bites.

pairs.tendency: The final score is a pile that grows all game, so the size of each player's stock at the end decides who wins.
pros: Scores show piles in plain view.
Players weigh long and short gains.
cons: Players may chase the score, not the system.
The final count can feel like a surprise.

pairs.tendency: A stock such as health or supplies drains with every turn, and players drop out as their piles run out, until one is left.
pros: A draining pile makes the risk clear.
Players watch each other's stocks.
cons: Players who run out early wait.
A big early pile can settle the game.

pairs.tendency: The team shares a pile that slowly wears down, such as food or fuel, and the game is lost when it runs out, so each turn takes a little.
pros: The shared pile gives a clear threat.
The team watches one number together.
cons: A falling pile can feel hopeless.
One player can speak for the whole team.

pairs.tendency: The group aims at a target stock, such as a full store or a clean river, and every turn nudges the pile closer or further away.
pros: One pile gives a clear target.
Players share a picture of progress.
cons: Little tension between players.
Some players can follow without thinking.

pairs.tendency: Each player secretly wants a different pile to grow or shrink, so the same stock is pushed in different ways and nobody is sure why it moves.
pros: One pile shows several aims.
Players guess others' goals from the stock.
cons: A moving pile is hard to read.
Secret aims can hide the system.

pairs.tendency: The story unfolds while stocks build in the background, such as grudges, debts or wealth, and the ending reflects the piles.
pros: Piles give the story a past.
Endings follow from what built up.
cons: The story can crowd the stocks out.
The numbers may be skipped.

pairs.tendency: With no winner, the piles that built up are what players look at and talk about when the game stops, so the stock becomes the result.
pros: Players read the piles freely.
Looking at the pile is the point.
cons: Without a target, nobody may watch the pile.
Little push to build one.

pairs.tendency: Each player names a pile they want to reach or avoid, so the same stock is judged by different aims at the end.
pros: Piles are read through each aim.
Players compare what they wanted.
cons: Players may pick goals the pile cannot reach.
Comparing aims can take time.

pairs.tendency: A pile such as debt or blame builds up and the player left with the largest one loses, so everyone watches the pile and tries to pass it on.
pros: Piles give the loss a clear cause.
Players watch and avoid the heaviest pile.
cons: The loser can feel singled out.
Players may only hand the pile on.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep a shared stock from running out or overflowing, so players watch the pile to keep play going and nobody tries to end it.
pros: The pile gives a reason to keep going.
Players care for the stock together.
cons: No ending to show where the pile led.
The game can drift on.

pairs.tendency: The piles grow whatever players do, so the game can show that some stocks only rise, such as debt or waste, and no choice wins.
pros: Piles show what players cannot fix.
A strong point about a real problem.
cons: Players may feel the game is unfair.
Some may stop trying.

pairs.tendency: The player works alone against a pile of cards that shrinks or jams as they play, so the table is a stock to be cleared.
pros: The pile gives a clear challenge.
Players learn by trying again.
cons: A stuck pile ends the game early.
Luck of the deal can decide the pile.

pairs.tendency: Each game starts with fresh stocks but a record of wins builds across games, so a second stock, the score, carries over from one game to the next.
pros: Players see two piles at once.
One lost game is not the end.
cons: The score can matter more than the system.
Players may skip learning from each pile.

pairs.tendency: Every point picked up adds to a pile that counts against you, so the pile players want smallest is the one they keep growing by acting.
pros: Players dodge growing piles.
Piles show the cost of acting.
cons: Players may stall to keep a pile small.
The reversed aim can confuse beginners.

pairs.tendency: A pile has to reach a target exactly, so a stock that grows too far has to be pulled back, and players weigh each addition against the line.
pros: The target makes the pile easy to read.
Players count carefully.
cons: One step too far can cost the whole pile.
Exact totals can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: Players want a pile to fall, so they give things away and watch the stock drain, which shows what emptying a store looks like.
pros: Draining a pile is easy to see.
Players view a stock from the other side.
cons: Players may mix up the aim.
Giving away can feel odd.

pairs.tendency: Each player grows their own pile side by side, so the piles can be compared at any point and rarely affect each other.
pros: Players compare piles directly.
Calm, steady play.
cons: Little contact between players.
Hard to see how people affect each other.

pairs.tendency: Players raid and spoil each other's piles, so stocks rise and fall by attack, and the biggest pile tends to draw the most attacks.
pros: Piles show who is ahead.
Raids have clear effects.
cons: Fights can matter more than the stock.
Players behind can feel picked on.

pairs.tendency: Players add to and take from a shared pile, such as soil or water, and each person's choices show in the stock the others meet.
pros: A shared pile shows how people affect each other.
Quiet, clear links.
cons: Hard to tell who made the pile.
Slow, thoughtful turns.

pairs.tendency: The whole team tends one pile together, adding to it, drawing from it and watching what it does, so every move shows in a shared total.
pros: One pile gives the team a shared picture.
Everyone has a part to play.
cons: One player can direct the rest.
Little tension.

pairs.tendency: Players share a pile they all need but draw on it for private gain, so the stock tends to fall when each player takes a little extra.
pros: The pile shows self against group.
Tense, honest choices.
cons: A pile can run out before anyone admits it.
Hard to keep trust.

pairs.tendency: Each team tends its own pile and tries to grow it past the other's, so team talk is mostly about what to add and what to protect.
pros: Teams compare piles side by side.
Team talk about stocks.
cons: One player can take over.
The contest can hide the system.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly drains or spoils the shared pile, so the team sees a stock fall and has to work out whether it is the system or a person.
pros: Falling piles raise suspicion.
Tense, close watching of the stock.
cons: Hard to tell a leak from a plain loss.
Accusations can upset people.

pairs.tendency: With turns that take days, the pile changes slowly between letters, so each reply meets a stock that has moved on, and waiting is part of the play.
pros: Slow change suits a slow game.
Players come back to a changed pile.
cons: Piles are hard to keep up to date.
Players may lose track between letters.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's stock keeps its place on the board, or grows by a fixed rule, so players deal with a pile nobody present controls.
pros: An absent pile acts like a distant force.
Players plan around a stock they cannot steer.
cons: Nobody present can explain it.
The pile may feel like a puzzle.

pairs.tendency: The game master keeps the books on each pile, such as food, trust or debt, and tells players what the stock has become after their choices.
pros: One keeper makes piles easy to follow.
The master can explain why a pile grew.
cons: The master's hand can steer the piles.
Players may rely on being told the numbers.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by join and leave while stocks such as chalk marks or counters stay on the ground, so the pile is built by many people across the day.
pros: Anyone can see the pile.
Players come and go but the stock stays.
cons: Nobody owns the pile or can track it.
New players join without knowing its history.

pairs.tendency: The lone player holds a stock of power or resources that the others try to wear down together, so the size of that pile shows who is winning.
pros: One pile makes the contest easy to read.
The group shares a clear target.
cons: The lone player may run out of stock early.
The pile may favour one side.

pairs.tendency: One player tends a pile and meets every result of their own past choices, with nobody else to blame for the stock they built.
pros: Players own every change to the pile.
Players can stop and study the stock.
cons: No other player shows another approach.
Alone, the pile may seem like a puzzle.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws add to and take from each pile, so stocks rise and fall for reasons players did not choose and cannot steer.
pros: Players see piles move with luck.
Quick, light play.
cons: Players cannot link choices to piles.
Little to learn about how stocks work.

pairs.tendency: Luck changes the piles, but players can build a reserve in advance, so a bigger pile softens a poor turn and a small one does not.
pros: A reserve shows what a pile is for.
Players prepare for poor luck.
cons: Building a reserve costs a turn.
Players with spare stock feel safe.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly decide how piles grow, with a little luck on top, so the stock built with most care tends to lead but not always.
pros: Piles mostly show choices.
Some surprise keeps play lively.
cons: Skilled players tend to win.
Luck can break a long build.

pairs.tendency: Piles grow only from what players do, so each stock is a plain record of past choices and the leader's pile shows a plan that worked.
pros: Every pile has a reason.
Players can learn from each stock.
cons: Real stocks are rarely so predictable.
Early errors stay in the pile for long.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a sign, and each reading is added to a growing record, so the pile is a collection of readings.
pros: A growing record builds a story.
Players return to earlier readings.
cons: The pile may seem about meaning, not numbers.
Players may not compare piles.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act in step, and each matched moment adds to a shared stock of trust, so the pile is felt more than counted.
pros: Trust builds up as a shared stock.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: A stock of trust is hard to count.
One slip can seem to undo it.

pairs.tendency: Rolls on a table add events, injuries or debts to the story, so each character carries a pile of what the dice have given them.
pros: Piles give characters a past.
The story gains memory.
cons: Dice decide what piles up.
Players may forget to track the stock.

pairs.tendency: Every pile is open to all, so players can read exactly how big each stock is and plan around it.
pros: Stocks can be compared at a glance.
Players discuss piles freely.
cons: Little surprise.
Leaders are easy to target.

pairs.tendency: Players keep part of their stock out of sight, so each pile is partly guessed from what others do and what they ask.
pros: Players read stocks from behaviour.
Guessing keeps play lively.
cons: Hard to compare piles exactly.
Players may bluff about stocks.

pairs.tendency: Players pile up resources while their true roles stay hidden, so the size of a stock tends to give someone away.
pros: A pile becomes a clue.
Watching stocks adds suspicion.
cons: Players may hide their piles.
The pile gets blamed for what a person did.

pairs.tendency: The sizes of visible piles are clues, and players work backwards from a stock to what had to be done, so each pile tells a small story.
pros: Piles become evidence.
Players reason about cause and effect.
cons: A pile can fit many causes.
Slow turns.

pairs.tendency: Players claim bigger or smaller piles than they hold, so the stock others believe in can differ from the real one.
pros: Players learn how claims shape a stock.
Mind games around the pile.
cons: Hard to track the real pile.
Lies about piles can upset people.

pairs.tendency: Players learn how piles behave by trying things and being told no, so a stock that grows too fast or fails to grow shows where a rule hides.
pros: Piles show hidden rules at work.
Discovery feels like real learning.
cons: Players can be left guessing at the pile.
The rule may seem unfair.

pairs.tendency: One player knows how the pile has grown but can only hint, so the others have to work out the stock from clues.
pros: Hints give a pile a shape.
Players read the stock together.
cons: Hints about size are hard to give.
The knower can feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: Piles are found as areas are explored, so each new region adds its stock to the known world and the whole pile is learned in pieces.
pros: Discovery adds to the pile.
Players are curious about what is next.
cons: Early piles are known only partly.
Players may plan on guesses.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so one pile is fully known while the rest stay secret, and players use the open stock to reason about the hidden ones.
pros: One known pile helps players guess others.
Open stock makes planning easier.
cons: The open pile can steer the game.
A known pile may seem unfair to its owner.

pairs.tendency: Points and money pile up out of sight, so nobody knows who has the biggest stock and players have to guess from what others do.
pros: Hidden piles keep players guessing.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: Nobody can read the whole system.
A big pile can win without warning.

pairs.tendency: One player changes the pile at a time, so everyone else watches the stock move and can see each turn's small effect on the total.
pros: Each change to the pile is easy to see.
Players have time to think.
cons: Waiting turns can drag.
Slow piles can feel slow to play.

pairs.tendency: Everyone adds to or takes from the pile in the same moment, so the stock jumps by the sum of all choices and nobody sees one cause.
pros: The pile moves as a group does.
Players share one turn together.
cons: Hard to tell whose choice made the pile.
Players cannot adjust to each other.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can add to or take from the pile at any moment, so the stock changes in a rush and the quickest players grow the largest piles.
pros: The pile shifts as fast as players act.
Lively, urgent play.
cons: Quick players can empty a pile.
Hard to follow the pile.

pairs.tendency: The clock gives each player little time to react to the pile, so players tend to act on a stock they have only half read.
pros: Time pressure shows how piles are misjudged.
Short turns keep play moving.
cons: Players may miss a pile growing.
Hasty moves can empty a stock.

pairs.tendency: Piles change a little each day, so players come back to a stock that has grown or shrunk, and waiting is part of the pile.
pros: Slow piles feel like real time.
Players return to a changed stock.
cons: A pile can be forgotten between turns.
Players may lose interest.

pairs.tendency: The pause before each move gives players time to look at the pile and think about what it will be next, so slow growth gets noticed.
pros: Players have time to watch piles.
Quiet play suits slow change.
cons: Slow turns can feel dull.
Players may lose patience with a small pile.

pairs.tendency: Piles grow faster as the game speeds up, so the stock that was small in early rounds can outrun players near the end.
pros: Piles seem to run away.
Players feel growth speed up.
cons: Late rounds are hard to follow.
Early piles shape everything that follows.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn lets one player add to their pile again at once, so one lucky player can build a stock while others wait.
pros: Players see a pile jump.
Lucky turns feel exciting.
cons: A lead in one pile can grow quickly.
Others wait while the pile grows.

pairs.tendency: The first stage builds a stock that the second stage uses up, so piles made early decide what players can do later.
pros: Early piles shape later choices.
Players see cause and effect across stages.
cons: Poor first-stage piles hurt late play.
Stage rules take time to explain.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system, such as a village's grain store, and the pile in each place shows how that system holds or loses stock.
pros: A real stock becomes easy to see.
Players link piles to the real thing.
cons: The pile can be hard to read at first.
Simplifying may hide parts of the real system.

pairs.tendency: Each role holds a different pile, such as the farmer's grain or the council's funds, so the same system gives some roles large stocks and others small ones.
pros: Unequal piles show who has what.
Players see the system from each seat.
cons: Small piles leave a role little to do.
Players may blame roles for the piles.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws on one pile, so what one player takes lowers the stock for all, and the pile shrinks faster than any one person notices.
pros: Players see a pile being used up.
Shared stocks show why restraint is hard.
cons: A pile can run out before anyone stops.
Players may take quickly out of fear.

pairs.tendency: What players do now changes a pile later, so the stock keeps growing or shrinking after a choice is made and its cause is already in the past.
pros: Piles show effects arriving late.
Players learn to look ahead.
cons: Players may blame the wrong choice.
Hard to link a pile to its cause.

pairs.tendency: A new rule changes how fast a pile grows or shrinks, and players see its effect only after the stock has had time to move.
pros: A pile shows what the rule did.
Players test a rule on a safe pile.
cons: A single round shows little change.
Old piles can hide a rule's effect.

pairs.tendency: After play, the final piles give players something to point at, and talk about how each stock got that size and what it matches in real life.
pros: Piles give the talk something to hold.
Players trace a stock to its causes.
cons: Players may remember only the final totals.
Piles from early rounds can be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: A stock that cannot be rebuilt, such as soil lost or a torn card, carries into the next game, so a pile built or used up stays that way.
pros: Players feel what a lost stock means.
Each choice about a pile counts.
cons: A used-up pile can make later games hard.
Players may fear touching the pile.

pairs.tendency: What the rules reward in a pile makes the game's point, such as scoring only for a big stock, which claims how the real world treats it.
pros: The pile makes a point without words.
Players question what the rules count.
cons: Players may miss the argument.
A pile can look like a plain score.

pairs.tendency: A pile in the game stands for something real, such as favours owed or time promised, so its size matters beyond the table.
pros: The pile feels weighty.
Players think hard about each addition.
cons: Real debts can cause arguments.
Some players feel pressured.

pairs.tendency: Points pile up for something that matters, such as health or kindness, so players chase the stock and may forget what it stands for.
pros: Players see a number replace a value.
The pile makes the trade-off plain.
cons: A big pile can hide what was lost.
Players may chase the pile blindly.

pairs.tendency: Players build up the stocks a new way of living would need, such as shared food or trust, to see how long they take to grow.
pros: Slow piles show what change takes.
Players feel a possible future.
cons: Real piles grow slower than a game can show.
Players may expect results too soon.

pairs.tendency: The world's rule adds to or takes from each pile between turns, so stocks keep changing even when no player acts.
pros: Piles move on their own.
Players see the system at work.
cons: Hard to tell the world's effect from a player's.
Players may feel they cannot stop the change.

pairs.tendency: A sudden event hits the piles, so a large stock can cushion a shock and a small one may be wiped out.
pros: Reserves show what they are for.
Shocks give piles a test.
cons: A shock can empty a pile through chance.
Players with large piles feel safe.

pairs.tendency: Each round adds a year of change to the pile, so a slow stock such as soil or debt shows decades of growth within one sitting.
pros: Slow piles grow within one sitting.
Long trends become easy to see.
cons: Years of detail are skipped.
Players may miss small yearly changes.

pairs.tendency: The gauges show the size of each pile, such as water level or trust, so every move shows in a number everyone can read.
pros: Piles are always in view.
Players share one picture.
cons: Players may watch gauges and skip causes.
A gauge shows size but not who made it.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with piles of different sizes, and since stocks tend to compound, the early gap tends to widen as play goes on.
pros: Players see how a start shapes a pile.
Unequal piles raise real questions.
cons: Players with small piles can feel stuck.
The gap can end the contest early.

pairs.tendency: The player with the largest pile writes the rules, so a big stock gives power to change how piles grow for everyone else.
pros: Players see a pile turn into power.
The link between stock and rule is plain.
cons: Players behind can feel shut out.
The gap between piles can grow quickly.

pairs.tendency: Each role wants a different pile to grow or shrink, such as fish in the lake and fish in the boat, so one stock is pulled both ways.
pros: One pile shows opposed aims.
Players see why the pile will not settle.
cons: The pile can run out while players argue.
Roles may block each other all game.

pairs.tendency: The opening describes the piles already in place, such as debt or grain, so players begin with a history they did not build.
pros: Piles give the situation a past.
Players start with something to react to.
cons: A long list of piles is hard to read.
The starting piles can set the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Players argue how a move changes a pile, and the table agrees how much stock is added or lost, so the pile reflects the case made for it.
pros: Piles come from reasoned argument.
Players explain what a pile means.
cons: Persuasive players can inflate a pile.
Sizes can be hard to compare across moves.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points so players can look at how each pile has grown and ask why, before the stock moves on.
pros: Players read piles while they can change.
Stops show slow trends early.
cons: Breaks interrupt build-up.
Players may talk about piles and not act.

pairs.tendency: The same game is run again with one change, and the final piles are compared across plays, so the stock becomes the measure of the change.
pros: Piles show what one change did.
Players compare plays with real numbers.
cons: One luck-driven run can mislead.
A second run takes time.

pairs.tendency: The game says which stocks it ignores, such as the pile of waste or unpaid work, so players know what the visible piles do not show.
pros: Players see what the piles skip.
Honest limits make the stocks easier to trust.
cons: The list may be long.
Players may only look at the piles shown.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about help decide which piles to track and how fast they grow, so each stock matches what they actually live with.
pros: Piles match real experience.
Players trust the stocks they see.
cons: Piles can be argued over at length.
Some real piles are too complex to show.

pairs.tendency: Goods wait in a pile at every link, so each player has a stock of their own, and a late order grows one pile while the next link runs short.
pros: Piles show where goods get stuck.
Players see one link's pile affect another.
cons: Players only see their own pile at first.
Orders can overshoot and leave big piles.

pairs.tendency: Players see only their own pile and the orders reaching them, so a stock somewhere else can grow unseen and players guess at the whole.
pros: Players feel what hidden piles cost.
Guessing from one pile shows its limits.
cons: Players may blame others for piles they cannot see.
The whole system stays out of view.

pairs.tendency: Work waiting in front of the slowest step grows into a large pile, while the steps after it sit short of goods.
pros: The pile shows where the slow step is.
Players see why speeding up elsewhere changes little.
cons: The pile can grow before anyone notices.
Players may blame the wrong step.

pairs.tendency: Goods made ahead of orders pile up in stock, while goods made only on order keep piles small, so players see how each way fills the shelves.
pros: Piles show the cost of guessing.
Players compare piles from the two ways.
cons: Pushed piles can fill up unseen.
Pulling can leave customers waiting.

pairs.tendency: A big batch builds a large pile at once and a small one builds a thin trickle, so each choice shapes how much waits between steps.
pros: Piles show what a batch size costs.
Players see waiting time as a pile.
cons: Big batches can bury the next step.
Small batches take more set-up.

cons: Hard to tell the rule from sabotage.
Accusations can be unfair.

pairs.tendency: Players send turns by letter while the world's rule moves between each, so the system changes before replies arrive.
pros: The wait lets the world change a lot.
The step can be shared in each letter.
cons: Letters may refer to an old state.
Someone has to apply the rule.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and the world's rule can move for them, so an absent player's pieces may still be changed by the system.
pros: The absent player has a place.
The step can speak for them.
cons: Their pieces may suffer without a say.
The rule may seem unkind.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, and its fixed rule gives them a ready change to apply, so the game master does not have to decide each time.
pros: The rule gives the master a steady guide.
The world seems independent.
cons: The master can feel tied to the rule.
Fixed steps leave less to improvise.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or park, and the world's rule moves between turns, so passers-by can see the system change and join in.
pros: Onlookers can read the change.
Joining in is easy.
cons: Someone has to apply the step.
Rules may be forgotten across a crowd.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, and the world moves by its rule, so the lone player may also be helped or harmed by the system.
pros: The world is a third force.
The rule can even a lopsided game.
cons: The step may favour one side.
The lone player may feel doubly pressed.

pairs.tendency: One player takes every turn and the world moves by its own rule between them, so the system acts like a second player with a fixed plan.
pros: A solo game has an opponent.
The player learns the rule by watching.
cons: A fixed step can be learnt and beaten.
Little surprise after a few plays.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most things, and the world's rule moves between turns as well, so one source of change is random and the other follows a pattern.
pros: The rule gives some pattern.
Players can watch the world.
cons: Chance and rule may blur.
Skill still counts for little.

pairs.tendency: Random events hit players but they can prepare, and the world's fixed step adds a second change they can predict, so players soften one and plan for the other.
pros: One force can be planned for.
Preparing has a clear reason.
cons: More rules to track.
Preparing for both can feel heavy.

pairs.tendency: Choices mostly decide results with a little luck, and the world's rule adds a steady change, so players plan against a rule they can learn.
pros: The rule can be learnt and used.
Skill is tested by an outside force.
cons: Experienced players gain most.
The step can undo careful play.

pairs.tendency: Results come from player choices alone, and the world's fixed rule runs between turns, so the only outside force is one that players can work out.
pros: Every change has a reason.
Careful players can see it coming.
cons: Real systems are rarely this predictable.
Experienced players gain most.

pairs.tendency: Throws are read as a message, and the world moves by its own rule between turns, so players may read the system's step as a sign too.
pros: The world can be read as a message.
Play invites reflection.
cons: Players may read too much into a step.
Rule and sign can be mixed up.

pairs.tendency: Players try to sense when others will act, and the world's rule moves at set moments, so a fixed rhythm gives them a pulse to tune to.
pros: The rule gives a shared beat.
Players watch each other and the system.
cons: The step can break the rhythm.
Sensing is harder with a fixed rule.

pairs.tendency: Dice are looked up on a table for what happens next, and the world's rule moves between turns, so the story has a roll and a steady change.
pros: A steady pulse sits beside the dice.
The story gets a setting that moves.
cons: Two sources of change can confuse.
The rule can seem to overrule the dice.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sees everything, including the world's rule and its next step, so players can plan exactly for what the system will do.
pros: Nothing about the world is hidden.
Players can talk about the next step.
cons: Little surprise remains.
A visible rule can be exploited.

pairs.tendency: Players hold secret cards while the world moves by its own rule in public, so the only hidden things are in hands and the system's step is open to all.
pros: The world is shared knowledge.
Secrets stay in the hands.
cons: Hands may change worth with the step.
Hard to plan together.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and the world moves by its rule in view of all, so odd results can be blamed on the system or a hidden player.
pros: The rule offers cover.
Suspicion has two sources.
cons: Hard to tell the rule from sabotage.
Accusations can be wrong.

pairs.tendency: Players work out hidden facts from clues, and the world's rule changes things between turns, so some clues come from the system's step and not from a player.
pros: The step makes a clue.
Players learn the rule by watching.
cons: Old clues can go out of date.
Players may chase false leads.

pairs.tendency: Players lie about what they hold, and the world's rule moves in the open, so a bluff has to fit the change the system just made.
pros: A bluff has to suit the world.
The rule tests claims.
cons: Lies may be checked by the step.
Bluffing is harder to keep up.

pairs.tendency: Players learn a hidden rule by breaking it, and the world's own rule moves between turns, so there may be two rules to work out.
pros: The step can be learnt like a rule.
Discovery feels like learning a world.
cons: Two rules can overload.
Players may confuse the two.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer and can only hint, and the world's rule changes the scene between turns, so the hints have to follow the change.
pros: Hints have a shifting setting.
The world gives more to point at.
cons: The step can make hints stale.
Guessers may lose the thread.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over by exploring, and the world's rule moves what players have already found, so a place seen earlier may have changed.
pros: Seen places may not stay as they were.
Exploration stays lively.
cons: Old knowledge cannot be trusted.
Players may need to re-check.

pairs.tendency: One hand is face up and the rest are secret, and the world's rule moves in view of all, so the open hand shows how the step changes things.
pros: The open hand shows the rule's effect.
Players can plan around the step.
cons: Open cards may lose worth.
Players may study the hand and not the world.

pairs.tendency: Some points are hidden while the world's rule moves between turns, so players guess who is ahead and the system also shifts the scores.
pros: Nobody can add up the system's effect.
Guessing has more to guess at.
cons: Hidden scores are hard to trace.
Players may suspect cheating.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, and the world takes its own turn between them, so the system is a participant that always moves by the same rule.
pros: The world has a clear place in the order.
Waiting players watch the step.
cons: The extra step lengthens the round.
Players may wait too long.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at once, then the world's rule runs, so the step becomes the one moment when all players watch the same thing.
pros: The step is a natural pause.
Choices are made before the rule shows.
cons: The rule can add delay.
Players may stop paying attention.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so the world's step needs a trigger such as a clock or a count, and players act while the system keeps moving.
pros: The world moves without waiting.
The rule gives the pace.
cons: The step can be missed in the rush.
Someone has to run the clock.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and the world's step runs at the end of each, so the world moves whether or not a player has finished.
pros: Pressure and a steady rule combine.
The world seems impatient.
cons: Rushed players miss the step.
Two kinds of timing can confuse.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks, and the world's rule moves a little each day, so the system keeps changing while players are away.
pros: The world seems to live on.
Waiting becomes part of the system.
cons: Someone has to apply the rule each day.
Missed steps can pile up.

pairs.tendency: The game slows on purpose, and the world's rule moves at the same slow pace, so each change is felt and talked over before the next.
pros: Each step can be noticed.
Slowness suits a gentle rule.
cons: Players may lose patience.
The world's change can feel small.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, and the world's rule runs more often or with greater force, so the system itself seems to quicken.
pros: The rule can build pressure.
The end comes in a rush.
cons: Late steps may be hard to follow.
Players may miss the cause of a change.

pairs.tendency: Some throws give a player another go, but the world still moves only at its own moment, so the lucky player can act many times before the system steps.
pros: A lucky run is limited by the rule.
The step offers a chance to catch up.
cons: A run can feel long.
The world may seem to wait for them.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages with different rules, and the world's step may differ in each, so what the system does can change as play moves on.
pros: The rule can follow the stage.
The world changes its pace.
cons: Players have to learn each step.
Switching may confuse.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system and the world's step is the way it moves on its own, so players see the system act as well as respond.
pros: The system acts as well as responds.
The step shows the cause.
cons: The rule needs checking against real life.
Players may take it for fact.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a real group, and the world's rule moves between turns, so every group meets a change it did not choose and each feels it differently.
pros: One step reaches groups unequally.
Roles share a common outside force.
cons: The step may favour one group.
Players may feel their group is picked on.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited stock while the world's rule renews or drains it, so the stock moves even when players take nothing.
pros: The stock has a life of its own.
Players watch the rule and each other.
cons: The system can empty the stock alone.
Players may blame each other for the rule.

pairs.tendency: Actions take a few rounds to show, and the world's rule runs every round, so a late effect lands on top of the step and is hard to tell apart.
pros: Late effects meet a steady rule.
Cause and change have to be traced.
cons: Players may not link action and effect.
Two timings are hard to track.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on, while the world's own rule keeps running, so the new rule is tested against a steady background.
pros: The fixed step shows what the new rule changes.
The test is clearer with a constant.
cons: The new rule may be blamed for the world.
Players may mix the two rules.

pairs.tendency: After the game players talk about what happened, and the world's rule gives them a plain thing to discuss: what it did and whether real life is like that.
pros: The step gives the talk a clear subject.
Players can ask whether the rule is true.
cons: The rule can take over the talk.
Players may forget their own part.

pairs.tendency: What happens is permanent, and the world's rule adds permanent changes of its own, so the next game may begin from a board the system has altered.
pros: The world leaves lasting marks.
Players feel the weight of each step.
cons: A step cannot be undone.
Later games may start in a poor state.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and the world's rule is part of that point, so the step is itself a claim about how a system behaves.
pros: The step carries a claim players can test.
The argument is visible in the play.
cons: A claim can pass as fact.
Players may not question the rule.

pairs.tendency: The game carries real consequences, and the world's rule moves between turns, so a step can change something real for a player they did not choose.
pros: The world has real weight.
Players take the rule seriously.
cons: A step can hurt a real feeling.
Players may blame each other for the rule.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, and the world's rule moves them between turns, so what the system does to the values is shown as plain numbers.
pros: The step shows loss of a value.
Players see the cost of chasing points.
cons: The number may replace the value.
Players may only chase the score.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future way of living, and the world's rule moves by itself, so the new arrangement has to survive changes that nobody planned.
pros: The future is tested by the world.
Players meet problems early.
cons: A fixed step may be unlike the real world.
The rehearsal may feel less free.

pairs.tendency: Cards or rolls bring sudden outside changes, and the world's rule moves steadily between them, so there is a steady change and a sudden one.
pros: The steady step makes shocks stand out.
Two kinds of change meet.
cons: Players may not tell which did the harm.
Too much change at once.

pairs.tendency: Each round stands for a year, and the world's rule moves once per round, so a step becomes a season or a decade of change.
pros: A long span fits in an afternoon.
The step has an easy meaning.
cons: A year's change can look too neat.
The rule hides what happened inside the year.

pairs.tendency: Gauges show the state of the system, and the world's rule moves them between turns, so players watch the needles shift by themselves.
pros: The gauges show the step plainly.
Players can predict the next change.
cons: Players may watch only the gauges.
A gauge can mislead.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with different money, land or links, and the world's rule affects everyone, so a step that is small for one player can be large for another.
pros: The same step lands unequally.
Players see who can absorb change.
cons: The poorer players may drop out.
The step can seem to punish them.

pairs.tendency: The leaders write the rules and the world moves by its own, so players see one rule they cannot change beside another their rivals can.
pros: Players see which rules are fixed.
The world offers a limit on the powerful.
cons: Leaders may bend the world too.
Others may see the step as fairest.

pairs.tendency: Each role wins by its own measure, and the world's rule moves between turns, so the same step helps one goal and hurts another.
pros: One step reveals who gains.
The rule is a shared fact.
cons: A step can seem to favour a role.
Players may argue about the rule.

pairs.tendency: Play opens on a described situation, and the world's rule then moves it on by itself, so the opening picture changes whether or not players act.
pros: The opening has a clear path.
Players see the rule change a known place.
cons: The starting picture may soon be gone.
The rule may overwhelm the scene.

pairs.tendency: Players try anything and argue why it would work while the world's fixed rule moves by itself, so the system does not need an argument.
pros: One part of the game is fixed.
Players argue only about their own moves.
cons: The rule can seem to ignore arguments.
The judge may be tempted to bend it.

pairs.tendency: Play stops so players can say what they notice, and the world's step is a plain thing to notice, so players can talk about what the system did.
pros: The step gives talk a clear subject.
Pauses can follow each step.
cons: The rule may be all that is discussed.
Pauses may slow the game.

pairs.tendency: The same game is played again with one thing changed, and the world's rule is the constant, so players can see what the other change did.
pros: The fixed step makes comparison fair.
Players learn what is player-made.
cons: Players may start to expect the step.
Replays may feel the same.

pairs.tendency: The game tells players what it left out, and the world's rule is one of its simplest parts, so the step invites asking what real life does differently.
pros: The rule is plainly a simplification.
Players can question the step.
cons: Players may only study the rule.
The list of leavings can be long.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about help design it, and the world's rule is one thing they can check against what they know, such as when the river really rises.
pros: The people can correct the rule.
The step rings true or does not.
cons: They may disagree about the rule.
Fixing it can be slow.

pairs.tendency: Each player is one link in a chain, and the world's rule, such as demand rising or falling, moves between turns, so every link meets it at a different delay.
pros: Demand moves without a player acting.
Players see how a change travels.
cons: The step can swamp the orders.
Players may blame the next link.

pairs.tendency: Players see only their own stock and orders, and the world's rule moves between turns, so each player sees the effect and not the cause.
pros: The step reaches players unseen.
Guessing the cause is a puzzle.
cons: The rule may look like another player's doing.
Players may feel in the dark.

pairs.tendency: The slowest step sets the pace, and the world's rule moves between turns, so the slow step may move or change on its own.
pros: The slow step can shift.
Players find where the limit is.
cons: Fixing a step may help only for a while.
Bottlenecks can seem to move for no reason.

pairs.tendency: Goods are made ahead to a guess or only on order, and the world's rule moves demand between turns, so each way meets the change differently.
pros: The step tests both ways.
Players feel which suits a shifting demand.
cons: Made-ahead goods can be left over.
Orders can arrive too late.

pairs.tendency: Players pick how many to make at once, and the world's rule moves demand between turns, so a large batch may meet less demand than it was made for.
pros: Batches meet a changing market.
The cost of each size shows.
cons: Large batches can sit unsold.
Small batches cost more in set-up.

pairs.tendency: Equipment fails at random and the world's rule moves other things by a fixed step, so there are two kinds of change, one random and one steady.
pros: Failures sit against a steady rule.
Plans have to allow for both.
cons: Too many changes at once.
A breakdown can be mistaken for the rule.

pairs.tendency: Holding stock costs something each round, running out costs more, and the world's rule moves demand, so players keep guessing the right amount.
pros: The step keeps the balance moving.
Players feel the cost of each side.
cons: Both costs can be hard to track.
A big shift can leave everyone out of stock.

pairs.tendency: A shock card is drawn when someone lands on certain spaces, so the same roll that moves you can also bring a flood or a price crash.
pros: Luck of the dice meets luck of the world.
Shocks arrive at a pace players can see coming.
cons: Two kinds of luck stack up.
Players may blame the dice for what the shock did.

pairs.tendency: Players pick cards for their own plans, then an event card changes what those picks are worth, so a plan made last round may no longer fit.
pros: Picks have to allow for surprises.
Players talk about hedging their choices.
cons: Careful plans can be undone by one card.
Players may stop planning if shocks are frequent.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes what things are worth just before or after an auction, so bidders guess how a crash or shortage will move the prices.
pros: Bids reflect fear and hope about the future.
Price swings feel like a real market.
cons: Players who overbid before a crash are stuck.
Shocks can make earlier bids seem pointless.
