pairs.tendency: Players keep pushing for more while an outside event may strike at any draw, so the risk comes both from your own greed and from the world.
pros: Two sources of risk keep the table tense.
Players read the deck for signs of a shock.
cons: Players cannot tell which risk hurt them.
One shock can end a long run at once.

pairs.tendency: An event hits a region of the map, such as a flood or an election, and every player holding that area feels it, whoever is winning there.
pros: Shocks can reshuffle who is ahead.
Holding many areas spreads the risk.
cons: Players who held the hit area lose at once.
Fights over areas can be erased by one card.

pairs.tendency: An event removes or changes some action spaces, so workers placed on a plan find the job closed or paying differently, and players re-plan.
pros: Players have to adapt plans mid-round.
Spare workers become worth keeping.
cons: Careful placement can be cancelled by a card.
Slow turns while everyone re-plans.

pairs.tendency: A shock card disturbs a pattern you are building, by removing a piece or forcing a change, and players learn to build patterns that survive.
pros: Players think about sturdy patterns.
Repairing a pattern gives a new puzzle.
cons: Long builds can be broken by one card.
Players may avoid ambitious patterns.

pairs.tendency: Players keep cards back for use, and an event can make the held cards more or less useful, so keeping a spare card for a crisis pays off.
pros: Holding cards in reserve gets a reason.
Timing feels more meaningful.
cons: Hoarded cards may lose value overnight.
Players may hold on too long and miss turns.

pairs.tendency: Between hands an event card changes a rule, such as which suit counts most, so tricks are played under conditions nobody planned for.
pros: A familiar game gets an unfamiliar turn.
Players re-read their hands after each event.
cons: The event can overrule hand skill.
The link between event and trick can feel thin.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits some players harder than others, and those who are hurt turn to the rest for help, so deals are made under pressure.
pros: Real need drives lively deals.
Players see who helps in a crisis.
cons: Hard-hit players can be pushed into poor terms.
Talk can turn into asking for pity.

pairs.tendency: An event can wipe out or change the value of a set type, so players collecting one kind find that a crash has hit what they chose.
pros: Mixed collections feel safer than single ones.
Surprises give collectors a reason to trade.
cons: Long collecting can be lost in one card.
Players may feel punished for focusing.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes the map under the tiles, such as a flood over low tiles, so what players built is tested by something they did not choose.
pros: Players learn which tiles hold up.
The map changes after it is built.
cons: Strong layouts can be damaged without cause.
Tidy maps become messy to fix.

pairs.tendency: A call comes from an event card, and each player answers with a move of their own, so the whole table responds in turn to what the world did.
pros: Everyone gets a turn to react.
The event gives each call a start.
cons: Answers can get slower as events pile up.
Players may repeat each other's replies.

pairs.tendency: An event strikes and nobody may talk, so players show how they will respond only by the cards they play and when.
pros: Silent reactions are tense and clear.
Players read each other closely.
cons: Players may respond in different ways by mistake.
Nobody can warn a player about an event.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes the rules as well as the board, so a shock and a player's own rule change can pile onto each other.
pros: Rule changes feel like part of the world.
Players adapt to rules from two sources.
cons: Hard to tell who changed what.
The rule set can become hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: When an event card is read out, each player decides how their character would respond, so a flood or a crash becomes a scene to act out.
pros: Events give characters something to react to.
Stories come out of shared trouble.
cons: Events can pull a scene away from a character's plan.
Quiet players may stay silent after a shock.

pairs.tendency: A shock card changes the conditions for a physical task, such as a tower being shaken, so hands have to cope with what the world did.
pros: Physical tests feel tied to events.
Players react in the moment.
cons: Event and task can feel unrelated.
Shaky hands add to the shock's luck.

pairs.tendency: When an event card is drawn, players change the map they have drawn, adding a flood or removing a road, so the world is marked by what happened.
pros: Events leave a visible mark on the map.
Players share the story of what happened.
cons: Neat maps can be spoilt by many events.
Players may argue over how an event ought to be drawn.

pairs.tendency: An event card forces players to hand over or discard cards, so the cards you ask for may be gone before you can claim them.
pros: Asking has to allow for loss.
Events shake up what players hold.
cons: Long asking runs can be stopped by an event.
Lost cards can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: An event changes the odds the bank pays, so players deciding how much to bet have to also guess what the world might do next.
pros: The bank feels like part of a larger market.
Bets change when the rates change.
cons: Players may bet wildly after a shock.
Odds become hard to read.

pairs.tendency: A shock card changes what a throw is worth or who may bet, so players betting on a throw are also betting on what the world brings.
pros: Bets carry two sources of risk.
Players watch events as well as dice.
cons: Too many random inputs.
Players may feel nothing they do matters.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes the pot or the cards in play, so players betting on a hidden hand have to also guess what the world might do.
pros: Bets have to allow for outside change.
Bluffs have a new thing to lean on.
cons: A strong hand can be spoilt by an event.
Players may fold early after a shock.

pairs.tendency: A shock lands on every side, but a side built to withstand floods copes in one and not in another, so builds are tested by the world.
pros: Builds show what each player planned for.
Different builds feel different in a crisis.
cons: One build can be made weak by the event deck.
Players may blame the deck, not the build.

pairs.tendency: You promise a result at the start, then an event card strikes during play, so a contract that looked safe can fail through no fault of yours.
pros: Promises are tested by the unexpected.
Players learn to call cautiously.
cons: Honest plans can fail from outside change.
Contracts may feel unfair after a shock.

pairs.tendency: An event card turns some pieces to another side or removes them, so captured pieces may change sides again for reasons no player chose.
pros: The board can shift under players' feet.
Players watch event cards as well as pieces.
cons: Hard to follow whose piece is whose.
Captures can be undone without a fight.

pairs.tendency: An event can free or trap whole groups of pieces, so a rescue that was going to work or fail changes when a shock card comes up.
pros: Events add drama to rescues.
Teams have to change plans suddenly.
cons: Rescues can feel pointless when a card undoes them.
Jail times can swing too much.

pairs.tendency: An event removes or moves some pieces, so a group that was about to surround another finds the ring has gaps, or the other group is gone.
pros: The board changes in a way both sides see.
Players learn to build links that last.
cons: Long surrounding plans can fail from a single card.
Hard to plan many moves ahead.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits players who are ahead more often, or helps those who are behind, so the world acts as an extra catch-up rule.
pros: Leads can feel less safe.
Players behind get a reason to stay in.
cons: Players may feel punished for leading.
Catch-up may feel too much like luck.

pairs.tendency: Both the moves and the world are decided by cards or dice, so the shocks add to a game where nobody's choices change what happens.
pros: Quick and simple for any age.
Shocks make little extra to learn.
cons: Players have nothing to respond to.
Shocks lose their meaning when everything is luck.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes the play space mid-chase, such as a blocked corner or a new safe zone, so chasers and runners both have to adjust.
pros: Chases get new turns.
Rules shift at a moment everyone sees.
cons: Players may argue about an event's reach.
Running and events can feel unconnected.

pairs.tendency: When a shock arrives, players pick which rival to blame or hit, so outside hard luck becomes a reason to turn on one another.
pros: Pressure gives targeting a reason.
Players see who gets chosen in a crisis.
cons: Shocks can become an excuse to gang up.
Players hit by luck and by rivals feel doubly low.

pairs.tendency: An event breaks a link in the middle of a chain players are building, so a path that was nearly complete needs a new route.
pros: Players keep several routes open.
Repairs are tense and clear.
cons: Long chains can be cut by one card.
Strong players are hurt most by a break.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes which choice beats which, such as a flood making one option weak, so players guessing each other's picks have to guess the world too.
pros: The cycle gets a new twist each time.
Players learn to read what an event favours.
cons: A shock can make one choice always win.
Guessing becomes confusing.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes what a combination is worth, so players holding a pair or a run to show may find its points raised or cut by outside news.
pros: Declaring gets a timing question.
Hands feel tied to a changing world.
cons: Planned combinations can lose value.
Hard to remember what each combination is worth.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits all players, but each player's power eases it or makes it harder in a different way, so one event has a different effect for each.
pros: Each player's power gets a clear use.
Players see how roles differ in a crisis.
cons: Some powers may be made useless by the event deck.
One player's power can seem to matter most.

pairs.tendency: A player may double the stakes just before a shock is drawn, so offers are made with an unknown event hanging over them.
pros: Doubling feels tense and risky.
Players watch for signs of a crash.
cons: Players can be wiped out by one doubled loss.
Doubling can seem like gambling on the deck.

pairs.tendency: An event moves or removes pieces so a capture that was forced last turn is gone, or a new one is forced, so a rule that guides play is shaken.
pros: Players plan traps with events in mind.
Shocks can change the board in a clear way.
cons: Traps can fail through no skill.
Players may feel the shock decides who is trapped.

pairs.tendency: A shock tests characters as they grow, and strong ones ride it out where weak ones do not, so growth is shown against what the world does.
pros: Growth feels as though it matters.
Players see the payoff of building up.
cons: Early shocks can end a character before it grows.
Late shocks may feel too small to matter.

pairs.tendency: A shock card changes what the list has to contain, so players reciting a long list have to hold the new item too and adjust what they say.
pros: Events make the memory task fresh.
Players laugh at changes.
cons: Long lists get hard after a change.
Players can lose their place in the list.

pairs.tendency: A shock lands on both players, but the one with a handicap has fewer resources to absorb it, so the gap between them can grow or shrink.
pros: Players see how handicaps matter in a crisis.
Shocks can give the weaker side a chance.
cons: Handicap and shock may add up to too much for one player.
Hard to tell which cause decided the result.

pairs.tendency: An event changes the place where someone is hiding, such as a closed room or a new open space, so hiders and seekers have to both adjust.
pros: Searches get new turns.
Hiders cannot rely on a plan.
cons: Hiding places can be taken away unfairly.
Events can end a search too early.

pairs.tendency: An event moves or removes some pieces, so a hop that was set up for next turn may no longer be possible or may open a new one.
pros: Hops become harder to plan.
Players watch the board closely.
cons: Careful chains of hops can be broken by a card.
Players may feel shocks decide the game.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes what a roll have to reach, or what a kept die is worth, so players choosing what to keep have to guess what the world will ask for.
pros: Keeping dice gets a second question.
Players plan for more than one outcome.
cons: Too much to keep in mind with each roll.
The event can make kept dice useless.

pairs.tendency: A shock card sends pieces back or forward, so players already sent back by a landing can be sent back again by the world, with no player to blame.
pros: Setbacks can come from the world as well.
Players watch both the board and the deck.
cons: Being set back twice feels very harsh.
Hard to tell if a loss was chosen or luck.

pairs.tendency: An event removes pieces from rows, so a row that was about to be formed is broken, or a stronger row appears by chance.
pros: Players look for spare rows.
Events give a close game a sudden turn.
cons: A near-finished row can be lost without cause.
Players may not trust their own plans.

pairs.tendency: A shock card changes which letters are available or how words score, so players building words have to adjust to a changed supply.
pros: Players try new words under a change.
A clear shared moment of surprise.
cons: A long word can lose points after a shock.
Players with small vocabularies are hit hardest.

pairs.tendency: An event closes some open ends or opens new ones, so a tile you were holding for a certain number may have nothing to match, or more than before.
pros: Players hold a mix of tiles.
The line changes in front of everyone.
cons: A held tile may be left without a use.
Hard to plan ahead.

pairs.tendency: An event can take cards from melds on the table, or add to them, so sets laid face up are put at risk by something no player chose.
pros: Laid sets no longer feel safe.
Players watch what others have on the table.
cons: Meld work can be lost to one card.
Hard to rebuild a meld after a shock.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives and each player decides whether to spend a one-use power now, so the world forces a choice about when to use it.
pros: A crisis gives powers a reason to be used.
Players save and spend with care.
cons: Players may save a power and never see a shock big enough.
A power used early can leave nothing for a harder event.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes what each side can offer, so the other player's say now depends on what the world just did to both of you.
pros: Offers become more careful.
Both players share the pressure.
cons: Replies can slow the game after each event.
Players may refuse out of fear.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes the message on the way, such as a garbled line, so players passing it along cannot tell if the change came from a person or the world.
pros: Shocks fit naturally into a message that changes.
Players laugh at how it ends.
cons: Hard to tell who changed the message.
Events can make passing feel random.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards before play, then an event changes what cards are worth, so the cards you gave or kept may suddenly matter more or less.
pros: Passing choices get a delayed test.
Players learn to give with the world in mind.
cons: Passed cards cannot be taken back.
Players may blame the one who passed to them.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the start and the other picks a side, then an event strikes, so both players have to judge a fair start that the world may soon change.
pros: Both players study the setup.
The event can be a fair test for both sides.
cons: A fair split can be broken by one card.
Hard to judge fairness when events can change it.

pairs.tendency: A shock removes or changes pieces close to the far end, so a piece that was about to be promoted may be lost or promoted by luck.
pros: Reaching the far end feels uncertain.
Players guard pieces on the way.
cons: Long journeys can be wasted.
Promotion may feel less earned.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes the course part-way through a team race, so one leg is longer, blocked or easier, and the team have to adapt on the next hand-over.
pros: Teams cope with change together.
Each leg gets a different challenge.
cons: One runner may carry the hit of the shock.
Teams may lose time arguing about the event.

pairs.tendency: A shock card removes protection from shapes or breaks them, so a shape that was safe may be unsafe, and players who relied on it are exposed.
pros: Safe shapes feel valuable.
Players think about backup shapes.
cons: A shape can lose its safety for no reason.
Players may stop trusting shapes.

pairs.tendency: An event changes which cards are worth points, so winning a trick for a named prize can become more or less useful when the world shifts.
pros: Prize hunting gets a changing target.
Players read events as clues to value.
cons: Plans for one prize can be lost.
Hard to keep track of what scores.

pairs.tendency: An event changes the cards in the middle, so every player's hand is affected at once, and each have to decide how much to rely on what is shared.
pros: Everyone feels the shock together.
Shared cards get a reason to be watched.
cons: One shock can help someone by chance.
Players with weak hands may gain or lose by luck.

pairs.tendency: An event adds to or takes from the pot, so the prize everyone is playing for can grow or shrink on the turn of a card.
pros: The prize feels alive.
Players watch the pot closely.
cons: A crashing pot can make play feel wasted.
A growing pot may tempt players to take risks.

pairs.tendency: A shock card removes or adds seeds in some pits, so a sowing plan that counted on a certain count of seeds fails or comes out differently.
pros: Counting skill meets surprise.
Players recount after every event.
cons: Planned sowings can be wrecked by a card.
Hard to count for those who are new.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes what the spare hand is worth, so a player choosing whether to take it have to guess what the world will do next.
pros: The choice of the spare hand feels weightier.
Players watch the deck for signs.
cons: The spare hand can become useless after a shock.
One player may gain more than others by luck.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes some special squares, such as turning a safe square into a trap, so players who relied on the track have to learn it again.
pros: Track knowledge is tested.
Surprises feel tied to the board.
cons: Players can be sent back by a square they trusted.
Many rules to recall.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes prices, so what a card or unit costs to use goes up or down overnight, and players who planned their spending have to re-plan.
pros: Spending takes account of changing prices.
Players learn how prices move.
cons: Savings can lose value fast.
Players short of money feel hit twice.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits one place or job, so players who split forces evenly are less exposed, and those who put most in one place can lose most.
pros: Spreading forces gets a clear reason.
Players see what spreading protects.
cons: Players who guessed right can look lucky.
Spreading thin can leave no force strong enough.

pairs.tendency: An event acts as the signal, so players keep moving until a shock is revealed, then freeze or grab a place, and the slowest are caught out.
pros: Events get a sharp, shared moment.
Players stay alert between events.
cons: Players may feel a surprise signal is unfair.
Quick reactions count for more than plans.

pairs.tendency: An event changes the value of cards on the table, so a swap that looked fair when you made it may look very different after the next shock.
pros: Swaps carry a bet on the future.
Players watch which cards others take.
cons: Fair swaps can be undone by the world.
Hard to guess what a card will be worth.

pairs.tendency: An event card is added to the discard pile or changes what the pile does, so a player taking the pile may be taking a shock as well as cards.
pros: Taking the pile becomes a risk.
Players watch what goes in the pile.
cons: The pile can be poison without warning.
Players may avoid the pile out of fear.

pairs.tendency: An event changes the trump suit or drops its power, so a hand built around one strong suit may suddenly be weak.
pros: Players think about their second suit.
Rule changes feel part of the world.
cons: A carefully built hand can be lost in one card.
Players may avoid building around one suit.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits one of the two boards, so a player who was a side in both feels the effect twice, once as helped and once as hurt.
pros: The two games get a link.
Players weigh effects across both boards.
cons: Hard to track two boards and an event deck.
One board may feel more important after a shock.

pairs.tendency: An event makes some cards scarce or removes wilds, so a player who was relying on a wild card to finish a set may find the plan gone.
pros: Wild cards become a risk to depend on.
Players plan set by set.
cons: Wilds can be lost to an outside change.
Players who held wilds feel cheated.

pairs.tendency: An event on a board with joined edges can strike places that seem far apart but touch, so a flood on the left edge also reaches the right.
pros: The board's shape affects events.
Players learn the real reach of a shock.
cons: Players may be unsure what counts as near.
Edge events are hard to draw.

pairs.tendency: An event card changes the secret or the facts a questioner has gathered, so a long run of yes and no answers may no longer point to the same answer.
pros: Long question runs have a risk.
Players have to re-check facts after an event.
cons: Careful questioning can be wasted.
The one who knows the secret may feel pressure.

pairs.tendency: A shock slows or speeds some players along the track, so the leader may be caught up, and a race that looked won can change in one draw.
pros: Races stay close and lively.
Players hold back some reserve.
cons: Winning can feel like luck.
Skilled planning is worth less in a short race.

pairs.tendency: Shocks add or remove points from players or their holdings across the game, so the final tally shows how each player stood up to what the world did.
pros: Players think about how to protect points.
Final scores tell a story.
cons: The score can be moved by late events.
Players may feel the total was decided by luck.

pairs.tendency: Shocks knock players out as well as rivals do, so the last one alive may be the one who was spared by the world, not the one who played strongest.
pros: Shocks keep the table tense.
Players watch for who is weakest.
cons: A knocked-out player waits while events go on.
Early outs may come from luck alone.

pairs.tendency: Each shock is a test of whether the team can last, so players share the loss of a flood or a crash and plan together for what may come next.
pros: Everyone feels the same threat.
Shocks give the team clear things to deal with.
cons: Players may feel crushed by a run of hard events.
One strong player may take over the planning.

pairs.tendency: A shock moves the group's goal further away, such as a crash that raises the price of the target, so the team have to adjust its plan together.
pros: The team adjusts as one.
Shocks make the shared goal feel real.
cons: Plans can be undone by a single card.
Players may disagree on how to adapt.

pairs.tendency: An event helps some secret goals and hurts others, so players may guess a rival's goal from how they respond to a shock.
pros: Reactions give away hints.
A shock can help one player by chance.
cons: Players may feel a goal was hit unfairly.
Hard to tell if a response was honest.

pairs.tendency: Events become turns in the story, such as a flood or a death, and the game ends when the story does, so shocks shape the plot as much as players do.
pros: Events give the story its turns.
Players find endings they did not plan.
cons: A story can be pushed off course by one card.
Players may feel the story belongs to the deck.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives in a game with no winner, so players simply look at how the world and their choices changed things, and talk about it.
pros: Shocks become something to talk over.
No one needs to protect a lead.
cons: Players may not see why a shock matters.
Play can feel aimless without a stake.

pairs.tendency: A shock tests each player's own idea of doing well, so one player may think a flood a disaster and another may count it as a chance.
pros: Events show what each goal needs.
Players learn how others measure success.
cons: Goals can be hard to compare after a shock.
A shock can make a personal goal impossible.

pairs.tendency: A shock makes it more likely that one player will be the one who loses, so everyone watches the weakest and wonders who the next event will hit.
pros: Tension builds with every event.
Players look out for the weakest.
cons: Players hit by luck may feel singled out.
A run of events can decide the loser early.

pairs.tendency: A shock threatens the game itself, so the aim of players is to keep playing through floods and crashes, and each event is a test of that.
pros: Events give the game things to survive.
Players help each other recover.
cons: Too many shocks can end the game.
Too few shocks leave little to keep going through.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives in a game nobody can win, so each event shows something about how the world works, and nothing the players do turns it round.
pros: Events carry the point of the game.
Players feel the weight of what they cannot change.
cons: Players may stop trying after the first shock.
A bleak game can feel pointless to some.

pairs.tendency: The layout fights back through shocks, such as cards that are removed or buried, so a solo player trying to clear it have to respond to events as well as plan.
pros: A solo game gets surprises.
A clear way to raise difficulty.
cons: A cleared table can be undone by one card.
Winning can feel like luck.

pairs.tendency: A shock in one game may be remembered in the next, so players choose differently once they have seen what the world might do.
pros: Players learn between games.
Shocks stay in memory for the next round.
cons: One game can be settled by a shock alone.
Players may play too carefully in the last game.

pairs.tendency: Shocks can add points to some players, so the one who keeps a low score may be the one the world spared, as much as the one who played carefully.
pros: Players try to keep clear of shocks.
Low scores get a surprise element.
cons: Players hit by events lose through no fault.
Players may think low scores are made by luck.

pairs.tendency: A shock moves players off the number they were aiming for, so a player close to an exact finish may be pushed back by an event.
pros: Last steps stay tense.
Players plan for ways to recover.
cons: Being so close and set back is frustrating.
Games can go on for a long time.

pairs.tendency: A shock pushes players away from the losing aim, such as a card that gives them something back, so those trying to give everything away may be set back by luck.
pros: Shocks give the aim a twist.
Players laugh at reversals.
cons: The aim can be confusing with events.
A shock may feel like it helps the wrong player.

pairs.tendency: The same shock hits every player's own board, but each has built differently, so players compare how their own plans held up without touching each other.
pros: Players learn from each other's boards.
Shocks give separate games a shared moment.
cons: There is little to do but watch.
Players may blame luck without comparing.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits during a fight, so players already attacking each other have to also cope with the world, and some use the event to hit harder.
pros: Fights get new turns.
Events can slow down a runaway leader.
cons: Shocks can be blamed for what a player did.
Players may use events as an excuse to attack.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes the board that players use to affect each other, so changes players made to the board are tested by what the world does.
pros: Players see board changes more clearly.
Shocks can reset a crowded board.
cons: Hard to know what changed the board.
Long board plans can be lost to events.

pairs.tendency: The team shares each shock, so players take it in turn to respond and share out the loss, and plans are made with the next event in mind.
pros: A shock draws the team together.
Everyone has a part in the response.
cons: One loud player can steer the reply.
The team may feel crushed by events.

pairs.tendency: A shock hurts everyone, but each player also wants to come out ahead, so players share the response and quietly look after their own position.
pros: Players weigh group and own interest.
Crises show who helps.
cons: Players may blame each other for a shock.
Private aims can slow the group's response.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits both teams, but one may be placed to cope more easily, so teams plan together for what the world might bring and watch the other side.
pros: Teams plan for shocks together.
Shocks can bring a close game.
cons: One team may be luckier than the other.
A team hit hard may feel the match is decided.

pairs.tendency: A shock hurts the team, and players wonder whether it was chance or the traitor's doing, so events become a reason to accuse.
pros: Shocks add to suspicion.
The traitor can hide behind events.
cons: Players may accuse the wrong person.
Honest players may feel blamed for hard luck.

pairs.tendency: Events arrive by post or message and every player answers in their own time, so a shock can sit for days before anyone responds.
pros: Events give a long game something to wait for.
Players have time to think about a reply.
cons: Players may miss an event or answer late.
A game can stall while an event waits.

pairs.tendency: A shock may come from the absent player, such as a ghost or an earlier game, so an event can feel like the missing person acting on the table.
pros: Events make the absent person felt.
Players have a reason to talk about them.
cons: Players may disagree on what the absent player would do.
The absent player may be blamed for each shock.

pairs.tendency: The game master reads or invents events, so shocks come from a person who can see how the players are doing, and can be made to fit them.
pros: Events can fit the moment.
The game master can adjust the pace.
cons: Players may feel shocks are aimed at them.
The game master carries more work.

pairs.tendency: An event in a street or park game, such as rain or a passing crowd, changes play, and players who are not playing may take part by chance.
pros: Real events can be used as shocks.
Passers-by may join in.
cons: Real events are hard to control.
Rules may be unclear for newcomers.

pairs.tendency: A shock hurts the lone player or the group, and the team of many may use it to press their advantage, or the lone player may use it to escape.
pros: A shock can swing the odds.
A lone player gets a chance to recover.
cons: The lone player can be buried by events.
The group may feel an event helped them too much.

pairs.tendency: A solo player draws shock cards and has no one to share them with, so each event is faced alone, and luck and choice both decide the result.
pros: Events give a solo game surprises.
A solo player can try many plans.
cons: A run of shocks can end the game early.
No one else to talk it through with.

pairs.tendency: Shocks join dice and draws in deciding what happens, so the game moves along by luck with another source of it, and players have little to plan.
pros: Easy and quick for any age.
Shocks add to the sense of surprise.
cons: Players have little to learn from a shock.
Skill hardly changes the result.

pairs.tendency: Players can soften a shock with a spare card, a reserve or a reroll, so the event is random but what it costs depends on how well they prepared.
pros: Preparing is worth something.
Players have ways to answer hard luck.
cons: Reserves can sit idle for many rounds.
Players may over-prepare against shocks.

pairs.tendency: Shocks are the small luck in a mostly skilful game, so strong players can plan around them and weaker players are not shut out.
pros: Luck keeps close games open.
Skilled players are tested on how they adapt.
cons: A shock can undo a long plan.
Skilled players may resent the luck.

pairs.tendency: A shock enters a game with no dice, so it becomes the one outside surprise, and a plan that was set by skill alone meets something nobody chose.
pros: Shocks test how players adapt.
Players think about contingency.
cons: One shock can overturn long thought.
Players may resent the one random element.

pairs.tendency: An event card is read as a message about the world, so a flood or a crash is a sign to interpret as well as something to survive.
pros: Events give players something to discuss.
Players find meaning in what turns up.
cons: Different readings of one event can lead to argument.
The sign may not mean much if players already know the rules.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes how players sense each other, so players who are in step before an event may drift out of step after it, and need time to find each other again.
pros: Shocks show how well players sense each other.
Players learn to recover as a group.
cons: Events can break a rhythm that took long to build.
Hard to feel in tune when the world keeps changing.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on an event table, so the shock itself is the story, and a flood or a price crash may be the next thing that happens on the road.
pros: Stories come from simple rolls.
The table makes events easy to run.
cons: A short table soon repeats.
Players may find the story random and thin.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible except the event deck, so players can see all that is in play and still cannot know what the world will do next.
pros: One hidden thing keeps a calm game alive.
Players plan with the facts in view.
cons: Skill games can be spoilt by one shock.
Players may resent the single secret.

pairs.tendency: Players hold secret cards, and a shock may change their value in a way each player alone can judge, so a hidden hand can become a hidden risk.
pros: Secret cards face a shared change.
Players guess how others are hit.
cons: Hard to tell who is hurt.
Players may bluff about how a shock hit them.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives and players watch how each person reacts, since a secret role may respond to a flood or a crash differently from the rest.
pros: Events give clues to roles.
Reactions become part of the play.
cons: Players may accuse someone for a normal reaction.
Shocks can cover a hidden player's moves.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes some of the facts, so players who were working out a hidden answer may find an old clue no longer holds.
pros: Players have to check their clues again.
A twist can make a mystery fresh.
cons: Careful work may be undone by one event.
Players may not trust their clues.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives and players claim it hit them harder or less than it did, so bluffing about the world's effect becomes part of the game.
pros: Shocks give bluffers something to use.
Players study each other's reactions.
cons: A real loss may be disbelieved.
Players may be stuck arguing about what happened.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives while players are still finding the secret rule, so they cannot tell whether a result came from the rule or from the world.
pros: Events add to the mystery.
Players test theories about both rule and shock.
cons: Hard to find a rule when events blur it.
Players may give up on the secret rule.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows the answer have to give hints, and an event may change what the answer is or how hints can be given, so the guessers' progress may be lost.
pros: A twist keeps a long guess lively.
The giver of hints faces a new task.
cons: Guessers may lose much progress.
Hints may become confusing after a shock.

pairs.tendency: Exploring may reveal an event as well as a place, so a newly turned area may carry a flood or a crash that players had no way to know about.
pros: Exploring carries real risk.
Each reveal is a surprise.
cons: Players may avoid exploring.
A shock tied to a reveal can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes the face-up hand or what it is worth, so a hand that everyone can read becomes the one thing that the world has changed in plain view.
pros: Everyone sees the effect of a shock.
Players plan with the open hand in mind.
cons: The open hand can mislead after a shock.
Players may feel certain about a hand that has changed.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes scores that nobody can see in full, so players guess how much it hurt rivals and cannot be sure who gained.
pros: Events add to the guessing.
Players watch behaviour after a shock for clues.
cons: Players may be unsure how they stand.
Shocks can hide who is really ahead.

pairs.tendency: An event card is drawn at the start or end of each round, so players wait their turn and then respond one at a time to what the world just did.
pros: A clear rhythm of event, then response.
Players have time to think after each shock.
cons: Players may wait long for their reply.
Early responders may shape what later players do.

pairs.tendency: A shock is revealed and every player responds at the same moment, so nobody can wait to see what the others do, and the table's reply is shared.
pros: Events get a fast, shared reaction.
Players compare their replies together.
cons: Players may not hear the event clearly.
Slow responders may be left behind.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives at any moment, and whoever notices first responds first, so the world can interrupt any plan and speed counts.
pros: Events keep players alert.
Quick players can save the table.
cons: Quiet players may miss an event.
Events can be lost in the noise.

pairs.tendency: A shock lands while the clock is running, so players have to respond in a few seconds, and a plan made before the event may not survive the time.
pros: Pressure and surprise add up.
Players learn to decide fast.
cons: Players may panic and make mistakes.
A timed reply can feel unfair after a hard event.

pairs.tendency: Events arrive over days or weeks, such as a message each morning, so players live with a shock for a long time before the next one comes.
pros: Shocks have time to sink in.
Players can plan and rethink over days.
cons: Players may forget an event or drop out.
A long wait can drain the tension.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives into a game that has been slowed down, so players have a long pause to think about the event before they may respond.
pros: Shocks can be thought about in full.
The pause makes each event feel weighty.
cons: A pause can drain the surprise.
Players may find the wait dull.

pairs.tendency: Shocks come faster as the game goes on, so players get less time to recover between events, and the end comes in a rush of events.
pros: Pressure builds in a clear way.
The ending feels hectic and memorable.
cons: Players may be overwhelmed late on.
Early rounds may feel calm and slow.

pairs.tendency: A shock gives some players an extra turn or takes one away, so the world decides who gets a second move, and a lucky player may do much before the others act.
pros: Events can reward luck with action.
A run of moves is exciting.
cons: A run can feel unfair to the others.
A player taking many turns can end a game quickly.

pairs.tendency: Each stage has its own events, so the shocks in the opening differ from those late on, and what players built early is tested at each new stage.
pros: Events mark the change of stage.
Early work is tested later.
cons: A shock may not suit every stage.
Players may feel a stage change is sudden.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system and a shock card hits it, so players see how the whole system, such as a village's wells and fields, responds to something outside it.
pros: Shocks show how the system is linked.
Players learn what a system can and cannot take.
cons: One shock can look like the whole lesson.
Players may take a shock as a forecast of real life.

pairs.tendency: One event looks different to each role, so a flood costs the farmer a crop, helps the boat owner, and puts the village council on the spot.
pros: Events show whose problem it is.
Players see one shock from many sides.
cons: One role may be hurt every time.
Players may care only about their own role's loss.

pairs.tendency: A shock strikes the shared resource itself, such as a dry year for the village well, so everyone's supply drops together and players have to decide who goes without.
pros: Shocks make the shared stock matter.
Players have to talk about sharing.
cons: A hard event may empty the stock at once.
Players may blame each other for the shortage.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives now and shows its full effect only a few rounds later, so players cannot tell at once whether they handled it well.
pros: Shocks give plans a delayed test.
Players learn to look ahead.
cons: Players may forget which shock caused a loss.
The link between event and result may be missed.

pairs.tendency: Players test a new rule and an event strikes, so the table sees how the rule behaves under pressure, not only when all is calm.
pros: A rule is tried in a crisis.
Players learn how it holds up.
cons: One event may unfairly judge a rule.
Hard to tell if the rule or the shock caused a result.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about each shock: what it did, who it hit and whether they could have seen it coming.
pros: Shocks give the talk clear things to discuss.
Players link events to real life.
cons: Players may talk about luck, not choices.
Hard to remember the order of events.

pairs.tendency: A shock leaves a permanent mark, such as a torn card or a sticker, so the world after a flood is not the same one as before it.
pros: Events have lasting weight.
The next game starts from a changed world.
cons: A harsh shock can ruin later games.
Players may feel nothing can be repaired.

pairs.tendency: The shocks that the game includes make a point about the world, such as a rule that floods only hit the poorest, so the deck itself argues.
pros: Events carry the game's message.
Players can argue about which shocks are included.
cons: Players may see the deck as unfair.
The point may be missed when events look random.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits what is at stake in real life, such as a forfeit or a promise, so an event can cost players something real.
pros: Shocks feel serious.
Players learn how others handle pressure.
cons: Real costs from chance can cause hurt.
Players may refuse to play after a harsh event.

pairs.tendency: A shock takes points away, such as health or trust, so players see in numbers what a crisis costs a thing that matters.
pros: Events show what a loss is worth.
Players think about what they protect.
cons: Points can make a real loss seem small.
Players may chase points and ignore the meaning.

pairs.tendency: A shock strikes a future the players are practising, such as a shared village in a drought, so they find out how it holds up under strain.
pros: Players test a future against trouble.
Weak spots in a plan show up.
cons: A single shock may seem to decide the result.
Players may think the shocks are a forecast.

pairs.tendency: One event card stands for a year or more, such as a drought or a price crash, so players see the effect of large events across a long span of time.
pros: Events feel as large as in real life.
Years of change fit in one sitting.
cons: A year's shock may be hard to picture at the table.
One card may carry too much weight.

pairs.tendency: A shock moves the gauges on the board, such as water level or trust, so everyone sees at once how much the event changed the whole system.
pros: The effect of a shock is clear to all.
Players link events to the gauges.
cons: Players may watch gauges and not the cause.
One big move can feel like the end of the game.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits everyone, but a player who began with more money or land can ride it out, and a player who began with less may be ruined.
pros: Players see how a start affects a crisis.
Shocks make inequality plain.
cons: Those who start poor may feel set up to fail.
The same event may look fair to some and not others.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits, and the powerful may use the crisis to change the rules, so those hurt most find the rules shifting at the hardest moment.
pros: Crises show how rules get changed.
Players see power at work.
cons: Players hurt by luck and rules may feel crushed.
Players may stop playing if the rules shift too often.

pairs.tendency: A shock helps one role and hurts another, such as a drought that raises the price for the seller and ruins the farmer, so each reads the same event differently.
pros: One event gives roles a reason to clash.
Players see why groups disagree.
cons: A role that is always hurt may lose interest.
Players may argue over what the shock means.

pairs.tendency: The opening is a described situation, and a shock is the first thing that changes it, so players have to act as soon as the scene is set.
pros: The game starts with something happening.
The starting scene feels alive.
cons: An early shock may undo a carefully built opening.
Players may feel rushed into action.

pairs.tendency: A shock arrives and players argue how they would respond, so the table judges whether a plan for a flood or a crash would work.
pros: Events invite real reasoning.
Players learn to defend a plan.
cons: Arguments about an event may run long.
The strongest talker may win rather than the strongest plan.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a shock so players can say what they notice, so an event becomes a moment to think rather than only to react.
pros: Shocks give a natural place to pause.
Players understand an event before moving on.
cons: Stops can break the mood of a shock.
Players may repeat the same remarks each time.

pairs.tendency: The same shocks are played again with one thing changed, so players can see how the same flood or crash plays out under different choices.
pros: Players can compare how plans handle the same event.
Players see what really changed the result.
cons: Players may remember the shocks and play to them.
A repeat of the same events loses surprise.

pairs.tendency: The game states which real shocks it left out, such as an illness or a war, so players know that events in the game are only a few of those that could happen.
pros: Players know the limits of the events.
Players think of shocks the game left out.
cons: The list of left-out events can be long.
Players may feel the shocks shown are not enough.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about help choose which shocks go in, so events come from what has really happened to them, not from a designer's guess.
pros: Events ring true to those who lived them.
Players hear real accounts of shocks.
cons: Painful events may be hard to see on a card.
People may disagree on what counts as a shock.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits one link in the chain, such as a factory fire or a closed port, and its effect travels down the line to every later player.
pros: Players see how one event reaches many.
Links learn to hold some spare stock.
cons: Players far from the shock may not see where it began.
Late links can be hit hardest.

pairs.tendency: A shock reaches you only through the orders and stock you can see, so you feel the effect without knowing what the cause was or who else was hit.
pros: Players learn how little one link can see.
Shocks feel like real surprises.
cons: Players may blame the wrong neighbour.
Players may feel left in the dark.

pairs.tendency: A shock hits the slowest step, so the whole line slows further, or hits another step and changes nothing, and players learn which step the event really matters for.
pros: Players learn which step really matters.
A shock at the bottleneck is felt by all.
cons: A shock elsewhere may seem to do nothing.
Players may stop caring about other steps.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes demand suddenly, so goods made ahead to a guess may pile up, while a line that makes to order waits and then rushes to fill orders.
pros: Players feel the cost of each way.
Shocks show which way copes with change.
cons: The comparison may need several rounds.
Players may blame the event, not the method.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes demand or breaks a step, so a large batch ordered before it may be too much or too late, and a small batch is easier to change.
pros: Small batches show a clear use.
Players see the price of a big batch.
cons: A small batch may cost more in set-up.
Players may judge batch size by one lucky event.

pairs.tendency: A breakdown is itself a shock, and an outside event can strike at the same time, so a line already short of a machine is hit by another problem.
pros: Players learn why spare capacity matters.
Two kinds of failure test one plan.
cons: Two shocks together can end a round at once.
Hard to tell which one caused the delay.

pairs.tendency: A shock changes demand, so stock that was a fair amount yesterday may be too much or too little today, and the cost of either shows at once.
pros: Players see the cost of each mistake.
Stock levels feel like real choices.
cons: A sudden shock can make any level wrong.
Players may keep too much stock after one event.

pairs.tendency: Each roll moves your piece through a year, so a few throws carry a whole lifetime along the path and luck sets how fast you age.
pros: A lifetime fits on one path.
Quick, familiar turns.
cons: Dice decide how many years pass.
Little to choose within a year.

pairs.tendency: Each pass of the cards is a year, so the hand you pick from changes with the seasons and early picks shape the decades that follow.
pros: Picks pile up into a visible history.
Fast rounds cover many years.
cons: Players forget which year a card came from.
Passing cards can feel unlike time passing.

pairs.tendency: Players bid once a year for land, labour or tools, and prices climb or fall as years go by, so a bid is a bet on later years.
pros: Prices show how scarcity changes over time.
Bids look ahead across many years.
cons: Money spent early cannot be seen paying off.
Early and late bids are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Each round is a year and players decide how far to push before it ends, so one risky year can undo many careful ones.
pros: A lost year feels heavy.
Short rounds keep the risk quick.
cons: One bust can end a long run.
Losses can feel too sudden for a decade.

pairs.tendency: The map changes hands once a year, so players watch borders and holdings drift across decades instead of fighting over one afternoon's turn.
pros: Borders shift slowly enough to read.
Long holdings feel earned.
cons: Little happens inside a single round.
Players lose track of past years.

pairs.tendency: Each placement round is a year's work, so workers are sent to jobs for a season and the same few spaces fill up again every year.
pros: A yearly routine is easy to learn.
Planning for the next season feels natural.
cons: The same spaces repeat every year.
Days inside a year go unseen.

pairs.tendency: Pieces laid each round add one year to a growing pattern, so the finished pattern reads as a record of decades, like rings in a tree.
pros: The pattern becomes a record of time.
Calm and easy to read at the end.
cons: One year adds very little.
Early placements are hard to change later.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand are plans for future years, so holding one back means waiting for a season that suits it.
pros: Waiting for the right year feels real.
Hand size shows how much is planned.
cons: Held cards go stale over long spans.
Players may hoard instead of letting time pass.

pairs.tendency: Each trick is one year's contest, so a hand of tricks reads as a run of years in which first one side and then another comes out ahead.
pros: Quick contests cover many years.
Familiar rhythm of play.
cons: Card strength says little about what the year was like.
The link to time passing is thin.

pairs.tendency: Players make their deals once a year, so promises have to last across seasons and a broken deal is remembered when the next year comes round.
pros: Promises have to last many years.
Trust builds and wears down in view.
cons: Talk can fill a year and stall the game.
Forgotten deals cause arguments.

pairs.tendency: Each year players add one more piece to a set, so a collection becomes a slow harvest of many seasons rather than one lucky draw.
pros: A finished set shows years of patient work.
Progress is easy to count each round.
cons: Sets can feel like stamps, not time.
Waiting for the last piece can drag.

pairs.tendency: Each tile is a year of growth, so the shared map of roads and fields fills slowly and shows what decades of building leave behind.
pros: The map becomes a record of years.
Slow growth is easy to see.
cons: Early tiles shape everything after.
One round adds very little.

pairs.tendency: A call and its answer pass in each round, so every exchange is a year and the chain of replies reads like a history told back and forth.
pros: The chain of replies records the years.
Easy to keep in rhythm.
cons: A year can shrink to a single line.
Players lose the thread across many rounds.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks while the years pass, so players show what they mean only by what they play and feel time move through the cards alone.
pros: Quiet makes time feel long.
Players read each other closely.
cons: Which year it is can be unclear.
Nobody can explain what a year stands for.

pairs.tendency: A rule changed in one round holds for all the years after, so players watch one rule shape a community over decades in a single sitting.
pros: Rule effects show over many years.
Players see rules grow old.
cons: Early rule changes can lock in everything after.
Long play makes the rules hard to track.

pairs.tendency: Each round players speak as their characters for a year, so characters age, change jobs and settle quarrels over a long game.
pros: Characters change over the years.
Players explain what happened between years.
cons: Skipped years leave gaps in the story.
Players disagree about what happened meanwhile.

pairs.tendency: A flick, stack or throw each round stands for a year, so steady hands carry on across decades and a shaky tower leans with age.
pros: A tower shows time passing.
Hands-on play stays lively.
cons: Skill at the table has little to do with years.
One flick is a thin stand-in for a year.

pairs.tendency: Each round the players add one year to the map, so a settlement's growth, losses and moves are drawn on the paper in order.
pros: The finished map holds decades of history.
Players make the record together.
cons: Drawing takes longer than a year feels.
Years are hard to tell apart on one sheet.

pairs.tendency: Each round is a year in which one player asks another for a card, so what each person holds becomes known as the years add up.
pros: Knowledge of each other builds over years.
Short rounds are quick to play.
cons: A year shrinks to one question.
Asking has little to do with time passing.

pairs.tendency: The bank pays or collects each year, so a run of rounds reads as rich and lean times over a lifetime while the bank passes round.
pros: Runs of luck read as rich and lean years.
The passing bank gives the span a shape.
cons: Fixed odds do not change as years pass.
A year is only one throw.

pairs.tendency: Each year one throw decides who takes the stakes, so luck alone sets whether a year is kind, and players bet before they know.
pros: Years of luck feel like weather.
Betting looks ahead one season.
cons: Nothing players do changes the year.
Every year can feel the same.

pairs.tendency: Chips stay in the pot as years go by, and players weigh whether to stay in for another year or drop out and lose what they put in.
pros: Staying in costs more each year.
Dropping out is a real choice.
cons: Hidden hands do not show years passing.
Losses can feel sudden.

pairs.tendency: Each side is built once and then plays through many years, so choices made at the start show their results long after, in the last rounds.
pros: Early choices show results decades later.
Different sides age in different ways.
cons: A weak start is felt for many rounds.
A side is hard to adjust once it is built.

pairs.tendency: A contract names what a side will do across the years of a hand, so players promise a result for a long stretch and are held to it at the end.
pros: One promise covers many years.
Failure is easy to see at the end.
cons: Plans are hard to change as years pass.
One poor year can sink the whole contract.

pairs.tendency: A piece that changes sides stays changed for the years after, so a conquest in one round shapes the balance for the decades that follow.
pros: Conquests show their effects over time.
The lead can change within a few years.
cons: Swings can look like sudden fate.
Turns of fortune can feel too fast for decades.

pairs.tendency: A prisoner waits in jail for rounds, so a capture is felt as years lost, and a rescue comes only after the cost has been paid.
pros: Waiting in jail shows the cost of time.
A rescue feels earned.
cons: Captured players sit out many years.
Years in jail can be dull.

pairs.tendency: Stones close in on each other round after round, so a surround takes years to finish and the board shows slow pressure building.
pros: Slow pressure is easy to watch.
Long plans pay off late.
cons: One year adds a single stone.
The squeeze may only show late.

pairs.tendency: Help for players who are behind arrives as the years pass, so a late recovery reads like a change of fortune after a hard decade.
pros: A comeback feels like a change of era.
Players who are behind stay in the game.
cons: Leaders see years of work undone.
Help can feel arbitrary.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards settle each year with no choice at all, so the game reads as seasons that nobody steers, like weather over a lifetime.
pros: Years feel like weather nobody steers.
Very quick to play.
cons: Players only watch the years go by.
No choices to look back on.

pairs.tendency: Each round of chasing stands for a year, so who is It and who runs changes over a long stretch of time that fits into a few minutes.
pros: Running and tagging stay lively.
Roles swap, like fortunes over years.
cons: Fast running does not feel like a year.
Many years pass with no sense of time.

pairs.tendency: Each year you pick who is hit or helped, so grudges and favours stack up across rounds like old quarrels between neighbours.
pros: Grudges build as years pass.
Choices carry a history.
cons: Players can be picked on year after year.
One year's pick can seem small.

pairs.tendency: A chain of stones lengthens a little each year, so a link across the board takes decades to finish and the other side can cut it at any time.
pros: A long chain shows years of effort.
A cut feels like lost decades.
cons: One round adds a single stone.
A year's work can look slight.

pairs.tendency: Each year players choose between options that beat and lose to each other, so over many years nobody holds the lead and the cycle turns like the seasons.
pros: The cycle feels like turning seasons.
No choice stays on top for decades.
cons: One year is just one pick.
Players may feel they repeat the same year.

pairs.tendency: Players show a pair or a run each year and score for it, so a hand shows what has built up over a long span while cards stay held.
pros: Scores add up like years of work.
Showing a run marks a year.
cons: A declaration says little about what the year was like.
Held cards sit still while years pass.

pairs.tendency: Each player's power shapes how their years go, so players live through the same span under different rules, like people in places with different laws.
pros: Each player's years feel different.
Powers show unequal histories.
cons: More rules to remember each year.
A power can fade into the background.

pairs.tendency: Doubling raises what a long game is worth, so offering it is a bet that the years ahead will go your way.
pros: A double is a bet on the future.
Players weigh a decade of risk.
cons: Giving up loses everything already earned.
Doubling too early leaves many years to run.

pairs.tendency: A forced capture binds a player to a move in a given year, so choices narrow as years pass and a trap set early shapes the decades after.
pros: Traps set early show their price later.
Forced moves feel like events pressing in.
cons: Choices shrink over many years.
Years can feel out of the player's hands.

pairs.tendency: A character gains power every year, so one afternoon shows a whole career, from a weak start to the strength of many years of work.
pros: A whole career fits in the game.
Growth is easy to see year by year.
cons: Early years can feel slow and weak.
Late years can feel too easy.

pairs.tendency: Each year the list gets one more item, so it becomes a record of every year gone by and has to be said whole each round.
pros: The list is a record of the years.
Memory stands in for history.
cons: Long lists slow the late years.
One slip of memory spoils many years.

pairs.tendency: A handicap sets how the years begin, so a weaker player starts with less and the game shows how long a head start lasts.
pros: Shows how long a head start lasts.
Weaker players stay in the game.
cons: A head start can fade within a few years.
Players argue about the starting gap.

pairs.tendency: Something stays hidden through many rounds and each search is a year, so the longer it stays hidden the more years pass with nothing found.
pros: Long searches feel like years passing.
Finding it ends the long wait.
cons: A round of searching is short for a year.
Years can pass with nothing happening.

pairs.tendency: Each round's hop stands for a year, so a piece's path across the board becomes a long journey made one jump at a time.
pros: A path shows a journey across years.
Jumps are easy to follow.
cons: One jump per year can feel slow.
Time and space blur together.

pairs.tendency: Each year you roll, keep what you like and roll again, so a lifetime's luck can be partly steered across years but never fully.
pros: Players can steer a few years of luck.
Rolls feel like seasons.
cons: Each year takes up to three rolls.
Unlucky streaks still show up.

pairs.tendency: A piece sent back to the start loses years of travel, so one landing in one round can wipe out a decade of progress.
pros: Setbacks feel like lost years.
Safe squares feel like rest.
cons: Years of progress can vanish in one round.
Players may stop caring about the long run.

pairs.tendency: Rows build up over years and a finished row lets you take a piece, so slow work across many rounds pays off in one moment.
pros: Slow building pays off in one move.
Years of work feel earned.
cons: A take seems sudden after quiet years.
Early years can feel empty.

pairs.tendency: Letters add up year by year, so a word grows slowly and a finished word stands for many years of work, though spelling takes time.
pros: Words leave a lasting record.
The dictionary settles arguments.
cons: Finding a word takes longer than a year.
Letters have little to do with years.

pairs.tendency: Each tile extends the line by a year and a missed turn means a year passes with nothing added, so the line reads as a history.
pros: The line reads as a history.
Missed turns show lost years.
cons: A year can pass with nothing happening.
Players with no match just wait.

pairs.tendency: A meld stays on the table for the rest of the game, so a set laid in one year can be added to by the years that follow.
pros: A meld becomes a lasting record.
Others can build on past years.
cons: Early melds shape all later play.
Years are hard to tell apart on the table.

pairs.tendency: Each power can be spent once, so players choose which year is the one to use it, and timing becomes a question across a lifetime.
pros: Choosing the right year is a real choice.
Powers mark turning points.
cons: Unused powers can sit out the whole game.
A power feels small beside a whole year.

pairs.tendency: Each year the other player can turn down your offer or choose between two moves, so what happens in a year is agreed, not just done.
pros: Years are shaped by both players.
Offers show what each side wants.
cons: Refusals can stall a year.
Players may argue over every move.

pairs.tendency: A message passes along over rounds and changes on the way, so a year's news can arrive altered, like a story retold across generations.
pros: Retelling shows how stories change over time.
Nobody can check it until the end.
cons: A year's news may be lost on the way.
Players only learn the change at the end.

pairs.tendency: Cards are handed on before play, so each player starts a long span with something they did not choose, as people inherit from the years before them.
pros: Inherited cards feel like a past.
Players start with something unplanned.
cons: Players cannot look before they choose.
Handing on happens once, not each year.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the starting year and the other picks a side, so the first year is made even and the long span after it begins level.
pros: The years that follow start level.
The setter has to think about both sides.
cons: An even start can fade within a few years.
The rule only matters once.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes more powerful, so a long march of many years ends in a change of rank, like a career.
pros: A long march ends in a new rank.
Pushing forward feels like a career.
cons: Pieces may hold back for years.
Promotion comes once, late.

pairs.tendency: A team passes the baton over many legs, so each leg stands for a year or a generation and the team finishes a long journey together.
pros: Each leg feels like a generation.
The whole team shares the finish.
cons: Waiting for a leg to end is slow.
One slow leg holds up the whole span.

pairs.tendency: Stones that form a safe shape stay safe for the rest of the game, so a shape built over a few years holds through the decades after.
pros: A safe shape lasts like a settled home.
Long plans get a clear goal.
cons: Years go into one shape.
Rivals can wait years to surround it.

pairs.tendency: Named cards carry the prizes, so each year's tricks are a step towards a prize the whole span has been heading for.
pros: A prize gives the years a goal.
One card can win much at the end.
cons: Prizes can be settled in the first years.
A year's tricks matter less than the prize.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle stay up for the year, so everyone draws on the same conditions, as people all face the same weather or prices.
pros: Everyone faces the same year.
Shared cards show common conditions.
cons: Different years can look alike.
Players see the year but not each other's plans.

pairs.tendency: The pot grows each year nobody wins, so a run of empty years makes the prize worth waiting for and a win suddenly counts for far more.
pros: Waiting years add to the prize.
A big pot raises the stakes.
cons: Many empty years can feel flat.
A late win swamps the early years.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are sown one year and gathered the next, so the board counts a farm's seasons and an empty pit is a lean year.
pros: Seeds and seasons fit together.
An empty pit shows a lean year.
cons: Sowing takes long for one year.
Counting seeds can hide the years.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand is dealt once before play, so one player may take a second chance at the start of a long span and carry it for years.
pros: A second chance opens the long span.
Choices come before any years pass.
cons: It happens once, not each year.
A hidden extra hand can look unfair.

pairs.tendency: A special square sits at some year of the track, so the path across the board becomes a calendar with feast days and hard seasons.
pros: The track works like a calendar.
Squares mark kind and hard seasons.
cons: Landing on one is chance, not planning.
Players may not read squares as seasons.

pairs.tendency: Each year players spend to buy what they need, so costs add up across the span and what is bought early has years to repay itself.
pros: Early buys have years to pay back.
Costs are easy to compare.
cons: Spending in early years hurts later.
Players may save for too long.

pairs.tendency: Each year you share a fixed amount between places, so what you neglect piles up and shows its cost some years later.
pros: Neglect shows up later.
Sharing out is a clear choice.
cons: Early shares are hard to take back.
One year's split gives little to see.

pairs.tendency: A signal ends the year and everyone freezes, so players move at their own pace until the season ends and the slowest is caught.
pros: A signal marks a year clearly.
Players feel the season end.
cons: Signals feel frantic, not slow like years.
Freezing feels like a game, not time.

pairs.tendency: Cards swapped each year let players trade old plans for new ones, so a hand changes with the seasons and shows what each player learned.
pros: A hand changes as years pass.
Players adapt to new conditions.
cons: Swapping can slow every year.
Some players hold on to old cards.

pairs.tendency: The pile grows round after round, and whoever takes it gets every year's leftovers at once, so a long wait pays off in one go.
pros: The pile shows what years left behind.
Taking it feels like a harvest.
cons: One player can gain many years at once.
Waiting can feel like nothing happens.

pairs.tendency: One suit is trump for the hand, so a hand stands for an era when one kind of power rules, and the next hand begins a new era.
pros: Each hand feels like an era.
Trump shows what rules a period.
cons: Eras change on the deal, not by play.
One suit can decide a whole era.

pairs.tendency: Two boards run over the same years, so a gain on one board may cost on the other and a long span holds two stories at once.
pros: Two stories share one span of years.
Gains and losses balance over time.
cons: Two boards double the work each year.
Players lose track of each board's year.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for whatever a year needs, so luck can fill a gap whenever a long run of rounds comes up short.
pros: A wild card fills a hard year.
Surprise breaks up a long run.
cons: Wilds blur what each year was about.
Players may save wilds for a later year.

pairs.tendency: A line that runs off one edge returns at the other, so years can come back round like seasons and the board suggests a cycle.
pros: The board feels like a cycle of seasons.
Years can return.
cons: Joined edges can confuse players.
A cycle can hide the long climb of change.

pairs.tendency: One yes or no answer is given each year, so the secret narrows slowly and a long span of rounds adds up to knowing.
pros: Each year narrows the answer.
Players learn bit by bit.
cons: One answer can feel small for a year.
Long hunts can drag.

pairs.tendency: The race runs across years, so the first to reach the end has lived the fastest lifetime and every round is one step on the road.
pros: Each round marks a year of the race.
The winner is clear.
cons: Speed can crowd out what a year means.
Years can feel the same as turns.

pairs.tendency: Points come in each year, so the final score is the sum of a long span and a player can lead for decades and still fall behind in the last few years.
pros: The score shows a whole span.
Late years can change the result.
cons: Players may chase points, not the years' events.
An early lead can be hard to see.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out one year at a time, so survival is counted in years and the last player left has lived through the most.
pros: Survival feels like years lived.
Knockouts mark time passing.
cons: Players knocked out early sit and wait.
The last years can drag.

pairs.tendency: Players hold out together for a set number of years, so each round survived is a year gained and a shared run of seasons.
pros: Each year survived feels earned.
Players share the span.
cons: Late years can drag if early ones are easy.
One hard year can end it for everyone.

pairs.tendency: All players work towards one aim over the years, so each round is a year closer to it and a late finish shows how long the aim took.
pros: Progress is read year by year.
Everyone shares the long aim.
cons: Years of work may show little.
A single player may steer every year.

pairs.tendency: Each player follows a secret aim across the years, so choices that look random in one round may make sense when the span is looked back on.
pros: Years look different in hindsight.
Secret aims feel like private lives.
cons: Hard to read what each year meant.
Aims can be forgotten across many rounds.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story ends, so each round is a year of that story and the finish comes when the long tale reaches its close.
pros: Years become chapters of a story.
The end is clear when it comes.
cons: A year may be skipped to reach the end.
Players may not agree what each year held.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so years pass with nothing to chase and at the end players look back over what a long stretch left behind.
pros: Players watch the years rather than a score.
Looking back is easy.
cons: Nothing marks a year of progress.
Play may drift.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what counts as a worthwhile life, so the same span of years is judged by different measures at the end.
pros: Players judge their own years.
Many kinds of life fit.
cons: Years are hard to compare between players.
Players may drift without a measure.

pairs.tendency: The game runs year after year until one player loses, so the rest are simply safe and each round survived is a year gained.
pros: Years of safety feel like relief.
The loss is clearly marked.
cons: One player carries the whole loss.
A long run to the end can drag.

pairs.tendency: Years go on for as long as players want to carry on, so the long span becomes the point, like a campaign that runs for years.
pros: Years can run on as long as players want.
A long span feels like a life.
cons: Nothing marks the end of a year.
Play may drift without a finish line.

pairs.tendency: Years pass and nobody can win, so the game holds on to a long span and shows something by refusing the usual finish.
pros: Years show what no win can fix.
Players see time without a prize.
cons: Players may stop caring after a few years.
Years can feel pointless without a goal.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards and each round is a year, so clearing the table is a long task and being stuck is a lost lifetime.
pros: One person sets the pace of the years.
Getting stuck is clear.
cons: A stuck year can end the whole game.
Years against cards can feel empty.

pairs.tendency: Each game is a year or a decade, so a match of several games reads as a history and the winner comes out ahead across many eras.
pros: Many games make a history.
A loss in one era can be recovered.
cons: Each short game has little time.
The winner can be settled early.

pairs.tendency: Every year adds points against you, so the player with the fewest has lost least over a long span and a quiet year counts for something.
pros: Quiet years count for something.
Slow years add up.
cons: Years of loss pile up.
Doing nothing can look like a plan.

pairs.tendency: Landing exactly on the target takes years of steady steps and overshooting costs the win, so players slow down as the end nears.
pros: Careful steps near the end add tension.
Players count years as the end nears.
cons: Years can be wasted missing by one.
The end can drag.

pairs.tendency: Players give things away across the years, so a lifetime of letting go is the aim and the finish is reached by loss, not gain.
pros: Letting go reads as a life's work.
The upside-down aim makes a point.
cons: Players may find the aim confusing.
Years of losing can feel like waste.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays their own years side by side, so each player builds a separate history and comparing them afterwards shows how different years can be.
pros: Each player builds their own history.
Comparing years afterwards is easy.
cons: Years rarely meet.
Little to do while others take their year.

pairs.tendency: Players attack one another each year, so quarrels build into long feuds and a hit in one year is paid back in the years after.
pros: Feuds grow over years.
A hit is paid back later.
cons: Players can be picked on for years.
Fighting can fill every year.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board each year and feel one another's marks later, so a wall built in one year affects the decades after.
pros: Marks on the board last for years.
Players meet through what is left.
cons: Years of building can go unseen by others.
Hard to say who caused what.

pairs.tendency: Everyone shares one team through the years, so a hard year is faced together and the whole span ends in one shared result.
pros: Hard years are faced together.
The span has one shared result.
cons: A strong voice can decide every year.
Quiet players can be left out.

pairs.tendency: Players work together through the years but each has a private reason, so a shared year can hide a quiet advantage that shows later.
pros: Private aims show in hindsight.
Years of trust can wear thin.
cons: Players may doubt each year's choices.
Cooperation can break late.

pairs.tendency: Two teams run through the years against each other, so each round is a year of a long rivalry and teams answer last year's move.
pros: A rivalry builds over years.
Teams answer each other's last year.
cons: Players on the weaker team may give up.
One year can decide for all.

pairs.tendency: A traitor works against the team across the years, so a hard year may have been sabotage and the team looks back to find the turn.
pros: Looking back over years may reveal the traitor.
Trust wears over time.
cons: Every hard year looks like sabotage.
Accusations can end the years early.

pairs.tendency: Letters between far-off players take weeks, so each exchange can stand for a year and the slow post makes the long span feel true.
pros: Slow letters make the years feel real.
Waiting is part of play.
cons: Years take real months to play.
Players may drop out while waiting.

pairs.tendency: A player who is not there still has years, so the table fills in what that person would have done while their years pass unseen.
pros: Absent years can be filled in by stories.
The missing player's years still count.
cons: Their years are guessed, not played.
Players may disagree about what they did.

pairs.tendency: One person describes what each year held, so the master tells the passing of seasons and decides which events fill each round.
pros: A narrator can cover years at once.
Years can be told in a few words.
cons: The master's view shapes every year.
One person carries the whole span.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by join and leave in the middle, so each round of the street game is a year with new faces and the span is made by whoever stops.
pros: New players bring new years.
Anyone can join mid-span.
cons: Long spans do not fit short stops.
Nobody sees all the years.

pairs.tendency: One player faces the rest through the years, so each round is a year of a lone struggle and the pack can wear the single player down.
pros: A lone struggle over years feels heavy.
Years of pressure show the odds.
cons: The single player may tire over many rounds.
The pack can win with little effort.
