cons: Watching dials can break the feeling of being in step.
Players may act for the dial and not for each other.

pairs.tendency: Rolls on a table decide what happens next, and the gauges show how each event has changed the world the story is set in.
pros: Events leave a visible mark.
The story has a measure.
cons: Dice can move the dials without a reason.
Players may lean on the dials, not the story.

pairs.tendency: Everything is open to see and the gauges add a shared reading of the world, so nothing about the state of the system is hidden.
pros: Everyone argues from the same facts.
Easy to talk over what the dials mean.
cons: Little surprise left.
Players can overthink every move.

pairs.tendency: Cards stay secret while the gauges are open to all, so players learn about each other's hands from how the dials move.
pros: The open dials hint at what is held.
A shared reading sits beside private knowledge.
cons: Gauges can give hands away.
Secret and open information mix awkwardly.

pairs.tendency: Roles are secret and the gauges are public, so players guess who is who from how each move shifts the dials.
pros: The dials give evidence about roles.
Suspicion has something to work with.
cons: A gauge can look like proof when it is not.
A reading that points at someone can start an unfair accusation.

pairs.tendency: Players work out a hidden fact and the gauges give them clues, such as which resource is draining and so who is using it.
pros: The dials are a source of clues.
Detective work can follow a reading.
cons: Gauges may give away too much.
Players may ignore clues the dials do not show.

pairs.tendency: Players can lie about what they hold, but the gauges are open, so a claim can be checked against what the dials show.
pros: Open dials keep lies in check.
Players read bluffs against the readings.
cons: Dials can limit what a bluff can claim.
Gauges may make bluffing too risky to try.

pairs.tendency: Players learn a hidden rule by breaking it, and the gauges show the effect of each attempt, so the dials act as part of the answer.
pros: The dials show the rule's effect.
Learning from a reading is quick.
cons: Gauges can give the rule away.
Players may chase the dials, not the rule.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer and can only hint, and the gauges show what the guessing is costing, such as time or tries left.
pros: Guessing gets a visible cost.
The group sees how close it is.
cons: Gauges can give hints that are not meant to be given.
Dials may add pressure on the player who knows.

pairs.tendency: Parts of the map are turned over as players explore, and the gauges show what exploring costs the world, such as supplies spent.
pros: Exploring has a visible cost.
The unknown is measured.
cons: Gauges may move before the map is understood.
A partly hidden map makes dials hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid open while the others stay secret, and the gauges show the open information from another angle, so players reason with two readings.
pros: There is more to work out from open information.
Open hand and dials support each other.
cons: The open hand already shows a lot.
Hidden hands can leave the dials unclear.

pairs.tendency: Some points are secret while the gauges are open, so players can see how the world is doing but not who is ahead.
pros: The open reading is about the world, not rank.
Players guess standings from the dials.
cons: Gauges can leak what the scores hide.
Secret scores and open dials pull attention apart.

pairs.tendency: One player moves at a time, and after each move everyone sees the gauges shift, so every turn has a clear effect on the shared world.
pros: Each move has a visible result.
Easy to follow turn by turn.
cons: Waiting players may only watch the dials.
Slow turns when readings are discussed.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at the same time, and the gauges show the combined effect of all the choices once they are revealed.
pros: The sum of everyone's moves is seen.
No one waits to read the dials.
cons: It is hard to tell whose choice moved a gauge.
The reveal can bring too much change to take in.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment and the gauges move as they do, so the dials show a world that never waits for players to catch up.
pros: The dials keep pace with play.
A lively sense of a world in motion.
cons: Readings can change faster than people can read them.
Quick players may move the dials alone.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so players glance at the gauges and decide in seconds, and the dials give the quickest picture of the world's state.
pros: Dials give a fast read of the state.
The clock adds pressure to the readings.
cons: Little time to study the gauges.
Players may act on a misread dial.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks, so players come back to the gauges each morning and see what time and other people's moves have done.
pros: Slow change is easy to follow.
A reading gives a place to pick up.
cons: Gauges may be left unchanged for long stretches.
Players may forget what the dials last said.

pairs.tendency: Play is slowed on purpose, so players have time to read the gauges and think about what each move has done to the world.
pros: Time to study the dials.
Calm, careful play.
cons: Slow play can leave the dials feeling still.
Some players lose patience.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes and the gauges move faster too, so the dials show a world that is picking up pace and harder to keep up with.
pros: The speeding up is visible.
Players feel pressure rise with the dials.
cons: Gauges can move faster than players read them.
The rush may leave no time to think.

pairs.tendency: Some moves give a player another go at once, and the gauges can swing a long way before anyone else acts, so one player's run is read on the dials.
pros: A long run shows its full effect.
Others see how much one turn changed.
cons: Extra turns can push the dials too far.
The others watch and wait.

pairs.tendency: Play comes in stages and the gauges carry over from one stage to the next, so what players did first shows in how the second stage starts.
pros: Early choices have a visible effect later.
The dials link the stages.
cons: A stage that starts with the dials low may feel hopeless.
Reading the carried gauges takes time.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system and the gauges give its overall state, so each move is shown doing what it would do in real life.
pros: The system's state is easy to read.
Cause and effect show on the dials.
cons: Gauges can seem like a summary of the board.
A single dial can hide the parts behind it.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a real group and the gauges show how the whole system is doing, while each group's own aims can pull against the readings.
pros: Each group's actions show on shared dials.
Players see the system from every side.
cons: One gauge may not fit every group's measure.
Players may only read the dial that suits their role.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws on one limited stock and the gauge shows how much is left, so players watch it fall as each of them takes a share.
pros: The shrinking stock is plain to see.
Everyone can read the same level.
cons: Players may race to take before it runs out.
The gauge can show the limit too late.

pairs.tendency: What players do now shows on the gauges only some rounds later, so a dial may move on a choice that was made long ago.
pros: The delay between act and effect is visible.
Players see the dials catch up.
cons: Players may link a reading to the wrong move.
A calm dial can hide trouble on its way.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on, and the gauges show what the rule has changed, so its effect can be read and not guessed.
pros: A rule's effect can be checked.
Players see the result of their own choice.
cons: Gauges can change for reasons other than the rule.
One round may not be enough to show an effect.

pairs.tendency: After play the gauges give players something to point at, so the talk about what happened can start from the readings and not from memory.
pros: The dials give the talk something to work from.
Players recall what happened and when.
cons: Gauges can narrow talk to what they measure.
A dial may be taken for the whole story.

pairs.tendency: Changes cannot be undone, and the gauges show what has been lost for ever, so a dial that has fallen stays down for the next game.
pros: Permanent loss can be seen.
Players weigh every move against the dials.
cons: Players may freeze up with the dials low.
A ruined reading can leave later games without hope.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world and the gauges show what they reward, so the dials are the argument made visible.
pros: The point of the rules shows in the dials.
Players can see what the game values.
cons: Gauges may argue more loudly than the rules intend.
Players can miss the point if the dials are unclear.

pairs.tendency: Play carries into real life, and the gauges show a shared state that players know will matter afterwards, so each reading is read with care.
pros: Real stakes show on a shared dial.
Players take every reading seriously.
cons: A falling gauge can start a real argument.
Players may feel watched by the dials.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for things like health or kindness, and the gauges show the real things alongside, so players can see where chasing points leaves the world.
pros: The gap between points and values is visible.
Players notice when a number replaces what it measures.
cons: Gauges can also be chased like a score.
The points and dials may confuse players.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, and the gauges show how that world is doing, so each choice is read against the future they are trying out.
pros: The imagined world has a visible state.
Players see how a new way of living holds up.
cons: Gauges can look more exact than a guess about the future.
Players may judge the future by the dials alone.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different amounts, and the gauges show how the whole world is doing, so who is ahead and how the world fares are two different readings.
pros: The world's state is separate from who is winning.
Unequal starts show their effect on the dials.
cons: A single gauge can hide who is carrying the cost.
Poorer players may feel a gauge is blaming them.

pairs.tendency: Whoever is ahead sets the rules, and the gauges show what those rules are doing to everyone else, so the effect of power can be read on the dials.
pros: The effect of rule-making can be seen.
Players can name what their rules cause.
cons: The powerful may ignore a falling gauge.
Others may blame the dials for what the rules did.

pairs.tendency: Each role has its own measure and the gauges show the shared state each one is pulling on, so players see whose goal is moving the dials.
pros: Competing goals show up on shared dials.
Everyone sees the cost of the tug.
cons: One gauge may suit one role's goal.
Players may argue about which dial counts.

pairs.tendency: Play opens on a described situation and the gauges set its starting numbers, so everyone begins with the same picture of how the world stands.
pros: The opening is easy to share.
Players can compare later readings with the start.
cons: The starting numbers may feel set by the writer.
Players may read too much into the first readings.

pairs.tendency: A player argues for a move and the table decides, and the gauges give the table something to judge it by, so a claim can be tested against the dials.
pros: Arguments have evidence to point at.
Players read the effect of a move before agreeing.
cons: Gauges can limit what an argument may claim.
Players may argue about the dials, not the move.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points and players read the gauges together, so each pause starts from what the dials say about the world.
pros: Pauses have a shared reading.
Players notice what changed.
cons: Players may talk about the dials only.
Pauses can break the pace of play.

pairs.tendency: The game is played again with one thing changed, and the gauges give each round a reading that can be set beside the last.
pros: Rounds can be compared on the same dials.
Players see what one change did.
cons: Players may read too much into a single difference.
Gauges can be set back to the start and lost.

pairs.tendency: The game says what it left out, and the gauges show only what is in, so players know the dials leave parts of the real world unmeasured.
pros: Players learn where the dials stop.
Absent things can be talked about.
cons: The dials can still be taken for the whole world.
Players may trust a gauge more than the game's own warning.

pairs.tendency: The people whose situation is modelled helped choose what the gauges show, so the dials measure things those people say matter.
pros: The dials reflect what matters to them.
Players can check readings against real lives.
cons: The people may disagree about what to measure.
A dial may hide what some of them care about.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a link in a chain and the gauges show the state of the whole chain, such as stock held and orders waiting, which no single link sees.
pros: The whole chain can be read.
Players see how one link's choice reaches the others.
cons: Seeing the whole chain removes what each link would not know.
Many gauges for many links.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own stock and orders, while the gauges show the whole system, so the open dials cut across what each player cannot see.
pros: Players compare their corner with the whole.
A gauge can show where a guess was wrong.
cons: Gauges can remove the point of seeing a corner only.
Players may rely on the dials and stop guessing.

pairs.tendency: The gauges show where work is piling up, so the slowest step stands out and players see that speeding up elsewhere changes nothing.
pros: The bottleneck shows itself on the dials.
Players see why faster steps do not help.
cons: A pile-up can show before anyone has found the cause.
Players may blame the wrong step.

pairs.tendency: Gauges show stock waiting and orders arriving, so players can see goods pushed ahead piling up or orders pulling goods only as asked.
pros: The effect of making ahead is visible.
Players feel the difference between push and pull.
cons: Gauges can show a pile only after it has formed.
Both ways need several dials to read.

pairs.tendency: Gauges show waiting time and stock as players choose big or small batches, so the cost of a batch size appears on the dials.
pros: Choices of batch size show their costs.
Players see waiting and set-up traded off.
cons: Players may read the dials for a single round only.
The dials can look the same for different batch sizes.

pairs.tendency: A breakdown shows at once on the gauges as output falls and queues grow, so players see how much one failed machine does to the whole line.
pros: A breakdown's cost is easy to see.
Plans that assume nothing breaks are exposed.
cons: Gauges can fall for no cause players chose.
Repairs can take attention from other dials.

pairs.tendency: Gauges show stock held and orders missed side by side, so players see both costs and can tell when they have tipped too far toward either.
pros: Both costs can be read together.
Players see the balance as it shifts.
cons: Two dials moving opposite ways can confuse.
Players may fix one dial and ignore the other.

pairs.tendency: Players roll and move from different starting spaces or with different purses, so the same roll takes a lucky-born player further than a poor one.
pros: Dice make the gap feel like fate.
Easy to explain at the table.
cons: Behind players can only wait for rolls.
Luck and the head start blur together.

pairs.tendency: Players pick cards from the passed hand while starting with different stocks, so a richer player can afford the strong picks and a poorer one takes what is left.
pros: Picks show what a head start buys.
Everyone sees the same cards go round.
cons: Poor players may only get leftovers.
Early picks can lock in the lead.

pairs.tendency: Players bid from purses of different sizes, so the richest can outbid anyone on the first lot and the others learn to pick their fights.
pros: Prices show what money buys.
Poor players bid for cheap things cleverly.
cons: Rich players win the early auctions easily.
Poor players may stop bidding altogether.

pairs.tendency: A player with a big cushion can risk another throw and survive a bust, while a player with little cannot afford to push at all.
pros: Risk means different things to different players.
Tense decisions for the poor.
cons: Poor players cannot take the risks that pay.
Rich players lose little by busting.

pairs.tendency: Players start holding different amounts of the map, so some begin with whole regions and others with a single square to defend.
pros: The map shows who began with what.
Small holders play scrappily.
cons: Large holders can sit and wait.
Early fights lean towards those already ahead.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with different numbers of workers, so some fill many jobs a turn while others wait for the spaces that remain.
pros: Missing workers are easy to see.
Small players have to choose jobs carefully.
cons: Big players take the useful spaces first.
Players with few workers may feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: Players build patterns from different starting piles of tiles, so some have colours to hand while others have to build around what they were given.
pros: Each player works with their own limits.
Building patterns stays calm.
cons: Tile piles decide the first shapes.
Poor players may never catch up.

pairs.tendency: Players are dealt hands of different strength or size, so one holds many options and another have to save every card for the right moment.
pros: Small hands make timing matter.
Players see what a full hand allows.
cons: Big hands give far more choices.
Small hands leave little to plan.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different hands or points, so a player already ahead needs few tricks while a player behind have to win nearly all of them.
pros: Targets differ for each player.
Trailing players take risks.
cons: Leaders can play safe and slow.
The trailing player's hand may simply be weak.

pairs.tendency: Players with more at the start have more to trade, while poorer players bring promises and need what the others hold.
pros: Deals show who needs whom.
Poor players find ways to matter.
cons: Rich players can dictate terms.
Weak players may be talked into poor deals.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different sets already in hand, so some are one card from scoring while others have nothing matching at all.
pros: Head starts are easy to count.
Poor players aim for cheap sets.
cons: Leaders finish sets in a few turns.
Late sets rarely catch the early ones.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of tiles already placed, so some begin with a village and a road while others hold an empty corner.
pros: The shared map shows the head start.
Late players choose their spot freely.
cons: Early players shape the whole map.
Poor corners can stay poor.

pairs.tendency: Players answer each other in turn, but some begin with a longer line or a stronger reply to hand, so the exchange leans towards them.
pros: Each voice sounds different.
Answers can be shaped by the head start.
cons: The chain can tilt to one player.
Players with less to say may fall quiet.

pairs.tendency: Players cannot talk about who started with more, so the gap shows only in what each can afford to play and when.
pros: The gap is felt, not argued.
Players read each other's means from play.
cons: No way to protest the unfairness.
Resentment may build unspoken.

pairs.tendency: Players change the rules while starting from different places, so those with more can write rules that keep their lead and the others try to rewrite them.
pros: Rules become a tool for the unequal.
Players learn how rules favour someone.
cons: Rich players can lock in the head start.
Rule fights may swallow the game.

pairs.tendency: Each character begins with different wealth, family or contacts, and players act those differences out, from the person who is let in to the one kept waiting.
pros: Characters feel like real people.
Players see how doors open or stay shut.
cons: Playing a poor role can feel uncomfortable.
Rich roles may have less to do.

pairs.tendency: Players flick or stack with the same hands but start with different scores or advantages, so skill has to make up a gap set before play.
pros: Skill can close a gap.
Everyone can see what is owed.
cons: Poor players may feel the gap is too big.
A steady hand cannot fix a large head start.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map but begin with different amounts of it, so one holds the richest land while another is handed a margin.
pros: The map keeps the start visible.
Poor players can draw their way out.
cons: Rich players draw the richest parts first.
Those left a corner may lose interest.

pairs.tendency: Players ask for cards while starting with different hand sizes, so a player with many cards is asked often and one with few is rarely worth asking.
pros: Questions show who holds most.
Small hands are hard to read.
cons: Big hands give away information.
Small hands may rarely get a turn that matters.

pairs.tendency: Players place bets from purses of different sizes, so big players stake a lot and small players can only stay in with small bets.
pros: Odds feel different to each player.
Small bets last longer.
cons: Big purses absorb many losses.
Poor players can be wiped out in one throw.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on a throw while holding different amounts, so the same coin flip is a small matter for one and a ruin for another.
pros: One throw shows the gap clearly.
Risk feels different for each person.
cons: Rich players can bet and lose without worry.
Poor players are pushed out fast.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on hidden hands from stacks of different size, so a big stack can raise just to push a small one out.
pros: Pressure comes from the stack, not the cards.
Bluffing becomes a tool for the poor.
cons: Big stacks can bully.
Short stacks may fold for most of the game.

pairs.tendency: Players build their own sides from different budgets or collections, so some arrive with strong armies and others with what they could afford.
pros: The gap appears before play starts.
Choices show what each can afford.
cons: Poor sides may look weak from the start.
Building can matter more than playing.

pairs.tendency: Players call contracts from different starting positions, so a leading player can call a small safe one while a trailing player have to call a hard one.
pros: Calls show how each player sees their chances.
Behind players have a reason to dare.
cons: Leaders can coast on safe calls.
Hard calls often fail.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of pieces, and every capture changes sides, so a big army can grow while a small one is eaten and turned.
pros: The gap can grow or close quickly.
Small armies can still surprise.
cons: Big armies snowball.
Early losses may end a small player's game.

pairs.tendency: Teams start with different numbers of players or head starts, so a short team is jailed fast and has few free members left to rescue anyone.
pros: Teamwork matters more for the small team.
Rescues feel dramatic.
cons: Short teams may be jailed in minutes.
Players in jail wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of stones already on the board, so one side begins with more territory and the other has to find gaps.
pros: Small players look for gaps.
Territory is easy to see.
cons: Large sides can surround quickly.
Small players run out of room.

pairs.tendency: The game starts players unevenly, then gives those behind extra moves or cards, so the gap may close or may only slow down.
pros: Players behind keep hope.
The gap itself becomes a talking point.
cons: Help can cancel out the started gap.
Leaders may feel punished for what they were given.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal and the dice decide everything after, so the head start is the only thing that is not luck.
pros: The gap is the only real difference.
Nobody can blame choices.
cons: Players cannot act on their position.
The start may seem pointless.

pairs.tendency: Players have different head starts or speeds when the chase begins, so some are already far from It while others stand close.
pros: Everyone sees the unfair start.
Fast play and loud laughter.
cons: Close players are caught at once.
Caught players may drop out early.

pairs.tendency: Players pick whom to hit or help while starting at different levels, so the weak are tempting to attack and the strong become targets of the others.
pros: Targets show who the table fears.
Alliances form against the leader.
cons: Weak players get picked on.
Players may gang up on the richest.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with different stones already placed, so one side starts with a chain half built while the other have to cut it or build elsewhere.
pros: A head start is clear on the board.
Players learn to block as well as build.
cons: The side with more stones is nearly there.
The other side may have too few moves left.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, but players start with different numbers of each choice, so a player short of one type is open to attack.
pros: Stocks of each choice matter.
Players guess which kind others hold.
cons: A larger stock breaks the cycle.
Players with fewer kinds are predictable.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different hands, so some can declare a pair or a run in the first turn while others hold scattered cards.
pros: Early declarations show the head start.
Poor hands find smaller scores.
cons: Strong hands score again and again.
Weak hands may never declare anything.

pairs.tendency: Players already have different powers, and now start with different amounts as well, so the powers add to the head start or soften it.
pros: Two kinds of difference show up together.
Players find how the differences combine.
cons: It is hard to tell which gap matters.
Too many differences may confuse players.

pairs.tendency: One player offers to double while the other starts with less, so the poorer player cannot afford to accept and gives up the game.
pros: Doubling shows who can bear a loss.
Cautious play for the poorer player.
cons: The richer player can double to bully.
Poor players give up before the game is played.

pairs.tendency: Players have to capture when they can, and starting with more pieces means more captures forced on the smaller side, who may be drawn into traps.
pros: Forced moves show a gap in options.
The weaker side can set traps.
cons: The smaller side has fewer free choices.
The larger side wins by forcing.

pairs.tendency: Characters start at different strength and grow with play, so a stronger one meets later tests easily and a weaker one has to climb.
pros: Growth lets the weak catch up in time.
Players feel progress.
cons: The strong grow faster than the weak.
Weak characters may fail early tests.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different amounts to remember, such as a few items against a long list, so some recite a lot on the first turn while others begin easily.
pros: Memory is a head start too.
Early rounds are easy for some.
cons: A long list is hard from the start.
Players lose track at different points.

pairs.tendency: A handicap tries to even out what the unequal start would give, so players can compare a game that adjusts the gap with one that leaves it.
pros: Players see both ways side by side.
Fairness becomes a choice.
cons: A handicap can cancel the lesson of the gap.
Players may argue about the right amount.

pairs.tendency: Players hide and seek with different head starts or numbers of helpers, so some searchers cover many places while others cover few.
pros: Unequal numbers show quickly.
Hiders feel clever.
cons: A large search team finds fast.
The small team may give up early.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of pieces, and a hop needs gaps, so a crowded side blocks itself while a small side finds room.
pros: Gaps and crowding are easy to see.
Small armies can hop through.
cons: Large sides can run out of space.
The gap can reverse in a few moves.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of dice or rerolls, so some reroll three times and others only once.
pros: The difference is easy to count.
Fewer dice make each roll count.
cons: More rerolls smooth out poor luck.
Players with few dice cannot fix a poor throw.

pairs.tendency: Players start from different places along the track, and a landing sends a piece back, so those far ahead have more to lose from each hit.
pros: Leaders fear the pack behind them.
Those behind can bring a leader down.
cons: Leaders can be sent home by one throw.
Pieces far back have little to lose or gain.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different pieces on the board, so one has a row half done and takes a piece quickly while the other breaks rows apart.
pros: Defence matters as much as building.
The head start is easy to read.
cons: Pieces taken early are hard to replace.
The side with fewer pieces falls behind.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with different letters in hand, so one holds useful vowels and another holds a mix of awkward letters.
pros: Words show who got what.
Players with few letters invent short words.
cons: Hard letters leave little to play.
A word list cannot fix a poor draw.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different tiles to match the open ends, so some always have a tile to play and others pass again and again.
pros: Passing shows who was short.
Tile counts are simple to read.
cons: Players with few matches may miss many turns.
A poor starting hand can last the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different cards, so one lays a set on the first turn and others wait for the cards they need, adding to sets already down.
pros: Players can add to the sets of others.
Early melds are easy to see.
cons: A strong hand melds fast.
Players left behind are only adding to sets.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of one-use powers, so some have many chances to turn a game and others have only one.
pros: Spending a power is a clear moment.
Players with few powers think hard before using one.
cons: Players with many powers can spend them freely.
Powers run out for those who had few.

pairs.tendency: One player offers a move and the other can refuse, and position changes what each can afford to turn down or accept.
pros: Players see how position shapes choice.
The weaker player can still say no.
cons: A poor player may have to accept.
Refusing can cost more than accepting.

pairs.tendency: Players start in different places in the chain, so a person near the start has more say over a message than a person at the end.
pros: Position in the chain changes what you hear.
Messages show who stands where.
cons: The end of the line hears the shakiest version.
Players may feel blamed for changes.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards to others before play while starting with unequal hands, so a rich hand can pass the weakest cards and a poor hand can spare little.
pros: Gifts show what each can afford.
Poor players choose carefully.
cons: Players with little cannot spare any.
A rich hand can pass its junk.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the start and the other picks a side, so the setter tries to even out the very gap this block creates.
pros: The setter learns what fair looks like.
Chooser and setter both think hard.
cons: An uneven start is hard to cut evenly.
Players may argue whether it is even.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different pieces, so one is already close to the far end and a promotion while the other is far back and has to travel.
pros: Distance to the end is easy to see.
Those behind can still push forward.
cons: Players near the end promote quickly.
Players far back may never promote.

pairs.tendency: Teams start with different head starts or numbers of runners, so one team begins a leg ahead and the others have to make it up in their own legs.
pros: Everyone can see the gap on the course.
Teams can plan who runs when.
cons: Teams behind may lose heart.
A short team runs more legs each.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of stones, so one side can quickly make a safe shape while the other has too few stones to make one.
pros: Safe shapes show what a head start buys.
A small side aims for one safe corner.
cons: The bigger side builds many safe shapes.
The smaller side may never make one.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different scoring cards or points, so the prizes named in advance are already closer to some players than to others.
pros: Prizes show the head start.
Plans form around the named cards.
cons: Early holders keep the strongest prizes.
Players with no prize card have little to chase.

pairs.tendency: Shared cards in the middle are the same for everyone, but players hold different hands, so the same middle helps a rich hand far more than a poor one.
pros: The middle is fair; the hands are not.
Players see how a head start combines.
cons: Some hands gain a lot from the middle.
Weak hands gain little.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different amounts and all pay into one pot, so the same ante is a small cost to one and a large share of everything to another.
pros: The same payment feels different.
A big pot tempts the poor.
cons: Poor players give up a large share.
Rich players can pay and not notice.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of seeds in their pits, so one has many to sow in long moves while another has few and short ones.
pros: Seed counts show the gap at once.
Small pits move quickly.
cons: Big pits allow long captures.
A pit with few seeds is emptied fast.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand is dealt in the middle and one player may take it, so a player with a weak start may grab it to catch up.
pros: The spare hand can level things.
Choosing to take it is a real decision.
cons: Richer players may buy it too.
Taking it may just widen the gap.

pairs.tendency: Players start at different points on a track with special squares, so those ahead meet safe and sending-back squares sooner than those behind.
pros: Squares show who meets them first.
Behind players know what lies ahead.
cons: Leaders may land on a poor square early.
The track decides more than the start.

pairs.tendency: Everything has a price in the game and players start with different amounts, so one can buy the strong items and another can only afford cheap ones.
pros: Prices show what money buys.
Poor players find cheap tricks.
cons: Rich players buy their way ahead.
Poor players may never afford the strongest items.

pairs.tendency: Players share out different totals between places, so one has plenty to spread and another has to choose which places to leave empty.
pros: Small totals make hard choices.
Spreading shows what each player values.
cons: Large totals cover everywhere.
Small totals leave places unguarded.

pairs.tendency: Players start nearer or further from safety when the signal comes, so some are in reach of a seat and others are far from one.
pros: The unfair start is quick to feel.
Everyone is moving and laughing.
cons: Those far from safety lose often.
Players out early wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different hands and may swap cards for new ones, so a poor hand swaps often while a rich hand keeps what it has.
pros: Swapping gives the poor a way up.
Players choose what to give up.
cons: Swaps use turns that the rich can spend elsewhere.
Poor hands may stay poor after swapping.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different hand sizes and may take the discard pile, so a player with few cards finds a big pile heavy and a full hand takes it easily.
pros: The pile shows how much each can carry.
Big piles bring big risks.
cons: A full hand can take any pile.
A small hand can be buried.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of trump cards, so one holds many winners in the named suit and another holds only low cards.
pros: Trump counts show the head start.
Players with few trumps play sneakily.
cons: One strong suit can decide the hand.
Players without trumps lose most tricks.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal on one board and may be even on the other, so a gap in one game can be traded for an edge in the other.
pros: Trade-offs between boards appear.
Players see the head start from two sides.
cons: Two boards are hard to follow.
A weak player may lose on both.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of wild cards, so one can finish any set while another has only fixed cards in hand.
pros: Wild cards show what flexibility is worth.
A single wild can close a gap.
cons: Players with many wilds finish sets easily.
Players with none are stuck with what they hold.

pairs.tendency: Players start at different spots on a board whose edges join, so nobody is truly in a corner, but some still sit closer to the action.
pros: No one is stuck at an edge.
Distance is easier to judge.
cons: The wrap can confuse a new player.
The unequal start can still hold.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different clues or numbers of questions, so one begins knowing half the answer while another begins knowing nothing.
pros: Knowledge is a head start.
Questions show what each already knows.
cons: Players with clues finish fast.
Players with none may ask too many questions.

pairs.tendency: Players start at different distances from the finish, so a race is already partly decided and the players behind have to find a faster route.
pros: The head start is a visible gap.
Players behind take risks.
cons: Players ahead can walk it.
Races may feel fixed before they begin.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different scores, so those with a lead need less to win and those behind have to score more in every turn.
pros: The gap is a single number.
Trailing players have a clear target.
cons: Leaders can play safe.
A big lead can end hope early.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different numbers of lives or pieces, so the poorest are knocked out first and the richest outlast the others.
pros: Survival depends on the start.
Players form alliances against the strong.
cons: Weak players leave early.
Players out of the game have to wait.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with different supplies but win or lose together, so the rich have to decide whether to share with the poor or lose with them.
pros: Sharing becomes a clear choice.
Everyone feels the gap together.
cons: The group may lean on the player with most.
Players with little may feel they are a burden.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different resources and work to one goal, so each gives what they can and the gap shows in who carries most.
pros: The gap becomes a plan.
Each player brings something different.
cons: Players with more may do all the work.
Players with less may be left out of decisions.

pairs.tendency: Players start with unequal means and each hides a private goal, so nobody knows whether a poor player is really behind or aiming somewhere else.
pros: Hidden goals muddy the gap.
Players guess at each other's aims.
cons: Hard to tell a head start from a trick.
The poor may be suspected unfairly.

pairs.tendency: Characters begin with different amounts in a story, and play ends when the story does, so the gap shapes who gets the big scenes.
pros: The story grows out of the gap.
Players see who gets to act.
cons: Rich characters take the main scenes.
Poor characters may have thin parts.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal but nobody wins, so the gap can be looked at and talked about without anyone racing to close it.
pros: The gap is easy to discuss.
Players notice it without pressure.
cons: Nothing pushes anyone to change it.
The gap may go unremarked.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different means and each decides what doing well means, so a poor player may count a small gain as a success.
pros: Players define their own measure.
The gap matters less than the aim.
cons: Players may pick goals that excuse the gap.
Nobody agrees on who was ahead.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal and the game goes on until someone loses, so the poorest are the likely loser and everyone else tries to stay out of that place.
pros: Everyone feels the loser's seat.
Players ahead watch the one behind.
cons: The poor player may lose from the start.
Nobody has to win, so the leaders can coast.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal but the aim is to keep playing, so those with more may prop up those with less to stop the game ending.
pros: Sharing is part of the point.
The gap is something to manage together.
cons: Those with more carry the load.
Players with less may feel looked after.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal in a game that cannot be won, so the gap has no prize at the end and is felt only as a different way of being stuck.
pros: The gap stands out without a prize.
Players ask what the start is for.
cons: Players may see no reason to care.
Poor players may find it unfair for nothing.

pairs.tendency: One player works against the cards and starts with a fixed layout that may be easier or harder than another's, so the same effort gives different outcomes.
pros: A hard layout is a gap you can see.
Different layouts can be compared.
cons: Some layouts cannot be cleared.
A lost game may say little about the player.

pairs.tendency: Players play several games with unequal starts, so the poor in one game may be rich in the next, and wins are counted across them.
pros: Starts can be swapped between games.
Players see the gap from both sides.
cons: A poor start can cost early games.
Leaders may stop trying once safe.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different scores and the lowest wins, so a player who starts with few points is already near winning and others have to avoid every point.
pros: Lead and trail are reversed.
Everyone avoids points.
cons: A low start is a real head start.
Players with many points may give up.

pairs.tendency: Players start at different distances from the exact target, so a player close to it can wait for the right roll while another have to travel.
pros: Near players have to stop and wait.
Far players have time to plan.
cons: Near players may miss the number again and again.
The exact number can make the head start worthless.

pairs.tendency: Players aim to lose while starting unequal, so those who begin with the most have the most to give away and the poor have little to lose.
pros: The gap runs the other way.
Players have to rethink what rich means.
cons: Rich players may be slow to lose anything.
Poor players have almost nothing to give up.

pairs.tendency: Players build their own things side by side from different starting piles, and nothing one does touches another, so the gap stays exactly as it began.
pros: The unfair start is plain to see.
Players cannot blame each other.
cons: Nobody can close the gap by playing.
Poor players watch the rich player's tableau grow.

pairs.tendency: Players attack and steal from each other while starting unequal, so the strong pick on the weak or the weak team up against the strong.
pros: Fights show who is vulnerable.
Teaming up against a leader is easy.
cons: Poor players are attacked first.
A big gap can end the fight early.

pairs.tendency: Players act on the board rather than on each other, so a head start shows up as spaces taken and the poor feel it as less room.
pros: Position is easy to see on the board.
Nobody has to attack to win.
cons: Poor players are crowded out quietly.
The rich can wall off the board.

pairs.tendency: Players work together against the game from unequal starts, so the strong carry more and the weak need help for the group to win.
pros: The gap becomes a shared problem.
Players learn to share fairly.
cons: Strong players can take over.
A weak start may be blamed on a person.

pairs.tendency: Players work together but each has a private reason to win more, so the rich can help and stay ahead while the poor choose between helping and catching up.
pros: Cooperation tests who gives up what.
The gap shapes every deal.
cons: Those ahead may help only a little.
Trust can break when the poor fall behind.

pairs.tendency: Teams start with different resources or numbers, so one team is stronger from the first turn and the other has to make up for it with teamwork.
pros: Teammates can plan for the gap.
Teams can see each other's strength.
cons: A weaker team may feel beaten before play.
One team may have to carry its weakest member.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal while one is a secret traitor, so a rich player who helps the group may be suspected and a poor player who fails may be suspected too.
pros: Suspicion falls on the odd one out.
The gap gives a traitor cover.
cons: Players may accuse the unlucky.
A poor start can look like sabotage.

pairs.tendency: Players far apart play by letter from unequal starts, so a player with more can send more letters and a player with less waits for each reply.
pros: Waiting shows the gap.
The slow pace gives time to think.
cons: Poor players fall behind over weeks.
Letters can be lost or delayed.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table and starts with a fixed position, so the gap between them and the others cannot be argued over or changed.
pros: The absent player's start stays put.
Players work around a fixed position.
cons: Nobody can speak for the absent player.
The unequal start may seem arbitrary.

pairs.tendency: A game master describes the world and decides how the starting gap matters, so a rich character is let through doors a poor one has to knock on.
pros: Players feel what unequal starts are like.
Stories respond to wealth.
cons: The game master may tilt things by accident.
Players may feel the world is set against them.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a public place and passers-by join with whatever they bring, so players start with different skill, numbers and kit.
pros: Anyone can join as they are.
Unequal start is a normal part of play.
cons: Late joiners start at a disadvantage.
Regulars may dominate newcomers.

pairs.tendency: One player faces the rest and starts with more or less than the others, so the lone player may hold a large stock to match the group's numbers.
pros: The gap sits between sides, not people.
Lone players have a reason to be clever.
cons: Many players may still outweigh one.
Fair stock for one against many is argued over.

pairs.tendency: One player plays alone from a start that may be easy or hard, so the gap is between the player's luck and the game's draw rather than between people.
pros: The start can be compared with others later.
Nobody is blamed for the gap.
cons: A hard start feels like poor luck.
No other player to share the gap with.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most things, and players start unequal, so the head start is quickly drowned out or confirmed by luck.
pros: Luck can shake up the order.
Everyone has some hope.
cons: The start may seem to matter little.
Players cannot learn why they lost.

pairs.tendency: Players start unequal and have ways to soften poor luck, so a rich player can buy re-rolls while a poor player lives with the dice.
pros: Re-rolls show what money buys.
Poor players keep a few small tools.
cons: Rich players can fix almost any roll.
Tools may matter more than the dice.

pairs.tendency: Choices matter most and a little luck is added, so the unequal start is the main thing a skilled player has to overcome, with some help from luck.
pros: Skill can still pay off.
A little luck keeps hope alive.
cons: A big gap may be too hard to overcome.
A skilled poor player may feel cheated.

pairs.tendency: Nothing is left to dice, so the starting gap decides a lot and the less well placed player needs careful choices to close it.
pros: Close results come from skill alone.
The gap is clear and traceable.
cons: There is no luck to rescue a poor start.
A strong head start is hard to overturn.

pairs.tendency: Dice are read as signs while players start unequal, so a rich player may read a useful omen and a poor player a poor one from the same throw.
pros: Signs mean different things to each player.
Players talk about what a throw means.
cons: Signs may seem to justify the gap.
Players may read unfair luck as destiny.

pairs.tendency: Players try to sense each other's moves while starting unequal, so the stronger placed can afford to wait and the others have to guess when to act.
pros: Players watch each other closely.
The gap does not stop timing.
cons: Players with less may act too soon.
The gap is hard to see without numbers.

pairs.tendency: A table says what happens from each roll, and the unequal start changes which rows suit whom, so a rich character meets helpers and a poor one meets hard ones.
pros: Rolls feel linked to position.
The story reflects the start.
cons: Poor characters may get all the hard rows.
Rich characters rarely meet trouble.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sees everything, including who started with more, so the gap is out in the open and every player can plan against it.
pros: Nobody can hide the gap.
Players plan with the same facts.
cons: Poor players see exactly how far behind they are.
Nothing is left to hope for.

pairs.tendency: Players hold hidden cards from unequal starts, so nobody can tell how big the gap is and each has to guess from how the others play.
pros: Guessing replaces counting.
Bluffing can hide a poor hand.
cons: Players may overestimate the gap.
A strong hand looks like a bluff.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles and unequal starts, so a rich player may be taken for a leader and a poor one for a helper, whatever their real roles.
pros: Wealth is a clue and a disguise.
Players read each other's starting means.
cons: The gap can mislead the whole table.
Players may accuse the poor unfairly.

pairs.tendency: Players use clues to find hidden facts while starting with unequal clues, so one begins with half the answer and another with nothing.
pros: Clues are a head start.
Everyone works from different facts.
cons: A rich clue stock finishes first.
Players with few clues may feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: Players lie about what they hold from unequal starts, so a poor player may bluff to look rich and a rich one may play poor.
pros: The gap is something to pretend about.
Bluffing gives the poor a weapon.
cons: Rich players can bluff with little to lose.
Players may stop trusting any show of strength.

pairs.tendency: Newcomers learn the secret rules by being told no, so those who already knew the rules begin ahead of those who did not, on top of any gap in stock.
pros: Knowing the rules is a head start.
Players feel the gap in knowledge.
cons: Newcomers face two gaps at once.
Players may feel the game is a trap.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer and may only hint, and unequal starts mean the others begin with different guesses, so some are nearer the answer.
pros: Hints reach players differently.
Players with more clues can help others.
cons: Poor players may never get a hint they follow.
The hinting player may not know who is behind.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over as it is explored, so players start unequal and what they find is unequal too, with some landing on rich ground and some on bare.
pros: Exploring shows who is lucky.
Nobody knows the gap at first.
cons: A poor start may reveal poor land.
Early finds can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up while the others are secret, and players start unequal, so the open hand shows the gap and the hidden hands guess at it.
pros: The open hand makes the gap plain.
Players compare it with their own.
cons: Hidden hands can hide a larger gap.
The open hand may give away too much.

pairs.tendency: Players keep part of their points or money secret while starting unequal, so nobody knows who truly began ahead and everyone guesses.
pros: The gap is a rumour.
Players watch for signs.
cons: A poor player may be treated as rich.
Players may feel cheated when scores come out.

pairs.tendency: Players go one at a time from unequal starts, so each turn shows what a player's position lets them do while the others wait and watch.
pros: Each turn shows the gap.
Players plan for their own turn.
cons: Poor players wait to act.
Rich players use every turn well.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret at the same moment from unequal positions, so the rich act freely and the poor are forced to commit before seeing others.
pros: Players choose at the same time.
Nobody waits for their turn.
cons: Poor players may be forced to choose blind.
The gap decides many choices at once.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns and players start unequal, so the quick and the well placed take the strongest things first and the slow take what is left.
pros: Speed and position both count.
The gap shows in who reaches things first.
cons: Quick players can ignore the gap.
Slow, poor players may get nothing.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock and players start unequal, so a player with many options runs out of time choosing while a player with few decides fast.
pros: Few options save time.
The clock hurries everyone.
cons: Rich players may waste time on many choices.
Poor players may run out of moves.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks and players start unequal, so a small head start can grow over many mornings.
pros: The gap has time to widen.
Players can see the change.
cons: A long wait may feel unfair for the poor.
Players may lose interest before it matters.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose while they start unequal, so there is time to notice the gap and sit with it before making a move.
pros: Players have time to look at the gap.
Slow play makes the gap feel real.
cons: The wait can feel long for the poor.
The pause may make the unfairness feel heavier.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes and players start unequal, so the gap has less time to close and the head start is carried to the end.
pros: The head start matters more.
A hurried finish stays clear.
cons: Poor players have little time to catch up.
Leaders can run out the clock.

pairs.tendency: Some throws give another go while players start unequal, so a lucky rich player can pull far ahead and the poor have to depend on extra turns to catch up.
pros: Extra turns are a way to catch up.
Lucky streaks are exciting.
cons: A rich player with extra turns can win fast.
Poor players need a lot of luck.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, and the unequal start carries from the first stage into the second, so a head start from early choices shapes what players can do later.
pros: Early choices matter later.
Players can see the gap grow.
cons: A poor first stage hurts the whole game.
The second stage may feel decided.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system, such as a village's wells, and players start with unequal shares, so the gap shows how the real system treats people.
pros: A real gap is easy to recognise.
The system shows why the gap holds.
cons: The system can look unfair by design.
Players may blame the game for the gap.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a real group, such as landowners or tenants, and the groups start with unequal means, so players see the problem from very different positions.
pros: Players feel what each group has.
Roles make the gap understandable.
cons: Players in poor roles may feel stuck.
Rich roles may feel they have nothing to solve.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited thing, such as the water under a village, and players start with unequal access, so the poor are first to see it run dry.
pros: The gap shows who feels scarcity first.
Players see how access differs.
cons: Poor players have less to take.
Rich players may drain it for everyone.

pairs.tendency: A head start from the first round may only show its effect a few rounds later, so a small gap at the start has grown by the time players notice.
pros: Players see the gap grow over time.
Early choices have lasting effects.
cons: Players may blame the wrong round.
Poor players may notice too late.

pairs.tendency: Players test a new rule on unequal starts, so one rule may help the poor and hurt the rich, and the game shows how a rule treats each position.
pros: A rule's effect is easy to see.
Players can change it and compare.
cons: A rule that suits one position may hurt another.
Players may vote by their own position.

pairs.tendency: After play, everyone talks about the unequal start, what it gave and what it took, and how it is like the real problem.
pros: The talk can name the gap.
Players say how each position felt.
cons: Players with more may feel blamed.
Players with less may find it hard to speak.

pairs.tendency: Changes in play stay permanently and the start was unequal, so the gap passes to the next game and the poor start the next one poor.
pros: Players see a gap carry forward.
Nothing can be quietly undone.
cons: A poor start may be locked in.
Players may lose hope after one game.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and unequal starts are part of it, so the game says that where you start shapes where you end.
pros: The unfairness is part of the message.
Players see the argument at work.
cons: Players may think the game is simply unfair.
The point is missed if the start looks random.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the game carries into real life, and players start unequal, so a real gap in money or standing may be felt as a game one.
pros: The gap is taken seriously.
Players think hard about fairness.
cons: A real disadvantage can sting.
Players may feel pressed to agree to unequal terms.

pairs.tendency: The game turns things that matter into points while players start unequal, so those with more points may seem to have more worth.
pros: Players see how numbers shape worth.
The gap can be talked about as a value.
cons: Points may seem to rank people.
Players may chase points and forget the values.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future that does not exist yet, such as a village sharing everything, from unequal starts, so they find out what happens to the gap there.
pros: Players see if the gap stays or fades.
A new way of living can be tried.
cons: The old gap may come back unnoticed.
Rich players may resist sharing.

pairs.tendency: Whoever is ahead writes the rules, and the unequal start decides who that is, so the head start becomes the power to keep it.
pros: Power and wealth show up together.
Players feel how rules are made.
cons: Rules can lock in the gap.
The poor follow rules they did not write.

pairs.tendency: Each role wins by its own measure and starts with unequal means, so the strong can reach their goal while the weak have to bargain to reach theirs.
pros: Goals and means pull in different ways.
Players know everyone's aim.
cons: The well placed can reach their goals alone.
Weak roles may never reach theirs.

pairs.tendency: Play opens on a described situation, and the unequal start is part of that description, so every player reads who has what before the first move.
pros: The start is stated and clear.
Players understand the gap from the first turn.
cons: A long description can slow the start.
Players may argue about whether it is fair.

pairs.tendency: A player explains why a move would work and the table decides, and the unequal start changes how easily each player is believed.
pros: Players talk about how position changes belief.
Moves can be creative.
cons: The rich may be believed more often.
A poor player's strongest argument may be ignored.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points so players can say what they notice, and the unequal start gives them something to say after the first rounds.
pros: The gap is named while play goes on.
Players can change their play.
cons: Pauses may break the mood.
Players with less may not want to speak.

pairs.tendency: The same game is played again with the start changed, so players can compare how the same people do from rich and poor positions.
pros: Players see what the start did.
Switching places makes the gap personal.
cons: Players may remember the first game and play differently.
The comparison may not be fair if skill grows.

pairs.tendency: The game tells players what it left out of the real situation, so they know the unequal start is only part of how real unfairness works.
pros: Players know where the game stops being true.
The gap is not mistaken for the story.
cons: The list of omissions can be long.
Players may fix on what is left out.

pairs.tendency: The people whose situation the game models help design the start, so the gap matches what they actually live with rather than a guess.
pros: The gap rings true to them.
Players trust the numbers more.
cons: The designers may disagree on the real gap.
Others may find the real gap hard to play.

pairs.tendency: Each link in the chain starts with different stock or money, so a maker with a full store ships easily while a shop with an empty one waits for orders.
pros: Players see how stock moves along the chain.
One link's start shapes the others.
cons: A poor link can starve those after it.
A rich link can hold goods back.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own stock and orders and starts with different amounts, so nobody can tell whether the gap is large or small.

cons: The absent player has no voice.
Rules can be written without them.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs the world, and the leading player writes rules the game master has to apply. Others live with them.
pros: Shows rule power between two roles.
The game master can judge the change.
cons: Others may feel the game master is overruled.
Players may argue over who decides.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street, and whoever holds the spot or the crowd writes the rules. Passers-by join under them.
pros: Shows power over who joins.
New players see the rules at once.
cons: Newcomers can be turned away.
Rules can change with the crowd.

pairs.tendency: The one player takes on all the others, and the one who is ahead writes the rules. The side behind plays under them.
pros: Shows power running one way.
Players see who benefits.
cons: The lone player may be pushed hard.
The many may impose rules on one.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone, you are both the leader and the one under the rules, so any change you make is your own.
pros: Shows rules you choose for yourself.
Players learn how rule changes feel.
cons: Nobody is there to object.
Changes can make the game too easy.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide who gets ahead, then that player writes the rules. The rest play under them with little to do.
pros: Shows luck turning into power.
Players see how a lead is unearned.
cons: Others have few moves in answer.
A lucky lead can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide a lot, and the leader writes rules on how poor luck may be softened, such as only for themselves.
pros: Shows who gets help against chance.
Players see how protection is shared out.
cons: Others have less help against poor rolls.
Help for one can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: Skill takes a player ahead, and then they write the rules. A little luck still shakes things up for the others.
pros: Shows skill turning into rule power.
Players feel skill rewarded, then used.
cons: Luck gives others little comfort.
The gap between players widens.

pairs.tendency: The most skilled player takes the lead and then writes rules for the rest. No luck can undo it.
pros: Shows how skill can become control.
Every result has a reason.
cons: Trailing players cannot catch up.
The lead can become permanent.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes how throws are read, such as their sign counting as a lucky omen. Others read their own throws under it.
pros: Shows meaning given by whoever leads.
Players reflect on who reads the signs.
cons: Signs can be made to suit the leader.
Others may stop trusting the readings.

pairs.tendency: Players sense each other's timing, and the leader writes a rule that changes it, such as a signal only they give.
pros: Shows how a shared sense can be broken.
Players notice the change by feel.
cons: Trust between players can wear down.
The sense may be hard to rebuild.

pairs.tendency: Dice write the story, and the leader writes new tables for them. Others roll on tables that no longer favour them.
pros: Shows who sets the odds of events.
Story and rules shift together.
cons: Others' events turn out harsher.
The table can feel rigged.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so every player sees the leader's rule change and what it does. They can plan around it.
pros: Shows power with nothing hidden.
Players can talk through the change.
cons: Seeing it does not mean they can stop it.
Open power can feel harsher.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes a rule, and nobody can see how it helps their hand. Others guess and play under it.
pros: Players read rules for what they hide.
Suspicion adds to the play.
cons: Rule changes may seem unfair.
Others cannot check the change.

pairs.tendency: Roles are hidden, and the leader writes rules that others try to read for clues about who they are.
pros: Rules become clues about identity.
Suspicion shapes each change.
cons: Players may accuse the wrong person.
Hidden roles may hide self-serving rules.

pairs.tendency: Players work out facts from clues, then the leader writes a rule about which clues may be used. Others keep deducing.
pros: Shows access to clues shaped by power.
Rules become part of the puzzle.
cons: Others lose clues they relied on.
Deduction can stall under new rules.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes rules about claims, such as challenges costing others more. Players keep bluffing under them.
pros: Shows who can afford to challenge.
Bluffs change in price.
cons: Others may stop challenging.
Lies are safer for the leader.

pairs.tendency: Newcomers learn rules by breaking them, and then the leader rewrites them. Others have to learn the rules again.
pros: Shows rules that keep shifting.
Players pay attention to every no.
cons: Learning can feel pointless.
Newcomers may give up.

pairs.tendency: One player holds the answer but cannot say it, and the leader writes a rule on hints. Others guess under it.
pros: Shows hints shaped by power.
The guessing game takes on new rules.
cons: Guessers have fewer hints.
The one who knows may feel muzzled.

pairs.tendency: The map is revealed as players explore, and the leader writes rules about exploring. Others uncover tiles under them.
pros: Shows who gets to see more.
Exploring has a cost.
cons: Others may explore less.
The leader can see more than they say.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, and the leader writes a rule about who may play it. Others still hold hidden hands.
pros: Shows access to shared resources.
Everyone can see how the open hand is used.
cons: Others lose use of the open hand.
Open hands can become the leader's alone.

pairs.tendency: Scores are secret, so nobody knows for sure who is ahead, yet someone writes the rules. Others wonder whether it is fair.
pros: Shows power without proof.
Players guess who leads.
cons: Rule changes can seem random.
The wrong player may end up writing rules.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns, then the leader writes new rules for turn order or turn length. Others wait their turn under them.
pros: Shows power over who goes when.
Changes are easy to follow.
cons: Waiting players cannot answer at once.
Others sit through the rule change.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at once, and the leader writes a rule about how choices are revealed. Others choose under it.
pros: Shows how power can change what is shared.
Players adapt in the same moment.
cons: Others may not see the change in time.
Simultaneous play can hide who ruled.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so the one who gets ahead writes rules at any moment. Others keep grabbing under them.
pros: Shows how quick players take power.
Rule changes happen in flow.
cons: Others may miss changes.
Quick players keep gaining.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes a rule about the clock, such as shorter turns for others. Everyone plays under it.
pros: Shows time used as power.
The clock makes change felt.
cons: Others have less time to think.
Hurried moves can lead to errors.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks, and the leader posts a new rule partway. Others find it on their next move.
pros: Shows power at a slow pace.
Players have time to respond.
cons: Others can miss a post.
Change in slow play can be hard to answer.

pairs.tendency: The game is slow on purpose, and the leader writes a rule at a calm moment. Others have time to think about it.
pros: Shows power in a slow setting.
Players can reflect on each change.
cons: Slow play can drag.
The change can seem to come from nowhere.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, and the leader writes rules as the pace climbs. Others have less time to read each change.
pros: Shows how speed helps whoever writes rules.
Tension rises with pace.
cons: Others cannot keep up with changes.
Late changes arrive in a rush.

pairs.tendency: A player who earns extra turns often pulls ahead, then writes the rules. Others see the lead growing.
pros: Shows a chain of gains.
An early lead is easy to spot.
cons: Extra turns can make the lead permanent.
Others take few turns before rules change.

pairs.tendency: A game in stages lets the leader of stage one write the rules for stage two. What others did earlier shapes their start.
pros: Shows how early results set later rules.
Stages give a clear moment for change.
cons: The first-stage winner holds the second.
Others may feel stage one was wasted.

pairs.tendency: The board models a real system, and whoever is ahead rewrites its rules, such as taking more water. Others play on in the changed model.
pros: Shows how real systems get shaped by the strong.
Players see who benefits from rules.
cons: The model can stop matching reality.
Players may blame the model.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a real group, and the group with most power writes the rules. Others act in role under them.
pros: Shows how rules favour some groups.
Players feel what it is to be under them.
cons: Weaker roles can feel stuck.
The strong role can dominate.

pairs.tendency: Players draw from one limited stock, and the leader writes the rules on who may take how much. Others share what is left.
pros: Shows how access to a shared stock gets decided.
The stock shows who gained.
cons: Others can be locked out.
The stock can run out faster.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes a rule whose effects show only a few rounds later. Others find out slowly what it did.
pros: Shows how rule changes can hide results.
Players trace cause and effect.
cons: Others may not link effect to rule.
Mistakes show up too late.

pairs.tendency: Players agree on rules to test, but here only the leader writes them. Others play on to see what it changes.
pros: Shows how rules are tested by few.
Players compare rules and results.
cons: The test can serve one player.
Others have no say in what is tried.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about who wrote the rules and why. They compare it with real life.
pros: Players name how power worked.
Rule changes become something to discuss.
cons: Strong feelings can come up.
Players may blame the leader.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes a rule that cannot be undone, such as tearing up a card. Others live with it in later games.
pros: Shows how rule changes can last.
Players feel the weight of a rule.
cons: Others cannot reverse it.
One change can shape every later game.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes a rule, and the game itself makes a point about who decides. Players see the rules as an argument.
pros: Players see rules as a claim.
The point comes from play.
cons: The point may read as one-sided.
Some may reject it.

pairs.tendency: Rules written by the leader carry real stakes, such as who does a chore. Others live with the outcome after play.
pros: Shows power with real effects.
Players take rules seriously.
cons: Others can feel it as real unfairness.
Arguments can carry over after play.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, and the leader writes the rules on what earns them. Others chase what the leader defines.
pros: Shows who decides what counts.
Players question what is being measured.
cons: Others may chase points over values.
The leader can redefine worth.

pairs.tendency: Players rehearse a way of living, and the leader writes its rules as it goes. Others try to live under them.
pros: Shows future rules shaped by a few.
Players feel how a rule might sit.
cons: Rules may feel set by one voice.
The future can end up one player's.

pairs.tendency: Roles have goals that pull against each other, and the leader writes rules that favour their own role's goal.
pros: Shows rules serving one goal.
Players see the others' aims clearly.
cons: Opposing roles lose ground.
Goals may stop being fair to each role.

pairs.tendency: The opening situation sets who is where, and the leader later rewrites rules on top of it. Others see how the start led there.
pros: Players can trace the lead back to the start.
A clear start makes the change visible.
cons: A fixed start can feel unfair afterwards.
Others may blame the setup.

pairs.tendency: Players argue their moves, and the leader writes rules on how arguments are judged. Others argue under them.
pros: Shows who decides what is accepted.
Arguing gets more careful.
cons: Others' arguments may count for less.
Judges can be swayed by the leader.

pairs.tendency: Play pauses so players can say what they notice, and the rule change is named out loud before play goes on.
pros: Players get to speak on the change.
Power becomes something to discuss.
cons: Pauses can slow play.
The leader may still go ahead regardless.

pairs.tendency: The same game is played again with the rule change dropped or kept, and players compare.
pros: Shows what the rule change did.
Players see the lead's effect plainly.
cons: A replay takes more time.
Players may argue over which game was fair.

pairs.tendency: The game says what it left out, such as who agreed to the rule changes. Players know where the model stops.
pros: Shows where the model's limits lie.
Players can question the rule-making.
cons: Players may think the whole game is too simple.
Real rule-making is far more complex.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about help design it, including how rule-making is shown. They check that it rings true.
pros: Shows power as those who live it know it.
Players trust the model more.
cons: Designers may disagree on how to show it.
Real stories can be painful to play.

pairs.tendency: Each player is one link in a chain, and the strongest link writes rules for the rest, such as who gets paid first.
pros: Shows how strong links shape a chain.
Players see weaker links squeezed.
cons: Weak links can be dropped.
The chain can break at its weakest.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own corner, and the leader writes rules others see only through their own stock.
pros: Shows how rules can arrive unseen.
Players guess where changes come from.
cons: Others cannot tell who made a rule.
Guessing may be wrong.

pairs.tendency: The player who holds the bottleneck writes the rules, such as who goes first. Others wait at the slowest step.
pros: Shows how a pinch point turns into power.
Players see where the pace is set.
cons: Those downstream wait on the rule-maker.
The bottleneck can be kept slow on purpose.

pairs.tendency: The strongest link decides whether goods are pushed or pulled, and others work under that choice.
pros: Shows a strong link setting how goods flow.
Players feel the gap between push and pull.
cons: Others carry stock they did not choose.
Orders and guesses can pile up.

pairs.tendency: The player with the most weight writes a rule on batch size, such as others making bigger batches. Others pay for it in waiting.
pros: Shows how rules can push costs along.
Players feel waiting and set-up costs.
cons: Others pay for choices they did not make.
Big batches can leave stock unused.

pairs.tendency: Machines break at random, and whoever is ahead writes the rules on repairs, such as their own getting fixed first.
pros: Shows who gets help when things fail.
Players plan for failure.
cons: Others wait longer for repairs.
Breakdowns can pile up on the weak.

pairs.tendency: The leader writes a rule on holding costs, such as lower costs for their own stock. Others balance too much against too little.
pros: Shows how costs can be shifted.
Players weigh stock carefully.
cons: Others pay more to hold the same.
Running out hits the weak hardest.

pairs.tendency: Players move by dice along a track, and each role scores by a different measure, so the same landing space is a gain for one role and a loss for another.
pros: Same space means different things to each role.
Easy turns leave room to talk about goals.
cons: Dice can drown out the goal clash.
Roles may ignore each other and just race.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks cards for their own role's measure, and a card one role wants is often the card another role needs to keep away from them.
pros: Picks show what each role values.
Passing cards reveals rival goals.
cons: Players may take cards only to block.
Roles with fewer fitting cards fall behind early.

pairs.tendency: Roles bid for the same things, but each values them by a different measure, so one bid can be cheap for a farmer and costly for a conservationist.
pros: Prices show how differently roles value things.
Bids make the clash open and clear.
cons: Richer roles can outbid the rest every time.
Bidding can bury the reasons behind the goals.

pairs.tendency: Each role pushes for more of what it wants, and the more one role takes, the more the opposed role stands to lose when it ends.
pros: Greed in one role is felt by another.
Tension rises as the taking goes on.
cons: Players may push only to spoil a rival.
Bust turns can feel like plain luck, not conflict.

pairs.tendency: Roles fight over the same map areas, but each wants them for a different reason, such as a field to farm against a marsh to leave alone.
pros: Same land, different uses, easy to see.
Fights over places have clear reasons.
cons: The map can turn into plain fighting.
Roles with fewer natural areas feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: Roles place workers on shared jobs, and one role's job often undoes what another role's workers have just done.
pros: Taking a space also blocks a rival's aim.
Planning around other roles' goals feels real.
cons: Blocked roles may wait many turns.
Players may block out of habit, not need.

pairs.tendency: Each role builds toward its own pattern, and the pieces one role lays down can break the pattern another is making.
pros: Each role has a clear shape to chase.
Quiet building shows whose goal is whose.
cons: Patterns can feel abstract against real goals.
Spoiling a neighbour can matter more than building.

pairs.tendency: Each role holds cards that serve its own measure, and playing one can help your role while hurting someone else's.
pros: Timing a card matters for every role.
Players learn what rival roles hold dear.
cons: Roles with weaker hands feel stuck.
Cards can be saved too long to show any conflict.

pairs.tendency: Players win tricks for their roles, but what counts as a prize differs by role, so winning a trick can be a loss for another role's aim.
pros: Each trick means something different to each role.
