Short rounds keep the goals in view.
cons: Tricks can feel like plain card play.
Goals can fade once the cards are dealt.

pairs.tendency: Roles with opposed measures talk and trade, looking for deals where each gives up something it values less than the other values it.
pros: Talk brings out what each role really needs.
Deals show where goals can and cannot meet.
cons: Loud players can talk quiet roles out of things.
Players may hide their goals, though all are known.

pairs.tendency: Each role collects a different set, and some of the pieces one role needs are the very pieces another role has to hold back from.
pros: Each role has its own clear target.
Collecting makes progress easy to see.
cons: Rival sets may never overlap, so little clash.
Hoarding can stall the whole table.

pairs.tendency: Roles lay tiles into one shared map, and a tile that helps one role's goal can spoil a place another role is trying to keep.
pros: The shared map holds every role's mark.
Each placement is a visible argument.
cons: Tiles can be laid just to block.
The map can end up as a patchwork of spite.

pairs.tendency: One role makes a move or a statement and the next role answers it from its own measure, so the talk goes back and forth between opposed aims.
pros: Each answer shows a role's own view.
Conversation carries the conflict.
cons: Players may answer as themselves, not their role.
Quiet players can fall out of the chain.

pairs.tendency: Roles pull against each other but nobody may talk, so each role's aim shows only in what it plays and when.
pros: Goals are read from actions alone.
Players pay close attention to each other.
cons: Rivals cannot explain or bargain.
Players can misread a move as a spoiling one.

pairs.tendency: Players can change a rule on their turn, and each role changes it toward its own measure, so the rules become the thing the roles fight over.
pros: Rule changes show whose goal is winning.
The game shifts as the roles push.
cons: Rule changes can swamp the original goals.
Players with a clever mind may rewrite their way to the win.

pairs.tendency: Players speak as characters with opposed aims, so the conflict is argued in the voice of a fisher or a conservationist, not only scored.
pros: The clash is acted out, not only counted.
Players hear each role's reasons.
cons: Players may play a role as a villain.
Some players find speaking for an opposed role hard.

pairs.tendency: Roles with opposed aims also have to use their hands, so a steady hand can win a goal that another role wanted.
pros: Skill of the hand gives each role a turn.
Lively, with a lot of laughter and groans.
cons: Hand skill can matter more than role goals.
The clash of goals can fall into the background.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and each role draws it toward its own aim, so one sheet of paper holds every role's wishes.
pros: The map records what each role wanted.
Players see the effect of their own marks.
cons: Drawing can turn into a fight over the pen.
Players with less drawing skill may hang back.

pairs.tendency: Players ask each other for cards, and since each role wants different cards, asking can hand a rival the very card it was after.
pros: Questions reveal what each role holds.
Easy to learn, with clear goals.
cons: Asking can tell rivals too much.
A lucky draw can end a role's whole plan.

pairs.tendency: The bank sets odds and the others bet, and each role has a different reason to risk its counters, so the same bet means something else to each.
pros: The bank gives a simple fixed rule.
Bets show how bold each role is.
cons: The bank role has an odd, lonely goal.
Roles with fewer counters stay out of play.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on a throw nobody controls, and roles with different measures stake different things, so one throw pays out differently to each.
pros: Stakes show what each role values.
Short, tense moments.
cons: Chance decides, so goals barely matter.
Roles may lose through the dice alone.

pairs.tendency: Players raise and match bets on hidden cards, and each role has its own reason to stay in, so one bet can mean different aims.
pros: Bets hint at each role's hidden plan.
Hidden cards add doubt to open goals.
cons: Bluffing can hide the real role goals.
A player with a poor hand may leave the clash.

pairs.tendency: Players pick their own side and goals before play, and a side built for one aim tends to run straight into sides built for others.
pros: Choosing a side shows a player's aim.
Players own their own goal.
cons: Sides may be tuned so no real clash occurs.
Unequal sides can leave one role far ahead.

pairs.tendency: Players say what they will achieve before play, and a contract for one role often fails if another role reaches its own aim.
pros: Players state their aim out loud.
Success or failure is clear to see.
cons: Stated contracts can be too safe.
A failed contract can feel like a rival's doing.

pairs.tendency: Pieces taken from one role change sides and serve another, so one role's loss is a rival's gain and the aims swap hands.
pros: Captured pieces show whose side wins.
Leads can swing at any time.
cons: A role can fall behind through one move.
Pieces may change hands with little to do with goals.

pairs.tendency: A caught piece waits for rescue, and roles with opposed aims may choose whether to free or hold it, since freeing one role hurts another.
pros: Rescue gives roles a reason to work together.
Strong team spirit.
cons: Waiting in jail is dull.
Roles may rescue only their own friends.

pairs.tendency: Roles take pieces by surrounding them, and each role has its own reason to hem in a rival's piece, so goals show on the board.
pros: Takes are clear and easy to read.
Players can see a rival's aim in its plan.
cons: Surrounding can crowd out the role goals.
A role can be shut out of the board.

pairs.tendency: Help for players who are behind softens a clash that would otherwise be one-sided, so a role losing on its own measure gets another chance.
pros: Losing roles stay in the game.
The clash lasts to the last turn.
cons: Leaders feel held back by the help.
Players may hold back to win from behind.

pairs.tendency: The dice or cards decide everything, so each role's opposed goals are only scored after chance has spoken, and no choice changes them.
pros: Quick, light, and everyone starts equal.
Opposed goals are plain to read.
cons: Players can change nothing about the clash.
Roles feel pointless when luck alone settles them.

pairs.tendency: One role chases the others and each role has its own reason to be caught or to escape, so running away can serve one aim and hurt another.
pros: Fast, loud and active.
Aims are easy to follow from where you run.
cons: Quick runners can win every time.
Goals can be forgotten in the chase.

pairs.tendency: Each turn players choose who to hit, help or trade with, and an opposed role is an easy target since its aim cuts against yours.
pros: Choosing targets shows who is the rival.
Alliances can form around shared aims.
cons: One role may be picked on by all.
A player aimed at by everyone can lose heart.

pairs.tendency: Roles try to join their own chains across the board, and a chain for one role can cut off a chain another role needs.
pros: Aims show up as lines on the board.
Cutting a rival has a clear reason.
cons: Only one chain may fit, so one role loses.
Block moves can become the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, and each role has its own measure, so winning a round does not always mean winning on your goal.
pros: Short rounds are easy to play.
Guessing a rival's goal adds a layer.
cons: The cycle may overshadow role goals.
A round won can be a goal lost.

pairs.tendency: Players show a pair or a run to score, and a combination that serves one role's goal may leave another role's goal further off.
pros: Showing sets reveals aims in the open.
Scoring moments are easy to follow.
cons: Combinations may be too far from the role goals.
Showing a set can give rivals a target.

pairs.tendency: Each role has its own power as well as its own goal, so a role's power is made for its own aim and often cuts across a rival's.
pros: Powers fit roles and their goals.
Each player feels unlike the rest.
cons: A strong power can end the clash early.
Players have to learn many powers.

pairs.tendency: A player can offer to double what the game is worth, and the role that is behind on its own measure may refuse and give up the points.
pros: Doubling shows how sure a role is.
Raises feel risky and sharp.
cons: A role behind may lose more than it gains.
The offer can pressure quiet players.

pairs.tendency: When a capture is possible a role has to take it, and a forced take can pull a role off its own aim and hand a rival an opening.
pros: Forced takes create clear traps.
Rivals can plan around a role's duty.
cons: A forced take can harm the role's own goal.
Players may feel the game plays for them.

pairs.tendency: Roles gain power as they play, and the stronger a role becomes at its own aim the harder it presses on the opposed role.
pros: Progress is easy to feel.
Roles can see their own growth.
cons: A role that grows early may overwhelm the rest.
Opposed aims can drift as powers outgrow them.

pairs.tendency: Each player recites the list so far and adds an item, and each role adds what serves its own aim, so the list shows the clash grow.
pros: The list holds everyone's priorities.
Easy to play without a board.
cons: A long list is hard to remember.
The conflict stays on the surface.

pairs.tendency: A stronger player starts with less, which lets roles with unequal power still press their own aims against each other.
pros: Unequal players meet on a fairer footing.
Weaker roles have a real chance.
cons: Choosing the handicap can cause arguments.
A handicap may hide the clash of goals.

pairs.tendency: Some players hide while others seek, and each role may want something found or kept hidden, such as a fish stock to protect or to catch.
pros: The search gives a clear reason to oppose.
Roles each want a different outcome.
cons: Hiding can end the game quickly.
Seeking can leave hiders with little to do.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hop over others to move forward, and a hop that helps one role's goal can clear a piece another role was using.
pros: Moves are quick to see.
Hops have clear effects on rivals.
cons: Hopping can become chain reactions nobody planned.
Goals can be lost beneath tactics.

pairs.tendency: Players set aside dice they like and roll the rest, and each role keeps the dice that serve its own aim, so a die one role keeps another needed.
pros: Choosing dice shows each role's measure.
Rerolls give some control.
cons: Dice can still undo a carefully kept plan.
Roles may chase dice, not goals.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a rival sends them back, so a role's progress toward its aim can be undone by a rival simply landing on it.
pros: Send-backs make the clash direct.
Setbacks are quick to grasp.
cons: Sent-back roles may lose heart.
Luck of the dice decides who is sent back.

pairs.tendency: A row lets a player take a piece, and each role builds rows for its own aim while breaking up the rows that serve another role.
pros: Rows are easy to see and aim for.
Taking pieces has clear targets.
cons: Players can focus on rows and ignore role goals.
A role with few pieces can fall away.

pairs.tendency: Players make words from letters, and each role scores by its own measure, so a word that helps one role can use up letters another needs.
pros: Words are easy to check.
Players talk about what they spell.
cons: The word game can overshadow the goals.
Players with a larger vocabulary get ahead.

pairs.tendency: Tiles go on matching ends, and a role that plays a tile may close an end another role needed, so each placement can help one aim and block another.
pros: Matching rules are quick to learn.
Blocking is natural and clear.
cons: Players with no match can be stuck.
Goals may be lost in the matching.

pairs.tendency: Players lay sets face up and others can add to them, so a set made for one role can be used by another role against its own aim.
pros: Laid sets are open for all to read.
Others can build on your set.
cons: Adding to a set may help a rival's goal.
The table can fill with long, hard sets.

pairs.tendency: Each role holds a power that works once, so players decide when to use it against a rival's aim, and a power spent early cannot be used later.
pros: Timing a power becomes a real choice.
Used powers show what each role fears.
cons: A power used wrongly can end a role's chances.
Players may sit on their powers too long.

pairs.tendency: A player offers a move and the other may turn it down or pick between options, so a rival role can steer you away from your own aim.
pros: Rivals have a voice in each move.
Moves have to suit more than one role.
cons: Offers can be turned down every time.
A role with no say can feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: A message goes from player to player and may change on the way, and each role may bend it toward its own aim.
pros: The shifted message shows each role's bias.
Light, funny and quick.
cons: The goal clash is mostly in the background.
Players may bend a message for fun.

pairs.tendency: Players hand cards to a neighbour before play, and each role passes what serves its aim least, so you hand a rival cards for its own goal.
pros: Passing shows what a role values least.
Players trade without talk.
cons: A neighbour's goal may be helped by your pass.
A weak hand can come from a rival's pass.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up and the other chooses a side, so a role has reason to make both sides even, since a rival with an opposed aim will pick the stronger.
pros: Setup becomes a careful act.
Both roles start on level ground.
cons: Setups can feel long and fussy.
The pie rule fits two roles more than many.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes stronger, and each role pushes forward for its own aim while rivals try to stop it or reach their own end first.
pros: Pushing forward has a clear prize.
Each role has a reason to risk pieces.
cons: Promoted pieces may end the clash early.
Roles may rush, ignoring their goals.

pairs.tendency: Teams race in legs, handing over one to the next, and when each team's legs serve opposed measures, passing the baton can mean handing work to a rival aim.
pros: The team passes work clearly.
Every player has a part.
cons: A team can lose through one slow leg.
Opposed aims inside a race can get lost.

pairs.tendency: A safe shape can't be captured, so roles build shapes that protect their own aim while rivals try to hem them in or work around them.
pros: Safe shapes give roles a clear goal.
Players see how protection is built.
cons: Protected roles may stop interacting.
Safe shapes can leave a role walled off.

pairs.tendency: Prizes are named in advance, so each role knows which prizes serve its measure, and one card a role wants may be the card a rival needs to deny it.
pros: Named prizes show what each role wants.
Players plan for a few clear cards.
cons: One card can end a rival's plan.
Prizes may matter more than the goals.

pairs.tendency: Everyone can use the cards in the middle, so a card one role takes for its own aim is gone for the role that needed it.
pros: Open cards show every role's needs.
Players can read each other's plans.
cons: Players may take shared cards only to spoil.
A busy middle can be hard to track.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts counters in the middle and one wins it all, so a pot that is a gain for one role is a loss for every other role's aim.
pros: The pot is a clear, simple prize.
Everyone can see what is at stake.
cons: One winner can leave the rest with nothing.
Pots can grow until the goals no longer matter.

pairs.tendency: Players scoop seeds and drop them round the pits, and each role sows to serve its own aim while a sown seed may land in a rival's pit.
pros: Moves are physical and easy to learn.
Each sowing helps or hurts someone clearly.
cons: Seeds can pass to rivals by accident.
Roles are hard to track through the sowing.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand sits in the middle and one player may take, swap or buy it, so roles with opposed aims bargain over who gets the stronger start.
pros: A spare hand gives a second chance.
Players weigh what each role needs.
cons: The spare hand can favour one role.
Taking it may reveal a player's aim.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces carry their own rule, and a space that helps one role's measure may send another role's piece back or skip its turn.
pros: Squares stand for real events.
Space effects are easy to read.
cons: Special spaces may favour one role.
Dice may decide who lands on them.

pairs.tendency: Everything has a price, so roles with opposed aims choose what to buy with limited funds, and what one role buys may cost another dearly.
pros: Spending shows what each role values.
Choices are easy to compare.
cons: A rich role can buy its way ahead.
Spending can be about money, not goals.

pairs.tendency: A fixed amount is shared between several places, so each role spreads its effort across its own aims, and a rival's choice can leave one place thin.
pros: Spreading effort shows a role's priorities.
Rivals can guess where to press.
cons: Roles can end up spread too thin.
A leaning toward one place can overlook others.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until a signal stops them, and roles with opposed aims all freeze together, so the slowest role loses what the quickest one reached.
pros: Signals create a quick, shared moment.
Everyone is alert at once.
cons: Goals may be forgotten in the scramble.
The same players tend to be slow.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards back and take new ones, and each role swaps toward its own aim, so a card one role gives up may serve a rival.
pros: Swaps let roles shape their hand.
Returned cards tell rivals something.
cons: Swapped cards may help the rival role.
Swapping can slow the game down.

pairs.tendency: A player may pick up the whole discard pile, and each role wants different cards from it, so taking it can help one role and burden another.
pros: Piles hold what everyone threw away.
A pile can swing a role's fortune.
cons: A big pile can end a role's plans.
Players may take piles only to stop a rival.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats all others, so a role whose measure suits the trump suit has a strong edge over roles whose aims lie in other suits.
pros: A clear ranking is easy to follow.
Trumps give roles a reason to plan.
cons: One suit can favour one role every time.
Goals may be lost behind the card ranking.

pairs.tendency: Players are one side on one board and the other on another, so a role's gain in one game can be its own loss in the other.
pros: Players feel both sides of the clash.
Two boards show different views.
cons: Two boards are slow to learn.
Players may favour one board over the other.

pairs.tendency: Wild cards stand for any card, so a role can finish its own set with one, and the same wild card is lost to a rival whose aim it would also serve.
pros: Wilds give roles a way out.
A wild card is a clear, easy prize.
cons: Wilds can make goals too easy to reach.
Players may fight for wilds.

pairs.tendency: The board edges are joined, so no role can be pushed to the side, and a role's line running off one edge may come back on another to meet its rival.
pros: No edge gives a role cover.
Movement feels open and free.
cons: Rivals can come from any direction.
The joined edges can confuse new players.

pairs.tendency: One player has a secret and the others ask yes-or-no questions, so a role with an opposed aim can ask questions that steer toward its own measure.
pros: Each question shows a role's interest.
Answers narrow the choices for everyone.
cons: Questions may drift away from the role goals.
A role with few questions loses ground.

pairs.tendency: Roles race to the end, but each role's measure of reaching the end differs, so reaching it first can be a loss for another role's aim.
pros: The finish line is clear for all.
A race keeps every role in motion.
cons: A race can crowd out the conflict of goals.
Roles who fall behind may give up the clash.

pairs.tendency: Roles add up points by their own measures, and since the measures pull apart, a high total for one role often comes from lowering another's.
pros: Scores make the clash easy to count.
Everyone can see who is ahead.
cons: One score can hide differing aims.
Points may push roles toward the same goal.

pairs.tendency: Players knock each other out, and each role's reason to stay in differs, so the last role standing wins its own aim and ends the others'.
pros: The ending is quick and clear.
Roles have a strong reason to hold on.
cons: Knocked-out players wait and watch.
Role goals may matter less than survival.

pairs.tendency: The group has to survive together while each role also has its own aim that pulls against the rest, so survival is shared but how to reach it is not.
pros: Shared danger gives roles a reason to talk.
Aims clash inside a shared goal.
cons: Roles may sacrifice the group for a private aim.
Players may feel torn between two aims.

pairs.tendency: All players work toward one goal while each role holds its own measure, so the shared aim is reached only if each role gives something up.
pros: Roles have to meet in the middle.
A shared goal makes talk worthwhile.
cons: Roles may hang back and let others pay.
Players may agree too quickly and skip the conflict.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal on top of a role's open measure, so rivals know the role's aim but not what the player really wants.
pros: Secrets add doubt to open goals.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: Secret goals can cloud the known clash.
Hidden aims may be hard to read or trust.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story does, and roles with opposed aims push the story toward different endings, so the end shows whose aim had the upper hand.
pros: Roles shape the story together.
Many endings are possible.
cons: The story can end without any role winning.
Players with strong voices steer the tale.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so roles with opposed aims play on without a final score, and the clash is something to notice and talk about afterwards.
pros: Players can explore a clash without pressure.
Talk afterwards can be open.
cons: Roles may drift without a clear aim.
Some players lose interest with no prize.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means for them, so roles carry both a set measure and a chosen one, and the two may not agree.
pros: Players own their own goals.
Choices show what each player values.
cons: Self-set goals may be too easy to reach.
Roles can drift away from the set clash.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player loses, so roles with opposed aims try to push a rival into the loser's seat while staying safe themselves.
pros: Everyone else is safe, so tension is shared.
The ending is clear.
cons: One role may be picked on to lose.
Roles may play only to avoid loss.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going while roles still pull against each other, so the clash has to be kept alive instead of settled.
pros: The clash can be played over and over.
Players can keep trying new moves.
cons: Without an end, goals may slip away.
Roles may soften the clash to keep playing.

pairs.tendency: The game cannot be won, yet roles still pull in opposed directions, so the clash shows what is lost when every role chases its own aim.
pros: The clash is shown with no winner to hide it.
Players are left to think about it.
cons: Players may feel there is no point.
Roles may play without caring about goals.

pairs.tendency: One player plays alone against the cards, so the conflicting goals are held by one person who has to serve opposed measures in turn.
pros: A single player feels both pulls.
No rival is needed to show the clash.
cons: Opposed goals are harder to feel alone.
The clash can seem like a puzzle.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played in a row, so roles with opposed aims can win one game and lose another, and may swap approaches between games.
pros: Each game gives a fresh try at the clash.
Roles can learn from losing.
cons: A role that falls behind early may give up.
Results are mixed when goals differ by game.

pairs.tendency: Points count against you, so roles with opposed measures try to pass points to each other, and each role's loss can be a rival's gain.
pros: Dodging points makes goals easy to see.
Players guard against being burdened.
cons: Pushing points onto others can feel spiteful.
A role with many points may be left behind.

pairs.tendency: A role has to land on an exact number, so it may have to hold back while a rival with an opposed aim presses on, and overshooting costs it its goal.
pros: Exact aims add careful timing.
Waiting for the right moment builds tension.
cons: A role can be stuck waiting for one number.
A rival may spoil an exact landing.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, so a role may want to lose on its own measure while another role wants to win, and the clash is about who gives way.
pros: Opposed goals become surprising.
Players think about winning and losing in new ways.
cons: Players may lose track of whose aim is whose.
The twist can overshadow the roles.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays at once without affecting each other, so the clash between roles shows only in the final scores and not in play.
pros: Players focus on their own goals.
No one blocks anyone.
cons: Conflicting goals barely show during play.
The clash is only seen when scores are compared.

pairs.tendency: Players attack, steal or sabotage on purpose, and roles with opposed aims have a clear reason to target each other.
pros: Conflict is open and easy to see.
Aims give reasons for the attacks.
cons: Attacks can turn personal.
Players may attack out of habit.

pairs.tendency: Roles change the board, take spots and build walls, so the clash between opposed aims is felt through the board, not through attacks on a person.
pros: Conflict is felt, with less blame.
The board shows what each role did.
cons: The clash may be slow to notice.
Players may not see whose move hurt them.

pairs.tendency: All players are on one team against the game, yet roles still hold opposed measures, so cooperation is only possible by giving up some part of each aim.
pros: Roles have to work out trade-offs together.
A shared enemy keeps everyone talking.
cons: Opposed aims can weaken the shared plan.
One loud player may take over the team.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together but each has a private reason to win more, and roles with opposed aims make that private pull strong.
pros: Partners and rivals at once.
Players weigh trust at each move.
cons: A betrayal can sour the table.
Shared goals may be dropped for private ones.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play against each other, and each team's roles may hold opposed aims inside it, so a team can pull itself apart while facing a rival.
pros: Teammates can disagree openly.
Players learn to give and take.
cons: A team can lose through its own clash.
The enemy team may be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: A secret traitor works against the group while roles already hold opposed aims, so a role that blocks you could be a rival or a traitor.
pros: Mistrust is part of the play.
Players read each other's moves closely.
cons: Players can't tell a rival from a traitor.
Accusations can end the clash early.

pairs.tendency: Players far apart send moves by letter, so roles with opposed aims have weeks to think about each move, and the clash builds slowly in the post.
pros: There is time to think each reply.
Players can plan around rival goals.
cons: Waiting can be long.
Players may lose interest between letters.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so a role is played by a ghost or a record, and its aim pulls against the others without anyone speaking for it.
pros: An absent aim still shapes the table.
Players think about voices not heard.
cons: Nobody can bargain with an absent role.
An empty seat can slow the clash.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world while the others play roles with opposed aims, so the game master can bring in what each role wants and judge disputes.
pros: Someone can keep the clash fair.
The world can answer to all roles.
cons: The game master may favour one role.
One player does not get to take a role.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in the open and anyone can join, so passers-by take roles with opposed aims quickly, with little time to explain them.
pros: Newcomers can join easily.
Roles can be explained in a line.
cons: Passers-by may leave before the clash builds.
Rules for opposed goals may be hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all others, so the lone role's aim is opposed to the group, and the group's own roles may also pull against each other.
pros: The sides are clear and easy to see.
The lone player feels both pressure and power.
cons: The group may argue and lose to one player.
The lone player may be outnumbered every time.

pairs.tendency: Nobody else takes a turn, so one player holds roles with opposed aims and chooses which to serve, and every choice costs another aim.
pros: Players feel the trade-off for themselves.
No one waits for a turn.
cons: Without rivals, the clash can feel like a puzzle.
A single player may favour one role.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most things, so roles with opposed aims often win or lose by luck, and the clash is felt mainly in how the dice fall.
pros: Quick, open to all.
Everyone shares the lucky and unlucky turns.
cons: Luck decides, so aims barely matter.
Players can't act on what they learn.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide a lot but players have ways to soften an unlucky run, so each role can protect its own aim from the dice while rivals look for gaps.
pros: Players have a reply to an unlucky run.
Roles can plan despite the dice.
cons: Softening may favour a role that is already ahead.
Tools to soften luck add rules to learn.

pairs.tendency: Choices matter most, with a little luck, so roles with opposed aims can plan against each other and a lucky turn keeps the outcome open.
pros: Skill pays off, but luck stops a runaway.
The clash is open to planning.
cons: A lucky turn can feel unfair to a planner.
Skilled players may outplay the clash entirely.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so roles with opposed aims clash by choice alone, and the sharper planner can press its own aim hardest against the rest.
pros: Every outcome comes from a choice.
Goals are pursued with real planning.
cons: A more skilled player may dominate.
Newcomers may find the clash hard to read.

pairs.tendency: Throws are read as messages, so roles with opposed aims may each read the same throw to suit their own measure, and argue over what it means.
pros: A throw can be read from each role's side.
Players talk about meaning, not only score.
cons: Readings can differ with no way to settle.
The clash may turn into plain argument.

pairs.tendency: Players succeed by sensing when others will act, so roles with opposed aims have to read each other's moods and timing, not only what each one wants.
pros: Players tune into each other.
Quiet, attentive play.
cons: Opposed aims may block the sense of unity.
Players may feel left out if they do not sense it.

pairs.tendency: A table says what happens after each roll, so the dice write events that help one role's aim and harm another, and the story shows the clash.
pros: Rolls bring unexpected events to the clash.
Players share in the story told.
cons: Events may favour one role by chance.
The dice may drive the story away from the goals.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, and everyone already knows each other's goals, so roles with opposed aims can plan with full knowledge of the clash.
pros: Plans can be made with open facts.
Nobody is surprised by a hidden goal.
cons: Rivals can predict each other too well.
Open aims can make play slow.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards others cannot see, so roles with opposed aims have to guess what a rival holds, though the goals themselves are known.
pros: Players hint, bluff and guess.
Hidden cards add doubt to known aims.
cons: Guessing may overshadow the role goals.
A rival's hand can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, so opposed aims are known for open roles but not for hidden ones, and nobody can be sure who pulls against whom.
pros: Doubt gives open aims a twist.
Players study each other's choices.
cons: Secret roles can blur the known clash.
Distrust can spread among friends.

pairs.tendency: Players use clues to find hidden facts, and roles with opposed aims may share or hold back clues, since a clue that helps one role may hurt another.
pros: Clues have a clear reason to be hidden.
Roles learn each other's aims by reasoning.
cons: Hiding clues can stall the game.
Reasoning can take over from the clash.

pairs.tendency: Players lie about what they hold, so roles with opposed aims can bluff about both their cards and their aim, though the goals are known.
pros: Bluffs add depth to open goals.
Players learn to read each other.
cons: Lies can blur which aim is real.
Some players dislike lying at the table.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule that the others find by breaking it, so roles with opposed aims have to work out what the rules allow.
pros: Players discover the system as they go.
Rules are felt, not read.
cons: Newcomers can be shut out.
Goals may be lost while learning the rules.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer but can only hint, so roles with opposed aims hint toward their own measure while others guess.
pros: Hints show how each role thinks.
Guessing keeps everyone involved.
cons: Hints can be read in different ways.
The clash may be lost in the guessing.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over as players explore, so roles with opposed aims find out what the world holds together, and a find for one role may be a loss for another.
pros: Discovery gives the clash surprises.
Roles share the thrill of exploring.
cons: A hidden area can favour one role by luck.
Early finds may set the clash for the whole game.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up, so roles with opposed aims can see part of what is available and plan around an open hand.
pros: Open cards give some clear facts.
Players reason with partial knowledge.
cons: The open hand may favour one role.
One shown hand is a small part of the clash.

pairs.tendency: Some scores are hidden, so roles with opposed aims cannot be sure who is ahead on which measure, though they know each other's goals.
pros: Players have to judge progress without a count.
Final scores can be a surprise.
cons: Players may guess wrongly and play too safe.
Hidden scores can feel like hidden cheating.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so each role can answer the last move on its own measure, and the clash plays out in clear steps.
pros: Each move can be weighed in turn.
Players can watch and learn the clash.
cons: Waiting for a turn can be slow.
Players may lose track of the clash while waiting.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at once, so roles with opposed aims commit before they see each other's move, and the clash lands in a single reveal.
pros: Players act without waiting.
Reveals show the clash at once.
cons: Players may not have time to weigh aims.
Mistakes pile up before anyone can fix them.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so roles with opposed aims race to grab what suits their own measure, and the fastest tends to get there first.
pros: Fast, lively and tense.
Aims are chased with real urgency.
cons: Quicker players can take everything.
Few chances to talk or bargain over goals.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so roles with opposed aims have little time to weigh their own measure against the rest, and a rushed move can give ground.
pros: A clock keeps the game moving.
Quick choices show what a role values first.
cons: Hurried players may forget their own goals.
Players who think slowly lose their turn.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over real days or weeks, so roles with opposed aims live with their moves, and the clash builds over time.
pros: Players have time to think and talk.
Moves have lasting weight.
cons: Players may forget the game between turns.
The clash may fade over days.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose, so roles with opposed aims pause before each move and think about whose aim they are serving.
pros: Slowness makes room for the goals.
Players think before they act.
cons: Slow play can feel dull.
The pace may take the edge off the clash.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so roles with opposed aims have less time for each decision, and the clash comes to a rush near the end.
pros: Rising speed brings out the clash.
The ending feels tense and lively.
cons: Late rushes can wipe out careful plans.
Players have little time to talk about goals.

pairs.tendency: A hit or a throw gives a second go, so a role may gain two moves toward its aim before a rival can answer, and the clash tilts toward the lucky.
pros: Extra turns can feel thrilling.
Roles may reach their aims faster.
cons: A lucky run can end the clash early.
Players waiting for a turn may lose heart.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages with different rules, so roles with opposed aims may agree in one stage and clash in the next, and first-stage choices shape the second.
pros: Early choices carry weight later.
The clash can shift as stages change.
cons: Players have to learn more than one set of rules.
A strong first stage can lock in the result.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, and each role pulls it toward its own aim, so players see what happens when opposed measures act on one set of causes.
pros: Causes and effects are easy to follow.
Roles show different sides of one system.
cons: Roles may stop caring about the system itself.
One role's win can crash the whole model.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a real group with its own needs, and since needs differ, the game shows why people disagree before anyone is wrong.
pros: Roles stand for real groups.
Players see each group's reasons.
cons: A role can feel like a stereotype.
Players may ignore the real group's view.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited stock, and each role wants a different share, so what one role takes leaves less for the rest.
pros: The stock makes the clash plain.
Players feel the cost of taking.
cons: One role may drain the stock early.
The clash may end when the stock runs out.

pairs.tendency: A move shows its effect only a few rounds later, so roles with opposed aims may not see who caused a harm until it has grown.
pros: Players learn to think ahead.
Cause and effect show up in time.
cons: Blame can be hard to place.
Players may lose track of what caused what.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule for all and play on, and each role judges the rule by its own measure, so the same rule is a gain for one and a loss for another.
pros: Rule changes show who gains and who loses.
Players can test a rule safely.
cons: Roles may refuse a rule that costs them.
The rule can end up chosen by the loudest.

pairs.tendency: After play everyone talks it through, so roles with opposed aims can say what they wanted and see how their goals pulled against others.
pros: Talk brings out each role's reasons.
Players link the clash to real life.
cons: Roles may defend themselves instead of listening.
Short debriefs can skip the harder goals.

pairs.tendency: Changes can't be undone, so each role's push toward its own aim leaves a mark, and the next game starts from what the clash left behind.
pros: Marks show what each role did.
Players feel the weight of moves.
cons: An early loss can follow a role to the end.
Roles may be too wary to push their aim.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point, and opposed aims inside the rules show which role the game favours, so the argument is in how goals are scored.
pros: Scoring shows what the game values.
Players can question the point made.
cons: The rules may tip the clash toward one role.
Players may take the game's point as fixed.

pairs.tendency: What happens in play carries into real life, so roles with opposed aims may have real cost to a clash, such as a promise or a friendship.
pros: The clash feels real to players.
Players care about each outcome.
cons: Real stakes can make a role play for safety.
A real clash can spill past the table.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for things that matter, so roles with opposed aims chase different values, and a gain for one value is a number to give up for another.
pros: Numbers make the clash plain.
Players see how values pull against one another.
cons: Players may chase points and forget the values.
Some values get left out of a count.

pairs.tendency: Players try out a way of living that does not exist yet, so roles with opposed aims try to live it from their own side and meet the friction.
pros: Roles feel how a future might rub.
Players find tensions before real life does.
cons: A rehearsal may be too neat to be real.
Roles may agree too easily for the trial.

pairs.tendency: Play opens on a described situation, so roles with opposed aims begin from who is where and what is at stake, and the clash grows from that scene.
pros: Everyone starts from one shared scene.
The clash has an obvious cause.
cons: A scene may favour one role from the start.
A long description can delay play.

pairs.tendency: A player explains why a move works and the table decides, so roles with opposed aims argue for their own measure and a rival can argue against it.
pros: Players speak up for their aims.
Moves have reasons attached.
cons: Talk can favour the loudest speaker.
Decisions can take a long time.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points for players to say what they notice, so roles with opposed aims can say what the clash looks like as it grows.
pros: The clash is named while it is live.
Players can change approach midway.
cons: Pauses can break the pace.
Players may say what is expected, not what they feel.

pairs.tendency: The same game is played again with one thing changed, so roles with opposed aims can see how a small shift moves the clash.
pros: Players see cause and effect in the clash.
Roles can try a different approach.
cons: A second round may repeat the same fight.
Players may try to copy the first win.

pairs.tendency: The game says what it left out of the real situation, so players know the clash between roles is simpler than the real one and where it stops.
pros: Players know the limits of the model.
Opposed goals are not taken as the whole truth.
cons: A long list of gaps can distract.
Players may disagree on what was left out.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about helped design it, so opposed aims in the roles come from real accounts, and players can check that they ring true.
pros: Roles reflect real views.
Players trust the clash shown.
cons: Designers may disagree about which aims to include.
Real people may find a role too thin.

pairs.tendency: Each player is one link in a chain with its own measure, so a maker wants to sell and a shop wants stock, and what helps one link can leave another with little.
pros: Each link has a clear aim of its own.
Players see how a choice reaches others.
cons: Links may blame each other for shortages.
Players can lose sight of the whole chain.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own stock and orders, so roles with opposed aims guess at a rival's goal and cannot see where the measures pull apart.
pros: Players feel what limited sight does.
Guessing about others is part of play.
cons: Players may blame others for what they cannot see.
Opposed goals can stay hidden for too long.

pairs.tendency: The slowest step sets the pace, so a role whose aim is speed and a role whose aim is care may pull against each other at that one step.
pros: One step makes the clash easy to find.
Players see why speeding up elsewhere does nothing.
cons: The role at the bottleneck gets all the blame.
Other roles may sit and wait.

pairs.tendency: Goods are made ahead or only on order, and roles with opposed aims favour one or the other, such as a maker wanting steady work and a shop wanting little stock.
pros: The two ways can be compared directly.
Each role has a reason for its way.
cons: Players may not see why the other way suits a rival.
The clash can turn into a choice of method.

pairs.tendency: Large batches suit a role that wants low cost per item, and small batches suit one that wants a fast reply, so the roles pull on the same dial.
pros: One dial shows the clash plainly.
Players feel the trade between cost and speed.
cons: One role may set the batch for all.
The clash may shrink to a single number.

pairs.tendency: Machines fail by chance, so a role that wants steady output and a role that wants low upkeep cost pull against each other over repairs.
pros: Failures give roles a clear reason to argue.
Players learn why upkeep costs.
cons: Chance can decide who suffers a failure.
A failure may be blamed on the wrong role.

pairs.tendency: Too much stock costs money and too little loses sales, so roles with opposed aims each fear a different mistake and pull toward their own side.
pros: Both kinds of error have a clear cost.
Players see why no one setting suits all.
cons: Roles may settle on a middle that suits none.
Players can feel they lose either way.

pairs.tendency: Players read a short scene, such as a flooded village road, then roll and move along a path that runs through it.
pros: The scene gives each space a meaning.
Moves feel like a journey with a reason.
cons: Dice can pull attention away from the scene.
The opening text is forgotten after a few turns.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads the opening scene, then picks cards from a shared pool to answer it, so each pick is read against what was described.
pros: Picks share a common reference point.
Players can explain why they chose.
cons: Picks may drift away from the scene.
A long scene slows the first round.

pairs.tendency: After reading the opening scene, players bid for what it makes scarce, such as water in a dry village, so prices follow the story.
pros: Prices have a reason players can name.
Bids start from a common picture.
cons: Rich players can ignore the scene.
Bidding can take over from the opening.

pairs.tendency: The opening scene sets what is at risk, and each turn players decide how far to push before losing what they have.
pros: The risk feels like it belongs to someone.
Players can say what they are gambling.
cons: Busts can feel like dice, not the scene.
Cautious players may stop before the scene matters.

pairs.tendency: The opening scene says who holds which part of the map and what has just happened there, so the fight for areas starts from a story.
pros: Starting claims have reasons.
Players read the map as a place.
cons: Players may argue about who the scene favours.
Fights can bury the opening.

pairs.tendency: The scene names the jobs that need doing, such as repairs after a storm, and players place workers on them in the first round.
pros: Each action space has a clear cause.
Players start with a shared to-do list.
cons: Some jobs are obvious from the scene.
Players may place by habit, not the story.

pairs.tendency: Players read the opening scene and then build patterns on the board that stand for how they answer it.
pros: The build starts with a reason.
Calm, thoughtful opening.
cons: The scene and the pattern can feel unconnected.
Players may stop thinking about the scene once building starts.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the problem, and players hold cards that are tools for it, deciding which to play now and which to keep.
pros: Cards have a clear job.
Saving a card means saving it for something.
cons: Hands can become a puzzle apart from the scene.
A long scene crowds out reading the cards.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then play tricks that stand for the contest it describes, such as two sides over one market stall.
pros: Familiar play with a story behind it.
Winning a trick has a reason.
cons: The tie to the scene can feel thin.
Strong hands still decide a lot.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who has what and what is at stake, and players trade and make deals from those positions.
pros: Deals have something concrete to rest on.
Talk starts quickly.
cons: Players may argue about the facts of the scene.
A strong starting role can dominate the talk.

pairs.tendency: The opening scene names what everyone is short of, and players collect the sets that would fix it.
pros: Goals follow from the story.
Players know what a set is for.
cons: Collecting can turn into a checklist.
The scene is forgotten once sets build.

pairs.tendency: Players read a scene of a place, such as a village by a river, then place tiles to extend it from where it began.
pros: The map grows from a known start.
Tiles have a reason to go where they go.
cons: Early tiles can lock the map to the scene.
Tile luck can cut across the story.

pairs.tendency: The scene gives the first line, and each player answers in turn, so the game grows as a chain out of what was described.
pros: The first answer is easy to make.
Everyone shares the same setting.
cons: Players may drift from the scene.
A thin scene leaves too little to answer.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene aloud once, then play without speaking, so what the scene said is the only thing they share.
pros: Everyone starts from one picture.
Silence feels heavier after a clear scene.
cons: Players may read it differently with no way to check.
Nobody can ask what a line meant.

pairs.tendency: Play starts from a described scene, and later turns change the rules, so the scene may stop fitting the game.
pros: The scene gives a start to measure change against.
Players notice how far the rules have moved.
cons: Changed rules can make the scene untrue.
Players may argue whether a change breaks the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who each character is, where they stand and what just happened, and players then speak as those characters.
pros: Characters start with a place and a problem.
Players get into role quickly.
cons: Players may add facts the scene did not give.
A long scene uses up play time.

pairs.tendency: Players read a scene and then play with their hands, such as stacking or flicking, which has little to do with what was described.
pros: The scene gives the task a frame.
Short, lively contrast.
cons: Hands-on play can feel apart from the story.
Concentrating on balance pushes the scene out of mind.

pairs.tendency: The opening scene gives a starting place, and players draw the map outward from it as the game goes on.
pros: The first drawing has a start.
The map holds together as it grows.
cons: Players may draw things the scene ruled out.
A detailed scene leaves little to add.

pairs.tendency: After a scene that says who holds what, players ask each other for cards, and each question draws on what the scene made known.
pros: Questions have a known starting point.
Players can reason about who has what.
cons: The scene can matter little to the asking.
Questions can repeat.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who runs the bank and what players stand to win or lose, and then bets are placed against it at fixed odds.
pros: Players know whose side the bank is on.
Bets start with a reason.
cons: The odds can matter more than the scene.
The player acting as bank is stuck in one role.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then bet on a throw that stands for chance in it, such as whether the rains come.
pros: A bet has a reason beyond the dice.
Players see what luck is deciding.
cons: A single throw can end the scene's meaning.
Nobody can steer the outcome.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each player stands to gain or lose, and chips go in the pot while hidden hands are held.
pros: Stakes start out clear.
Each bet carries part of the story.
cons: Bluffing can pull away from the scene.
Folding players watch the story without acting.

pairs.tendency: After reading the scene, each player builds the side, deck or army that suits it, so players arrive in the scene with different answers.
pros: Choices come from a shared picture.
Players can compare how each read the scene.
cons: Players may read the scene as a puzzle to solve.
Building can take longer than the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what is possible, and before play each player calls what they will do, such as take three tricks.
pros: Calls rest on a known situation.
Players can judge a call against the scene.
cons: A scene that is too vague makes calls guesses.
A failed call can feel like blame.

pairs.tendency: The scene says which side each piece starts on, and captured pieces change sides, so the story shifts as pieces change hands.
pros: Changes of side read as events.
The opening gives a baseline to compare with.
cons: The starting picture soon no longer holds.
Players may stop caring who started where.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who has been caught and why, and teammates then try to free them, so rescue has a reason from the first move.
pros: Rescue has a clear target.
Teams share a cause.
cons: A plain scene can make rescues feel like a chore.
Caught players wait.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out who holds the board and what is at stake, and players then take pieces by surrounding them.
pros: Early positions have a meaning.
Players see land as something held.
cons: The scene can matter little once surrounding starts.
Early positions can feel fixed.

pairs.tendency: The scene shows who is ahead, and the game then helps those behind, so players can see how far the help is meant to reach.
pros: Players can see why help is given.
The opening scene sets the size of the gap.
cons: Help can feel like it ignores the scene.
Leaders may feel the story is bent against them.

pairs.tendency: Players read a scene, then dice or cards decide what happens, so the scene sets the stage and plays no part afterwards.
pros: The scene frames what chance does.
Play stays quick.
cons: Players make no choices to tie to the scene.
The scene can feel like decoration.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who is It and why, and the chase starts from that, so players run or tag with a reason.
pros: The chase starts with a story.
Everyone knows the reason at once.
cons: Running leaves little time for the scene.
The scene can feel like a delay before play.

pairs.tendency: The scene shows who stands where, and each turn a player picks who is hit, helped or traded with from that picture.
pros: Targets have clear reasons.
Players can explain why they picked someone.
cons: Players may gang up on the player the scene weakens.
Early picks can fix grudges.

pairs.tendency: After reading the scene, players try to link two sides of the board with a chain that stands for it, such as a road between two villages.
pros: The chain has a meaning.
Goals are easy to see.
cons: The scene can fade into a puzzle of lines.
The opening can feel unrelated to the chain.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets up opposing forces, and each choice beats one other and loses to a third, so no stance wins every time.
pros: The cycle feels like a real standoff.
Everyone sees why a counter exists.
cons: The cycle can feel arbitrary against the scene.
A fixed cycle can feel solved after a few rounds.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then show pairs or runs of cards to score, while the scene frames what a combination stands for.
pros: Each combination has a meaning.
Scoring moments are clear.
cons: A combination can score without touching the scene.
Players may collect for the score alone.

pairs.tendency: The scene places each player's role, and each role has a power nobody else has, so unequal starts begin in the story.
pros: Powers feel earned by the role.
Players see why they differ.
cons: Some roles can look stronger from the scene.
Players may argue about fairness at the start.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what is at stake, and part-way through a player may offer to double it, so the first reading shapes how big the offer feels.
pros: Doubling feels like a real risk.
Players know what is at stake from the start.
cons: A second offer can break from the scene.
The other player can feel pushed.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out the sides, and when a capture is possible a player has to take it, so the story is steered by what is forced.
pros: The forced move has a context.
Players can plan a trap from the scene.
cons: Forced moves can feel unrelated to the story.
Players may feel the board plays for them.

pairs.tendency: The scene says where each character starts, and as they grow, later challenges meet more power than they began with.
pros: Growth is measured against the start.
Players see how far they have come.
cons: Early scenes can look small by the end.
Players may chase power over the story.

pairs.tendency: The scene gives the first items, and each player repeats the list and adds one, so the list grows from what was described.
pros: Everyone begins from one list.
Memory is tied to a picture.
cons: The list can drift from the scene.
The list gets long and drags.

pairs.tendency: The scene shows who starts ahead, and the stronger side starts with less, so the gap in the story is visible on the board.
pros: Players see why one side starts lower.
Starts feel more even.
cons: The handicap can look arbitrary against the scene.
The stronger player may feel held back.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what has been lost or hidden and who is looking, and the hunt starts from that.
pros: The search has a reason.
Everyone knows what they are looking for.
cons: The scene can give away where to look.
The hunt can overtake the story.

pairs.tendency: The scene lays out who stands where on the board, and pieces then hop over each other, so every hop changes that picture.
pros: Each jump changes the opening scene.
Moves are easy to follow.
cons: Hops can feel unconnected to the story.
The opening is gone after a few turns.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then roll dice, keep some and roll the rest, so the scene frames what the dice stand for.
pros: Each keep has a reason.
Players weigh risk against the scene.
cons: Dice can stand apart from the story.
The scene is rarely referred to again.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out where each piece stands, and landing on a piece sends it back to start, so the opening position keeps being redrawn.
pros: Players remember where they started.
Setbacks have a reason in the story.
cons: Being sent back can feel like losing the scene.
Early leaders can lose a lot.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each side holds, and making a row of three lets a player take one of the other's pieces.
pros: Starting holdings have a meaning.
Taking a piece has a reason.
cons: The row can matter more than the scene.
Early rows can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then build words from letters, and a scene about a place or a trade suggests which words to look for.
pros: The scene hints at useful words.
Players start with the same set of ideas.
cons: Words can drift from the scene.
The scene helps some players more than others.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the first tile, and players add tiles that match the open ends, so the line grows out of what was described.
pros: The line has a known start.
Players follow each other's moves easily.
cons: The matching rule can feel apart from the scene.
A missed turn can leave a player out.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each player holds, and sets laid face up grow as others add to them, so the story builds in view.
pros: Everyone can see what has been laid.
Shared sets feel like shared history.
cons: The scene can fade behind the sets.
One set can grow too long to read.

pairs.tendency: The scene explains what each player or piece can do once, so spending a power is a choice with a known setting.
pros: Powers have a reason in the story.
The opening shows when to hold or spend.
cons: Players may spend too soon.
Used powers can leave the scene looking empty.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the stakes, and each move is offered to another player who may turn it down, so both read from the same picture.
pros: Both players know the stakes.
Offers feel fair.
cons: A flat scene leaves little to judge an offer by.
Refusals can slow play.

pairs.tendency: The scene gives the first message, and it travels from player to player, changing on the way, so players can compare the end with the start.
pros: The change is easy to see.
Everyone starts from one version.
cons: Players may remember the scene differently.
The gap can be blamed on listening, not on the system.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each player faces, and before play they pass cards to another player without seeing what comes back.
pros: Passing has a reason.
Players read the scene as they choose.
cons: The passed cards can bring a surprise.
A scene that is too vague makes passing a guess.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the opening situation, and the other picks a side, so the person who sets up the scene tries to make both sides even.
pros: The setter has to think about both sides.
Both sides begin on a shared picture.
cons: The setter may not see where it tips.
A strong picker can still win.

pairs.tendency: The scene shows where each piece starts, and a piece that reaches the far end turns into something stronger, so the journey is part of the story.
pros: The trip across has a reason.
Players see how a piece changes.
cons: The scene can be forgotten at the far end.
Players may push forward at any cost.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the course and who runs each leg, and teams then pass the baton from one player to the next.
pros: Every leg has a place in the story.
Teams share one picture of the course.
cons: The scene may matter little once running starts.
A weak leg holds the team up.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what is at stake, and players build shapes that cannot be captured, so safety has a meaning in the story.
pros: Safety has a reason.
Shapes give a clear goal.
cons: Safe play can crowd out the scene.
Players may build only to be safe.

pairs.tendency: The scene names what matters, and the cards worth points are named in advance, so players take tricks to reach them.
pros: The prizes follow from the story.
Players know what the game values.
cons: Players can chase cards and ignore the scene.
Early hints give some players an edge.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then use cards turned up in the middle, mixing them with their own, so everyone draws on the same picture.
pros: Shared cards ground the scene.
Players compare uses of one card.
cons: Shared cards can feel apart from the scene.
A strong shared card can decide the round.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what everyone puts in and why, and one player takes the pot, so the opening sets what the pot is worth.
pros: The pot has a reason.
Players share a picture of what is at stake.
cons: A growing pot can matter more than the scene.
Losers see their stake go.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each pit stands for, such as a field, and players scoop and drop seeds into the pits that follow.
pros: Each pit has a meaning.
Counting is easy to follow.
cons: The scene can fade into counting.
Players may not link pits to the story.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what is missing, and an extra hand is dealt to the middle, so a player may take it, swap it or buy it to fix the gap.
pros: The spare hand has a story.
Players choose with a clear reason.
cons: The first player to take it can gain a lot.
The scene can feel like set dressing.

pairs.tendency: The scene explains the place the track runs through, and special squares, such as a safe stop or a flood, give it detail.
pros: Squares feel like part of the place.
Each rule has a reason.
cons: The squares can outweigh the opening.
Players may read too much into them.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each player has to spend, and each card or item has a price, so players choose what to buy for the situation.
pros: Costs have a clear reason.
Players weigh needs against means.
cons: Players may spend by price alone.
A thin scene leaves nothing to weigh against.

pairs.tendency: The scene says where trouble is, and players share out a fixed amount between places or jobs, so each split answers what was read.
pros: Splits have a reason.
Trade-offs are easy to see.
cons: Players may split by habit.
A vague scene leaves the split a guess.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then keep moving until a signal, such as music stopping, so the scene sets why everyone is on the move.
pros: Everyone starts from one situation.
Play is lively.
cons: The signal can pull attention from the scene.
The last player caught can feel singled out.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each player needs, and they swap cards before the hand is played, so every swap answers the opening.
pros: Swaps have a clear goal.
Players use the scene to justify a swap.
cons: The scene may matter little to swaps.
Hoarded cards can limit what is on offer.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what everyone is working for, and a player may take the whole discard pile, so one choice moves a lot of cards.
pros: Taking the pile has a reason.
Players read each discard against the scene.
cons: A big pile can stand apart from the story.
Players may wait to take a big pile.

pairs.tendency: The scene says which side has the advantage, and one suit is named trump for the hand, so strength in play follows the story.
pros: The trump suit has a reason.
Players learn what the strong suit stands for.
cons: The scene can fade as tricks continue.
A low trump can feel odd against the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out two places at once, and each player plays one side on each board, so players read both from one opening.
pros: Both boards share a story.
Players see one choice felt in two places.
cons: Two boards can split attention from the scene.
Setting up and explaining both takes time.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what is scarce, and a wild card can stand in for anything, so it may fill a gap the scene named.
pros: Wild cards have an obvious use.
A missing piece can be solved quickly.
cons: Wild cards can work against the scene.
Their use can feel like an easy way out.

pairs.tendency: The scene describes a place with no edge, such as a ring road, and the board joins its sides so a line carries on at the other side.
pros: The board matches the place.
Moves feel open.
cons: Players may lose track of where they are.
The scene can feel unlike the board.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret, and the others ask yes-or-no questions, using the scene to guess which questions are worth asking.
pros: The scene narrows the questions.
Players start with something to ask.
cons: A thin scene leaves too wide a field.
A rich scene can give the secret away.

pairs.tendency: The scene says where everyone starts and what the finish stands for, and the game is a race to reach it.
pros: The finish has a meaning.
Everyone sees the same starting line.
cons: The race can crowd out the scene.
The leader soon stops needing it.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what matters, and at the end the highest score wins, so points are meant to reflect what was described.
pros: Scoring links back to the story.
Players compare scores against the opening.
cons: Points can drift from what the scene valued.
Players may chase points alone.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who is at risk and why, and players drop out one by one until one is left, so each exit has a story.
pros: Dropping out has a reason.
Players follow who is in danger.
cons: Players out early wait.
Early exits can lose the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene shows the danger, and the whole team tries to last through it, so everyone reads the same threat before the first move.
pros: Everyone sees the threat at once.
The team starts from one picture.
cons: A bleak scene can leave a team feeling it cannot win.
One reader can end up leading.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out a problem, and the group works together to reach a goal that answers it.
pros: Everyone knows the goal and why.
Planning starts at once.
cons: A clear goal leaves little to argue about.
Some players can follow without reading it.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads the same scene, then each player holds a secret goal inside it, so the same facts mean different things to each.
pros: One scene gives many motives.
Players compare their reading of it.
cons: Secret goals can pull from the scene.
Players may not know what they are aiming at.

pairs.tendency: The scene opens a story, and the game ends when the story does, so the first scene sets what an ending has to answer.
pros: The ending ties back to the opening.
The whole game reads as one story.
cons: A fixed scene can make the ending feel set.
A thin scene leaves too much open.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read and played from, but nobody wins, so players look at what happened against where it began.
pros: The opening gives something to look back at.
Gentle comparison at the end.
cons: Without a goal, the scene gets less attention.
Players may not know what the game was for.

pairs.tendency: Players read the same scene, then each says what doing well means for them in it, so goals start from one place.
pros: Goals have a shared background.
Players can compare how each read it.
cons: A goal can ignore the scene.
Players may set goals too easily met.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what is at risk, and play continues until one player loses and the others are safe.
pros: The loss has a story.
Everyone knows what is being avoided.
cons: One player can feel singled out.
The scene may be forgotten once the loser is clear.

pairs.tendency: The scene opens a situation that does not have an ending, and the aim is to keep it going, so what was read in turn one stays in view.
pros: The scene can be revisited again and again.
Play can build a long story.
cons: A first scene can go stale over many sessions.
Early details can be lost with time.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out a situation and the game refuses to be won, so the opening gives players something to push against.
pros: The refusal has a clear subject.
Players talk about why it cannot be won.
cons: A scene may make the loss feel planned.
Players may feel the game is hiding something.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what the layout stands for, and a lone player tries to clear or fill it, so the table is read as a situation.
pros: The cards stand for something.
Players have a clear picture of the task.
cons: The scene can feel like decoration on a puzzle.
A solo player has nobody to ask about it.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read once, and then several short games are played from it, so the opening can be compared across rounds.
pros: The same start can be played again.
Players see how games differ from one scene.
cons: Players may stop reading it after round one.
Repeated play can feel tedious.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what counts against players, and the one with the fewest points wins, so every point is read as a cost.
pros: Points have a story as costs.
Players see where the scene hurts.
cons: Avoiding points can drain the scene's meaning.
Players may play too safe.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what the target stands for, and a player has to land on it exactly, so the opening sets what a near miss means.
pros: The target has a reason.
Near misses feel like part of the story.
cons: Exact landing can feel apart from the scene.
A strong lead can stall for many turns.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what everyone wants to avoid giving away, and players try to lose, so the scene reads backwards from its usual sense.
pros: The reversal is easy to notice.
Players re-read the opening in a new way.
cons: The scene can seem to say one thing and the goal another.
Players may mix up what they are after.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads the same scene, then each builds their own answer alongside the others without much contact.
pros: All answers come from one start.
Players can compare at the end.
cons: Little contact during play.
The scene is rarely discussed.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who is on which side and what has just happened, and players then attack and sabotage each other from that start.
pros: Conflict has a cause.
Players know whom they are up against.
cons: Grudges can outlast the scene.
Players may attack for the sake of it.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets up the shared board, and players change it, so each player's moves affect the others without an attack.
pros: The board shows what has changed.
Effects are felt, not aimed.
cons: Effects can go unseen.
The scene can mislead about who is affected.

pairs.tendency: The whole team reads the scene together and then works against the game itself, so the group begins with one shared picture.
pros: Everyone starts with the same facts.
Talk starts at once.
cons: One reader can speak for the group.
Little tension in the opening.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads the same scene, and players mostly work together while each holds a small private reason to come out ahead.
pros: The common start makes secret aims stand out.
Players can see who gains.
cons: Private aims can pull away from the scene.
Trust can break early.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what each team stands for and what it wants, and the two teams then compete from that start.
pros: Each team has a reason to compete.
Teams talk about the scene together.
cons: A scene that favours one team can feel unfair.
One strong reader can speak for the whole team.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads the scene, then one player secretly works against the team, so the opening is the picture the traitor has to bend.
pros: Odd moves stand out against the scene.
Players know what normal looks like.
cons: The scene may hand the traitor an easy excuse.
Accusations can upset players.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read first, then players write their turns to each other over days or weeks, so the opening is what they keep returning to.
pros: A shared start holds players together over a long gap.
Letters have something to answer.
cons: The scene can be misremembered over weeks.
One late reply can leave the opening cold.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who is missing and what they left behind, and the others play for or around them, so their absence has a reason.
pros: Absence becomes part of the story.
Players think about who is missing.
cons: The absent person can be reduced to a prop.
The scene can feel heavy.

pairs.tendency: The game master describes the opening situation and the others respond, so the scene is the first thing the master gives them.
pros: One voice sets the scene for all.
Players know where they are at once.
cons: A game master can lock the scene too tightly.
Players may wait for the next description.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets up a game played in a street or a park, so passers-by can join in from what they can see.
pros: Anyone can pick the situation up from a sign.
The setting is the street itself.
cons: Passers-by may miss the scene.
A long reading is hard to hold in a crowd.

pairs.tendency: The scene describes who is alone and who stands against them, so the lone player and the group begin from one story.
pros: The imbalance has a reason.
Everyone knows who stands where.
cons: The lone player can feel exposed.
The scene can make the group seem to pile on.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read by one player, who then plays through it against the pack, so the opening is the player's own picture.
pros: The player starts with a clear setting.
Results are easy to compare with the start.
cons: Nobody else shares the reading.
The scene can feel like a note to oneself.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the stage, and dice and random draws decide most of what follows, so the scene shows little of what players do.
pros: The scene gives luck a setting.
Play stays easy to start.
cons: Few choices tie back to the scene.
The opening can seem to matter little.

pairs.tendency: The scene names what could go wrong, and players have ways to soften a poor roll, such as rerolls, so they prepare against it.
pros: Players can see what to prepare for.
Preparation has a reason.
cons: Softening luck can ignore the scene.
Preparation can fill the opening.

pairs.tendency: The scene gives the situation, and players' choices drive play with a small amount of luck, so planning and the scene go together.
pros: Choices start from clear facts.
A little luck keeps it open.
cons: Experienced players tend to read the scene faster.
A flat scene gives nothing to plan from.

pairs.tendency: The scene lays everything out, and only players' choices drive what comes next, so each outcome follows from the opening.
pros: Results have a reason.
Planning starts from clear facts.
cons: A fixed opening can leave the play solved.
Practised players gain from the first move.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets a question or a worry, and what the dice or cards show is read as a message about it.
pros: The sign has a subject.
Players think about the scene again.
cons: Players may read too much into a throw.
A vague scene makes any sign fit.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene together, then try to act at the same moment, so a shared picture helps them sense each other.
pros: Shared reading builds shared timing.
Players feel closer at the start.
cons: Players who read it differently drift apart.
Attunement is hard to explain to newcomers.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets where the story starts, and dice rolls are looked up on tables that say what happens next, such as who is met on the road.
pros: Tables continue what the scene began.
The story grows from a clear start.
cons: Table results can break from the scene.
Players may stop reading the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read aloud and every card and move is visible, so nothing is hidden from the start.
pros: Everyone starts with the same facts.
Talk comes easily.
cons: Nothing is left to find out.
Quick players can read the scene for others.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads one scene, then each holds cards nobody else sees, so the same picture meets different private knowledge.
pros: Shared start, private moves.
Hints can refer back to the scene.
cons: Players can invent facts that fit their hand.
Cards may not tie to the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene is public, but each player secretly holds a role in it, so the same facts hide different aims.
pros: Everyone starts with a shared picture.
The scene gives clues for guessing roles.
cons: Players may argue about what the scene allowed.
A role may fit the scene poorly.

pairs.tendency: The scene lays out the known facts, and players use clues to work out the hidden ones, so the opening is the first clue.
pros: The scene gives a start for reasoning.
Everyone has the same facts to work from.
cons: A detailed scene can give too much away.
A short scene can leave nothing to reason from.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what is true, and players can lie about what they hold, so everyone can check a claim against the opening.
pros: Lies can be tested against the scene.
Mind games have a clear base.
cons: Players can argue about what the scene said.
Lies can drift from the scene.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and everyone else learns it by breaking it, while the opening scene gives few clues about it.
pros: The scene is a place to test the rule from.
Players learn through the story.
