cons: The scene can hide too much.
Newcomers can feel lost.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read by everyone, and one player who knows the answer can only give hints, so the opening is the common ground for them.
pros: The hints connect to what everyone read.
Players share a picture to guess within.
cons: A thin scene gives few hints to use.
The hinter can feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: The scene tells players what they know of the place, and the map is turned over bit by bit, so each reveal is set against that opening.
pros: Reveals are felt against what was known.
The unknown has a clear edge.
cons: The first scene can mislead about what lies ahead.
Players can feel the opening told them too little.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the situation, and one hand is laid face up for all to see, so everyone can watch it used against the opening.
pros: One open hand grounds the scene.
Players can follow a plan out loud.
cons: The open hand can drown out the scene.
One player plays two hands.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what is at stake, and some points are kept secret, so players guess how others read the opening.
pros: Players wonder who is ahead.
The scene gives a basis for guessing.
cons: Guesses can drift from the scene.
Nobody can add up scores for certain.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene together, then one acts at a time, so the first mover sets a precedent the others answer.
pros: Everyone reads the scene before anyone acts.
Turns are easy to follow.
cons: The first mover shapes the story.
Waiting players can drift from the scene.

pairs.tendency: Everyone reads the scene, then all choose in secret and reveal together, so every player acts on the same opening.
pros: One scene, many answers at once.
Nobody waits.
cons: Players may read the scene differently.
Quick readers can start before others finish.

pairs.tendency: Players read the scene, then anyone acts at any moment, so those who read quickest act first.
pros: The scene gives everyone a start.
Play is lively.
cons: Slow readers can fall behind at once.
The scene is hard to keep in mind at speed.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read first, then each turn has a clock, so players decide how much of the scene to weigh in a short time.
pros: The scene shapes quick choices.
Players know what to look for.
cons: Reading the scene eats into the clock.
Rushed moves can ignore the scene.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the opening, and play runs over real days or weeks, so players come back to it between moves.
pros: Waiting becomes part of the story.
The opening stays in mind across days.
cons: Players may forget the opening over time.
Slow play can lose interest.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read slowly and play pauses before each move, so the opening gets time to sink in.
pros: The scene gets full attention.
Slow play suits a careful scene.
cons: A long wait can make the scene stale.
Impatient players may skim it.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the opening, and then the game speeds up, so the opening is only briefly in view before everything rushes.
pros: A clear start before the rush.
Contrast between slow and fast.
cons: The scene is quickly forgotten.
Players may skim it to start.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the stage, and some throws or hits give another go, so a lucky player can act many times in a row.
pros: The scene can explain a lucky run.
Streaks are exciting.
cons: A run can leave the scene behind.
Other players wait.

pairs.tendency: The scene opens the first stage, and later stages have different rules, so what was read at the start sets up what comes after.
pros: The scene links the stages.
Early choices carry into later ones.
cons: The scene may fit only the first stage.
Players can forget it by the last stage.

pairs.tendency: The scene describes the real system, such as the wells and fields of a village, and the board then works like it, so moves have real effects.
pros: Players start with the system in mind.
Cause and effect have a reference.
cons: Details can be wrong if the scene is.
A long scene can crowd out play.

pairs.tendency: The scene places each player's real group in the situation and says what has just happened to them, before anyone acts.
pros: Players see the problem from their group's side.
Every role starts with a clear need.
cons: Some groups can look weaker from the scene.
Players may argue about who it favours.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what everyone draws from, such as the water under a village, and how much is left, before the first take.
pros: Everyone sees what is limited.
Taking has a known starting point.
cons: The scene can suggest a safe level to take.
Players may take freely at the start.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets where things stand, and what players do shows its effect only a few rounds later, so they can look back at the opening.
pros: Players can compare then and now.
Delay feels like a real result.
cons: Early moves can seem to do nothing.
The scene is far away when effects arrive.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets what everyone starts from, and players agree a new rule and play on, so they can see what it changed from that start.
pros: The opening is a fixed point to compare with.
The new rule is easy to judge.
cons: A rule may not fit the scene.
Disagreement about the scene can spoil the test.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read at the start, and after the game players talk it through, so they can set what happened against the opening.
pros: The opening is something to return to.
Talk has a clear point of comparison.
cons: Players may remember the scene differently.
The scene can seem to explain too neatly.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the opening, and what players do changes the game for ever, so the next game starts from a different scene.
pros: The change can be seen against the first start.
Choices feel like they count.
cons: The first scene can no longer be replayed.
Players may be afraid to act.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets out a situation, and the rules reward some things and not others, so the game makes a point about it.
pros: The scene gives the argument a subject.
Players can say what the rules reward.
cons: The scene and the rules can disagree.
Players may take the point as settled.

pairs.tendency: The scene opens a situation that has a real counterpart, such as a shared studio, and what happens carries into real life.
pros: Players know what is really at stake.
The opening feels serious.
cons: A scene can start real arguments.
Some players may feel pressured.

pairs.tendency: The scene names what matters, such as health or kindness, and the game turns it into points, so players read each point against the scene.
pros: Points have a meaning.
The scene says what is being counted.
cons: Players can chase points over meaning.
Some values may not fit into points.

pairs.tendency: The scene describes a way of living that does not yet exist, and players try it out, so everyone starts from the same picture of it.
pros: The future has a clear shape.
Players test it from a shared start.
cons: The scene can sound too neat.
Players may play out their own wishes.

pairs.tendency: The scene gives the facts, and a player explains why a move would work, so the table can judge it against what was read.
pros: Arguments rest on stated facts.
The scene limits what can be claimed.
cons: Players may argue about what the scene allowed.
A thin scene leaves too much to argue.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read at the start, and play stops at set points so players can say what has changed since.
pros: The opening is something to compare with.
Pauses have a clear question.
cons: Pauses can break the flow.
Players may forget the scene by the first pause.

pairs.tendency: The same scene opens each game, and one thing is changed between games, so players can compare what happened from an identical start.
pros: The start is the same each time.
Differences are easy to trace.
cons: Players may skim the scene after the first game.
The scene can feel stale by the third game.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read and the game also says what it simplified, so players know where the opening stops being true.
pros: Players know the limits of the scene.
The scene is read with care.
cons: The list of gaps can be long.
Gaps can distract from play.

pairs.tendency: The scene was written with the people whose situation it shows, and they check it rings true, so the opening is theirs.
pros: The scene matches real life.
The people see their own situation.
cons: The scene may be hard to change later.
Several voices can leave the scene unclear.

pairs.tendency: The scene says who is where in the chain, such as maker, wholesaler and shop, and what orders and stock have just come in.
pros: Each link knows its place.
Players start with stock and orders to react to.
cons: A busy scene can bury the order.
Each link may read only its own part.

pairs.tendency: The scene is read aloud, but each player then sees only their own stock and orders, so the shared picture soon gives way to guessing.
pros: The opening is the one shared view.
Players compare what they guessed.
cons: Players can drift apart in what they believe.
The scene can mislead about the rest of the system.

pairs.tendency: The scene says which step is slowest, or leaves players to find it, and then everything after it waits on that step.
pros: The slow step can be found in the story.
Players see why speeding up elsewhere does nothing.
cons: Naming the slow step gives the game away.
A hidden bottleneck can look like plain misfortune.

pairs.tendency: The scene sets the stock and the orders at the start, and players make goods to a guess or only when ordered, so they feel the difference.
pros: Both ways start from the same facts.
The starting stock shows what a guess costs.
cons: A scene can favour one way from the start.
Early guesses can pile up unsold stock.

pairs.tendency: The scene gives the starting stock and orders, and players choose a big batch or one at a time, paying in waiting or in setting up.
pros: Batch choices rest on known facts.
Waiting and setup costs are easy to see.
cons: A scene can favour big batches without saying so.
Players may pick a size without reading it.

pairs.tendency: The scene says which machines are running and how old they are, and breakdowns then arrive without warning, so the opening shows what is at risk.
pros: Players see what could fail.
A breakdown feels like part of the story.
cons: A scene can suggest which machine fails first.
Breakdowns can wipe out a plan.

pairs.tendency: The scene says what stock is held and what is short, and players find that too much costs storage and too little costs lost orders.
pros: Both costs are visible from the start.
Players can see where they begin.
cons: The scene can show the balance too neatly.
Players may feel any choice is costly.

pairs.tendency: Dice set how far you go, but on some turns you argue for a different move and the table decides whether the dice or your reasons count.
pros: Players can answer a poor roll with a reason.
Talk gives a plain dice game some thought.
cons: Arguing against the dice can slow every turn.
Dice and judge can pull opposite ways.

pairs.tendency: You pick a card, then may argue that a card works in a way its text does not say, and the table rules on it.
pros: Cards get used in surprising ways.
Players learn what each card could stand for.
cons: Passed cards get argued over twice.
Picks slow down while the table debates.

pairs.tendency: Players bid, and may argue that a bid ought to count for more, such as a promise or a favour, and the table decides if it is accepted.
pros: Bids can carry reasons, not only money.
Players learn what others value.
cons: Fixed prices get argued over.
Persuasive players win auctions they could not pay for.

pairs.tendency: You press on for more, and when the risk bites you may argue why you ought to be spared, with the table deciding if it holds.
pros: Pleading after a bust is part of the play.
Risk and reasons mix in one moment.
cons: A bust can be talked away.
Players stop trusting the stopping rule.

pairs.tendency: Players claim areas by explaining why a move would work, and the table decides, so who holds a place depends on who argued it well.
pros: Claims come with reasons others can test.
Disputes over land are easy to see.
cons: Louder players can take more ground.
Positions can be settled by talk.

pairs.tendency: Workers go on action spaces, and a player may argue for a use of a space the board does not list, with the table deciding.
pros: Players find uses the designer did not list.
Each space can mean more than one thing.
cons: Spaces get less clear for new players.
Turns slow while players bargain over a spot.

pairs.tendency: You lay pieces into a pattern, and may argue that an odd shape still counts, with the table deciding if it does.
pros: Players see each other's reading of a pattern.
Odd shapes can be tried and talked about.
cons: Scoring needs a ruling each time.
Calm building turns into debate.

pairs.tendency: You hold cards and choose when to play them, and may argue that a card does something its text does not say.
pros: Cards become more flexible.
Saving a card can pay off in a reason.
cons: Hands become hard to value.
Rulings pile up and need remembering.

pairs.tendency: Players follow the suit rules for each trick, but may argue that a card wins or is allowed, and the table rules.
pros: Debate adds a layer to a familiar game.
Players say why one card beat another.
cons: Trick rules lose their firmness.
Stronger talkers win close tricks.

pairs.tendency: Players trade and talk anyway, and now a move itself can be argued for, so persuasion works on both deals and actions.
pros: Talk is the main tool.
Players learn how others reason.
cons: Persuasion can drown out the state of the game.
Quiet players get left out.

pairs.tendency: You collect sets, and may argue that a card counts toward a set it does not belong to, with the table ruling.
pros: Sets can be read in more than one way.
Players explain their thinking while collecting.
cons: Set counts get disputed at the end.
Clear sets lose their clear edges.

pairs.tendency: Tiles go down by edge rules, and a player may argue that a tile fits where it does not match, with the table deciding.
pros: Maps can grow in unplanned ways.
Players explain why a place suits a tile.
cons: Edge rules lose their firmness.
One argued tile can upset a whole map.

pairs.tendency: A line or move is answered with another, and an answer may be argued as a fit, so the table decides if the chain holds.
pros: The chain of answers becomes a conversation.
Players hear each other's reasons.
cons: Replies stop to be judged.
The rhythm of back and forth is lost.

pairs.tendency: Nobody may speak, so a player cannot argue a move aloud, and a judge or the table has to read intent from what is played.
pros: Intent shows through what is played.
Players read each other closely.
cons: The arguing half of the block cannot work.
Rulings may be guesses.

pairs.tendency: Players may change rules and may also argue any move through, so a ruling made today can become a rule tomorrow.
pros: Rules grow out of rulings.
Players see how a precedent forms.
cons: The game can lose its own shape.
Players hold different memories of what is allowed.

pairs.tendency: You speak as a character and say why an action would work for them, and a judge or the table decides what happens.
pros: Actions come from the character's view.
Players can try things no rule covers.
cons: Rulings can drift away from the character.
Confident talkers get more of the story.

pairs.tendency: Hands decide what happens in a flick or a stack, so an argument cannot change the result, and talk is left for disputes about the rules.
pros: Skill of the hands stays plain to see.
Arguing gets a small, separate place.
cons: Arguments cannot change a toppled tower.
The two parts of play rarely meet.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the world as they play and may argue that a drawn feature would hold, such as a bridge or a wall, with the table deciding.
pros: The map carries the table's reasons.
Drawn features are easy to question.
cons: Maps can fill with unchecked claims.
Arguing can crowd out the drawing.

pairs.tendency: You ask a player for a card by name, and may argue why they ought to hand one over, with the table ruling.
pros: Asking can carry reasons.
Players learn how others read the table.
cons: Hidden hands make rulings hard to check.
A plain question turns into a debate.

pairs.tendency: The bank throws at fixed odds, and a player may argue for a lower price or a different bet, with the table deciding.
pros: Odds become a point of debate.
Players notice how a price is set.
cons: Fixed odds lose their meaning.
The bank player can feel pushed around.

pairs.tendency: Players bet before a throw that nobody controls, so arguing can only change the bet or its size, not the throw.
pros: Reasons go into the bet itself.
Players see how others judge a risk.
cons: Argument has little to grip once the dice fall.
Disputes over stakes can outlast the throw.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on hidden cards, and may argue why a bet ought to stand or be matched, with the table ruling.
pros: Reasons add to the bluff.
Players hear how others justify a bet.
cons: Rulings can give away what is in a hand.
Plain bets lose their firm edge.

pairs.tendency: Each player brings a side of their own, and may argue that its parts would work together in a way the rules did not plan.
pros: Sides can be tried in odd ways.
Players explain their own choices.
cons: Sides can become hard to compare.
The judge has to know each side well.

pairs.tendency: You state what you will do before play, then may argue that a near miss still counts, with the table ruling on the result.
pros: Declared aims can be tested in talk.
Players explain what they meant.
cons: Contracts lose their pass or fail edge.
Arguments at the end settle the score.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece changes sides, and a player may argue why a capture counts or a piece switches, with the table deciding.
pros: Reversals have to be explained.
Players see why a swing happened.
cons: A single ruling can flip the whole game.
Disputes over who owns a piece grow.

pairs.tendency: Caught players wait in jail until a teammate frees them, and a player may argue that a tag or a rescue counted, with the table ruling.
pros: Disputed tags get an answer at once.
The chase keeps its quick pace.
cons: Arguments can stall a running game.
Rulings are hard when nobody saw the tag.

pairs.tendency: A piece is taken when it has no room left, and a player may argue that a gap counts as closed, with the table deciding.
pros: Edge cases become talking points.
Players learn to see shapes the same way.
cons: Clear capture rules turn grey.
Late arguments can undo captures.

pairs.tendency: The game helps players who are behind, and a player may argue they deserve a boost or a rescue, with the table deciding.
pros: Help can be asked for in words.
Players explain what is going wrong.
cons: Anyone can plead to be called behind.
Honest help and tactics are hard to tell apart.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide everything and players make no choices, so there is nothing to argue about and the argued-moves block has no room.
pros: The two blocks do not clash.
The game stays short.
cons: Players have nothing to argue for.
The block sits unused.

pairs.tendency: One player chases and tags the rest, and players may argue that a tag counted or a safe spot applied, with the table ruling.
pros: Disputes about a tag get settled.
Rules can be adjusted on the spot.
cons: Stopping to argue breaks the chase.
Arguments can end in shouting.

pairs.tendency: You pick which player is hit or helped, and may argue why that is fair, with the table deciding if it stands.
pros: Targets have to be explained.
Players see how others judge fairness.
cons: Reasons can hide a grudge.
Being the target can feel personal.

pairs.tendency: You build one chain across the board and the other player cuts it, and a player may argue that a link is joined, with the table deciding.
pros: Doubtful links can be talked through.
Players learn to read the board together.
cons: A close chain gets argued over.
A clear finish turns into a ruling.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, and a player may argue that a choice beats a different one, with the table deciding.
pros: The cycle can be tested and stretched.
Players find new reasons for old choices.
cons: The cycle loses its simple order.
Players keep arguing for the choice they just played.

pairs.tendency: You announce a pair or a run you hold, and may argue that an odd combination also scores, with the table ruling.
pros: New combinations can be proposed.
Players explain how cards fit together.
cons: Scoring turns into debate.
Declared hands are hard to check.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power of their own, and may argue that it applies in a case the rules left open, with the table deciding.
pros: Powers can be used in new ways.
Players explain their own strengths.
cons: Powers can grow past what was planned.
Some powers are easier to argue for than others.

pairs.tendency: You may offer to double what the game is worth, and may argue why the other player ought to accept, with the table watching.
pros: Offers come with reasons.
Players learn how others handle pressure.
cons: Pleas can turn pressure into nagging.
A clear take-it-or-leave-it turns soft.

pairs.tendency: If you can capture you have to, and a player may argue that a capture is not legal or not forced, with the table ruling.
pros: Forced moves can be questioned.
Players learn the rule by arguing it.
cons: A forced line can be talked away.
Opponents lose their way of forcing a move.

pairs.tendency: Your character grows with each challenge, and you may argue what that power can do, with a judge or the table ruling.
pros: Growth opens new things to try.
Players explain how they got stronger.
cons: Strong characters can argue past every limit.
Rulings may change as power grows.

pairs.tendency: Each player recites the list so far and adds an item, and a player may argue that a new item fits the list, with the table deciding.
pros: Odd items get explained.
Players remember by reasons.
cons: Memory games slow down when argued.
Disputes over a missed item grow long.

pairs.tendency: The stronger player starts with less, and a player may argue about what handicap is fair, with the table deciding.
pros: Players talk openly about fairness.
The handicap can be adjusted as play goes on.
cons: Haggling can outlast the game itself.
The weaker player can feel pitied.

pairs.tendency: One player hides and the others search, and players may argue that a hiding spot is allowed or a find counts, with the table deciding.
pros: Hiding rules get settled as they come up.
Rulings can be quick and on the spot.
cons: Searchers can argue the hider out of a spot.
Arguing can give away where the hider is.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another into an empty space, and a player may argue that a jump is allowed, with the table ruling.
pros: Odd jumps can be tested.
Players learn the board by arguing it.
cons: Plain moves get second-guessed.
Pieces can land where rules never planned.

pairs.tendency: You keep some dice and roll the rest, and may argue for an extra roll or a changed die, with the table deciding.
pros: Players can plead for a second chance.
Reasons add to the thrill of the roll.
cons: Dice results lose their final say.
Extra rolls can crowd out the real ones.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a piece sends it to the start, and a player may argue that the landing was not valid or the space was safe, with the table ruling.
pros: Safe spaces can be debated.
Players see why a rule exists.
cons: Loud arguments can undo a send-back.
The sting of landing weakens.

pairs.tendency: A row of three lets you take a piece, and a player may argue that a shape counts as a row, with the table deciding.
pros: Odd rows can be tried and talked over.
Players read the board the same way.
cons: A taken piece can be argued back.
The plain rule of three turns hazy.

pairs.tendency: Players build words from letters, and may argue that a word counts, with a dictionary or the table settling it.
pros: New words and slang get a hearing.
Players learn how others use words.
cons: The dictionary and the judge can disagree.
Close calls on spelling cause long pauses.

pairs.tendency: You add a tile whose number matches an open end, and a player may argue that a mismatch can still be played, with the table ruling.
pros: Matching rules can be tested.
Players explain why a tile fits.
cons: The simple matching test loses its firmness.
Missed turns become arguments.

pairs.tendency: You lay a set face up, and may argue that other cards can be added to it, with the table deciding if the meld stands.
pros: Sets can grow in new directions.
Players explain how cards belong together.
cons: Played melds get reopened later.
Slow turns while melds are checked.

pairs.tendency: Each piece has a power that works once, and a player may argue that it applies in a case the rules left open, with the table deciding.
pros: Players argue when to spend a power.
Powers get used in new ways.
cons: A power can be argued into two uses.
Rulings on timing are hard to keep fair.

pairs.tendency: You offer a move and the other player has a say, and either of you may argue for a different offer, so the move is shaped by two voices.
pros: Two players shape each move.
Players learn to offer reasons, not just moves.
cons: Every turn can become a negotiation.
One player can wear the other down.

pairs.tendency: A message passes along the line and may change, and players may argue what it meant, with the table deciding.
pros: Changes in the message get examined.
Players see how meaning shifts.
cons: Nobody can check the original.
Arguments about the message may never end.

pairs.tendency: You hand some cards to a neighbour before play, and may argue why a pass was fair or what a card is for, with the table ruling.
pros: Passed cards can carry a reason.
Players see what neighbours expect.
cons: Arguing before play can give away hands.
Disputes start before the game does.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up and the other picks a side, and either may argue that the split is even or not, with the table deciding.
pros: Talk about fairness comes first.
The setter has to justify the split.
cons: Players can argue until nobody wants to start.
A persuasive setter can sell an uneven start.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes stronger, and a player may argue what it turns into or that it has arrived, with the table ruling.
pros: Promotions can be argued for.
Players explain why a piece earned its change.
cons: Forward moves get stuck at the last step.
The promotion rule turns into a bargain.

pairs.tendency: Teams run a race in legs and a leg may be argued, such as whether a handover was clean, with a judge or the table ruling.
pros: Disputed handovers get an answer.
Teams learn to explain their moves.
cons: Arguing in the middle of a race slows it.
Rulings are hard when nobody saw the handover.

pairs.tendency: A shape cannot be captured, and a player may argue that their stones form it, with the table ruling.
pros: Shapes are checked in words.
Players learn what makes a shape safe.
cons: A safe shape loses its sure edge.
Claims of safety can be argued too far.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, and a player may argue that a card scores in a way its name does not say, with the table deciding.
pros: Prize cards can be read in several ways.
Players explain what a prize is worth.
cons: Scoring gets argued at the end.
The named prizes lose their clear count.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are shared by all, and a player may argue that a shared card plays a part its text does not give, with the table ruling.
pros: Shared cards get several readings.
Everyone hears the same argument.
cons: One argued card helps every player.
Middle cards are argued over repeatedly.

pairs.tendency: Everyone adds to a pot that one player wins, and a player may argue a claim to it, with the table deciding.
pros: Claims to the pot come with reasons.
Players learn what others think is fair.
cons: Disputes over a growing pot get sharper.
A pot that nobody can claim stays argued.

pairs.tendency: You scoop and drop seeds around the pits, and a player may argue about where the last seed lands or what it can take, with the table ruling.
pros: Disputed counts get settled.
Players learn the pattern of the pits.
cons: Counting is slow when stopped for argument.
A plain count turns into a ruling.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand is taken, swapped or bought, and a player may argue why it ought to be theirs, with the table deciding.
pros: The claim to the hand carries a reason.
Players hear what others value.
cons: The spare hand can go to the smoothest talker.
Arguing before play can show who needs it.

pairs.tendency: Some squares send you back or keep you safe, and a player may argue that a square does not apply this time, with the table ruling.
pros: Square rules can be tested.
Players learn why each square exists.
cons: Squares lose their sure effect.
Arguments can fill the track.

pairs.tendency: Every card and item has a price, and a player may argue that something costs less or does more, with the table deciding.
pros: Prices come with reasons.
Players learn what things are worth to others.
cons: Fixed prices lose their meaning.
Bargaining over costs can run long.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed amount between places and jobs, and may argue how a split would work, with the table deciding what happens.
pros: Plans can be explained and tested.
Players can try unusual splits.
cons: A clever case can make a poor split work.
Rulings on share sizes are hard to keep fair.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until a signal sounds and the slowest is caught, so there is no time to argue during play, only after it.
pros: Quick play stays quick.
Disputes can be settled after the round.
cons: Arguments cannot help in the moment.
Players may argue about who was slowest.

pairs.tendency: You put cards back and take new ones, and may argue why a swap is allowed, with the table ruling.
pros: Unlisted swaps can be tried.
Players explain what they want to change.
cons: Open swaps can wear out a deck.
Players may keep asking for more.

pairs.tendency: You may pick up the discard pile if you can use the top card, and a player may argue that they can, with the table deciding.
pros: Doubtful pickups can be talked through.
Players see how others read the top card.
cons: Piles get taken on weak reasons.
Disputes slow down a quick game.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, and a player may argue that a card ranks in a way the trump rule does not give, with the table ruling.
pros: The trump rule can be tested at its edges.
Players explain why a low card wins.
cons: The ranking loses its clear order.
A strong suit and a strong argument compete.

pairs.tendency: Two boards run at once and you play both sides, and a player may argue what a move on one board does to the other, with the table deciding.
pros: Links between boards come out in talk.
Players explain how they think both games meet.
cons: Two boards need two sets of rulings.
The judge can lose track of both games.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any card you choose, and a player may argue what it stands for, with the table ruling.
pros: Players explain why a stand-in fits.
Cards get used in unexpected ways.
cons: A wild card can be argued into almost anything.
The pull of the wild card grows too strong.

pairs.tendency: The edges are joined so lines carry on from the other side, and a player may argue that a line wraps or not, with the table deciding.
pros: Odd lines can be tested.
Players learn how the edges join.
cons: New players can get confused about wrapping.
Edge cases come up often.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret and answers yes or no, and the others may argue that a question fits or an answer was wrong, with the table ruling.
pros: Doubtful questions get settled.
Players learn to word a question well.
cons: Arguing about a question can leak the answer.
The keeper of the secret can feel doubted.

pairs.tendency: Players race to the end, and may argue that a move is allowed or a finish counts, with the table deciding who crossed first.
pros: Clever ideas can speed a player up.
Players explain their shortcuts.
cons: Winning moves can be argued at length.
Arguing can hold up the race.

pairs.tendency: Points decide the winner, and a player may argue for a move that scores, with the table deciding the total.
pros: Scores come with reasons.
Players see how others value points.
cons: Final scores can be argued.
A fluent talker can add unplanned points.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one, and a player may argue they are not out, with the table ruling.
pros: Players can plead to stay in.
The ruling says why someone is out.
cons: Knocked-out players keep arguing.
Elimination loses its edge.

pairs.tendency: The team argues together for what each move would do against the game, and the judge or table decides how the game answers.
pros: Everyone adds ideas to the plan.
Players learn how others reason.
cons: One confident voice can lead the team.
Plans that sound right fail by the ruling.

pairs.tendency: The group works toward one target and argues for moves that would get it there, with a judge or the table deciding.
pros: The group shapes its own plan.
Reasons are shared in the open.
cons: Little pressure between players.
A single strong talker can set the plan.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal and argues for moves, while the table decides, so reasons may hide what a player really wants.
pros: Players read each other's reasons.
Secrets and talk mix.
cons: An argued move can give a goal away.
Honest reasons are hard to tell from false ones.

pairs.tendency: The story ends when it ends, and each move is argued for as a fit with the story, with the table deciding.
pros: The table shapes the story together.
Players explain why a turn belongs.
cons: The ending can be argued away.
Story can pull away from the plan.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so arguments are about what would happen, not about who gains, and the table decides what the game shows.
pros: Reasons do not need a prize.
Players listen to each other.
cons: Talk can drift with no goal to hold it.
Rulings have little to settle.

pairs.tendency: Each player names what doing well means, and argues for moves toward it, with the table deciding what happens.
pros: Players explain what they want.
Different goals can sit side by side.
cons: Moves are hard to compare across goals.
Rulings may favour the goal that sounds nicest.

pairs.tendency: The game runs until one player loses, and a player may argue that they are safe or that another has lost, with the table deciding.
pros: Players argue for their own safety.
A ruling names the loser plainly.
cons: Arguing can single one player out.
A close finish turns into a trial.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, and players argue for moves that would carry it on, with the judge or table deciding.
pros: Talk keeps the story moving.
Players build on each other's ideas.
cons: Play can lose its direction.
Rulings tend to run long.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can win, so arguing is not about gaining ground, and the table decides what happens to shape what the game shows.
pros: Reasons are free of a prize.
Players explore what the game refuses.
cons: Players can drift without a point.
The argument half has little to push against.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards, and may argue to yourself why a move counts, with nobody but you to rule.
pros: You can test odd moves.
Solo play gets a thinking part.
cons: There is no judge, so rulings can be bent.
The game says lost while you say won.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played and the wins are counted, and a player may argue a result in any one game, with the table deciding.
pros: Rulings can settle between games.
Players see how earlier rulings shape later ones.
cons: One argued game can decide the whole match.
Players argue to win a match, not a game.

pairs.tendency: Points count against you, and a player may argue that a card scores less or not count, with the table deciding.
pros: Players can plead about what counts.
Scores come with reasons.
cons: Pleas can lower scores unfairly.
The fewest points rule gets argued over.

pairs.tendency: You have to land on the target exactly, and a player may argue that a near finish counts, with the table ruling.
pros: Near misses can be heard.
Players explain how close they came.
cons: The exact rule loses its sharp edge.
Rulings on a final count can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, and a player may argue that a move gives more away, with the table deciding how it counts.
pros: Players make a case for losing well.
Odd reasoning is allowed.
cons: Reasons for losing are hard to judge.
Players can argue in circles.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds their own thing alongside the rest, with a judge or the table ruling on each argued move, so players mostly ask for rulings, not fight.
pros: Each player can try their own ideas.
The table learns different approaches.
cons: Rulings are made for each player in turn.
Little for players to argue with each other about.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other and argue why a move works, with the table deciding, so a fight is also a debate.
pros: Conflict has to be explained.
Players see how others justify a move.
cons: Arguments can turn personal.
Quick fights slow down while players argue.

pairs.tendency: Players act through the board and argue what a change would do, so the table has to rule on effects nobody can touch directly.
pros: Effects on others are talked through.
Players spot chains of cause and effect.
cons: Hard-to-see effects are hard to rule on.
Slow turns while effects are argued.

pairs.tendency: The whole team argues together for moves against the game, and the judge or table decides how the game answers.
pros: Everyone adds to the plan.
Reasons are shared freely.
cons: One player can speak for the team.
Plans can be argued into a corner.

pairs.tendency: Players help the group but also want a private gain, so arguments for a move can serve the group and the arguer, and the table decides.
pros: Players weigh whose reason is whose.
Self-interest shows in the open.
cons: Reasons can hide a selfish aim.
Trust may wear down when rulings favour one voice.

pairs.tendency: Teams plan together and argue their moves to a judge or the table, so each team makes a case and the other can answer.
pros: Teams learn to argue as a group.
The other side keeps the case honest.
cons: A strong speaker can carry a team.
Teams can argue past the clock.

pairs.tendency: The traitor argues for moves like everyone else, so a persuasive case can be the secret sabotage, and the table decides whether to trust it.
pros: Suspicion hangs on how a move is argued.
Players watch each other's reasons closely.
cons: A smooth case can fool the table.
Honest players may be doubted for arguing clearly.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and write their moves with reasons, and a judge or the table rules by return, so each turn waits for a reply.
pros: Written reasons can be thought over.
Rulings can be kept as a record.
cons: Each ruling adds days of waiting.
Messages can be read in more than one way.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so the table argues for what their move would be, and the judge decides what they would have done.
pros: Absent players are still heard.
The table talks about what that player would do.
cons: Others speak for someone who cannot reply.
The table may bend the absent player's moves.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and decides what happens, so the argued-moves block gives the game master a natural job as judge.
pros: A single judge keeps rulings quick.
Players can try anything and be answered.
cons: One person carries all the rulings.
The game master may decide every dispute alone.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in the street and passers-by join in, so a ruling may come from whoever is watching, not a fixed judge.
pros: Newcomers can try things at once.
Passers-by hear reasons and join in.
cons: Rulings change from one crowd to the next.
Arguments in public can get heated.

pairs.tendency: The rest of the players team up against one player, and each side argues for its moves, so the lone player argues against a team.
pros: The lone player can speak up.
The team has to agree on a reason.
cons: The team can out-talk one player.
The single player can tire of arguing.

pairs.tendency: You play alone, so you argue a move to yourself and rule on it too, or a friend rules later when you compare results.
pros: Players can try odd moves.
Players learn their own reasoning.
cons: Nobody else judges, so reasons can bend.
Results are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most of what happens, and arguing for a different outcome fights the dice, so rulings may feel like overriding luck.
pros: Reasons give players a say against luck.
A dull dice game gains something to talk about.
cons: The table may feel the dice were set aside.
Little left to argue once the dice fall.

pairs.tendency: Dice rule, but players can soften poor luck, and a player may argue that one of the ways to soften it applies, with the table deciding.
pros: Players argue about their own safeguards.
Dice and reasons both matter.
cons: Safeguards can be argued past their limit.
Rulings on what softens the dice add rules.

pairs.tendency: Skill carries the game and some luck adds surprise, and a player may argue a move's merit, with the table ruling.
pros: Careful moves can be explained.
A little luck stops arguments from deciding all.
cons: Strong talkers can add to strong players.
Rulings and luck can both change a result.

pairs.tendency: Play is nearly all choice, and a player may argue that a move works, so the table is judging how clever a case is as well as a move.
pros: Players test ideas in the open.
Every result comes with a reason.
cons: The strongest arguer and player can differ.
Rulings can stand in for skill.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a message, and players argue what it means for them, with the table deciding which reading stands.
pros: Players share their own readings.
A single throw gives a lot to talk about.
cons: A reading can be pushed to suit the reader.
The table may not agree on a sign.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act in step without speaking, so there is little room to argue in play, and any ruling comes after the move.
pros: Players learn to sense one another.
Arguments are saved for afterwards.
cons: The timing of a move cannot be argued.
Talk after a moment can break its feel.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table, and players argue what the result means for their character, with the judge or table deciding.
pros: Players can add their own reading to a roll.
Dice and reasons build the story together.
cons: The table can read the roll in different ways.
An argued result can overrule the table of results.

pairs.tendency: Everything is on view, so arguments are about what a move would do, not about what is hidden, and the table can check each claim by looking.
pros: Claims can be tested by sight.
Rulings are easier to agree on.
cons: Little surprise left in what is claimed.
Players can argue over what is plainly visible.

pairs.tendency: Players hold secret cards and argue for moves, so a reason may show or hide what is held, and the table rules without seeing it all.
pros: Reasons can be part of a bluff.
Players learn to read each other.
cons: Rulings are hard to check.
Arguing can give away a hand.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles and argue for moves, so a reasoned case may be honest or a cover, and the table decides whether to believe it.
pros: Suspicion grows from how a case is made.
Players watch each other's reasons.
cons: A persuasive liar can hold the table.
Honest players get doubted for arguing well.

pairs.tendency: Players use clues to work out hidden facts, and may argue that a clue points one way, with the table deciding if the reasoning holds.
pros: Reasoning is spoken out loud.
Players check each other's logic.
cons: Arguing a clue can give away what you know.
The table may accept a wrong chain of reasons.

pairs.tendency: Players lie about what they have, and also argue for their moves, so a false claim can come wrapped in a reason.
pros: Bluffs come with reasons.
Players learn how others weigh a claim.
cons: A well-argued lie is hard to catch.
Arguing and lying can blur together.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule and the rest find it by breaking it, and arguing a move may help or confuse the search for the rule.
pros: Reasons can reveal how others think.
Players test the rule in words.
cons: The rule-keeper can be argued toward a hint.
Arguing can distract from finding the rule.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer and may only give hints, so they cannot argue a move aloud, while the others argue what the hints mean.
pros: Guessers explain their readings.
The table learns how hints can be taken.
cons: The hint-giver cannot answer back.
Arguments can lead the guessers astray.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over as players explore, and they may argue what lies ahead, so the table decides things that are not yet known.
pros: Players can reason about what might be found.
Arguments for exploring get a hearing.
cons: Rulings on unseen places are guesses.
A flipped tile can overturn an argued plan.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up while the rest stay secret, and a player may argue how the open hand is played, with the table deciding.
pros: The open hand gives something to point at.
Plays from the open hand can be explained.
cons: Players argue over a hand they cannot change.
Rulings need care about what is visible.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, and players argue for moves whose reasons may hide how far ahead they are.
pros: Claims are hard to check, which makes talk lively.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: Rulings can quietly change a hidden score.
Nobody can say if a ruling was fair.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so each argument gets its own turn and the table has time to rule before the next move.
pros: Each case is heard in full.
Rulings are easy to follow.
cons: Waiting players have to sit through every argument.
A long argument holds up the whole table.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses together, so arguments for each choice come at the same time, and the judge or table cannot rule on all of them at once.
pros: Many ideas are tried together.
Rounds can stay lively.
cons: Rulings pile up behind a single round.
Players talk over each other.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so arguments cross in the air, and a judge or the table rules on whichever came first.
pros: Fast ideas get through.
Play feels lively.
cons: Who spoke first can be unclear.
Arguments can turn into noise.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so a player has only seconds to argue for a move, and the table decides before the time runs out.
pros: Reasons have to be short.
Rulings keep up with play.
cons: Little time for a careful case.
Players run out of time before the ruling.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks, so an argued move can be made in writing and answered the next day, with the table deciding at its own pace.
pros: Players have time to think of reasons.
Rulings can be well thought out.
cons: Slow replies stretch each argument.
A ruling can be forgotten by the next move.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose, and arguing for a move fits the slow pace, with the table taking time to rule.
pros: Players weigh reasons carefully.
Rulings are calm.
cons: Debate can drag on.
Few quick moves to balance it.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so there is less time to argue each move, and rulings have to come faster as the end nears.
pros: Early rounds leave room for reasons.
Play builds toward a rush.
cons: Late rulings are hurried.
Arguments get cut short at the end.

pairs.tendency: Some throws give another go at once, and a player may argue that they deserve an extra turn, with the table deciding.
pros: Players plead for another turn.
A lucky run can be explained.
cons: Extra turns get argued onto the table.
One player can move many times.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages with different rules, and players argue moves in each one, with the table ruling on how the first stage carries into the second.
pros: Each stage can have its own kind of case.
Early reasons shape later play.
cons: Rulings have to stay steady across stages.
Past rulings need remembering.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system, and a player argues that a move would have a real effect, so the table decides if the argument matches how the system works.
pros: Players test what they know of the real system.
Reasons can be checked against how things work.
cons: The table may not know the system well.
A clever case can beat the model.

pairs.tendency: Each player argues as a real group would, saying what that group could do, and the table decides what the group gets.
pros: Each group's view is spoken aloud.
Players practise arguing for someone else.
cons: A weak speaker can leave a group unheard.
Players may argue for themselves, not the group.

pairs.tendency: Everyone takes from one limited stock, and players argue why they ought to take more, with the table deciding.
pros: The claims on a shared stock are spoken aloud.
Players practise arguing over a shared supply.
cons: The smoothest talker can drain the stock.
Quiet players can end up with the least.

pairs.tendency: A move shows its effect only a few rounds later, so the table has to rule on what will happen later, and players argue over how it will turn out.
pros: Players say what they expect to happen.
Later results show how sound the argument was.
cons: Arguments about the future are hard to judge.
Players forget what was ruled.

pairs.tendency: Players propose a new rule and play on to see what it changes, and the proposal is argued before it is tried.
pros: Rules are tested with reasons.
Players see what their argued rule does.
cons: The group can argue long before trying anything.
A strong case can pass a weak rule.

pairs.tendency: After play, players talk it through, and the argued moves give them rulings to look back on and ask why each went the way it did.
pros: Rulings are a record to discuss.
Players see why the table decided as it did.
cons: Old rulings may be forgotten by then.
The debrief can turn into a second argument.

pairs.tendency: What happens changes the game for ever, so every ruling stays, and an argued move that the table accepts cannot be taken back.
pros: Players think hard before arguing.
Rulings carry weight across games.
cons: A poor ruling stays for ever.
Players argue harder because nothing can be undone.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and arguing for moves lets players argue back at the game's own point, with the table deciding.
pros: Players can answer the game itself.
The game's argument can be tested.
cons: Players may argue the point out of the game.
The judge may side with the game's own view.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the game carries into real life, so an argued move that is ruled in has a real effect, and players argue with more at stake.
pros: Players take the reasons seriously.
Real stakes sharpen each case.
cons: Arguments can turn into real disputes.
Rulings feel heavier than a game ruling.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something like health or kindness, and players argue that a move is worth more points, with the table deciding what counts.
pros: Players debate what a value is worth.
The cost of turning values into points shows.
cons: Bargaining over points can cheapen kindness.
Players may chase points through talk.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living that does not exist yet and argue how it would work, with the table deciding what happens.
pros: The future is argued out, not just played.
Players say what they expect from it.
cons: Ideas can sound sounder than they play.
The table may not know what would really happen.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points so players can say what they notice, and rulings made so far can be looked at again before play goes on.
pros: Past rulings get a second look.
Players see how they have been arguing.
cons: Pauses can reopen settled rulings.
Stops break the flow of play.

pairs.tendency: The game is played again with one thing changed, and players compare the rulings from each round, so they can see what the changed rule did to the arguments.
pros: Rulings can be set side by side.
Players see what a change did.
cons: The table may not rule the same way twice.
A new judge can look like a new rule.

pairs.tendency: The game says what it left out of the real situation, and players argue moves that might use what was left out, with the table deciding.
pros: Players test the edges of the model.
The gaps become part of the talk.
cons: Arguments can drag in what was left out.
The table may not agree where the game stops.

pairs.tendency: The people whose situation the game shows helped build it, and they can argue whether a move rings true, with the table deciding.
pros: People close to the situation can speak with authority.
Rulings carry real knowledge.
cons: The table may defer to one voice.
Others may not feel they can argue back.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a link in a chain, and a player may argue that an order or a delivery goes differently, with the table deciding.
pros: Players explain choices that reach other links.
Rulings show how one change spreads.
cons: Arguments can undo the chain's delays.
A ruling for one link reaches every other.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own stock and orders, so their argument rests on a partial view, and the table decides without seeing it all.
pros: Players argue from what they actually know.
Gaps in what players know are made clear.
cons: Rulings are hard to check.
An argued guess can be taken as fact.

pairs.tendency: The slowest step sets the pace, and players may argue that a step could run faster, with the table deciding if it would change the pace.
pros: Claims about speed can be tested.
Players find the real limit by arguing.
cons: A clever case can wave a bottleneck away.
Arguments about the wrong step waste time.

pairs.tendency: Goods are made ahead or only when an order arrives, and players argue which way would work for them, with the table deciding.
pros: Players give reasons for how they make things.
Both ways can be argued and compared.
cons: Reasons can hide how each way really feels.
A ruling may favour one way unseen.

pairs.tendency: Players choose how many to make or move at once, and may argue why a batch size would work, with the table deciding what it costs.
pros: Players explain a batch choice.
The cost of waiting or setting up is argued.
cons: Rulings on cost can be guessed.
A fine argument can hide a poor batch.

pairs.tendency: Equipment fails at random, and a player may argue that a repair is quick or that a plan still holds, with the table deciding.
pros: Players argue about repair and backup.
Plans that assume everything works get tested.
cons: A smooth argument can talk a breakdown away.
Random failure loses its sting.

pairs.tendency: Stock costs each round and running out costs more, and players argue how much to hold, with the table deciding what it costs.
pros: Players reason about holding stock.
Both costs come up in the talk.
cons: Costs can be argued down without a count.
The balance between the two costs can be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: Players roll and move for a few rounds, then stop and say what the dice have done to each of them so far.
pros: Luck becomes something to talk about.
Easy rules leave attention free for noticing.
cons: Stops break the run of rolling.
Little to discuss when every move is a roll.

pairs.tendency: After a few rounds of picking and passing, play stops and players say what they took, what they left, and why.
pros: Picks become reasons said aloud.
Seeing what others passed is interesting.
cons: Stopping mid-pass can lose track of the hands.
Players may forget what they were weighing.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a few auctions and players say what they paid, what it was worth to them, and what surprised them.
pros: Prices get explained, not only paid.
Players hear how others valued things.
cons: Winners may defend bids rather than reflect.
Stopping cools the heat of the auction.

pairs.tendency: Players pause after a round of risks and say when they stopped, when they kept going, and what pulled them on.
pros: Risk habits become visible.
Players hear why others stopped.
cons: The pause breaks the tension.
Players who busted may not want to talk.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while the map is half held, and players say who holds what and which holds were chosen or forced.
pros: The map is read together.
Weak spots are seen before they are lost.
cons: Leaders can use the pause to plan.
Talk turns into planning attacks.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a round of placing workers, and players say which spaces filled first and which stayed empty.
pros: Crowding on spaces is noticed.
Each player hears why others chose differently.
cons: A pause during planning loses the plan.
Blocked players may stay quiet.

pairs.tendency: Players stop building and look at the patterns so far, saying what they were aiming for and what they now see.
pros: Makers see their own pattern from outside.
Calm play suits calm stops.
cons: The pause adds little to a quiet game.
Players can start to tidy rather than think.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players say what they have saved in hand, what they have played, and what they are waiting for.
pros: Holding back is explained.
Timing choices become clear.
cons: Saying a plan aloud can give it away.
Hands stay secret, so talk stays vague.

pairs.tendency: After a few tricks the play stops, and players say what they led, what they followed and what they read from the cards played.
pros: Reading cards gets named.
Newer players learn from the talk.
cons: Talk can reveal what is held.
Breaks the rhythm of quick tricks.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a round of deals and players say who they trusted, what they offered and what they felt about the outcome.
pros: Trust and pressure get named.
Quiet players get a turn to speak.
cons: Deals under way can be lost.
A pause can reopen settled arguments.

pairs.tendency: Players stop mid-game and say which sets they are building and what they have given up to do it.
pros: Hidden aims are said aloud.
Players see how many sets are still possible.
cons: Other players may use what they hear.
Talk can pull the game towards a checklist.

pairs.tendency: The shared map is looked at together part-way through, and players say what shape it is taking and who shaped it.
pros: The map is a shared thing to read.
Players notice plans that grew apart.
cons: Talk can start redesigning the map.
The pause can stretch out.

pairs.tendency: Between rounds of call and answer, players stop and say what the chain has become and how each answer was chosen.
pros: The chain is read as a whole.
Players hear how others listened.
cons: The flow of the exchange is broken.
Talk about the chain can replace the chain.

pairs.tendency: Players play without speaking, and the pause is the first time anyone may say what they meant by a move.
pros: Meanings are said after being only guessed.
Silence makes the pause matter.
cons: Players may talk too long once allowed.
Breaking the silence can end the mood.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after rules have been changed, and players say what each change did and whether it was meant that way.
pros: Effects of rules are checked.
The group sees who pushed which change.
cons: Stopping can cut short a rule's trial.
Rule talk can take over the game.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players step out of their characters to say what they were doing and why, then step back in.
pros: Players see their own choices.
Characters can be seen from outside.
cons: Stepping out can break the story.
Some find it hard to step back in.

pairs.tendency: Play stops between rounds of stacking or flicking, and players say what they noticed about their hands, nerves and the shaky parts.
pros: Players notice their own habits.
A rest relieves tired hands.
cons: The tension of a wobbling tower is lost.
Little to reflect on beyond steady or shaky.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players look over the map drawn so far, saying what is on it, what is missing and who drew what.
pros: The map becomes a record to read.
Gaps in the world get noticed.
cons: Talk can turn into redrawing.
Quiet drawers may stay unheard.

pairs.tendency: After some rounds of asking, play stops and players say what each question gave away and what they guessed from others'.
pros: The cost of asking is seen.
Players hear what others deduced.
cons: Saying guesses aloud can reveal hands.
The pause adds little to a short game.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a few throws and players say how they bet, how the bank felt, and what happened to their stake.
pros: Betting habits are shown.
Being the bank can be talked about.
cons: Talk can encourage chasing losses.
Stopping cools the pace of the betting.

pairs.tendency: Players stop after a few bets on throws and say why they bet as they did, when nothing they did could change the throw.
pros: Bets show what players believe.
Players see luck separate from choice.
cons: Little to reflect on beyond the bet.
Winners may credit themselves.

pairs.tendency: Play stops mid-hand or between hands, and players say what they thought their cards were worth and what made them raise or fold.
pros: Reasons for raising are heard.
Players learn how others read a hand.
cons: Saying too much shows the hand.
Stopping mid-hand breaks the nerve of it.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after the first clashes, and players say why they built their side as they did and what they would change.
pros: Choices of build get explained.
Players see which builds struggled.
cons: Talk can feel like blame.
Rebuilding mid-game may be tempting.

pairs.tendency: After some of the contract has been played, play stops and players say how likely they now think it is and what has changed.
pros: Hopes are checked against play.
Others see how a promise is going.
cons: Saying it aloud can help opponents.
The nerve of the call is lost.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a few captures and players say who is ahead and how quickly that has changed.
pros: Sudden swings are noticed.
Players see why a lead feels shaky.
cons: Leaders may feel uneasy being named.
Pauses can slow a game of sharp turns.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while some players are in jail, and players say how it feels to wait and what the rescuers are weighing.
pros: Waiting players are heard.
The risk of a rescue is spoken aloud.
cons: Stopping lets captured players rest.
The chase loses its pace.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while stones are closing in, and players say which groups look in danger and why.
pros: Slow danger becomes visible.
Beginners learn to read the board.
cons: Talk can pass on tips to the opponent.
Pausing a slow game can feel pointless.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some help has been given to trailing players, and players say whether it felt fair and who it helped.
pros: Fairness is discussed openly.
Leaders hear how their lead feels.
cons: Leaders may feel punished.
Trailing players may feel pitied.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some rounds of luck alone, and players say what happened and what, if anything, they could have done.
pros: Players see that nothing was decided by them.
Talk comes easily when nobody is to blame.
cons: Little to reflect on.
Reflecting on pure luck can feel empty.

pairs.tendency: Play stops, everyone stands still, and players say who is chasing whom, how it feels to run or to chase, and what they are doing.
pros: Fast play gets a breath.
Players notice who always runs or chases.
cons: Breaks the chase's energy.
Standing still can feel odd to players.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some rounds of picking targets, and players say who they chose and why, and who chose them.
pros: Reasons for picking someone are heard.
Players notice patterns in who gets hit.
cons: Targeted players may feel singled out.
Talk can turn into settling scores.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while two chains are racing across the board, and players say where the gaps are and what the other side is doing.
pros: The shape of the contest is seen.
Beginners see how a chain is cut.
cons: Naming gaps can help the opponent.
The pause can interrupt a plan.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after rounds of beating and losing to each other's choices, and players say what they guessed about each other.
pros: Guessing habits are shown.
Players find patterns they were using.
cons: Saying the pattern may change it.
Pausing breaks quick, simple rounds.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some declarations, and players say what they showed, what they kept back, and what that told others.
pros: What a declaration gives away is clear.
Players learn what others hold.
cons: Talk may reveal held cards.
The pause adds little to short rounds.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and each player says how their own power has helped or got in the way, and how others' powers look to them.
pros: Uneven powers get compared aloud.
Players learn what others' powers do.
cons: Strong powers may be resented.
Talk can drift to complaints about balance.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a double was offered, and players say what made them accept or give up and what they feared.
pros: Nerve and fear are named.
The cost of refusing is understood.
cons: Those who gave up may feel regret.
The tension of the offer drops.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some forced captures, and players say how it felt to have the move taken from them and how they used it.
pros: Hidden traps are explained.
The pull of a forced move is seen.
cons: Beginners may feel caught out.
Talk can warn the opponent of traps.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a few levels and players say how much stronger their characters are, and what that has changed about their choices.
pros: Growth is noticed, not just felt.
Players see how early choices paid off.
cons: Stronger characters may crowd out the talk.
Early gains can look bigger than they were.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after the list has grown long, and players say how they are holding on to it and what they do when they forget.
pros: Memory tricks are shared.
Players laugh about the slips.
cons: The list is lost when play breaks.
The game depends on pace, which the pause breaks.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players say how the handicap feels, to the one who carries it and to the one who gains from it.
pros: Feelings about fairness are said.
The weaker player is heard.
cons: The handicap can feel awkward when named.
Skilled players may feel judged.

pairs.tendency: Play stops with the hider still hidden, and the seekers say where they have looked and what they think.
pros: Search plans are explained.
The hider's choices become a story.
cons: The hunt loses its rush.
Seekers can give away where they have not looked.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some jumps and players say which jumps were chosen, which were forced, and what they planned.
pros: Chains of jumps are traced back.
Players see missed jumps.
cons: Talk can point out jumps to opponents.
Little to say in a quiet position.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a few turns and players say which dice they kept, which they sent back, and what they were hoping for.
pros: Hopes are set beside results.
Players see how others took risks.
cons: The quick pace is broken.
Players may only list their rolls.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after pieces have been sent back, and players say how it felt to send one and to be sent.
pros: Setbacks are said aloud.
Players see who has been hit most.
cons: Those sent back may feel sore.
Talk can become about getting even.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some mills, and players say which rows were built, which were broken up, and what they were watching.
pros: Both attack and defence are explained.
Players learn what a threat looks like.
cons: Pointing out threats helps the opponent.
A quiet game offers little to say.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while the letters are on the table, and players say how they hunted for words and which they nearly found.
pros: Ways of seeing words are shared.
Near misses become interesting.
cons: The hunt loses its speed.
Players may keep hunting while the others talk.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while the line has several open ends, and players say what they have in hand and which ends they have been steering.
pros: Hidden plans become clear.
Players see how ends close.
cons: Hands may be given away.
Little to reflect on in a simple line.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some melds and players say what they laid down, what they held back, and what they are waiting to add.
pros: The reasons for laying early or late are heard.
Players see what sets are open.
cons: Talk can reveal held cards.
The pause can slow a quick game.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some powers have been spent and players say when they used theirs, and when they held back.
pros: Timing of one-off moves is explained.
Players see which powers are still unused.
cons: Naming the unused powers helps opponents.
Players may regret a spent power.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after several offers and refusals, and players say how they chose what to offer and how they felt when refused.
pros: Offers are explained from both sides.
Players see how others judged fairness.
cons: Talk can feel like justifying.
Refused players may feel stung.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a message has travelled, and players say what they heard, what they passed on and what they changed.
pros: Small changes are traced.
Each link is heard.
cons: Players may feel blamed for changes.
The pause can end the surprise at the end.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after cards have been passed and players say what they gave, what they hoped for and what they got.
pros: Reasons for giving are heard.
Players see how others read them.
cons: Giving away hints can spoil the game.
Disappointment at what arrived is aired.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after the side has been chosen, and the one who set up the game and the one who chose say what they were thinking.
pros: The fairness of a split is said aloud.
Players see how the setter weighed it.
cons: The pause comes after the main choice.
Little more to say once play begins.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while pieces are racing to the far end, and players say who is ahead, who is holding back and why.
pros: The pull of promotion is named.
Patient players explain their holding back.
cons: Naming the plan can alert the opponent.
A quiet advance gives little to discuss.

pairs.tendency: Play stops between legs of the relay, and each runner says how the handover went and what they would try next.
pros: Handovers get attention.
Each runner is heard.
cons: Stopping a race feels odd.
The team loses pace and the cheer fades.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while players build towards a safe shape, and they say which shapes they are making and which are in danger.
pros: Slow plans are explained.
Beginners learn what is safe.
cons: Showing the plan helps the other side.
The pause may expose weak points.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some tricks and players say which named prizes they are aiming for and which they have given up on.
pros: Hidden goals are said aloud.
Players notice what each prize is worth.
cons: Naming prizes gives away plans.
The pause adds little once prizes are taken.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after the middle cards are turned, and players say how they read the middle and what they are holding.
pros: Different readings of one set of cards are heard.
Beginners learn how others judge odds.
cons: Talking about hands gives them away.
The suspense of the reveal is lost.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after the pot has grown for several rounds, and players say how it is changing what they are willing to risk.
pros: The pull of a growing pot is named.
Players see risk rising with the pot.
cons: Greed can be hard to admit.
Pauses can cool the excitement.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some sowing, and players say how they counted ahead and what they saw in the pits.
pros: Counting methods are shared.
Beginners see how a move is planned.
cons: Counting aloud helps the opponent.
A pause can interrupt a rhythm of quick scooping.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after the spare hand has been taken or swapped, and players say why they chose as they did.
pros: The choice of the spare hand is explained.
Players see how others valued it.
cons: Reasons may reveal the cards.
The pause comes after the one big choice.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some players have landed on special squares, and they say what the squares did and how it felt.
pros: Luck of the track is talked about.
Players spot which squares matter.
cons: Little to reflect on beyond lucky or unlucky.
The track's momentum is lost.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a few rounds of buying, and players say what they spent, what they saved, and what they regret not buying.
pros: Spending habits are named.
Prices are compared with value.
cons: Saving plans may be revealed.
Players may only list what they bought.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after players have shared out their forces and say how they split and what they guessed the others would do.
pros: Guesses about the opponent are aired.
Choices of spreading or piling in are explained.
cons: The split can be given away.
Talk can undo the surprise of the reveal.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at the signal as usual, and then stays stopped while players say what they were doing when it came.
pros: The frozen moment is looked at.
Players laugh at where they were caught.
cons: A longer stop kills the fun of a quick game.
Players eager to go again lose patience.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some swapping, and players say what they put back, what they took and what they were aiming for.
pros: Reasons for swapping are heard.
Players see how others judged their hands.
cons: Aims reveal what is held.
The pause slows a game of quick trades.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after a pile has been taken, and players say how they decided to take it and what it cost them.
pros: A big pickup is talked through.
Players see the weight of a big pile.
cons: Hands are given away in the talk.
Stops interrupt the flow of the pile.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after tricks where trumps won, and players say how the trump suit changed what they led and held.
pros: The pull of the trump suit is said aloud.
Players learn how others used it.
cons: Talk can reveal trump holdings.
Short rounds leave little to say.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players say how they are managing two boards, which one has taken their attention and which has been neglected.
pros: Split attention is noticed.
Players see how the two games affect each other.
cons: Pausing one board lets the other cool.
Players may pick sides rather than reflect.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after wild cards have been used, and players say when they spent theirs and what they would have done otherwise.
pros: Saving or spending a wild card is explained.
Players see what a wild card is worth.
cons: Wild cards held in hand are given away.
The pause adds little once they are gone.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while pieces are crossing the joined edges, and players say what they had not expected about the board.
pros: Surprise at the edge is shared.
Beginners work out how the edge behaves.
cons: Players may talk about the rule, not the game.
Little to reflect on once the rule is known.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after several yes and no answers, and the guessers say what they now rule out and what they still think possible.
pros: Narrowing down is said aloud.
The answerer hears how others are thinking.
cons: Saying guesses aloud helps the other guessers.
The chain of questions loses its rhythm.

pairs.tendency: Play stops partway through the race, and players say who is ahead, what is slowing them down and what it feels like to lead or trail.
pros: The gap between players is looked at.
Trailing players are heard.
cons: Stopping a race can cool the chase.
Leaders may talk about holding on rather than noticing.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players say how they are scoring, where their points come from and what they might be missing.
pros: Scoring sources are compared.
Players see strategies that differ.
cons: Talk can pull everyone to the same strategy.
Leaders may stay quiet about their plan.

pairs.tendency: Play stops after some players have dropped out, and the survivors and the knocked out say what they saw.
pros: Those who are out are heard.
Survivors say what kept them in.
cons: Knocked-out players have to watch more.
Stopping lets the winners rest.

pairs.tendency: Play stops when the team is under pressure, and players say what is going wrong, who is doing what and what is working.
pros: The team sees its own plans.
Quiet players can speak.
cons: One strong voice may steer the pause.
A grim position can feel heavier when named.

pairs.tendency: Play stops partway to the target and players say how far they are, who has done what and what is left.
pros: Progress is checked together.
The group can change plan on purpose.
cons: Talk can drift into one person giving orders.
Little tension in the pause.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players say what they have noticed about each other, while each keeps their own secret goal.
pros: Guesses about others are heard.
Players learn how they come across.
cons: Saying too much gives goals away.
The pause may turn into probing.

pairs.tendency: Play stops partway through the story, and players say what has happened so far and where they think it is heading.
pros: The story is retold in many voices.
Players find the story they share.
cons: The ending may feel fixed once it is said.
The mood of a story can be broken.

pairs.tendency: The game has no winner, so the pause is a stop to look at what has happened so far, with nothing to protect.
pros: Talk comes easily without a score.
Players say what they notice.
cons: Without a goal, pauses can wander.
The game and the pause can feel the same.

pairs.tendency: Play stops and players say what goal they set, how it is going and whether they would still choose it.
pros: Personal goals are checked mid-way.
Players can change course on purpose.
cons: Some may feel they are being tested.
Goals that were vague stay vague.

pairs.tendency: Play stops while nobody has lost yet, and players say who feels at risk and how they are avoiding being the one.
pros: Fear of losing is spoken aloud.
Players see who is protecting whom.
cons: The one at risk may feel watched.
Talk can single someone out early.

pairs.tendency: Play stops, and players say whether the game is still going well in the sense they want it to, and what keeps it alive.
