Players may repeat what failed.

pairs.tendency: Points count against players, and the slow step keeps players holding what they cannot pass on, so those held up pile up points.
pros: Players see who is stuck holding.
Clearing stock has a reason.
cons: The player at the jam is punished.
Points can seem unfair.

pairs.tendency: Players have to land exactly on the number, and the narrow step means a miss sends them to the back of the queue.
pros: Players weigh patience against rushing.
Near misses build tension.
cons: A miss costs a whole wait.
Players can stall in the queue.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to lose or give things away, and the slow step makes that slow too, so players who want to lose still have to wait their turn.
pros: Losing is slowed in a way players notice.
The jam works against its own aim.
cons: Players may be confused who is held up.
The game can feel upside down.

pairs.tendency: Each player runs their own line with its own slow step, so they compare where their jams sit without touching each other's.
pros: Players compare different jams.
Quiet, steady play.
cons: Little contact between players.
Players may not see why theirs differs.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other, and an attack on the slow step costs the victim the most, so every fight tends to aim at that one spot.
pros: The weak point is clear.
Fights have a focus.
cons: One player can be crushed by one hit.
Fights ignore the rest of the board.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board, and a change at the slow step is felt by everyone, so one player's moves there set the pace for all.
pros: Players feel each other's choices.
The key spot is easy to see.
cons: Effects can be hard to trace.
One player can quietly slow everyone.

pairs.tendency: The whole team works against the game, and all of them depend on the slow step, so they plan around it together.
pros: The team shares one problem.
Players learn to help each other.
cons: One player can direct the rest.
Players away from the jam may wait.

pairs.tendency: Players share the slow step but each wants a bigger share of what passes, so they help each other and still try to jump the queue.
pros: Shows tension about who goes first.
Players weigh helping against gaining.
cons: Selfish play can deepen the jam.
Trust can break.

pairs.tendency: Each team has its own slow step, and the team that clears its jam first tends to pull ahead, so teams watch each other's queues.
pros: Teams have a clear shared problem.
Team talk is about the jam.
cons: One player may take over their team's plan.
A team stuck at the jam can lose heart.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly works against the team, and a hold up at the slow step looks the same whether it is chance or sabotage.
pros: Suspicion has a place to land.
Delays get questioned.
cons: Hard to tell a jam from sabotage.
Accusations can upset players.

pairs.tendency: Turns go by letter, and the slowest reply sets the pace of the whole game, so one late post holds up every other move.
pros: Waiting is part of play.
Slow replies are easy to see.
cons: Games can take weeks.
Players may lose track of where things stand.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and if their step is the slow one, everyone waits on someone who cannot answer.
pros: The wait has a clear cause.
Players have to plan without them.
cons: Others wait on a missing player.
The game can stall for ever.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, and if their rulings are the slowest step, every other player waits on them to say what happens.
pros: Players see how one person sets the pace.
The game master can speed up or slow down.
cons: The game master carries the load.
Others may wait with nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in the open, and passers-by join at the narrow point, which fills up and holds back everyone else.
pros: Crowds make the jam easy to see.
People can join at any time.
cons: The jam grows with the crowd.
Late joiners may never reach the front.

pairs.tendency: One player faces the rest, and the lone player is the slow step if they act alone, so the group tends to wait on them each round.
pros: The slow step is a person.
The group can plan around them.
cons: The lone player feels watched.
The group may rush them.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the whole line alone, so the slow step is easy to find by watching where stock piles up, and nobody else is waiting.
pros: Players find the jam by themselves.
Time to think about it.
cons: Nobody to share the problem with.
Little reason to keep playing once found.

pairs.tendency: Dice or draws decide what goes through the slow step, so the queue grows and shrinks by luck and players can only watch it.
pros: Players feel how a jam is shaped by luck.
Light play.
cons: Nothing a player does changes the jam.
Some players blame luck for what is a limit.

pairs.tendency: Luck decides what goes through the slow step, but players can add a second route or spare capacity, so they can soften a jam.
pros: Players learn to prepare for it.
Choices have a clear effect.
cons: Spare capacity costs something.
Preparation can feel small beside luck.

pairs.tendency: Careful players find the slow step and plan around it, with a little luck in what arrives, so planning tends to pay off.
pros: Finding the jam is rewarded.
Some surprise stays.
cons: Experienced players tend to find it first.
Beginners can feel left behind.

pairs.tendency: The slow step is fixed and plain to see, so skilled players plan around it from the first round and the rest tend to learn it late.
pros: Every jam has a reason.
Planning has clear value.
cons: Experienced players tend to find it first.
Little surprise after the first game.

pairs.tendency: Players read dice as a sign, and a hold up at the slow step may be read as a message, not as a limit in the system.
pros: Players find meaning in the jam.
Talk is about what it means.
cons: Players may read a sign where there is a cause.
The real limit can go unseen.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others will act, and the slowest person at the step sets the rhythm, so everyone tunes to them.
pros: Players learn each other's pace.
The group moves as one.
cons: The slow player feels the pull.
Players out of step spoil the rhythm.

pairs.tendency: Rolls are looked up on a table, and an entry that says the road is blocked makes the story pile up behind it.
pros: Jams become part of the story.
Players tell why they are held up.
cons: Entries may block the story for too long.
Dice decide where the jam falls.

pairs.tendency: Everyone can see the whole line, so the slow step shows itself at once and every player knows where the queue is.
pros: The jam is plain to see.
Planning together is easy.
cons: Seeing a jam does not clear it.
Little surprise after the first look.

pairs.tendency: Players hold hidden cards, so nobody can see who holds the slow step, and they have to guess who is holding things up.
pros: Guessing who holds the jam is tense.
Players learn to read each other.
cons: Hard to find the cause.
Players may blame the wrong person.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles, so a hold up at the slow step could be a limit or someone's plan, and nobody can be sure which.
pros: Delays raise suspicion.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: Hard to tell a jam from sabotage.
A real limit can be mistaken for a plot.

pairs.tendency: Players work out where the hold up is from what piles up and where, so the slow step is the answer to the puzzle.
pros: Piles of stock are the clue.
Finding the cause feels satisfying.
cons: Players may look in the wrong place.
Slow to work out.

pairs.tendency: Players can lie about their stock or speed, so the slow step can be hidden behind false claims about who is waiting.
pros: Claims about the jam can be tested.
Mind games have something to fight over.
cons: Hard to find the real jam.
Lies can upset people.

pairs.tendency: Players find the rules by breaking them, and the slow step is one rule they learn only when stock begins to pile up.
pros: Players find the limit by hitting it.
Learning feels earned.
cons: Early rounds can feel confusing.
Players may waste effort before they find it.

pairs.tendency: One player knows where the slow step is but cannot say, so they can only hint while the others work on the wrong part.
pros: Hints can point at the jam.
Others learn by watching.
cons: The knower feels stuck.
Others may speed up the wrong steps.

pairs.tendency: The map is revealed as players explore, so the narrow point is found only when someone reaches it and sees the queue.
pros: Finding the jam is a surprise.
Exploring has a reason.
cons: Players may build before they find it.
Early moves are blind.

pairs.tendency: One hand is face up for all to see, so the slow step in that hand is clear and the others can plan around it.
pros: Everyone can read one hand.
Teaching by example is easy.
cons: The open hand can give the jam away.
Other jams stay hidden.

pairs.tendency: Scores are secret, so players cannot tell who is held up by the slow step and who is ahead, until the end.
pros: Surprise at the end.
Players watch the jam, not scores.
cons: Hard to tell who is stuck.
Players can feel in the dark.

pairs.tendency: Players take one turn at a time, so the slow step makes everyone else wait for the same player, and the table can see the wait.
pros: Waiting is plain to see.
Easy to follow.
cons: Others sit idle during the long turn.
Slow turns stretch the game.

pairs.tendency: Everyone acts at once, so only the slow step makes anyone wait, and the rest finish early and sit with spare time.
pros: Speed gaps show at once.
Everyone is busy until the jam.
cons: The fast finish and then wait.
The slow player feels watched.

pairs.tendency: Players act whenever they like, so work races ahead of the slow step and piles up before it, as in a factory line with one slow machine.
pros: Players watch stock build up.
Quick players see the cost of speed.
cons: Rushing adds no progress.
Piles can grow out of hand.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and the slow step may not finish in time, so unfinished work carries over and the queue grows.
pros: The clock makes the limit felt.
Players learn to pace themselves.
cons: Unfinished work piles up.
Time pressure can spoil careful play.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks, so a slow step shows as real waiting, and players feel a jam from one day to the next.
pros: The wait is real.
Players see the jam grow over days.
cons: Players may lose interest in between.
Long games can be dropped.

pairs.tendency: The game slows everyone on purpose, so the slow step is one more pause, and speeding up other steps matters even less.
pros: Slowness has a reason.
Players notice the pause.
cons: The jam may not stand out.
Long waits can bore players.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so the slow step falls further behind each round and the queue in front of it grows faster.
pros: Players see a jam growing.
Pressure rises round by round.
cons: The queue becomes unmanageable.
Players can feel swamped.

pairs.tendency: Some moves earn another turn, but an extra turn at a fast step adds nothing, so only an extra turn at the slow step speeds the game up.
pros: Players see which turns count.
Extra turns have a reason.
cons: Extra turns elsewhere go to waste.
Players may chase the wrong ones.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages, and the slow step moves from one stage to the next, so a fix in stage one may not carry to stage two.
pros: Players meet a new jam each stage.
Earlier choices show up later.
cons: A fix can stop working.
Players may repeat the same mistake.

pairs.tendency: The board models a real system, and the slow step in it is the narrow point that every output passes, so changes elsewhere show little.
pros: The real system's weak point is plain.
Players test where effort helps.
cons: The model may seem too simple.
Players may not link it to real life.

pairs.tendency: Players act as groups along one line, and the group with the slowest job holds up the rest, so all of them depend on it.
pros: Each group sees how it depends on others.
The slow role has a real voice.
cons: The slow role can feel blamed.
Other groups can feel idle.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited supply, and the slow step is how fast it can be refilled, so taking faster does not bring more.
pros: The limit on refilling is plain.
Players see the cost of taking.
cons: Players may keep taking until it runs out.
Arguments about fair shares.

pairs.tendency: A fix at the slow step shows its result only after a few rounds, so players may change it again before the first change has worked.
pros: Players learn to wait and watch.
The delay and the jam are seen together.
cons: Impatient players may undo a fix that was working.
Hard to tell which change worked.

pairs.tendency: Players try a rule for the slow step, such as a second worker, and play on to see whether the queue shrinks.
pros: Testing a fix is safe.
Players see the effect in play.
cons: Some rules change nothing.
One round may not show the effect.

pairs.tendency: After play, the group talks about where stock piled up and why, so the slow step is found by looking back and not by feeling it.
pros: Talk can name the real jam.
Players link the game to their own work.
cons: Players may argue about the cause.
The jam is found too late to fix.

pairs.tendency: A change at the slow step stays, so a widened or damaged step carries into later games and later rounds, and a hasty fix cannot be undone.
pros: Choices at the jam have a lasting effect.
Players think before they fix it.
cons: A poor fix stays in the game.
Players may be afraid to change anything.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point that one slow step limits the whole system, so players come away seeing where speed does and does not matter.
pros: The point is made by play.
Players find it for themselves.
cons: Players may think the point is too neat.
Real systems are less simple.

pairs.tendency: The queue at the slow step carries a real consequence, such as who does a chore, so waiting in it matters beyond the table.
pros: Waiting feels real.
Players care about the order.
cons: Real disputes can start about who is first.
Some players feel unfairly held.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, and the slow step caps how many can be earned, so players find that effort has a limit.
pros: Players see value held back by one step.
The limit is a topic for talk.
cons: Players may chase points and miss the cause.
Caps can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future way of working and find where it would jam, as a village sharing tools finds one tool that everyone waits for.
pros: Players find a jam before it happens.
A safe place to practise.
cons: The game may miss real jams.
Players may take the model for a forecast.

pairs.tendency: Goods made ahead to a guess pile up in front of the slow step, while goods pulled by orders only pass when it is ready, so each shows the jam differently.
pros: Pushing and pulling show different piles.
Players see the cost of each.
cons: Pulling can leave later steps idle.
Pushing can fill the line with stock.

pairs.tendency: Bigger batches make the slow step wait for a full batch, and smaller ones cost it setting up again, so batch size changes how long the queue is.
pros: Batch size has a clear effect on the queue.
Players try sizes and see the change.
cons: Small batches cost more in set up.
Large batches leave later steps waiting.

pairs.tendency: A machine at the slow step breaks and the whole line stops, so a breakdown there costs far more than a breakdown anywhere else.
pros: The cost of a breakdown is plain.
Players value spare machines.
cons: One breakdown can stop everyone.
Luck decides who is hit.

pairs.tendency: Stock piles up in front of the slow step and costs something every round, while the steps after it run short, so players pay both ways.
pros: Players see both costs at once.
The pile shows where stock is wasted.
cons: Players may cut stock too far.
Balancing takes careful counting.

pairs.tendency: Players roll and move along a path while orders either wait for them or travel ahead of them, so a die roll decides whether stock arrives where it is wanted.
pros: Easy way to feel stock moving down a line.
Each space shows a delay or a pile-up.
cons: Dice can hide whether the pull or push rule caused a stall.
Luck can outweigh the planning being taught.

pairs.tendency: Players pick cards that stand for goods made to a forecast or made to an order, then pass the rest, so each pick shows what the next player is left with.
pros: Picks show who gets stuck with leftovers.
Passing makes the line of hand-offs visible.
cons: Many cards to explain.
Picks can feel like collecting, not planning.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for goods or orders, and bids show whether stock made ahead sells cheaply or an order pulls a higher price.
pros: Prices show the cost of unsold stock.
Bids make demand easy to read.
cons: Players short on money drop out of the line.
Bidding can take over from the production rule.

pairs.tendency: Players keep making more ahead of orders for a bigger payout, and stop when they fear a pile of unsold stock.
pros: Over-making is felt, not just told.
Tension comes from a guess about demand.
cons: A bust turn can feel random, not caused.
Careful players may stay on the pull side throughout.

pairs.tendency: Players hold parts of a map that make and ship goods, either to a forecast or on an order, so each area's stock depends on who holds the next area.
pros: The map shows where stock piles up.
Links between places are clear.
cons: Fights over areas can hide the production rule.
Busy boards are hard to read.

pairs.tendency: Workers go to spaces that make goods, either ahead of orders or only when one arrives, so players see idle workers on one rule and rushed ones on the other.
pros: Idle time and rush time are both visible.
Planning feels like running a real line.
cons: Blocked spaces can look like a pull problem.
Many spaces to explain.

pairs.tendency: Players build patterns that stand for a line of work, and filling a gap ahead of the order is a push, while waiting for it is a pull.
pros: Gaps in the line become visible.
Calm, thoughtful building.
cons: The link to production can feel abstract.
Little sense of time passing.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand are goods or orders, and players decide whether to make what they hold ahead of time or wait for an order card.
pros: Holding a card shows what waiting costs.
Planning ahead has a clear price.
cons: Many cards to learn.
Hands can pile up and bury the rule.

pairs.tendency: Each trick is a small sale, and players who made ahead hold cards that may not match what is led, while those who wait have little to play.
pros: Familiar card play with a stock meaning.
Quick rounds show hits and misses.
cons: The link to production can feel thin.
Strong hands decide a lot.

pairs.tendency: Players talk over who makes what, and deals decide whether stock goes ahead to a buyer on a guess or waits for a firm order.
pros: Talk covers real supply-chain trade-offs.
Trust between buyer and maker becomes visible.
cons: Talk can drift away from the line.
Loud players can steer what gets made.

pairs.tendency: Players collect sets of parts, and either the parts are made ahead and pushed to them, or each part is made when a set is short.
pros: Collecting shows which parts are missing.
Clear goals for what to make.
cons: Sets can feel like a checklist.
Little sense of cause and effect.

pairs.tendency: Players lay tiles that build a factory floor or delivery map, so the layout shows how far goods have to travel to meet an order.
pros: The line grows in front of you.
Layout choices have a visible effect on delay.
cons: Building can matter more than the rule.
Tile luck can distort the result.

pairs.tendency: One player calls an order and the next answers with what they can supply, so each answer shows how far back the pull reaches.
pros: Orders travel back down the line.
Easy to explain with voices alone.
cons: Chains can wander away from stock.
Quiet players may be left out.

pairs.tendency: Without talking, players pass goods or orders along a line, so a push or pull only shows when something piles up or runs short.
pros: Shortages show without any explaining.
Silence makes everyone watch the stock.
cons: Nobody can ask what an order meant.
Mistakes may go unnoticed until late.

pairs.tendency: A player changes a rule on their turn, such as when goods may be made, so the group can swap between push and pull mid-game.
pros: The two rules can be compared directly.
Players see what each rule changes.
cons: Rule changes can bury the line itself.
Arguments over whose change counts.

pairs.tendency: Players speak as a planner, a shop owner or a machine operator, and each defends making ahead or waiting for orders from where they stand.
pros: Each role has a reason for its habit.
Arguments show why people disagree about stock.
cons: Players may play to type and skip the numbers.
Quiet players can be talked over.

pairs.tendency: Players stack, flick or balance pieces that stand for goods, so a steady hand decides whether a batch reaches the next stage.
pros: Physical goods make a hand-off feel real.
Lively and easy to watch.
cons: Skill with the hands can outweigh the rule.
Shaky players may feel left out.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the factory, store and delivery routes as they go, and the drawn distance shows how long an order waits to be pulled through.
pros: Players make the line themselves.
Routes show delay in plain view.
cons: Drawing skill varies a lot.
Slow to start.

pairs.tendency: You ask a player for a card, which is like placing an order, and they either already have it made or have to find it.
pros: Asking works like a pull signal.
Stock held by others is guessed from answers.
cons: Asks can feel like guessing, not planning.
Players can ask the same thing repeatedly.

pairs.tendency: The bank holds the stock and players bet on whether it will meet demand, so a made-ahead supply is a bet the bank may lose.
pros: Risk of unsold stock is felt at once.
Fixed odds make the cost clear.
cons: Bets can overshadow the production rule.
Players who lose chips stop caring.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on a throw that stands for demand, so a pile of goods made ahead pays only if the throw goes their way.
pros: Demand uncertainty is easy to feel.
Quick rounds.
cons: Players only choose the bet, not the production.
Little room to learn from the result.

pairs.tendency: Players raise or fold while their hidden cards stand for goods, so betting on stock made ahead feels like betting on a forecast.
pros: Risk and forecast feel alike.
Dropping out shows when to cut losses.
cons: Bluffing can take over from the rule.
A losing player has little left to do.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a make-ahead side or a make-to-order side before play, and then the two meet in the same market.
pros: The two ways run side by side.
Differences show up in the same rounds.
cons: One side may be clearly easier to start with.
Mismatched sides can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: Before play, a player names how many orders they will fill, so a contract on a pulled order meets a pushed forecast.
pros: Promises put a number on the forecast.
Missing a contract shows its cost.
cons: A failed contract can sting.
Cautious players call small.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece changes sides, so a stock of goods pushed to a front may end up working for the other player.
pros: Over-pushed stock becomes a risk.
A lead can reverse in one move.
cons: Players may stop making anything ahead.
A swing can feel arbitrary.

pairs.tendency: Players jailed with stock have to wait for a teammate to free them, so goods made ahead can sit stuck while an order pulls rescue.
pros: Waiting for help shows idle stock.
Teamwork pulls things forward.
cons: Players in jail wait without a task.
Rescues can overshadow the line.

pairs.tendency: Players surround pieces until they run out of room, like a store room filling up with goods made ahead of orders.
pros: Running out of space shows the cost of stock.
Quiet, thoughtful play.
cons: The link to production is loose.
Slow positional turns.

pairs.tendency: Players who are behind get a boost, such as extra goods or orders, so a late order can still pull a trailing player back in.
pros: Late starters stay in the game.
The rule helps show how a pull can rescue.
cons: The boost can hide the production rule.
Leaders may feel held back.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide demand and nothing else, so players with stock made ahead and players waiting are both only watching luck.
pros: Shows demand nobody can control.
Quick and light.
cons: Players make few real choices.
The production rule has little effect.

pairs.tendency: One player chases the rest around a space, so goods pushed out are caught, and those made only when an order comes are slower to leave.
pros: Running makes speed easy to feel.
Lively and physical.
cons: The line can turn into a chase.
Slow players are caught often.

pairs.tendency: Each turn a player picks who receives goods or orders, so a push can overload one buyer while a pull follows the buyer asking most.
pros: Targets show who gets the stock.
Choices have a clear who.
cons: Players can gang up on one buyer.
The line can be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: Players link one side of the board to the other, like a chain of makers and stores, and a gap shows where orders cannot reach.
pros: A gap in the chain is plain to see.
The goal ties to the whole line.
cons: Cutting a link can feel like a fight, not a stall.
Hard for new players to read.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, so making ahead beats a slow pull, but a surprise order beats a big stock.
pros: Neither rule wins every time.
Players keep trying both.
cons: Can feel like guessing.
The link to real stock is loose.

pairs.tendency: Players announce a pair or run they hold, like announcing stock made ahead, while the cards stay hidden in hand.
pros: Announcing stock shows what it costs to hold.
Points arrive during play.
cons: Pairs can feel like a side game.
Unlike real orders, nobody asks for them.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a special power, such as making goods in advance or on demand, so players run the line by slightly different rules.
pros: Different habits meet in one market.
Easy to compare approaches.
cons: Some powers may fit the game more easily.
Many powers to learn.

pairs.tendency: A player can double what the game is worth, like a big order that rewards a pushed stock but ruins an empty one.
pros: Big orders make risk plain.
Dramatic moments.
cons: A double can end a round suddenly.
Cautious players give up early.

pairs.tendency: A player who can capture has to, so stock made ahead can force a move, while an order-led player has more choice.
pros: Stock held ahead limits choices.
Forced moves can be planned around.
cons: Players can feel they have no say.
Can turn into a puzzle.

pairs.tendency: What players do builds their power, so a line that pulls steadily may grow into larger orders over rounds.
pros: Growth shows the long game.
Early choices carry forward.
cons: Early leads can run away.
Later challenges can swamp the line.

pairs.tendency: Players recite a growing list of goods made so far, and the longer list shows how much was pushed against how much was asked for.
pros: Memory shows the pile building up.
Easy to play anywhere.
cons: Players forget items and lose the thread.
Turns slow as the list grows.

pairs.tendency: The stronger player starts with less stock or time, so a pull-led line can face a pushed one on near-equal terms.
pros: The two rules meet on more even ground.
A newer player has a chance.
cons: Handicaps can hide what the rule does.
Setting the amount takes some trial.

pairs.tendency: Someone hides goods and others hunt for them, so stock made ahead can be lost in a store, and an order may find nothing.
pros: Lost stock is felt, not told.
Lively search.
cons: The search can overtake the lesson.
Hiding spots may be too easy.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another into a space behind, so pushed goods leap ahead and orders may need the way cleared first.
pros: Gaps show where goods can pass.
Hops give quick, clear moves.
cons: Jumping may seem unlike a supply line.
Long chains of jumps can confuse.

pairs.tendency: Players keep some dice and reroll the rest, like keeping stock made already while pulling more only for what is missing.
pros: Keeping dice feels like holding stock.
Rerolls act like fresh orders.
cons: A lot of luck remains.
Players stop thinking about the line.

pairs.tendency: A landing sends a piece back to the start, like a rejected batch that has to be made again, and pushed stock risks being sent back in bulk.
pros: Rework is felt directly.
Safe spaces act like checked stages.
cons: Setbacks can feel unfair.
Players may avoid risk altogether.

pairs.tendency: Players build rows to take an opponent's piece, so a row made ahead of need can be broken up before it pays off.
pros: Built stock can be lost to a rival.
Rows give a clear short goal.
cons: Fighting can hide the production rule.
Slow to explain to new players.

pairs.tendency: Players make words from letters, so letters held ahead may not fit, while waiting to draw what a word needs costs time.
pros: Letters in hand feel like stock.
Dictionary settles every argument.
cons: The word game can outweigh the rule.
Vocabulary gaps decide a lot.

pairs.tendency: A tile can only join a matching end, so stock made ahead may fit nothing, and a missing match means a lost turn.
pros: Mismatched stock is easy to see.
Simple rule with a clear stall.
cons: Missing turns can feel dull.
Luck of the draw decides much.

pairs.tendency: Players lay down finished sets that others can add to, so batches made ahead can become a shared pile that grows.
pros: Shared stock shows what is held.
Adding to others' sets is quick.
cons: Sets on the table can lock in a plan.
Players may hold back cards.

pairs.tendency: Each player has powers that work once, so a push or a pull can be saved for the order that needs it.
pros: Timing of a single move matters.
Players weigh when to spend.
cons: Used powers leave players with little to do.
A power spent early can feel wasted.

pairs.tendency: The other player can turn down a move, like a buyer refusing goods that were pushed to them.
pros: Refusal makes the pull visible.
Players have to offer what is wanted.
cons: Refusals can stall the game.
Offers can feel like haggling.

pairs.tendency: A message moves from player to player and may change, like an order passing back down a line and getting garbled.
pros: Errors in passing become visible.
Easy and funny to play.
cons: Funny results can mask the point.
Hard to check where a change began.

pairs.tendency: Players hand cards to another player before play, like pushing stock to a buyer who cannot say what they want.
pros: Passing shows the cost of guessing.
Players think about the other's needs.
cons: A poor pass can wreck a hand.
Players can only guess what they receive.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the start and the other picks a side, like a maker forecasting demand for a buyer who chooses whether to take it.
pros: Forecasts get tested straight away.
Both sides stay even.
cons: Setup needs a careful eye.
Choosing a side can feel like guessing.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a stronger one, like a batch that keeps moving and becomes a finished product.
pros: Moving forward has a clear reward.
Finished goods feel worth reaching.
cons: Players may push too hard.
Staying back to wait becomes unlikely.

pairs.tendency: Teams run goods in legs, handing over to the next runner, so a stack pushed ahead meets a runner not yet ready to receive it.
pros: Hand-offs show where a line stalls.
Teams cheer each other.
cons: Fast runners may rush past the idea.
The race can overshadow the lesson.

pairs.tendency: Players build shapes that cannot be taken, like a buffer stock kept safe against surprises.
pros: Safe stock has a clear price.
Players aim for something firm.
cons: Safe shapes can slow the pace.
The link to orders is thin.

pairs.tendency: Named scoring cards are the prizes, so players decide whether to hold stock for a known prize or wait for it to be called.
pros: Known prizes shape what is made.
Waiting for a prize feels like pull.
cons: Prize cards can overshadow the production rule.
Players may chase the same prize.

pairs.tendency: Shared cards in the middle can be used by anyone, like a common stock that either side may draw on.
pros: Shared stock raises talk about use.
Everyone sees what is available.
cons: Players can lean on others' stock.
The rule can sit in the background.

pairs.tendency: Everyone adds to a pot, so over-making ahead feeds a growing pot nobody has asked for, while waiting leaves it small.
pros: Growing waste is easy to see.
Rounds get a rising stake.
cons: Pots can pull attention from the line.
A big pot can end in a hollow win.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are dropped one by one into pits, so each push moves stock along a loop and the last seed decides what comes back.
pros: Moving stock around a loop is clear.
Easy to read from pit counts.
cons: Hard to see an order in a loop.
The rule can feel like counting.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand is dealt and one player can take, swap or buy it, like spare stock that may or may not suit what is needed.
pros: Spare stock shows its use or waste.
Buying it feels like a clear choice.
cons: Spare hands can feel random.
One player gains a clear edge.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces keep goods safe, send them back or cost a turn, so a pushed batch meets delays at set points on the way.
pros: Fixed delays are easy to learn.
Spaces show where lines slow down.
cons: Squares can feel like arbitrary luck.
Players stop watching orders.

pairs.tendency: Everything has a price, so making ahead means spending now and hoping an order arrives, while a pull spends only when asked.
pros: Cash tied up in stock is plain.
Costs are clear at every step.
cons: Players with little cash fall behind.
Counting costs can slow turns.

pairs.tendency: A fixed amount is shared between places or jobs, so putting more into stock made ahead leaves less for orders on demand.
pros: Trade-offs between stock and orders are clear.
Each split can be compared.
cons: Players may feel any split is a guess.
A split made in error is hard to undo.

pairs.tendency: Everyone keeps moving until a signal comes, like stock made until an order stops the line, and the slowest is caught holding goods.
pros: Stopping shows who is left holding stock.
Lively and quick.
cons: Speed can matter more than the idea.
Slower players are caught often.

pairs.tendency: Players swap cards for new ones before the hand is played, like reworking stock to match what orders now want.
pros: Swapping shows the cost of changing stock.
Players adjust to what they see.
cons: Swaps can pile up.
Another player may block a swap.

pairs.tendency: A player can pick up the whole discard pile, like taking on a store of unsold stock that others made ahead.
pros: The pile shows how much went unsold.
Taking it back feels like a hard choice.
cons: Big piles can swing a game.
Players may avoid the pile out of fear.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the others, like a product whose demand is high this season, so stock made ahead of it pays more.
pros: A strong season rewards guesses.
Hands change value with the trump.
cons: Hands can be luck, not forecast.
The rule can sit behind the card play.

pairs.tendency: Two games run at once on two boards, so one board is pushed on a forecast while the other waits for orders.
pros: The two ways sit side by side.
Players compare them in one sitting.
cons: Two boards are a lot to follow.
Slow to set up.

pairs.tendency: Wild cards stand for any card, like flexible stock that can fill whichever order comes, so waiting costs less.
pros: Flexible stock shows its value.
Shortfalls can be patched.
cons: Wilds can cover mistakes.
The pull rule loses its edge.

pairs.tendency: The board edges join, so goods pushed off one side come back from the other, and a line never quite ends.
pros: Loops show goods coming back round.
Easy to learn in one go.
cons: Loops can blur where a line starts.
Nothing marks a finished order.

pairs.tendency: Players ask yes-or-no questions to find what one player knows, like asking what the buyer wants instead of guessing.
pros: Asking shows the value of knowing demand.
Questions narrow the field.
cons: Slow if the questions drift.
The one answering can feel pressed.

pairs.tendency: Players race to clear the line, and the first to finish decides who wins, so pushing ahead to hit a target can leave unused stock behind.
pros: Clear target.
The speed of the line is easy to feel.
cons: Racing can push players to ignore waste.
Leaders can pull away.

pairs.tendency: Points come from filling orders, so players weigh making ahead against waiting for orders that each carry points.
pros: Scores make the two rules comparable.
Players test different plans.
cons: Points can matter more than the line.
Scoring can take time.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out when their stock runs out or piles too high, until one line is left.
pros: Failing lines are easy to spot.
Tense.
cons: Players out early wait.
Can feel harsh.

pairs.tendency: The team keeps a line supplied against demand that keeps shifting, and a big pile or a stall can sink them all.
pros: Everyone sees the same stock.
Shared pressure on the line.
cons: One player can direct the rest.
Collapse can feel hopeless.

pairs.tendency: The group works to meet one shared target, such as filling every order in the round, using either rule.
pros: Teamwork on one real problem.
Clear goal.
cons: Little tension.
Some players can follow without thinking.

pairs.tendency: Each player secretly wants something different from the line, such as low stock or fast orders, so push and pull serve different aims.
pros: Shows one line serving different wants.
Mystery.
cons: Secret goals can hide the production rule.
Hard to read.

pairs.tendency: The line becomes a story of a factory or shop, until it reaches its end, and a pile-up or a stall becomes a turning point.
pros: A stall becomes a story.
Easy to remember.
cons: The story can blur the rule.
The ending can feel set in advance.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and players run a line either way and then look at the stock left over and the orders missed.
pros: Gentle way to compare the two rules.
Players can talk through what happened.
cons: No clear target to chase.
Hard to say what it was for.

pairs.tendency: Each player chooses what a run that worked looks like, such as no stock left or no late orders, and tests it under push or pull.
pros: Players pick the thing they care about.
Reflection on what to measure.
cons: Goals can be hard to compare.
Easy to choose a goal the rule cannot test.

pairs.tendency: Play goes on until one line fails, either buried in unsold stock or starved of orders, and everyone else is safe.
pros: The failing rule is clear to see.
Others stay relaxed.
cons: The loser can feel singled out.
Players may avoid any risky choice.

pairs.tendency: Players keep the line running round after round, so stock and orders go on shifting and neither rule ever finishes the job.
pros: Lasting runs show slow build-up.
Long-term effects appear.
cons: No end to draw lessons from.
Interest can fade.

pairs.tendency: The game refuses a winner, so stock made ahead and orders pulled both feel like effort with no finish.
pros: Shows that supply never fully settles.
Players talk about the point of it.
cons: Players can feel frustrated.
The rule can be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a fixed layout of orders, and either build stock ahead or wait to clear each one.
pros: Easy to test one rule at a time.
No pressure from others.
cons: No second player to compare against.
Stuck positions can feel flat.

pairs.tendency: Players run several short lines, perhaps one on push and one on pull, and whoever wins most rounds takes the match.
pros: The two rules can each have a round.
Short games show the difference quickly.
cons: One lucky round can skew the result.
Repeats can feel the same.

pairs.tendency: Every unsold item or late order counts against a player, and the lowest score wins, so waste on either rule shows in the score.
pros: Waste has a plain number.
Fits stock and delay costs.
cons: Counting losses can feel gloomy.
Players hold back from risk.

pairs.tendency: A player has to land exactly on a target, like making exactly the number of goods ordered, and extra stock costs the win.
pros: Over-making has a clear price.
Exact amounts suit orders.
cons: Near misses can sting.
Pushed batches rarely land exactly.

pairs.tendency: Players aim to give everything away, so the winner is the one whose stock is gone first, whether pushed out or pulled out.
pros: Moving stock is the whole aim.
Turns the usual fear of unsold stock upside down.
cons: Can confuse new players.
Players may lose track of the production rule.

pairs.tendency: Each player runs their own line side by side, one pushed and one pulled, and they compare stock and delay at the end.
pros: A fair side-by-side comparison.
Calm.
cons: Little contact.
Hard to see how people affect each other.

pairs.tendency: Players attack or steal from each other's stock, so a big pushed pile is a target and a thin pulled line is harder to hit.
pros: Large stock shows its risk.
Dramatic.
cons: Fights can hide the production rule.
Can feel mean.

pairs.tendency: Players share a supply line, so one player's stock made ahead blocks space or buyers for another.
pros: Shows how makers affect each other.
Quiet, clear links.
cons: Effects can be hard to trace.
Slow turns.

pairs.tendency: The whole team runs one line together, and everyone sees where stock piles up or runs short.
pros: Shared view of the line.
Everyone has a part.
cons: One player can direct the rest.
Little tension.

pairs.tendency: Players share a supply line but each wants more for themselves, so pushing stock onto a neighbour may help or hurt them.
pros: Shows tension between self and the chain.
Tense choices.
cons: Selfish play can wreck the line.
Hard to balance.

pairs.tendency: Two teams run their own lines against each other, one making ahead and one waiting for orders, in the same market.
pros: Clear contest between the two rules.
Team talk.
cons: One player can take over.
Competition can hide the rule.

pairs.tendency: The team runs a line while one player secretly adds extra stock or hides orders, so a pile-up may be sabotage or just a push.
pros: Suspicion about who caused a stall.
Tense.
cons: Hard to tell the rule from sabotage.
Accusations can upset people.

pairs.tendency: Players send orders and goods by letter over weeks, so waiting for a reply is itself the delay that pull rules face.
pros: Waiting shows the lead time.
Slow, thoughtful play.
cons: Letters can be misread.
Play is hard to keep going.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so their orders arrive as notes and made-ahead stock has to guess what they want.
pros: Absence shows what a forecast costs.
Players think of a far buyer.
cons: Guesses can feel empty.
The absent player may be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the market and sends orders, so makers either build stock to the master's hints or wait for a firm order.
pros: The master controls how clear demand is.
Demand can change as play goes on.
cons: The master can tilt the result.
A lot of work for one person.

pairs.tendency: A game played in a street or park, where passers-by join in, makes demand arrive at random and stock made ahead may suit nobody.
pros: Random buyers feel real.
Easy to join.
cons: Hard to control the line.
Rules may be played in different ways.

pairs.tendency: One player is the buyer and the rest are makers, so the buyer's orders pull while the makers have to guess ahead.
pros: Demand has a face.
A clear sides-split for push and pull.
cons: The lone player carries the load.
Makers can gang up on the buyer.

pairs.tendency: One player runs a whole line against dice and cards, trying push and pull in turn, with no one to compare with in the moment.
pros: Easy to try both rules alone.
No wait for others.
cons: Little sense of other people's demand.
Hard to tell if results are typical.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide demand, so stock made ahead is a gamble, and a pull rule can only wait for whatever turns up.
pros: Shows demand nobody controls.
Light.
cons: Few choices.
Players may feel nothing they do matters.

pairs.tendency: Demand is random, but players can soften it with spare stock, quick changeovers or a wait, so each rule has tools against a run of ill luck.
pros: Planning against surprise is clear.
Interesting choices.
cons: More rules.
Preparation can feel small.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly decide what to make and when, with some random demand, so forecasts and orders both matter.
pros: Clear cause and effect.
Some surprise.
cons: Experienced players tend to win.
Slow.

pairs.tendency: No dice, so demand follows rules players can work out, and push suits a known forecast while pull suits a puzzle.
pros: Every result has a reason.
Deep thinking.
cons: Real demand is rarely this steady.
Slow.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a message about demand, so players decide on stock by a sign rather than a number.
pros: Players talk about how they read demand.
Gentle and curious.
cons: Hard to connect to the rule.
Readings can seem empty.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others are about to need something, like a maker who starts a batch just before the order arrives.
pros: Reading each other works like a forecast.
Warm, close play.
cons: Hard to explain the rule.
Some players feel left out.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what order or delay comes next, so demand writes part of the story.
pros: Orders feel like events.
Story and stock go together.
cons: Tables can bury the rule.
Rolls can feel random.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sees every order and every pile of stock, so pull has little to hide and push can follow a known demand.
pros: Easy to discuss.
Fair.
cons: Real demand is rarely this visible.
Little surprise.

pairs.tendency: Players hold secret stock or orders, so a pushed batch may go to a buyer who cannot say what they hold.
pros: Shows how stock is hidden in a chain.
Mystery.
cons: Hard to plan together.
Confusing for some.

pairs.tendency: Players act inside a supply line while secretly on hidden sides, so a pile of stock may be a trap or a mistake.
pros: Hidden interests show in a chain.
Mystery.
cons: Hard to read.
Confusing for some.

pairs.tendency: Players work out the hidden demand from what has sold, so stock made ahead is a guess from clues and a pull reads the order directly.
pros: Detective work about demand.
Satisfying when it clicks.
cons: Hard for some.
Slow.

pairs.tendency: Players can mislead each other about their stock or orders, so a claim of a full store may hide an empty one.
pros: Shows how false claims upset a chain.
Mind games.
cons: Hard to read.
Lies can upset people.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, like when goods may be made, and others find it by breaking it and being told no.
pros: Players find a rule by trying it.
Curious.
cons: Players may feel foolish.
Hard to tie back to stock.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the real demand but can only hint, so others guess how much to make ahead.
pros: Shows the value of a clear order.
Hints build teamwork.
cons: Hints can mislead.
Frustrating for the one who knows.

pairs.tendency: The map is hidden until explored, so players make goods ahead for places they have not yet seen, while a pull waits to find out.
pros: Not knowing the buyer is felt.
Exploring is exciting.
cons: Stock may suit no one.
Slow start.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up, like a store whose stock everyone can see while other stock stays hidden.
pros: An open store shows what is on hand.
Players plan around it.
cons: Open stock can make the rest feel dull.
Fewer surprises.

pairs.tendency: Some scores are hidden, so players cannot tell whether a rival's stock is paying off or piling up.
pros: Hidden results mimic real uncertainty.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: Players cannot learn from the result.
Frustrating if scores stay hidden.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so each player watches stock or orders change on the table before their own go.
pros: Changes are easy to follow.
Time to plan.
cons: Waiting can be dull.
Slow with many players.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses what to make at the same moment, so all lines make ahead or wait together and the market shows the sum.
pros: Fast and shows the whole market.
No waiting.
cons: Hard to trace who caused what.
Mistakes pile up fast.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so whoever is quickest fills an order, and a pushed stock is already there while a pull has to start from scratch.
pros: Speed gives pushed stock a visible edge.
Lively.
cons: Quick players dominate.
Rule differences get lost in the rush.

pairs.tendency: A clock limits each turn, so a pull has to wait on an order within the time, while a pushed stock is ready to hand.
pros: Time pressure shows what waiting costs.
Quick rounds.
cons: Rushed turns can cause mistakes.
Players may skip thinking.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days, one move each morning, so a push waits days for its orders and a pull's delay is felt in real time.
pros: Real waiting shows real delay.
Slow build of stock.
cons: Players may forget the game.
Hard to gather everyone.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose, so each batch waits and the effect of a push or a pull has time to be noticed.
pros: Time to see a pile form.
Calm.
cons: Slow.
Players may lose interest.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so orders arrive faster and stock made ahead goes out of date more quickly as the end rushes in.
pros: Speed shows which rule copes.
Mounting tension.
cons: Late turns become a scramble.
Mistakes pile up near the end.

pairs.tendency: A player on a lucky throw gets another go at once, so a pushed batch can be sent twice before an order is even placed.
pros: Quick follow-ups reward made-ahead stock.
Lively.
cons: A lucky run can overwhelm others.
Pull rule gets little time to show.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages, like building a line first and running it after, so stage one sets stock policy for stage two.
pros: Setup choices show up later.
Planning ahead is clear.
cons: Early mistakes can carry over.
More rules to teach.

pairs.tendency: The board models a real line of makers and shops, and players switch it between making ahead and making to order to see how stock moves.
pros: The real line becomes visible.
Clear cause and effect.
cons: Real lines have more parts.
Models can seem simple.

pairs.tendency: Players play a planner, a buyer or a shopkeeper, and each sees the same stock differently depending on who pays for a pile or a gap.
pros: Each role has its own view.
Reasons for the habit show.
cons: Players may play to type.
Debates can drift.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited stock, and making ahead can drain it before an order appears, while pull leaves it for use.
pros: Shared stock runs low in view of all.
Talk about who takes what.
cons: Players may race to take first.
Blame can start.

pairs.tendency: A choice shows its effect a few rounds later, so a push may look fine until the unsold pile appears, while a pull shows delay at once.
pros: Late effects are felt.
Planning ahead has weight.
cons: Players can lose track of causes.
Slow to see what changed.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a rule such as make only to order, then play on to see what it changes in stock and waiting.
pros: Safe test of a new rule.
Players compare before and after.
cons: One short test may mislead.
Slow if rules multiply.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk through why stock piled up or orders waited, and link it to a real shop or factory.
pros: Connects the table to real life.
Players share what they noticed.
cons: Talk can wander.
Quiet players may say little.

pairs.tendency: Choices to make goods stay in the game for keeps, so a pile of stock made ahead stays at the start of the next game.
pros: Long effects of a push are felt.
Choices carry weight.
cons: Early mistakes stay.
Hard for new players to join.

pairs.tendency: The rules show how a line works, so a game that rewards only low stock makes a case for pull, and one that rewards fast filling makes a case for push.
pros: Rules show a point of view.
Players can argue with it.
cons: One side may look more correct.
Hard to see the argument at first.

pairs.tendency: Players make real things to order or ahead, such as sandwiches for the class, and leftovers or missed orders matter.
pros: Waste and waiting feel real.
Players care about orders.
cons: Real stock may go to waste.
Some feel pressured.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for service and savings, so players may chase low stock or fast orders at the cost of what the numbers were meant to show.
pros: Shows a number replacing the thing.
Makes people question the measure.
cons: Players may follow the points blindly.
Measures can hide real harm.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future shop or kitchen that makes only to order, to see how it feels before trying it for real.
pros: Safe rehearsal of a new way.
Staff feel the change.
cons: The rehearsal may be too neat.
Real stress is hard to copy.

pairs.tendency: Players choose big batches made ahead or small batches made on order, and pay in waiting or set-up time for the choice.
pros: Batch size links to both rules.
Costs are easy to compare.
cons: Players can overthink the sums.
Set-up costs may seem arbitrary.

pairs.tendency: A machine breaks at random, so stock made ahead covers the gap while a pull line stops and orders wait.
pros: Spare stock shows its use.
Planning for failure feels real.
cons: Breakdowns can feel unfair.
Players may over-make just in case.

pairs.tendency: Holding stock costs every round and running out costs more, so push drifts to too much and pull to too little.
pros: Both costs are seen at once.
The balance is easy to feel.
cons: Players can fixate on one cost.
Hard to find a steady middle.

pairs.tendency: Players choose to move a whole group of pieces on one roll or send single pieces, and the dice decide how far each batch goes.
pros: Group moves feel bold and quick.
Single moves react to each roll.
cons: One poor roll strands the whole batch.
Splitting pieces means more rolls and more waiting.

pairs.tendency: Players take several cards from the pack in one pick or one card at a time, trading speed against how much they see of what others take.
pros: Big picks finish the round fast.
Single picks show what rivals want.
cons: Big picks hide what the table is taking.
One card at a time slows the passing.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for a lot of goods in one go or one item at a time, and a big lot ties up money until it is settled.
pros: Lots cut the number of auctions.
Single items let prices settle slowly.
cons: Big lots lock up most of a player's money.
One item at a time makes a long auction.

pairs.tendency: Players press on for one big haul or bank small gains often, and the larger the batch the more there is to lose in one bust.
pros: Big hauls feel tense.
Small gains keep players in the game.
cons: A bust on a big batch wipes the turn.
Banking often slows the pace.

pairs.tendency: Players send a large force to one area or a few pieces to many, and big forces take ground fast but leave other areas open.
pros: Big forces win a place quickly.
Thin spreads cover more of the map.
cons: Big forces leave other areas undefended.
Thin spreads are easy to beat in each place.

pairs.tendency: Players place several workers on one job or one worker per job, and the job may need setting up before a bigger batch pays off.
pros: Big batches use one visit well.
One worker per job keeps options open.
cons: Big batches block spaces for the others.
Setting up each job costs actions.

pairs.tendency: Players lay down a whole row of pieces at once or add one piece at a time, and a big batch can finish a pattern in one turn.
pros: Big batches complete patterns in one go.
Single pieces allow changes of mind.
cons: A big batch is hard to undo.
Single pieces make building slow.

pairs.tendency: Players play several cards together in one turn or one card at a time, and a big batch empties the hand faster than it refills.
pros: Played together, cards can combine.
One at a time keeps cards in reserve.
cons: Big batches leave the hand empty.
Small plays can fall behind the table.

pairs.tendency: Players choose when to lead many cards of one suit at once or one card a trick, and long runs win several tricks while spending a whole suit.
pros: Long runs win many tricks at once.
Single leads keep a suit for later.
cons: Spending a whole suit leaves a gap.
Single leads reveal little progress.

pairs.tendency: Players trade a bundle of goods in one deal or one item per deal, and bundles cut the talking while single swaps keep each side honest.
pros: Bundles settle many things in one talk.
Single swaps are easy to check.
cons: Bundles hide an unfair price.
Many small deals take a lot of talk.

pairs.tendency: Players gather a whole set before cashing it in or hand in small sets as they go, and waiting for a big set risks losing the cards.
pros: Big sets score more in one go.
Small sets bring points early.
cons: Held cards can be stolen or lost.
Cashing in early leaves little to build.

pairs.tendency: Players place several tiles in one turn or one tile at a time, and a large batch can fill a gap before others see it coming.
pros: Several tiles shape the map quickly.
One tile leaves room to react.
cons: Big batches can block other players' plans.
One tile at a time slows the map.

pairs.tendency: Players answer with a long string of words or moves or one at a time, and a long string gives the next player more to answer and to remember.
pros: Long strings make rich answers.
Short answers keep the chain moving.
cons: Long strings are hard to remember.
Short answers can feel thin.

pairs.tendency: Players put down one card per signal or a run of cards at once, with no talk to say how many are coming.
pros: A run can show a plan without words.
One card at a time keeps others in step.
cons: Others cannot tell a run from a mistake.
One at a time leaves long silences.

pairs.tendency: Players change one rule at a time or a bundle of rules in one turn, and a bundle can rewrite the game before anyone has tested the parts.
pros: Bundles change the game fast.
One rule shows what it changes.
cons: Bundles hide which rule did what.
One rule at a time makes slow change.

pairs.tendency: A character does a long run of actions in one scene or one small action at a time, and the scene's length decides how much the others get to say.
pros: Long scenes build a rich story.
Small actions let others join in.
cons: Long scenes can leave other players idle.
Small actions can break the story up.

pairs.tendency: Players flick, stack or throw several pieces in one go or one at a time, and each extra piece in the batch raises the chance of a slip.
pros: Several pieces at once are exciting.
One piece at a time is steady.
cons: One slip can ruin the whole batch.
Single pieces drag out the turn.

pairs.tendency: Players draw a whole region in one turn or add a single feature at a time, and big additions leave the others little room to draw.
pros: Big additions fill the map fast.
Small additions are easy to build on.
cons: Big additions can crowd out others' ideas.
Small additions leave the map slow to grow.

pairs.tendency: Players ask for one card or for every card of a rank, and a larger ask can win more but tells everyone more about the hand.
pros: A big ask can win many cards.
A small ask gives little away.
cons: A big ask shows your whole hand.
Small asks make for a long game.

pairs.tendency: Players bet one chip at a time or a pile on a single throw, and a bigger stake makes the bank's turn matter more.
pros: Big stakes pay out quickly.
Small stakes make the game last.
cons: A big loss can end a player's game.
Small stakes make little difference.

pairs.tendency: Players put one small bet on each throw or a large bet on a single throw, and nothing but the stake can be changed.
pros: Big stakes make each throw count.
Small stakes spread the risk.
cons: One throw can wipe out a large stake.
Small bets make a long, flat game.

pairs.tendency: Players raise by a large amount or by one chip at a time, and large raises end the round quickly while small ones let others read them.
pros: Big raises can push rivals out.
Small raises keep the round open.
cons: Big raises risk a lot on one hand.
Small raises show how sure you are.

pairs.tendency: Players build a side with a few large units or many small ones, and big units are quick to field but cost more when lost.
pros: Big units are quick to set up.
Small units are easy to mix and swap.
cons: Losing one big unit hurts a lot.
Many small units take long to organise.

pairs.tendency: Players call a large contract or a series of small ones, and a large call pays more but depends on everything going right.
pros: A big call pays a lot.
Small calls are easier to keep.
cons: A big call fails if one thing goes wrong.
Many small calls slow the hand.

pairs.tendency: Players take one piece at a time or a chain of pieces in one move, and each captured piece then works for the taker.
pros: A chain can swing the game.
One capture keeps the game close.
cons: One long chain can end the game.
One at a time leaves the game slow.

pairs.tendency: Players rescue several jailed teammates at once or one at a time, and a big rescue empties the jail but exposes the rescuer.
pros: A big rescue frees the whole team.
One rescue is a small risk.
cons: A big rescue puts the runner at risk.
One at a time leaves players waiting in jail.

pairs.tendency: Players surround one piece at a time or close a ring around a whole group, and a large ring takes many moves to build.
pros: A big ring takes many pieces at once.
Small captures are quick and clear.
cons: A big ring is easy to see and break.
Small captures can be slow to add up.

pairs.tendency: Players who are behind take a large boost at once or small boosts across turns, and a large boost can overshoot and swap the leader.
pros: A big boost can close a gap.
Small boosts keep the game steady.
cons: A big boost can overshoot the leader.
Small boosts can arrive too late.

pairs.tendency: Players choose only how many throws or draws to put into one round, and the result of each is out of their hands.
pros: Fewer rounds finish the game fast.
Short rounds keep everyone involved.
cons: Big batches wait on a few draws.
The batch size is the only choice.

pairs.tendency: Players run in one large group or split into small ones, and a big group is hard for one chaser to catch but easy to spot.
pros: A big group is hard to catch.
Small groups spread the chaser out.
cons: A big group can all be tagged together.
Small groups tire sooner.

pairs.tendency: Players aim a whole batch of attacks or help at one player or spread single ones, and the target feels a big batch more.
pros: Big batches show a clear choice.
Spread-out moves stay under notice.
cons: A big batch can knock one player out.
Spreading it thin slows the pressure.

pairs.tendency: Players put down a long run of stones at once or a single stone at a time, and the rival can only cut the chain between turns.
pros: A run can build a chain fast.
One stone can answer a cut.
cons: A long run gives a rival one big cut.
Single stones make a slow chain.

pairs.tendency: Players commit several choices of one kind or play one at a time, and a big batch of one choice is easy to beat if it is read.
pros: A big batch can win a lot.
One at a time keeps players guessing.
cons: A read batch loses all at once.
One at a time gives slow rounds.

pairs.tendency: Players declare several combinations together or one at a time, and holding them back for a big batch hands the others time to react.
pros: A big declaration scores many points.
One at a time keeps hands hidden.
cons: Holding cards back leaves points unscored.
Early declarations show what you hold.

pairs.tendency: Players use a power on a large batch of pieces or on one at a time, and each player's power may suit a different batch size.
pros: Powers can suit different batch sizes.
Big uses show off a power.
cons: Uneven powers can favour big batches.
Players may use their power in unclear ways.

pairs.tendency: Players double after a long run of play or after each small step, and a big batch is a bigger bet to accept or refuse.
pros: Late doubles are tense.
Early doubles keep stakes in sight.
cons: A big double ends the game for the loser.
Many small doubles cause delay.

pairs.tendency: Players may be made to take one piece after another in a forced chain, and a big batch of captures can be set up by the opponent.
pros: Chains of forced captures are dramatic.
A trap can be laid in advance.
cons: A forced chain can empty one side.
A forced chain can end the game too soon.

pairs.tendency: Players spend a long stretch building up for one big challenge or take many small ones, and the bigger batch of growth arrives all at once.
pros: Big batches give clear jumps in power.
Small steps bring regular rewards.
cons: Long waits leave players weak for a while.
Small steps make growth feel slight.

pairs.tendency: Players add a single item or a chunk of items each turn, and a bigger chunk makes the list harder to recall for everyone.
pros: Chunks make the list grow quickly.
One item keeps the list fair.
cons: Big chunks are hard to remember.
One item can make slow turns.

pairs.tendency: Players give the stronger side a small head start or several handicaps at once, and the batch of handicaps changes how even it feels.
pros: Big handicaps are easy to see.
Small steps let players fine-tune.
cons: A big handicap can swing the game round.
Small adjustments take many games to find.

pairs.tendency: The hider hides a pile in one place or single things in many, and a big hide is quick to set up but easy to find all at once.
pros: A big hide is quick to set up.
Small hides spread the search out.
cons: One find ends a big hide.
Many hides take a long time to set.

pairs.tendency: Players make a long chain of jumps in one turn or a single hop, and a big chain can clear the board in a moment.
pros: Long chains feel powerful.
Single hops are easy to follow.
cons: A long chain can empty the other side.
Single hops make a slow game.

pairs.tendency: Players keep most dice and reroll a few, or reroll most of them, and a large reroll takes more risk for a larger payoff.
pros: Rerolling a lot can undo a poor throw.
Rerolling a few keeps the dice you like.
cons: A big reroll can lose a fine hand.
Rerolling a few moves slowly toward a result.

pairs.tendency: Players move a bunch of pieces together or one at a time, and a bunch is safe on one space but sent back as a whole if caught.
pros: A bunch can block the others.
Single pieces are easy to move on.
cons: A caught bunch goes all the way back.
Single pieces are easy to hit.

pairs.tendency: Players build a row in one go or one piece at a time, and a quick row takes a piece before the rival can break it up.
pros: A quick row takes a piece at once.
One piece at a time hides your plan.
cons: A big move shows the row coming.
Slow building lets the rival break it.

pairs.tendency: Players lay a long word at once or short words one after another, and a long word scores more but needs the right letters.
pros: Long words feel rewarding.
Short words are easy to find.
cons: Long words need a lot of waiting for letters.
Many short words fill the board slowly.

pairs.tendency: Players play several matching tiles in one turn or one at a time, and a long run uses up tiles but leaves the open ends for others.
pros: A run empties the hand fast.
One tile at a time keeps tiles in reserve.
cons: A run can leave the others stuck.
Single plays can leave you without a match.

pairs.tendency: Players lay a large meld at once or small melds as soon as they can, and a big one gives the others a long list to add to.
pros: A big meld scores in one move.
Small melds get cards out early.
cons: A big meld gives others places to add.
Small melds spend cards too soon.

pairs.tendency: Players spend several one-use powers in one turn or save them for single moments, and a big batch can win a turn but leaves none for later.
pros: Spending many powers can win a turn.
Saving them keeps a threat in hand.
cons: Powers cannot be used twice.
Waiting can leave powers unspent at the end.

pairs.tendency: Players offer a big batch of moves for the other to accept or refuse, and the other has more to judge than with a single move.
pros: A big offer gives the other more to weigh.
Small offers are quick to answer.
cons: A big offer can hide a poor deal.
Small offers make for slow turns.

pairs.tendency: Players pass on a long message or a short one, and the longer the batch the more may change on the way.
pros: Long messages show how errors grow.
Short messages travel quickly.
cons: Long messages lose most of their meaning.
Short messages change little and give less fun.

pairs.tendency: Players pass a big handful of cards or just one, and the more they pass the less they know of what comes back.
pros: A big pass changes the whole hand.
A single pass is a small step.
cons: A big pass is a blind gamble.
One card seldom changes the hand much.

pairs.tendency: The setter-up builds a large starting position or a small one, and the bigger it is the harder it is to judge which side is stronger.
pros: A big setup is hard to judge.
A small setup is quick to check.
cons: A big setup can hide an advantage.
A small setup gives the chooser little to weigh.

pairs.tendency: Players push several pieces forward together or one at a time, and a group can promote many at once but moves slowly.
pros: A group can promote several pieces.
One piece can run for the end alone.
cons: A group is slow and easy to block.
A single runner is easy to catch.

pairs.tendency: Teams pass the baton after a long leg or a short one, and fewer long legs mean fewer handovers but more weight on each runner.
pros: Long legs mean few handovers.
Short legs let more people take part.
cons: A tired runner slows a long leg.
Many handovers add up to lost time.

pairs.tendency: Players build a whole safe shape at once or one stone at a time, and a half-built shape is open to attack in between.
pros: A whole shape is safe at once.
Building slowly hides your plan.
cons: A half-built shape can be captured.
Placing many stones at once costs a turn.

pairs.tendency: Players hold back to win a big batch of tricks for one prize card or take tricks one at a time, and one trick can win several prizes.
pros: Waiting can win a lot at once.
Early tricks bring steady points.
cons: A big plan can fail on one trick.
Small tricks can miss the prize.

pairs.tendency: Players use several cards from the middle at once or one at a time, and a big batch makes a strong set but leaves less for others.
pros: Several cards make a strong set.
One card leaves choices open to all.
cons: A big batch strips the middle for the rest.
One card at a time slows the hand.

pairs.tendency: Players stake a big amount into the pot at once or small amounts over rounds, and a big pot gives a larger prize to the winner.
pros: A big pot makes a tense round.
Small stakes keep losses small.
cons: A big pot can be lost on one round.
Small stakes build a slow pot.

pairs.tendency: Players scoop a big pit or a small one, and a big pile sows far round the board while a small one stays close to home.
pros: A big pit reaches far.
A small pit is easy to count.
cons: A big pit can feed the rival's side.
Small pits take many turns to add up.

pairs.tendency: Players swap many cards from the spare hand or just one, and a big swap changes the hand but gives away what is held.
pros: A big swap can remake a hand.
One card is a small, safe change.
cons: A big swap leaves a hand of strangers.
One card seldom changes much.

pairs.tendency: Players move several pieces onto special squares in one turn or a piece at a time, and a big move sets off many squares at once.
pros: A big move can set off many squares.
Single moves let players pick the squares.
cons: Many pieces can land on one harmful square together.
One piece at a time makes the track slow.

pairs.tendency: Players spend a lot on one big item or buy small things often, and a big buy leaves nothing for the next turn.
pros: A big buy gives a strong item.
Small buys spread the cost.
cons: A big buy leaves players with nothing.
Many small buys add up to lost time.

pairs.tendency: Players send forces in a few big batches or many small ones, and a big batch wins its place but leaves the others thin.
pros: A big batch wins one place well.
Small batches cover many places.
cons: A big batch leaves other places open.
Small batches are weak in each place.

pairs.tendency: Players move a big group of pieces or one piece before the signal, and a big move has more to freeze when it comes.
pros: A big move gets far before the stop.
A single move is easy to freeze.
cons: A big move can be caught by the signal.
A single move may get nowhere.

pairs.tendency: Players swap a whole hand at once or one card at a time, and a big swap can fix a hand but tells others it needed fixing.
pros: A big swap can remake the hand.
One swap is a small, quiet step.
cons: A big swap shows how weak the hand was.
One swap at a time can be too slow.

pairs.tendency: Players take a big pile of cards or leave it to grow, and a big pile gives many cards and the top card has to be used at once.
pros: A big pile gives lots of cards.
A small pile is quick to take.
cons: A big pile can swamp the hand.
A small pile is cheap but gives little.

pairs.tendency: Players lead a long run of trump or spend one trump at a time, and a long run wins several tricks but uses up the strongest suit.
pros: A run of trump wins several tricks.
One trump at a time wins one key trick.
cons: A run uses up all the strong cards.
One at a time lets others out-trump a trick.

pairs.tendency: Players make a big move on one board or small moves on both, and a big move on one board leaves the other open.
pros: A big move can win one board.
Small moves keep both boards covered.
cons: A big move leaves the other board open.
Small moves can win neither board.

pairs.tendency: Players spend several wild cards in one turn or one at a time, and a big batch can finish a hand but spends the helpers quickly.
pros: Several wilds can finish a hand.
One wild can fix a single gap.
cons: A big batch leaves none for later.
One at a time may be too slow.

pairs.tendency: Players move a long line of pieces over the edge in one go or one at a time, and a long line can reach the far side without a stop.
pros: A long line reaches the far side quickly.
Single pieces are easy to follow across the edge.
cons: A long line is easy to cut.
Single pieces cross slowly.

pairs.tendency: Players ask one question at a time or bundle several together, and a bundle is quick but can turn a plain yes or no into a muddle.
pros: Bundled questions go quicker.
Single questions give clear answers.
cons: A bundle can get an unclear answer.
Single questions take many turns.

pairs.tendency: Players move a big group toward the end together or run one piece at a time, and the winner is whoever finishes the whole batch first.
pros: A big group is hard to stop.
One piece can sprint ahead.
cons: A big group moves slowly.
A single runner can be blocked.

pairs.tendency: Players score in a few large batches or many small ones, and big scores arrive late while small ones show the lead as the game goes.
pros: Big scores make late swings.
Small scores keep a clear score.
cons: Big scores can come too late to see.
Small scores take time to add up.

pairs.tendency: Players commit many pieces at once to knock others out or one at a time, and a big attack ends a player but leaves the attacker open.
pros: A big attack can knock a player out.
Small attacks wear the others down.
cons: A big attack leaves the attacker open.
Small attacks drag out the game.

cons: A shown set can be spoiled by chance.
Players may never declare.

pairs.tendency: Each player has one special ability, and a power that needs a machine stops working whenever it breaks.
pros: Powers have a visible weak point.
Players guard what their power rests on.
cons: Some powers fail more often than others.
Power balance gets harder to check.

pairs.tendency: A player offers to double the stakes, knowing a fault could change who is ahead before the game ends.
pros: Doubling becomes a bet on reliability.
Players read each other's plants.
cons: One fault after doubling can end it.
Players may double too early or never.

pairs.tendency: A player who has to capture is forced into a move even while a machine sits broken, so repairs wait.
pros: Forced moves show how pressure delays repair.
Opponents can plan around a fault.
cons: Players cannot choose repair first.
Feels harsh for the player with a fault.

pairs.tendency: A player's plant grows more powerful, but larger machines fail with bigger consequences and cost more to mend.
pros: Growth brings new risks.
Strength can be spent on repair.
cons: Late faults can be very costly.
Growing stronger can feel pointless.

pairs.tendency: Players recite a list of machines and faults so far and add one, so each breakdown is one more item to remember.
pros: Recalling the faults tells the plant's story.
Easy to start.
cons: Long lists tire players.
Faults become forgettable words.

pairs.tendency: The stronger player starts with fewer machines or less repair help, so a single fault hits them harder.
pros: Faults make a handicap felt.
A weaker player has more room.
cons: A handicap and a fault together can be too steep.
The stronger player may feel the dice decide.

pairs.tendency: Players hide the fault or search for the broken machine, and finding the failing part is the game.
pros: Repair begins with diagnosis.
Searching feels like fault-finding.
cons: Slow if the fault is well hidden.
Hiders may keep a machine broken a long time.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hop over others to move forward, and a broken machine becomes a blocked square that hops cannot use.
pros: Faults reshape the paths.
Broken pieces are easy to see.
cons: One fault can freeze a whole line.
Planning long hops gets hard.

pairs.tendency: Players roll dice to make output and set aside the ones they like, and a fault can cancel a kept die.
pros: Rerolls give some control over output.
A cancelled die stings in a clear way.
cons: Locked dice lose their meaning.
Luck on luck can feel flat.

pairs.tendency: Landing on another piece sends it back, and a broken machine is one more way to be sent back to the start.
pros: Setbacks come from two sources.
Safe spaces can double as repair bays.
cons: Being sent back and failing together is harsh.
Players may stop caring about the board.

pairs.tendency: Players build rows to take pieces, and a machine that fails breaks a row before it closes.
