pros: Rows can be built with spares in mind.
A mill gains a second weak point.
cons: Failures can break a mill in luck, not skill.
Players may stop making rows.

pairs.tendency: Players make words from letters, and a faulty machine can take away a letter, so the plan changes midway.
pros: A missing letter forces new words.
Faults are easy to picture.
cons: Words may have nothing to do with machines.
Faulty letters can feel arbitrary.

pairs.tendency: Players extend a line by matching its ends, and a broken machine can seal an end until it is mended.
pros: A blocked end changes the line.
Repair tiles have a clear role.
cons: A sealed end can leave players passing.
One fault may block everyone at once.

pairs.tendency: Players lay down finished sets and add to them, and a fault can strike a melded set so no one can add to it.
pros: Sets on the table become shared risk.
Repair of a meld helps all who add.
cons: A fault can strand a whole meld.
Melding early exposes it.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a one-time power, and the choice is whether to spend it on a breakdown or keep it for something else.
pros: Saving a power has a real cost.
A single repair can change a round.
cons: Players may hoard it until too late.
Powers lose their effect if faults are rare.

pairs.tendency: A player offers a repair plan and the other can refuse it, so a broken machine waits while they argue.
pros: Repair plans get tested.
Both players see the cost of delay.
cons: One refusal can stall the plant.
Players may refuse out of habit.

pairs.tendency: A fault report passes from player to player and may change on the way, so the repair crew gets a garbled message.
pros: Shows how fault reports can be misread.
Funny and quick.
cons: Repair goes to the wrong machine.
Players may enjoy the mix-up more than the plant.

pairs.tendency: Players hand over some cards before play, and what they give away decides what repair parts they will have when a machine fails.
pros: Giving away a part is a real cost.
Players guess at others' spares.
cons: Players may pass junk.
The first failure shows who guessed wrong.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the plant and the other picks a side, so the layout has to be even in how much it can fail.
pros: Fair layouts need failure risk counted.
The chooser studies faults carefully.
cons: Hard to check both sides for failure.
Players can miss a hidden weak machine.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the end becomes more powerful, and it may now fail more costly, so promotion brings a bigger risk.
pros: Rewards come with a visible price.
Promotion becomes a choice, not only a prize.
cons: Players may avoid promotion.
A promoted piece failing feels cruel.

pairs.tendency: Teammates pass the job along in legs, and a machine that fails during one leg stops every leg after it.
pros: One fault shows how stages depend on each other.
Teammates wait on one another.
cons: A single fault can ruin a team's run.
Late runners may wait doing nothing.

pairs.tendency: Some shapes cannot be captured, and a machine that fails can break the shape from inside rather than by attack.
pros: A safe shape stops being fully safe.
Players care about upkeep as well as attack.
cons: Safe shapes feel less safe.
Failure can undo careful building.

pairs.tendency: Named prize cards score points, and a fault on the machine that wins a prize can send it to someone else.
pros: Prizes stay open to the very end.
Repair can decide a prize.
cons: A late fault can flip the whole score.
Players may protect prizes instead of playing.

pairs.tendency: Shared cards in the middle include spares and faults, so everyone can use a repair part or suffer a fault.
pros: Everyone shares the same risk.
Players read the table for failures.
cons: A shared fault can hit all at once.
Players may wait for others to repair.

pairs.tendency: A pot grows while nobody wins, and every failed machine keeps the pot from being won, so it grows larger.
pros: Faults feed the stakes.
Waiting is tense.
cons: A huge pot can ride on a lucky repair.
Rounds can drag with no winner.

pairs.tendency: Players sow seeds into pits, and a pit that breaks is skipped or loses its seeds, so the sowing path changes.
pros: Broken pits change counting.
Repair has an easy rule to read.
cons: Counting gets harder with faults.
A lost pit can undo a long plan.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand can be taken before play, and it may hold repair parts that no one else will have.
pros: Spare parts become a choice.
A spare hand can save a plant.
cons: Players may guess wrong about faults.
Taking the spare may cost play cards.

pairs.tendency: Some squares send you back or make you miss a turn, and a breakdown square adds one more place where output stops.
pros: Squares can stand for repair stops.
Risk is easy to see on the board.
cons: Players may avoid the same squares each time.
Squares and random faults repeat each other.

pairs.tendency: Every machine has a price to run, and a repair adds a cost on top, so players weigh running a machine against mending it.
pros: Running costs and repair costs sit side by side.
Choices have visible prices.
cons: Repair can drain the budget.
Cheap machines may be bought and left to break.

pairs.tendency: Players share their workers or money between several machines, and a fault in one pulls them away from the others.
pros: Spreading thin shows its risk.
Repair is a clear trade-off.
cons: One breakdown can undo a plan.
Players may over-reserve forces for faults.

pairs.tendency: Everyone keeps working until a signal, and a machine that fails at the stop leaves one player caught short.
pros: Failure and timing meet in one moment.
Tense and quick.
cons: Being caught can feel unlucky.
Plant detail gets lost in the rush.

pairs.tendency: Players swap cards to get what they need, and a repair card is the first to be swapped for after a fault.
pros: Swapping answers a real shortage.
Repair parts have a visible price.
cons: Players can drain the pile of spares.
Swaps may slow the game.

pairs.tendency: Players can take the whole discard pile, and a pile with repair parts becomes worth more after a fault.
pros: Old cards can come back as repairs.
Reading the pile pays off.
cons: Taking a big pile slows the next player.
Players may hold off on discarding parts.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, and a machine failing in the trump suit leaves players holding cards they cannot use.
pros: A strong suit becomes a risk.
Players hold a mix of suits for repair.
cons: Trump faults can swing a hand.
Suits and machines can get muddled.

pairs.tendency: Players run two plants on two boards, and a fault on one board pulls attention from the other.
pros: Dividing attention is real.
Faults on one board show on the other.
cons: Too much to track.
A fault on one board can feel unrelated.

pairs.tendency: Wild cards can stand for a missing part, so one lucky wild card can mend a machine that nothing else could.
pros: Wild cards make faults easier to fix.
Players weigh saving a wild against using it.
cons: Wild cards can erase the cost of a fault.
A lucky draw can fix everything.

pairs.tendency: Edges are joined, so a failing machine at one edge can spread to the other side, and repairers can approach from either end.
pros: Faults have no safe corner.
Repair routes have two directions.
cons: Hard to see which side a fault is nearest.
Players may lose track of the layout.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which machine is faulty, and the others narrow it down with yes-or-no questions.
pros: Fault-finding becomes a real skill.
Each answer shrinks the list.
cons: The knower has little to decide.
Slow if the questions are poor.

pairs.tendency: Players race to finish a job while machines fail at random, so the fastest runner is sometimes the one who stopped to mend.
pros: Repair costs the racers a real turn.
Leaders can be caught after a fault.
cons: Chance can decide the race.
Players may skip repair to keep up.

pairs.tendency: Players score points from what their machines make, and each failure cuts the score and the repair adds a cost.
pros: Reliable plants show in the score.
Players compare how they handled failure.
cons: Scores can come down to who failed least.
Counting lost output takes time.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out as their plants stop working, until one plant is still running.
pros: Failure becomes a real danger.
Repair and defence feel tied.
cons: Early failures leave players out for long.
Players hit by ill luck feel it hard.

pairs.tendency: The team keeps a plant running against faults that come every round, and stays alive only as long as repairs keep up.
pros: Everyone sees what the repairs cost.
Teamwork has a clear job.
cons: Faults can pile up beyond help.
One player can run the repairs for all.

pairs.tendency: The group aims at one output target together, and each breakdown slows everyone toward it.
pros: A common aim makes faults a shared problem.
Teams plan spare capacity.
cons: Little tension if faults are mild.
Some players may stand back and watch.

pairs.tendency: Each player secretly wants something different from the plant, so who mends a machine can show what they want.
pros: Repair choices give away aims.
Faults feed suspicion.
cons: Players cannot tell goals from habit.
Secret aims may be dropped to mend a fault.

pairs.tendency: The plant's story runs through its breakdowns and repairs until the story ends.
pros: Faults become events in a tale.
A history of the plant builds.
cons: The story can feel like a list of faults.
Random faults can break the tale's shape.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and players watch how a plant copes with faults and talk about what they saw.
pros: Failure can be watched without a score.
Talk follows what actually broke.
cons: Little push to repair.
Play may drift with no stake.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what a working plant means, such as steady output or few repairs, and faults test that aim.
pros: Different aims meet the same faults.
Players learn what they value in a plant.
cons: Hard to compare results.
A player can set an aim that faults never touch.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one plant is lost, so each fault pushes the weakest player toward losing.
pros: Faults give the loser a clear cause.
Safe players feel relief.
cons: The unluckiest player can be singled out.
Faults can feel like the reason, not the plan.

pairs.tendency: Players aim to keep the plant running for as long as they can, so repair is the main job.
pros: Upkeep becomes the game.
Players think about how a plant lasts.
cons: Repair can feel like chores.
Little sense of progress.

pairs.tendency: The plant cannot be won, and failures keep coming, so repair is never done.
pros: Shows that maintenance has no end.
Players learn what a plant is like.
cons: Players may feel nothing counts.
Many will give up early.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone, you clear a layout while faults block cards, so you keep repairing and clearing together.
pros: Faults make a layout harder to read.
Alone, the cost of a fault is easy to see.
cons: One fault can leave you stuck.
A stuck layout can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short games, and each starts with machines in a new state of repair.
pros: Each game can try a different repair plan.
Players learn from the last failure.
cons: One unlucky fault can lose a short game.
Short games may not be long enough for repair to matter.

pairs.tendency: Points count against you, and each failure adds points, so keeping machines running is how you win.
pros: Repair has a clear reward.
Faults sting in a clear way.
cons: A string of faults can lock a player out.
Players may avoid running machines at all.

pairs.tendency: You have to land on the exact number to finish, and a fault can push you past it or set you back.
pros: Faults put an exact finish in doubt.
Tension rises near the end.
cons: A fault at the finish feels unfair.
Players may wait for the right moment.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, so players want their own machines to fail and the others to mend them.
pros: Failure becomes something to plan for.
Players think about repair backwards.
cons: Hard to keep the aim in mind.
Players may break machines and mend them to cheat.

pairs.tendency: Everyone runs their own plant side by side, and faults hit each one separately.
pros: Players compare their repair plans.
Faults feel fair.
cons: Little contact between players.
Few chances to help each other.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other's plants, and a random fault can look like an attack from another player.
pros: Attacks and faults make plants fragile.
Revenge has a place.
cons: Players cannot tell sabotage from chance.
A fault can feel like a hit.

pairs.tendency: Players share a board of machines, and one player's strain on a machine can make it fail for someone else.
pros: Shared machines show shared risk.
Quiet pressure between players.
cons: Hard to tell who caused a fault.
Slow to notice what changed.

pairs.tendency: The whole team keeps a plant running against faults and shares the cost of each repair.
pros: Teamwork on upkeep.
Everyone has a job.
cons: One player can direct all repair.
Little tension if the team agrees.

pairs.tendency: Players share a plant and need it to run, but each wants a bigger share, so repair work gets argued over.
pros: Who pays for repair becomes a real question.
Tense choices over a shared plant.
cons: Players can wait for others to repair.
Repair can be left until too late.

pairs.tendency: Two teams run rival plants, and each team spends turns on repair that its rival can use to get ahead.
pros: Teams plan around faults together.
Rivals watch each other's weak machines.
cons: One player can take over repair for the team.
Teams may stall each other.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly sabotages the plant, and the team cannot tell a traitor's fault from a random one.
pros: Faults give a traitor cover.
Suspicion has a real reason.
cons: Players may blame chance and the traitor goes free.
Accusations can upset people.

pairs.tendency: Players send fault reports and repair orders by letter, so a machine can stay broken for days while the reply travels.
pros: Delay becomes part of the repair.
Players see how slow messages cost a plant.
cons: Long waits can be dull.
A fault may be mended before the letter arrives.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so their plant may fail with nobody there to repair it.
pros: Shows what an unattended plant is like.
The gap has a clear cost.
cons: The absent player's plant can fall behind.
Faults can feel unfair for someone who cannot act.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the plant for the others and decides when machines break, so faults can be timed for the story.
pros: Faults can serve the story.
The master can shape the pace.
cons: Players may suspect faults are aimed.
The master has a lot to track.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in the open, and passers-by can join in and take over a broken machine, so repair is shared.
pros: Anyone can be a repairer.
Faults draw a crowd.
cons: Hard to keep track of who is mending what.
Players may come and go mid-repair.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the plant against many repairers, or many run it against the faults one player brings.
pros: The lone player's faults have a face.
Group repair is clear.
cons: The lone player can seem unfair.
The group may argue over who mends first.

pairs.tendency: You run a plant alone against the faults, so every repair is your own choice and every loss is yours.
pros: Clear view of cause and repair.
Easy to start and stop.
cons: No one to blame but luck.
Little to learn about teamwork.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide almost everything, including which machine breaks, so planning has little effect.
pros: Shows how random a plant can be.
Quick to play.
cons: Little to decide.
Players may feel nothing they do matters.

pairs.tendency: Faults come by chance, but players can soften them with spares, servicing or insurance.
pros: Prevention has a clear price.
Players plan against a known risk.
cons: More rules to learn.
Prevention may look wasted when no fault comes.

pairs.tendency: Skill decides most outcomes, and random breakdowns add a small, steady surprise.
pros: Faults add surprise to a skilled game.
Careful players can still recover.
cons: Experienced players may handle faults more easily.
A fault can seem to cancel a clever plan.

pairs.tendency: Players decide almost everything, so breakdowns are the one thing outside their control and they plan around them.
pros: Faults are the only surprise.
Planning around risk is clear.
cons: Chance may feel out of place.
One fault can overshadow skill.

pairs.tendency: A throw says which machine is in trouble and players read it as a message about the plant rather than a score.
pros: Faults become something to think about.
Players talk about what a fault means.
cons: Reading a fault as a sign can mislead.
Players may stop mending and just interpret.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others are about to act, so a team can notice a failing machine and move before it stops.
pros: Noticing signs of failure grows.
Teams feel in step.
cons: Hard to tell if anyone noticed.
Faults that come without signs feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: A roll on a table says what breaks and who comes to fix it, so the dice help write the plant's story.
pros: Faults have a cause in the story.
Tables can hold many kinds of fault.
cons: Tables can grow long.
Outcomes can be the same each time.

pairs.tendency: Everyone can see every machine's wear and every spare, so each failure is a risk everyone saw coming.
pros: Players can discuss faults openly.
Risk is plain to see.
cons: Little surprise.
Players may stall while checking everything.

pairs.tendency: Players hold repair parts in secret, so nobody knows who can mend a fault until they try.
pros: Spare parts become a secret.
Asking for help is a gamble.
cons: Hard to plan as a team.
Players may hide parts and let a plant stall.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret sides, so a machine that fails raises the question of who broke it and who is mending it.
pros: Faults feed suspicion.
A repair can hide its motive.
cons: Hard to tell fault from sabotage.
Players may blame the wrong person.

pairs.tendency: Players use clues from symptoms to work out which machine is failing and why.
pros: Fault-finding is the whole game.
Clues have real causes.
cons: Slow if clues are weak.
Players may guess instead of reasoning.

pairs.tendency: Players can claim a machine is working or broken, and others have to guess whether to believe it.
pros: A hidden fault can be hidden on purpose.
Claims about condition matter.
cons: Lies can upset people.
Players may stop trusting reports.

pairs.tendency: Players learn the rule for what makes a machine fail only by breaking it, and being told no.
pros: Learning how a plant fails by trying.
Discovery has a real cost.
cons: Players may break many machines to learn.
New players may feel lost.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which machine will fail but can only hint, such as by pointing at a gauge.
pros: Players watch signs.
Hints feel like a mechanic's hunch.
cons: Hints can be missed.
The knower may feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: The plant is hidden until explored, so machines reveal their condition only when a player reaches them.
pros: Exploring shows the state of the plant.
Faults come as surprises.
cons: Players may never see some faults.
A broken machine may be found too late.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, including its spares, so players can see which repairs are available and plan around them.
pros: Repair stock is open to all.
Planning around a known hand is easier.
cons: The open hand reduces surprise.
Players may rely on the open hand.

pairs.tendency: Some scores are hidden, so nobody can tell how much a fault has really cost another plant.
pros: Faults can be kept quiet.
Players guess who is hurting.
cons: Hard to judge your own standing.
Guessing can overtake repair.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so a fault waits until its owner's turn and the rest watch the plant wait.
pros: Waiting shows what a delay costs.
Each repair gets full attention.
cons: Players can be idle while a fault sits.
Long waits between turns.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses together in secret, so several plants may face faults and mend at the same moment.
pros: Fast, busy repair.
Players see each other's repair at once.
cons: Hard to follow every fault.
Mistakes can slip past.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so repairs go to whoever reaches a broken machine first.
pros: Faults create real urgency.
Quick hands decide who mends.
cons: Quick players mend everything.
Slower players may feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a fault that lands mid-turn leaves little time to find the right repair.
pros: Faults add real pressure.
Players learn to act under stress.
cons: Rushed repairs can be careless.
Players may run out of time reading rules.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks, so a breakdown can sit unrepaired overnight.
pros: Waiting for repair feels real.
Faults happen between moves.
cons: Plants can stay broken for a long time.
Players may lose track of the state.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down with a pause before each move, so a breakdown is met calmly, not in a rush.
pros: Time to look at the fault.
Careful repair is possible.
cons: A slow pace can feel dull.
Faults wait long for a fix.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so faults come more often and repairs have less time.
pros: Pressure builds steadily.
Players feel a plant under strain.
cons: Late rounds can be chaos.
Repair gets crowded out near the end.

pairs.tendency: Some moves give an extra go, so a player can mend a machine and move again, while others wait for their turn.
pros: A repair can be quick.
Extra turns feel like a quick mend.
cons: One player can pull far ahead.
Others sit by while a plant is mended.

pairs.tendency: The first stage sets up the plant, and the second runs it with faults, so early choices about spares show later.
pros: Early planning pays off or fails later.
Players see what they set up.
cons: Early choices can be forgotten.
A weak first stage can ruin the second.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real plant, and breakdowns show how one fault spreads to the machines around it.
pros: Cause and effect are visible.
Players learn how a plant depends on each machine.
cons: Chance faults can hide the pattern.
Players may not link the board to a real plant.

pairs.tendency: Players act as operator, mechanic, manager and owner, and each sees a breakdown from a different side.
pros: Each role feels the fault differently.
Players see who pays for a fault.
cons: Blame can pile on one role.
Some roles can seem unimportant.

pairs.tendency: All players draw on one pool of spares or one mechanic, and a run of faults can use it up for everyone.
pros: Shared spares show the cost of sharing.
Players weigh taking now against keeping some.
cons: One player's faults can drain the pool.
Waiting for the pool can slow everyone.

pairs.tendency: A fault caused by neglect shows up only a few rounds later, so skipping a service now costs later.
pros: Delayed cause and effect becomes clear.
Neglect has a price.
cons: Hard to link a fault to its cause.
Players may blame luck.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new maintenance rule and play on to see how often machines fail, so the rule can be tested safely.
pros: Rules about repair are tested at no real cost.
Players see the effect of the rule.
cons: A rule may look sound from one game.
Faults are random, so effects can be hard to read.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk through which machines failed, why, and what they would change in a real plant.
pros: Faults give plenty to talk about.
Players link luck to cause.
cons: Players may blame luck for everything.
Talk can drift to who failed.

pairs.tendency: A machine that breaks can be scrapped for ever, and the next game starts without it.
pros: Failure leaves a lasting mark.
Players think hard about wear.
cons: Early loss can ruin later games.
Players may never risk a machine.

pairs.tendency: The rules about faults make a point, such as that maintenance is cheaper than repair, by how they reward each.
pros: The rules show how upkeep is valued.
Players can talk about what the rules say.
cons: The point can seem heavy-handed.
Players may play against the argument.

pairs.tendency: A breakdown in the game costs something real, such as time or a chore, so faults feel like they matter.
pros: Faults carry real weight.
Players take repair seriously.
cons: Luck decides real costs.
Some players may feel uneasy.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something like safety, and breakdowns cost points, so players chase the number and neglect what it stands for.
pros: Shows how a number can replace real safety.
Players notice what repair leaves out.
cons: Players may skip repairs that earn no points.
The idea can be lost in the scoring.

pairs.tendency: Players practise running a shared workshop with a repair rota, and breakdowns show how the plan holds up.
pros: Faults test a new way of working.
Players feel the plan before trying it.
cons: Random faults may not match real ones.
A plan may look sound only because faults were few.

pairs.tendency: Players hold spare parts that cost something each round, while a breakdown without a spare costs more, so they balance the two.
pros: Spare stock has a clear price.
Players learn how much cover is enough.
cons: Players may over-stock to be safe.
A run of luck can mislead them.

pairs.tendency: Players roll to move along a track while the stock they hold costs something each round, so a short roll can leave a player holding too much or too little.
pros: Easy to read stock rising and falling.
Spaces on the track can stand for stores.
cons: Dice decide shortages more than planning does.
Players cannot plan stock against a roll.

pairs.tendency: Each pick adds to the stock a player carries, and every card kept costs something each round, so players weigh taking one more against running short.
pros: Every pick shows the cost of holding.
Passed cards show what others need.
cons: Players may take cards only to deny others.
Late picks leave some players short.

pairs.tendency: Players bid to restock, and the price of running out pushes bids up while the cost of holding stock pulls them down.
pros: Prices show how much a shortage hurts.
Bids make the two costs easy to compare.
cons: A rich player can buy stock and starve others.
Overbidding leaves stock too costly to hold.

pairs.tendency: Players keep drawing to build up stock, but each extra unit costs more to hold and one bust can lose it all, so stopping is a real choice.
pros: The balance is felt, not just read.
Stopping early has a visible cost.
cons: Bust turns can feel like dice, not stock sense.
Careful players stop before they learn the limit.

pairs.tendency: Players hold stock in several areas of a map, and an area that runs dry or sits overfull is easy for another player to take.
pros: Stock links to place on the map.
Weak areas show up clearly.
cons: Fighting can matter more than stock.
Spreading stock thin leaves every area open.

pairs.tendency: Workers go to spaces that bring in or use up stock, so players choose between topping up and saving the turn, with holding costs due each round.
pros: Each placement has a clear stock reason.
Players plan several rounds ahead.
cons: A blocked space can leave a player short.
The stock count adds to slow turns.

pairs.tendency: Players build patterns from pieces they hold, and spare pieces cost something each round while a missing piece stalls the pattern.
pros: Players see why each spare piece is a cost.
Planning ahead feels natural.
cons: A pattern can stall for one missing piece.
Players may hoard pieces they do not need.

pairs.tendency: The hand is the stock: each card held costs something every round, and a thin hand leaves a player without a move when it counts.
pros: Hand size becomes a real choice.
Players learn to time their plays.
cons: Players may dump cards to dodge the cost.
An empty hand can leave a player stuck.

pairs.tendency: Players want strong cards to win tricks, but holding unplayed cards costs something each round, so hands are kept lean and risky.
pros: Cards in hand show a visible cost.
Each trick teaches about spending stock.
cons: Hand cost can pull attention from the trick.
Weak hands run short with little recourse.

pairs.tendency: Players with too much stock offer it to players with too little, and talk turns into trades that settle both holding costs and shortages.
pros: Trades show who is overstocked or short.
Talk comes from a real need.
cons: A short player has to accept a poor price.
Players may hide stock to avoid trading it away.

pairs.tendency: Players gather items to finish sets, but items held while waiting for the rest cost something every round, so hoarding for a set is costly.
pros: Waiting for a set has a visible price.
Players weigh partial sets against cost.
cons: One missing item can strand a whole set.
Players may drop sets to save cost.

pairs.tendency: Players keep a supply of tiles to place, and spare tiles cost something each round while a missing tile stops a planned extension.
pros: The map shows what was spent.
Players choose when to place or wait.
cons: Tile luck can force overstock.
Stalled players build nothing for a round.

pairs.tendency: Each answer in the chain uses up a word or item from the player's store, and a store that is too large or too small makes the next answer harder.
pros: Players feel the strain of keeping up.
The chain shows when a store runs dry.
cons: Holding costs can interrupt the back-and-forth.
Stock can feel bolted onto a word game.

pairs.tendency: Players cannot talk about who holds too much or too little, so they read stock from what others play and when, and guess who is running short.
pros: Players learn to read each other's stock.
Quiet play keeps attention on the cost.
cons: Shortages go unmentioned until too late.
Overstocked players cannot offer help.

pairs.tendency: A player can rewrite the cost of holding or running out, so the balance players were managing shifts under them mid-game.
pros: Players see how a cost shapes choices.
Rule changes become a way to test costs.
cons: A new rule can wipe out stock plans.
Players may change costs to rescue themselves.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a character who has to keep stock, such as a shopkeeper, and decides how much to hold knowing storage costs and empty shelves cost more.
pros: Stock choices come with a reason.
Characters can argue over stock in role.
cons: Players may stay in character and ignore the costs.
Counting stock can slow the story.

pairs.tendency: Players move or stack stock with their hands, so a clumsy move can spill stock and the cost of holding more is a shakier stack.
pros: A bigger pile is felt with the hands.
Mistakes show their cost at once.
cons: Hand skill can matter more than stock sense.
A steady player can hold too much without paying.

pairs.tendency: Players draw stores and routes as they go, and each store they draw has to be kept stocked while an unstocked one costs more.
pros: The map shows where stock sits.
Players decide where stock matters.
cons: Drawing can take time from stock counting.
Players may draw more stores than they stock.

pairs.tendency: A player asks for a card and gives away what they hold, so keeping spare cards costs something while asking for missing ones tells others what you lack.
pros: Asking shows the price of a shortage.
Players learn what others hold.
cons: Players may hold back questions to hide need.
A well-stocked player is easy to ask.

pairs.tendency: The bank holds a pool that has to pay winners, and a large pool costs the bank each round while a small one risks being unable to pay.
pros: The bank player feels the pool's cost.
Odds and stock link together.
cons: Bank turns can be much harder than others.
A thin pool can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: Players put stock on a throw they cannot steer, so too little stock means a small win and too much means a bigger loss.
pros: Bets show how much stock a player will risk.
Quick, tense rounds.
cons: No skill reaches the stock choice but the bet.
Dice decide whether stock holds up.

pairs.tendency: Players put chips in a pot while their hand looks strong, and chips kept back cost nothing to hold but win nothing, so players weigh staying in against holding back.
pros: Chip stacks show who is short.
Folding feels like a real choice.
cons: A short stack is forced out early.
Players may fold to dodge the cost.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a side and decides how much stock to bring, since a large side costs more to keep up and a lean one can run dry.
pros: Side choice has a clear trade-off.
Players with different sides face different costs.
cons: Some builds make the cost very light.
Players need to know all the costs before choosing.

pairs.tendency: A player names a target before play and has to stock to meet it, since holding too much costs and falling short loses the contract.
pros: The target ties stock to a promise.
Players learn to plan before acting.
cons: A wrong call can be lost before play begins.
Players may call low to keep stock safe.

pairs.tendency: Captured pieces change sides and count as stock for the new owner, so a large army costs more to hold while a lost piece shrinks it.
pros: A swing in pieces swings stock too.
Leaders can fall behind quickly.
cons: Captured pieces add cost to hold at once.
Players may avoid capturing to keep costs low.

pairs.tendency: A jail holds captured players, who stop adding to the team's stock, so the team feels the cost of every capture and every rescue attempt.
pros: A capture shows its cost to the whole team.
Rescue becomes a stock decision.
cons: A team can run short awaiting rescue.
Players in jail wait with nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: Players spread pieces to surround others, and a piece stretched thin is cheap to hold but easy to take, while a packed group costs more to keep.
pros: Spreading and packing both show a cost.
The board shows how thin stock is.
cons: Players with many pieces may overextend.
Surrounding can matter more than stock counts.

pairs.tendency: The game gives help to players who are behind, which can ease the cost of running short but also reward a player who let stock run out.
pros: Behind players stay in the game.
Shortages need not end a player's game.
cons: Players may run short on purpose to get help.
Leaders can feel punished for holding stock.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards set stock levels and costs, and players make no choices, so they watch the balance swing without steering it.
pros: Quick play with nothing to learn first.
Both costs are easy to see.
cons: Players cannot act on stock at all.
The lesson gives players nothing to act on.

pairs.tendency: Chasers and runners carry something that costs effort to hold, so a runner holding a lot slows down while one with little has less to gain.
pros: Stock costs show up in running speed.
Fast rounds with a clear cost.
cons: Counting stock can interrupt the chase.
Fit players can ignore the cost.

pairs.tendency: Players choose whom to hit or help, and a well-stocked player is a target for theft while a short one is a target for pity or pressure.
pros: Stock makes some players targets.
Players weigh whom to help or hit.
cons: Holding more stock can draw the attacks.
Players may hide stock to stay unnoticed.

pairs.tendency: Players build a chain from one side to the other, and the chain pieces cost something to hold while a gap in supply can stop it.
pros: A chain shows exactly where supply is thin.
Quiet, thoughtful play.
cons: Cutting the chain matters more than stock.
The cost can feel extra to a clean contest.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, and stock held for the wrong choice is wasted while too little leaves a player open.
pros: Players guess which stock to hold.
Quick rounds with a clear risk.
cons: Stock choices turn into guesses.
Players may stop trying to count stock.

pairs.tendency: Players hold cards to declare scoring pairs or runs, and cards kept for combinations cost something each round while a missing card delays the score.
pros: Players weigh waiting for a card against its cost.
Declaring shows what stock is for.
cons: Waiting for a pair can lose a whole round.
Scoring can outweigh the stock cost.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that shifts how stock works for them, so one player's holding cost or shortage differs from another's.
pros: Players learn why costs differ.
Powers give each player a different plan.
cons: Some powers make the cost nearly vanish.
Players have to track others' stock rules.

pairs.tendency: A player may double what the game is worth, so holding back stock cuts the risk while holding a lot raises both the stake and the cost.
pros: Doubling puts a price on stock.
Tense choices about when to raise.
cons: A short player may have to give up.
A richer player can push a weaker one out.

pairs.tendency: A player who can capture has to, so stock can be drained by a forced move and a thin position can be pushed into running short.
pros: Forced moves show how stock can be drained.
Opponents can plan around the rule.
cons: Forced moves can strip stock a player needed.
Players may dodge stock rather than plan it.

pairs.tendency: A character gains power through play, but each gain needs stock to keep going and costs something to hold, so growth has an upkeep.
pros: Growth shows what it costs to keep up.
Players choose when to build and when to save.
cons: Strong characters can outrun the cost.
Players may stop growing to save stock.

pairs.tendency: Players recite a longer list each turn, so each added item is more to hold in memory and a forgotten item ends the player's turn.
pros: Memory shows the cost of holding too much.
A list is a simple stock to see.
cons: Memory skill matters more than planning.
Players who forget drop out early.

pairs.tendency: The stronger player starts with less stock, so they feel the cost of running short sooner while the weaker player has room to hold more.
pros: A gap in stock levels the contest.
Stock shows the size of the handicap.
cons: A handicap can feel like a punishment.
The balance tips if the gap is wrongly set.

pairs.tendency: A hider keeps something hidden and a finder carries supplies to search, so a heavy pack slows the search while a light one runs out.
pros: The cost of carrying shows in the search.
Simple rounds.
cons: Searching can be slow while stock runs out.
Hiders have no stock to balance.

pairs.tendency: Players hop pieces over others to reach spaces, and each piece kept on the board costs something while a missing piece leaves a gap in a hop.
pros: A hop shows how many pieces were needed.
Players plan chains of hops.
cons: Hopping can matter more than stock.
Players may hold back pieces to lower cost.

pairs.tendency: Players keep some dice and reroll the rest, so each kept die is stock that costs a roll and each reroll risks losing what was enough.
pros: Each reroll puts a number on stock.
Quick rounds with a clear choice.
cons: Dice decide whether stock holds up.
Players may reroll too little to avoid losing stock.

pairs.tendency: A piece landing on another sends it back to the start, so a player far ahead holds more to lose while a short player has little.
pros: Players see the cost of holding a lead.
Safe spaces act like a store.
cons: One big loss can wipe out stock.
Players may stay back to keep stock safe.

pairs.tendency: A row of three lets a player take a piece, so pieces kept for rows cost something to hold and taken pieces cut stock for the other player.
pros: Taking a piece shows what stock was worth.
Rows give stock a clear use.
cons: Fighting over rows can bury the stock cost.
A short player may fail to form a row.

pairs.tendency: Players hold letter tiles to make words, and a hand with too many tiles costs something each round while too few limits the words they can make.
pros: A tile hand makes stock easy to see.
Players learn to trade or spend letters.
cons: Word skill can matter more than stock sense.
Awkward letters can stay and cost round after round.

pairs.tendency: Players add tiles that match an open end, and tiles held cost something each round while a missing number leaves a player passing.
pros: Passing turns show a shortage plainly.
Holding the right tile has a clear value.
cons: Tile luck can leave one player stuck.
Players may hold on to tiles to block others.

pairs.tendency: Players lay down sets and add to them, so cards kept in hand cost something while a played set stops costing and can be added to by others.
pros: Laying down a set shows a cost is over.
Melds give stock a clear use.
cons: Waiting to meld can be costly.
Players who meld early may run out of cards.

pairs.tendency: Each power works once, so holding it costs something while using it early leaves nothing for later, and the choice is when to spend it.
pros: Spending a power is a clear stock choice.
Players learn to save and spend.
cons: Unused powers can feel wasted at the end.
Players may hold powers and never use them.

pairs.tendency: A player offers a move and the other may turn it down, so moves that add stock can be refused and moves that run it down can be forced.
pros: Refusing a move shows what it costs.
Players learn what a rival will accept.
cons: A refused move can leave a player short.
Players may offer moves that hide the cost.

pairs.tendency: A message passes along a line and may change, so a long message costs more to hold and a short one may leave out what the last player needs.
pros: Players feel the cost of a long message.
Both costs show at once in the message.
cons: The message can break on the way.
Stock is hard to explain through a message.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards before play without seeing what they will get, so passing too many leaves a player thin and passing too few leaves them with costly cards.
pros: Passing sets how much stock to carry.
Players learn to give up what costs.
cons: Players cannot judge what they will receive.
A player can pass the wrong cards.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the start and the other picks a side, so the setter tries to split stock evenly so neither side faces more holding cost.
pros: Setting stock evenly is a clear task.
The chooser sees the costs of both sides.
cons: Setting up needs care to be even.
A small gap in stock tilts one side.

pairs.tendency: A piece reaching the far end gains power, so keeping spare pieces back costs something while pushing forward leaves the back short.
pros: Promotion gives stock a reason to move.
Players weigh pushing against holding.
cons: Players may rush a piece and leave gaps.
A promoted piece costs more to keep safe.

pairs.tendency: Teams pass a baton in legs, and a runner carrying a heavy load slows the team while an empty hand has nothing to pass on.
pros: Each leg shows what a load costs.
Team play with a clear job per runner.
cons: Fast runners can ignore the cost.
The stock idea can be lost in the race.

pairs.tendency: Players build shapes that cannot be taken, so stones kept for a shape cost something to hold while a missing stone leaves the shape open.
pros: A shape shows exactly how many pieces it needs.
Building to a goal feels steady.
cons: The shape can matter more than the count.
A player may spend many stones on one shape.

pairs.tendency: Tricks lead to named prize cards, so players hold cards for prizes at a cost each round, while giving up a prize leaves it for others.
pros: Prizes give stock a clear aim.
Players weigh holding against spending.
cons: Prizes can decide the game over stock.
Holding for a prize may run out the turns.

pairs.tendency: Face-up cards are open to everyone, so players use them to cut what they hold, and a shared card removes some of the cost of stock.
pros: Open cards lower the need to hold.
Players read shared stock at a glance.
cons: Everyone sees the same shortage.
Players may wait on others to use shared cards.

pairs.tendency: Everyone adds to a middle pot that grows each round, so what a player puts in costs them while a bigger pot raises the cost of missing it.
pros: The pot shows stock building up.
Players see what the pool is worth.
cons: The pot can matter more than own stock.
Players may stop adding to avoid cost.

pairs.tendency: Players scoop and sow seeds, so a full pit costs a turn to empty while an empty pit leaves a player with nothing to move.
pros: The pits show stock at a glance.
A move changes the stock of both players.
cons: Counting seeds is slow for new players.
An empty side leaves a player passing.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand is dealt face down and one player can take, swap or buy it, so buying costs something and passing it up leaves a hand thin.
pros: The spare hand shows a price for stock.
Choosing is a clear stock trade-off.
cons: One player may gain stock the others lack.
An unused spare hand is wasted.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces give, use up or protect stock, so a track with these spaces makes players aim for or avoid spots to keep stock balanced.
pros: Spaces turn stock into a map.
Players plan a route around costs.
cons: A costly space can wipe out stock.
Players may stop on safe spaces and not move.

pairs.tendency: Every card or unit has a price, so players choose what to buy and what to hold, with each unit held costing something every round.
pros: Price and holding cost sit side by side.
Players learn to budget.
cons: Players may hold too much and spend too little.
Counting prices adds to turn time.

pairs.tendency: Players share out a fixed amount across places, so too much in one place leaves another short and too little in a place invites a loss.
pros: Sharing out shows both costs at once.
Players learn to spread stock.
cons: A split can leave every place thin.
One surprise can ruin a careful split.

pairs.tendency: Players keep moving until a signal, and a player carrying a lot is slow to stop while one with little can move fast but has less to show.
pros: Stock costs show in how fast a player stops.
Fast, lively rounds.
cons: Counting stock can slow the pace.
The signal can matter more than stock.

pairs.tendency: Players put back and take cards to shape a hand, so a swap can cut the cost of holding or fill a gap, and a failed swap leaves it thinner.
pros: Swaps are a clear way to fix stock.
Players test what they need.
cons: A failed swap deepens the shortage.
Waiting for another player's agreement can stall play.

pairs.tendency: A player may pick up the whole pile, which adds stock that costs something each round, while leaving it means running short.
pros: The pile shows the cost of taking too much.
Players weigh a big pile against its cost.
cons: A big pile can bury a player.
Players may avoid the pile and run short.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, so players hold trumps at a cost each round, and a hand with no trumps is weak when it counts.
pros: The trump suit shows what stock matters.
Players decide how many trumps to keep.
cons: A hand with no trumps has few options.
Holding trumps can lock a player into one plan.

pairs.tendency: A player runs stock on two boards at once, so holding too much on one leaves the other short and each board has its own costs.
pros: Two boards show two stock stories.
Players trade stock between the boards.
cons: Keeping track is heavy.
A shortage on one board can be missed.

pairs.tendency: Wild cards fill any gap, so a few cut the cost of running short but each one held costs something and can be saved for later.
pros: A wild card gives stock a clear price.
Players weigh using or keeping one.
cons: Many wilds can remove the shortage.
Players may hold wilds and stall the game.

pairs.tendency: Edges join, so stock can flow round the board, and a store on one edge can reach the other edge while empty spots can be reached from either side.
pros: Stock can move in any direction.
A shortage has more ways out.
cons: Players may find the board harder to read.
A joined edge can hide where stock is thin.

pairs.tendency: Each question uses up a limited number of asks, so too many questions cost the player their allowance and too few leave the secret unfound.
pros: Questions become stock a player spends.
Players learn to ask what matters.
cons: Players may waste asks early.
A short allowance can end the game at once.

pairs.tendency: Players race to the end while carrying stock that costs weight each round, and running short on the way can stop a player where they stand.
pros: A race shows both stock costs quickly.
Players hold or drop stock as they go.
cons: Racing can leave stock out of mind.
A leader can run short and be caught.

pairs.tendency: Points are scored for how well a player balances stock, so holding too much costs points each round and running out costs more.
pros: Points put a number on the balance.
Players compare ways of holding stock.
cons: Chasing points can hide the stock lesson.
Scoring costs each round slows play.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out as they run short of stock, so the last one still stocked wins and holding too much only slows a player.
pros: Running out has a clear and sharp cost.
Players watch each other's stock.
cons: Early drop-outs wait for the rest.
Players may hoard stock rather than use it.

pairs.tendency: The team shares stock and holding costs, and one player's shortage becomes the team's shortage, so the group balances together.
pros: Everyone shares in the stock problem.
Players talk through each cost.
cons: One player can direct all stock choices.
A shortage can feel hopeless for the whole team.

pairs.tendency: The group reaches a target together while managing stock, so holding costs eat into progress and a shortage stalls the whole team.
pros: Stock becomes a common problem.
Players divide who holds what.
cons: Little tension beyond the stock count.
One player may take over the planning.

pairs.tendency: Each player secretly aims for a different stock level, so what looks like hoarding to one is the goal of another and shortages are hard to read.
pros: Shows why people hold different amounts.
Players guess goals from stock.
cons: A shortage can be mistaken for a plan.
Secret goals can hide the cost.

pairs.tendency: A story moves forward while stock costs add up, so the tale shows what holding too much or running short does to the people in it.
pros: Stock costs turn into story events.
Easy to remember afterwards.
cons: The story can drift from the stock idea.
The ending can feel set before play.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so players manage stock only to see what happens, and the costs of holding and running out can be looked at after play.
pros: Players can look at costs freely.
Calm play with room to talk.
cons: Without a goal, stock choices may feel pointless.
Players may stop trying to balance.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what a balanced stock means, so one holds a large stock to be safe while another runs lean, and the costs fall differently.
pros: Players choose which cost to accept.
Choices show different attitudes to risk.
cons: Goals are hard to compare.
A goal can be set to dodge the cost.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the player who runs lowest on stock loses, so every player watches holding costs and shortages to avoid last place.
pros: Everyone has a reason to watch stock.
Tension builds around a shared cost.
cons: The loser can feel singled out.
Players may help others fail to stay safe.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, so players balance stock so no one runs out or is crushed by holding costs, and play ends only if stock fails.
pros: Stock balance becomes a shared aim.
Players help each other keep going.
cons: The game can drag on with no end.
One shortage can end an otherwise calm game.

pairs.tendency: The game cannot be won, so the balance of stock is the only thing to watch, and costs keep coming whatever players do.
pros: The stock problem is plain to see.
Players talk about the balance itself.
cons: Players may find no reason to play on.
Costs can feel like a trap without an exit.

pairs.tendency: One player manages stock against a layout of cards, and the layout costs more as cards stay unplaced while an empty row leaves the player stuck.
pros: A solo player sees both costs plainly.
Players can test plans safely.
cons: Nobody else shares the stock problem.
A stuck layout can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short games, so stock lessons from one game carry over, and a poor balance in one costs only that game.
pros: Players try a new balance each game.
A single loss is easy to recover from.
cons: Stock costs may be forgotten between games.
Early games can decide the whole set.

pairs.tendency: Stock held adds points against the player, so holding too much costs directly and running out may cost more through a penalty.
pros: Costs are plain to read on the scoreboard.
Players weigh holding against penalty.
cons: Players may spend stock early to cut points.
A shortage penalty can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: Players have to land on an exact number, so holding too much stock can overshoot and holding too little falls short, and both cost the win.
pros: Both costs show in one target.
Players count carefully near the end.
cons: Stock may be dumped near the end.
A player can lose by one unit.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to give stock away or hold least, so a player short of stock is winning, and the cost of too much becomes the point.
pros: Players see the cost from the other side.
Familiar ideas turn upside down.
cons: Players may be confused about which stock to keep.
Running out stops being a cost, so balance fades.

pairs.tendency: Everyone manages their own stock side by side, so players compare how each holds or runs short without affecting each other.
pros: Players compare ways of balancing.
Calm play with little pressure.
cons: Little contact between players.
No one feels another's shortage.

pairs.tendency: Players attack stock directly by stealing or sabotage, so a large stock draws attacks while a thin one can be knocked to zero.
pros: Theft shows the cost of holding stock.
Players need to defend what they hold.
cons: Fighting can bury the balance idea.
A player with little stock can be crushed.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board so that others find stock harder or easier to reach, and no one is attacked directly.
pros: Players feel the effect of others' choices.
Quiet pressure on stock.
cons: Players may not see why stock ran short.
Slow turns while players read the board.

pairs.tendency: The whole team shares stock against the game, so holding costs and shortages are shared problems, and no player wins alone.
pros: Everyone feels the same cost.
Players divide up who holds stock.
cons: One player may plan for the team.
The game can feel hopeless if stock runs out.

pairs.tendency: Players share a stock problem but each wants more for themselves, so hoarding helps one player while it leaves the group short.
pros: Shows the pull between self and group.
Tense choices about sharing.
cons: Hoarders can sink the group.
Players may accuse each other of holding too much.

pairs.tendency: Two teams manage their own stock against each other, so a team that holds too much pays for it and one that runs short is easy to beat.
pros: Teams plan stock together.
Each team can see the other's cost.
cons: One player may take over team stock.
A short team can be written off early.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly drains or over-fills the team's stock, so players cannot tell whether a shortage is chance or sabotage.
pros: Suspicion grows around shortages.
Players watch stock closely.
cons: Real shortages look like sabotage.
Accusations can upset players.

pairs.tendency: Players move by letter over days or weeks, so stock costs run on a slow clock and a shortage may wait many days before anyone can act.
pros: Waiting makes shortages feel real.
Players think hard before each move.
cons: Costs may be forgotten between letters.
A slow reply can leave a player short.

pairs.tendency: A player who is absent holds stock the others cannot touch, so their stock still costs and their shortage still bites although they never play.
pros: Absent stock shows costs left unattended.
A ghost player makes a clear example.
cons: An absent player cannot respond to stock.
Players may forget the absent stock.

pairs.tendency: A game master sets and runs the costs of holding and running out, so players deal with a world that charges for stock and the master decides how hard.
pros: The master can fit costs to the group.
Players can ask what a cost means.
cons: A master can make the costs feel unfair.
The master has more to track than the players.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or park, so stock is shared with passers-by who can add or take, and holding costs are felt in the open.
pros: Players see stock in the open.
Newcomers can join and change the balance.
cons: Stock can vanish when passers-by walk off.
Keeping count is hard in the open.

pairs.tendency: The lone player and the team each manage stock, and the lone player has more to hold alone while the team can share the cost.
pros: Shows how a group can share a cost.
The lone player has a clear task.
cons: A lone player can run short with no help.
The team can leave the lone player short.

pairs.tendency: One player manages stock against the game, so the costs of holding and running out are felt directly and no other player is to blame.
pros: Costs are plain to see.
A player can test plans safely.
cons: No other player to compare stock with.
A mistake in stock is only the player's own.

pairs.tendency: Dice and random draws change stock levels each round, so players see shortages and surpluses they did not plan and can do little about.
pros: Players feel how luck changes stock.
Light, quick play.
cons: Players cannot plan stock against the dice.
Costs can feel unrelated to choices.

pairs.tendency: Random events change stock, but players can build reserves or insure, so holding some extra pays against ill luck at a cost each round.
pros: Players weigh a reserve against its cost.
Choices stay open despite luck.
cons: Extra rules to learn.
A reserve can feel too costly to try.

pairs.tendency: Careful stock planning mostly decides results, with some random events that shift stock, so careful plans can still be knocked off by luck.
pros: Planning shows clear gains.
A small chance of surprise.
cons: Experienced players tend to manage stock sooner.
Planning can slow turns.

pairs.tendency: No luck changes stock, so every shortage and every holding cost comes from a player's own choice and the balance can be worked out.
pros: Every result has a clear reason.
Players can learn to plan stock.
cons: Real stock rarely behaves this predictably.
Slow turns while players calculate.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a message about stock, so players consider whether they hold too much or too little and what the sign tells them.
pros: Players reflect on their stock.
Quiet, thoughtful play.
cons: A sign cannot say how much stock to hold.
Players may ignore costs and read only the sign.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others will act and time stock to match, so holding costs are paid when players misjudge and running short happens when they are out of step.
pros: Players learn to read each other's timing.
Stock comes from a shared sense.
cons: Costs are hard to see in the play.
Mistakes in timing cannot be traced to stock.

pairs.tendency: A roll on a table brings events that raise or cut stock, so the story shows what a surplus or shortage does to the characters.
pros: Events show stock in story form.
Rolls give a lively sense of risk.
cons: Dice can bury a plan for stock.
Story can drift away from the stock cost.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sees all stock and all costs, so players can tell who holds too much or too little and plan against it.
pros: Players discuss stock openly.
Fair, clear play.
cons: Little surprise in stock.
A short player is easy to target.

pairs.tendency: Stock is held in hidden cards, so players cannot tell who holds too much or too little and have to guess from what is played.
pros: Players learn to read stock from play.
Mystery around who is short.
cons: Hard to plan with others.
Shortages can go unseen.

pairs.tendency: Players hide their sides while managing stock, so a player's stock choices may give away their side, and others read shortage as a clue.
pros: Stock choices become clues.
Suspicion around who holds what.
cons: Players may stock to mislead.
Reading identity can distract from the costs.

pairs.tendency: Players work out from clues how much stock each holds, since a hidden stock still shows in what a player pays or runs short of.
pros: Costs leave clues to follow.
Detective work about stock.
cons: Players may find clues hard to read.
Slow rounds while players reason.

pairs.tendency: Players claim to hold more or less stock than they do, so a bluff of plenty can ward off a rival while a bluff of need can win help.
pros: Bluffs show the value of stock.
Mind games around holding.
cons: Stock lies can upset players.
A bluff of need can cost real trust.

pairs.tendency: A hidden rule decides what stock costs, so players find out the price of holding or running out only by breaking it and being told.
pros: Costs are found by trying.
Learning feels like discovery.
cons: Early mistakes in stock can be expensive.
One player knows the cost and others do not.

pairs.tendency: One player knows how much stock is right but can only hint, so the others guess whether they hold too much or too little.
pros: Hints stand in for a stock count.
Players talk about stock carefully.
cons: Hints can be misread.
The hinting player may be frustrated by errors.

pairs.tendency: A hidden map shows stores and supplies only when explored, so players carry stock into the unknown, and holding extra costs while a short supply can strand them.
pros: Exploring puts a price on stock.
Players guess what lies ahead.
cons: A hidden store can be out of reach.
Players may carry too little and turn back.

pairs.tendency: One hand is open to all, so stock in the open hand is known while the others stay hidden, and players can play the open hand too.
pros: The open hand makes stock easy to read.
Players plan around known stock.
cons: The open hand can steer the whole game.
Hidden hands are still guesses.

pairs.tendency: Part of each player's stock or score is hidden, so nobody knows who holds too much or too little and players guess who is ahead.
pros: Players learn to guess from clues.
Surprise at the end.
cons: Costs are hard to compare.
Players may feel unsure of their own position.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so each turn is a chance to adjust stock and holding costs build up while others wait.
pros: Each turn has a clear stock choice.
Players can watch others' stock.
cons: Waiting time can be long.
Costs may feel far apart between turns.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses stock in secret and reveals together, so players cannot react to each other and a wrong guess shows at once in the cost.
pros: Quick rounds with no waiting.
Players learn from the reveal.
cons: Guessing can replace planning.
Mistakes are all revealed at the same time.

pairs.tendency: Anyone acts at any moment, so stock can run short before a player notices and quick players can take stock before it runs out.
pros: Shortages arrive with pressure.
Fast, busy play.
cons: Counting stock is hard in the rush.
Slower players run short first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so players decide stock fast and a rushed choice can leave them holding too much or too little.
pros: Time shows how stock choices feel under pressure.
Quick rounds.
cons: Rushed counting leads to errors.
The clock can matter more than the stock.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over real days, so holding costs are due each morning and a shortage may last until the next move.
pros: Waiting makes stock costs felt.
Players think before each move.
cons: Costs can feel slow and dull.
A forgotten turn leaves stock to run short.

pairs.tendency: The game slows play on purpose, so players have time to count stock and weigh holding against running out before each move.
pros: Time to think about the balance.
Calm play.
cons: The slow pace can feel dull.
Slow play can hide the cost of delay.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so stock costs rise and shortages come faster, and players have less time to correct them.
pros: Pressure builds around the balance.
The end feels tense.
cons: Late rounds can overwhelm players.
Early mistakes grow into big losses.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn can restock a player or run them out, so a lucky run can build up stock that then costs something to hold.
pros: Extra turns show how stock builds.
Quick bursts of play.
cons: A lucky player can get far ahead in stock.
Players may take turns just to avoid a cost.

pairs.tendency: Stages bring different stock needs, so what a player holds in the first stage sets up the second and too much or too little carries forward.
pros: Early choices show their later cost.
Players plan across stages.
cons: A poor first stage can ruin the second.
Rules change between stages.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system with stores, so a move changes stock as it would in life and costs of holding and running out show how that system behaves.
pros: Stock behaves like the real thing.
Players see cause and effect.
cons: Many rules to explain.
Stock counting can hide the larger system.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group, such as a shopkeeper or a farmer, who holds stock differently, so the costs fall unevenly on each role.
pros: Shows why groups hold different amounts.
Players argue from their role's needs.
cons: Some roles feel the cost more than others.
Players may blame each other for shortages.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws on one limited store, so taking more costs the others and a store left unused wastes what it could give.
pros: Shows how a shared store runs short.
Players can see the cost of taking.
cons: One player can drain the store for all.
Little reason to hold back without a rule.

pairs.tendency: What a player holds or runs out of shows its cost only a few rounds later, so a shortage can arrive long after the choice that made it.
pros: Shows why costs feel unfair when late.
Players learn to look ahead.
cons: Players may blame the wrong move.
Early mistakes are hard to trace.

pairs.tendency: Players try a new rule about stock, such as a cap on holding or a price for running out, and see what it changes.
pros: Safe way to test a stock rule.
Players see the effect of a new cost.
cons: A rule can break the balance.
Players may argue over which rule to try.

pairs.tendency: After play, players talk through how much stock they held, what it cost and when they ran short, and link it to real stores.
pros: The costs get named and compared.
Players link the game to real stock.
cons: Memory of costs can fade.
A short debrief may skip the costs.

pairs.tendency: What a player does with stock cannot be undone, so a wasted surplus or a shortage stays with the game into the next round.
pros: Costs of a choice are permanent.
Players take more care with stock.
cons: A deep shortage can ruin later games.
Players may avoid any choice to avoid loss.

pairs.tendency: The rules charge for holding stock and for running out, so the game says something about how stores ought to be kept without saying it aloud.
pros: The cost carries a point.
Players can spot what the rules argue.
cons: The argument may be read wrongly.
Players may take the rule for a fact.

pairs.tendency: Stock stands for something real, such as chores or time, so holding too much or running short has a real cost beyond the table.
pros: The cost feels real.
Players pay close attention.
cons: Real costs can cause arguments.
Some players feel pressured.

pairs.tendency: Stock is tied to points that stand for values, so players chase the balance of points and may forget what the stock was meant to measure.
pros: Shows how a number replaces a value.
Players notice the swap.
cons: Points can crowd out the value itself.
Players may balance the number, not the thing.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future store or village sharing, so holding costs and shortages show how a new way of living might feel.
pros: Costs of a new way show early.
Players can test a plan safely.
cons: Real costs may differ from the game's.
A plan can look easier than it will be.

pairs.tendency: The dice say how many lines you draw each turn, so a high throw can close several squares at once while a low one leaves you a single line.
pros: Dice give a quiet drawing game some surprise.
A big throw can finish a whole run.
cons: Careful planning of safe lines counts for less.
One lucky throw can undo a long lead.

pairs.tendency: Cards that name which kind of line you may draw are picked and passed round, so your pick limits which lines you can add and which you leave for others.
pros: Each pick shapes what the grid will look like.
Players watch which lines others want to draw.
cons: The cards you pass can hand someone a square.
Picking slows down a game that is quick alone.

pairs.tendency: When a chain of nearly closed squares appears, players bid for the right to start it, so the price shows how many squares each player thinks it holds.
pros: Bids show what a chain is worth.
Players learn to count squares before they pay.
cons: A player can overpay for a short chain.
Bidding takes more time than drawing a line.

pairs.tendency: After you close a square you may keep drawing, but a line that sets up the third side of a square hands it to your rival and ends the run.
pros: Every extra line is a small gamble.
Players feel a run of squares building.
cons: One careless line gives away all you gathered.
Cautious players stop after a single square.

pairs.tendency: The dots sit on a map of regions, and whoever closes the most squares inside a region holds it, so one square can swing a whole area.
pros: Squares have a clear reason beyond their count.
Players fight over the same dots.
cons: Strong players can pick which region to close first.
The map makes the drawing harder to read.

pairs.tendency: A worker placed on a spot on the board gives you the right to draw one line, and a taken spot means that line stays free for others.
pros: Spots decide who draws which lines.
Planning ahead matters as much as drawing.
cons: A taken spot can leave you without a line.
Two kinds of choice slow each turn.

pairs.tendency: The squares you close are also the shapes of a larger pattern, so you draw a line for its place in the pattern as well as for the square.
pros: Every line has two reasons.
Rivals can read your pattern from the grid.
cons: A rival can draw the line that breaks it.
A player can lose sight of the squares.

pairs.tendency: Cards in your hand allow certain lines, so you decide whether to spend a card now to close a square or keep it for a longer run later.
pros: Saving a card feels like a real choice.
Players plan a run of squares ahead.
cons: A card you wait on can be made useless.
Holding cards slows play on the grid.

pairs.tendency: Each trick is won with a card, and the winner draws a line, so players fight over cards for the chance to close the next square.
pros: The line becomes a prize for the trick.
Card play and drawing feed each other.
cons: Strong cards can give a player every line.
Players need to follow two games at once.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about which lines to leave open, offering to skip a square now for one later, though only the player holding the pen decides.
pros: Players trade squares they cannot both take.
Talk adds a human side to a drawing game.
cons: A promise to leave a line open can break.
Talking can drag out a quick turn.

pairs.tendency: Each square you close is a piece of a set, such as the four corners of a block, and you count squares by the sets they complete.
pros: Squares have a reason to be chosen.
Counting becomes clearer than a plain total.
cons: Sets can push you to close the wrong squares.
Rivals can take the one you lack.

pairs.tendency: Tiles placed on the table add new dots and new boxes to the grid, so each tile changes which squares are close to closing.
pros: The grid grows as the game goes on.
Every tile opens fresh chances for squares.
cons: A tile can leave a square for your rival.
The shared grid is harder to keep in mind.

pairs.tendency: One player draws a line and the next answers with a line next to it, so the grid grows like a chain of replies, with squares closing as it goes.
pros: Each line answers the last.
The drawing becomes a pattern both players made.
cons: Answering can force you to give a square away.
The chain can wander off from the squares.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a player shows their plan only by which line is drawn, and a rival has to read a lone line without a word.
pros: Lines say things without talk.
Players learn to read the grid closely.
cons: A line can look like a trap.
A silent table can feel dull.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may change a rule, such as how many sides close a square or whether closing one lets you go again.
pros: The game changes shape from turn to turn.
Players invent new ways to close a square.
cons: A change can undo a plan the others made.
The rule of going again can vanish overnight.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, such as a farmer fencing fields, and every line is drawn as something that character would do.
pros: The grid gets a small story.
Closing a square feels like an event.
cons: The talk takes longer than the lines.
Quiet players can feel left out of the story.

pairs.tendency: You draw each line with a steady hand, perhaps with a long pen held at arm's length, so a slip lands in the wrong place on the grid.
pros: Hands matter as much as plans.
A hard line is a real achievement.
cons: A slip can close a square for a rival.
Tired hands can decide a late game.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and the dots mark places on it, so a closed square becomes a field or a town that its owner can name.
pros: Squares turn into places with a story.
The map and the score grow together.
cons: Players may close squares to fit the map.
A crowded sheet gets hard to read.

pairs.tendency: You ask a player for a card to earn the right to draw a line, and a yes lets you draw while a no leaves the grid as it was.
pros: Asking gives each line a price.
A question shows which squares you want.
cons: A no can leave a square for a rival.
Questions slow a game that is quick alone.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on who will close the next square, and the bank pays fixed odds, so a player can win a bet without drawing a single line.
pros: Odds show which squares are close to closing.
Even a player behind can win a bet.
cons: Bets can matter more than the squares.
The bank player has two jobs to follow.

pairs.tendency: Before the dice land, players put counters on the table, and the throw says who draws first or how many lines each may add.
pros: The throw gives each bet something to rest on.
A bet adds a stake to every line.
cons: An unlucky throw can hand a rival squares.
Bets can pull attention from the grid.

pairs.tendency: Players put chips in the pot while they think their hidden cards can win, and the cards decide who may draw a line and close the next square.
pros: A bet shows how sure you are.
Hidden cards bring bluffing to a plain grid.
cons: A strong hand can give a long run.
The pot can count for more than the squares.

pairs.tendency: Before play each player picks a side with its own way of drawing, such as lines that start only from an edge, and then plays on the same grid.
pros: Each player draws in a different style.
A side shapes the whole plan for the grid.
cons: Two sides can fit the grid unevenly.
Players need time to learn each other's side.

pairs.tendency: Before play you say how many squares you will close, and every line you draw afterwards is either helping the promise or giving a rival a square.
pros: A spoken aim gives each line a reason.
Rivals know what to try to stop.
cons: A promise too big can fail early.
A small promise leaves little to play for.

pairs.tendency: A closed square can be taken over when a rival draws the line that completes a larger shape around it, so a lead of squares can swing in one move.
pros: A closed square is not yet safe.
A player who is behind can win it back.
cons: Squares change owners so often that scores blur.
A winning run can turn into a loss.

pairs.tendency: A square can be freed from a rival, and a teammate who draws the missing line can win it back, so players watch each other's squares too.
pros: Teammates have a reason to cover for each other.
A lost square is not lost for ever.
cons: Rescuers can walk into the same trap.
Waiting teammates have little to do.

pairs.tendency: Squares you close become walls, and a rival's squares caught inside a ring of yours are taken, so closing a square can start a second contest.
pros: Closing a square can win more than one.
Players plan a ring of squares before drawing.
cons: The rules for a ring are hard to follow.
A ring fails if one line is left open.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind may draw two lines in a turn, so a short run can start where a rival thought the squares were safe.
pros: The player behind keeps a real chance.
A lead stays small and tense.
cons: The leader may close fewer squares on purpose.
Players can hold back so they get the help.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards say which line goes where, so players only watch the grid fill in and count the squares that close along the way.
pros: The game is quick and light.
Anyone can win, whatever they know.
cons: There are no choices left in the lines.
Players may drift away from the game.

pairs.tendency: Players run round a floor grid, and a runner who is touched has to draw the next line, so the chase decides who gets to try for a square.
pros: Running and drawing share one game.
Quick bodies matter as much as clever lines.
cons: Players are sent hurrying to draw.
The squares can be forgotten in the chase.

pairs.tendency: With three or more players, you pick whose open square to close or whose chain to break, so who you pick counts as much as the line you draw.
pros: Choosing a target is a decision of its own.
Players have to read the whole table.
cons: The player with most squares gets picked on.
More players make each turn slower.

pairs.tendency: Players draw lines from one side of the grid to the other, and a line that closes a square also lengthens the chain, so both aims share the dots.
pros: One line can serve two aims.
Closing squares helps build the chain.
cons: A rival can cut the chain and close squares.
Players may chase squares and lose the chain.

pairs.tendency: Each kind of line beats one other kind and loses to a third, so a player picks which line to draw knowing a rival may answer with its counter.
pros: No kind of line wins every time.
Players guess what a rival will draw.
cons: Guessing can replace the planning of chains.
A run of squares can depend on a guess.
