pairs.tendency: You show a pair of cards you hold to score points while the game goes on, and those points sit beside the squares that close on the grid.
pros: Two kinds of score feed one total.
Players plan their cards around the grid.
cons: Shown pairs tell rivals what you hold.
Two scores are harder to follow than one.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that bends one rule of the grid, such as drawing two lines when a square is one line short.
pros: Each player plays a different game.
A power gives a clear plan.
cons: One power can make closing squares too easy.
Players spend time learning each other's powers.

pairs.tendency: Part-way through, a player offers to double the game's value, and the other either plays on with the squares as they stand or gives up the game.
pros: The grid shows who leads before the offer.
A big offer tests nerve.
cons: A player can be bluffed out of a lead.
Doubling can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: If a square can be closed, you have to close it, so a player can force a rival to take squares and then open a bigger chain.
pros: A trap becomes a way to win.
Players think several lines ahead.
cons: A beginner is forced to take unwanted squares.
Long chains can seem unfair.

pairs.tendency: Each square you close adds to your power, so a player who closes the early squares can draw longer runs in the later part of the game.
pros: An early square gives a lasting gain.
The game builds up as it goes.
cons: A lead grows and is hard to catch.
Players behind can drop out in spirit.

pairs.tendency: Each turn a player says the whole list of squares closed so far, then adds one more, so the record of the game gets longer as the grid fills.
pros: The grid and the memory fill together.
Players remember who took which square.
cons: Mistakes in the list start arguments.
A long list slows the last turns.

pairs.tendency: The stronger player starts with fewer squares or draws with a shorter turn, so a weaker player can still close the first squares.
pros: A weaker player has a real chance.
The game stays close to the end.
cons: A player may feel they are seen as weak.
Setting the handicap takes time.

pairs.tendency: One player hides a mark on the grid, and the others draw lines to close squares round it until it is found.
pros: Closing a square can uncover the mark.
Players watch each line for a clue.
cons: The hider has nothing to do while others draw.
The hunt can take over from the squares.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops across a closed square to land beyond it, and the squares you close make the path your piece can use.
pros: Closed squares open new routes.
A hop can win more ground in one move.
cons: Pieces and lines add two sets of rules.
A piece can jump over the squares you wanted.

pairs.tendency: You roll dice, keep some and roll the rest, and the lines you may draw this turn depend on the dice you keep.
pros: You choose how many lines to risk for.
A late reroll can close a square.
cons: The dice can leave you a single useless line.
Rerolling slows the turn before drawing.

pairs.tendency: A piece that lands on a rival's piece sends it back, and a rival who is sent back loses the right to draw until it returns.
pros: A sent-back piece costs a rival a turn.
Squares and sending back both swing a lead.
cons: Players can be sent back again and again.
The grid slows down while pieces wander.

pairs.tendency: A row of three marks lets you take a rival's mark, and the squares you close help you build rows, so taking a piece can break a square open.
pros: A closed square can help make a row.
A row can undo a rival's square.
cons: Players track two kinds of shape at once.
Taking a mark can reopen a chain.

pairs.tendency: Each dot holds a letter, and a closed square scores only if its four letters read as a word, so drawing lines means choosing which words to leave open.
pros: Squares are worth more when they spell something.
A dictionary settles arguments about a word.
cons: Players can close a square that spells nothing.
Players with small vocabularies fall behind.

pairs.tendency: Each line you draw has to join the open end of an earlier line, so the grid grows as one chain and a square closes only where two chains meet.
pros: The grid grows in one connected piece.
Open ends show where squares may close soon.
cons: A player with no matching line misses a turn.
A tight chain leaves few squares to claim.

pairs.tendency: You lay down a set of cards face up, and the squares you close let you add matching cards to it, so the grid and the table both grow.
pros: Squares add to a set already shown.
Rivals can add to a set too.
cons: A laid set tells rivals what you hold.
Cards on the table crowd the grid.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a special power that works once, such as drawing two lines, so the main question is which square is worth spending it on.
pros: Spending a power is a clear decision.
A power can end a rival's chain.
cons: A power left unused is wasted at the end.
One use can swing a game too far.

pairs.tendency: You offer a line and the other player may turn it down or choose between two lines you offer, so every line has to be safe in two ways.
pros: An offer shows how you think a rival draws.
Players learn to offer lines that are safe.
cons: A refused line can hand over a square.
Offering takes longer than drawing.

pairs.tendency: A note about the grid passes from player to player, and what arrives may not match what was sent, so squares are drawn on a half-known picture.
pros: The message is a small surprise.
Players learn how a picture changes in passing.
cons: A wrong message can close the wrong square.
The game stops while the note travels.

pairs.tendency: Before play, you hand some cards to another player, and the cards you get let you draw certain lines, so a gift can start a run of squares.
pros: What you pass shapes your rival's lines.
You choose without seeing what you get.
cons: A card passed may close a square for them.
Passing happens before you see the grid.

pairs.tendency: One player draws the first few lines, and the other chooses which side to play, so the opening has to leave squares even for both sides.
pros: The first player has a reason to be fair.
The opening gets careful thought.
cons: A tricky opening can be hard to judge.
One side can end up with the long chain.

pairs.tendency: A closed square at the far end of the grid is marked as a stronger square that scores double, so players push their lines towards that edge.
pros: A far square gives a reason to push on.
A small square can turn into a big one.
cons: The far edge can become crowded with traps.
Players may hold back close squares to reach it.

pairs.tendency: A team draws the grid in legs, each player taking a turn and passing the pen on, and the first team to close every square in its leg wins.
pros: Teammates depend on each other's lines.
Passing the pen keeps everyone drawing.
cons: A teammate can leave a square for a rival.
A slow leg holds back everyone after it.

pairs.tendency: A group of squares that cannot be split by a rival line is safe, so players aim to close such a block while a rival tries to cut it.
pros: A safe block gives a clear goal.
Rivals have a reason to strike early.
cons: Players can draw only for the shape.
A safe block may leave other squares open.

pairs.tendency: Closing squares earns the right to claim named prizes, and a single prize can be won with more than one square.
pros: Prizes make some squares worth more than others.
Players aim for the prize, not only the count.
cons: Squares not tied to a prize lose their appeal.
A prize named early can steer the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle can be used by everyone, and a closed square lets you combine them with your hand to score more.
pros: Everyone sees which cards are available.
A square can be worth more than one point.
cons: A rival can use the card you waited for.
The middle cards crowd the table.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter into the middle, and the player who closes the last square takes the pot, which grows if nobody manages it.
pros: The last square becomes worth a lot.
Players push for the final line.
cons: The last square can feel too big a prize.
A pot that grows can drag the game on.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are sown one at a time round a row of pits, and where the last seed lands decides which square you may close next.
pros: Both games turn on where a count ends.
Players plan how many seeds to sow.
cons: Counting and drawing double the work each turn.
One miscount can close the wrong square.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand of cards lies face down, and one player may take it before play, so the lines you can draw may change in a single swap.
pros: One swap can reshape the lines.
The first player to choose gets a clue.
cons: A strong-looking hand can be a weak one.
The swap comes before any lines exist.

pairs.tendency: Some squares on the grid have a rule of their own, such as keeping a player safe or sending them back, so closing one can bring more than a point.
pros: A square can carry a surprise.
Players choose which squares to chase.
cons: A square with a penalty can be a trap.
Special squares can pull play from long chains.

pairs.tendency: Every line type has a price, and a longer run of squares costs more to start, so players spend what they have on the squares they want.
pros: A run of squares has a clear cost.
Players weigh a price against the squares won.
cons: Players short of money cannot draw.
Counting the cost slows the drawing.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed number of lines between several grids, so a lot spent on one square leaves less for another, while your rival splits theirs too.
pros: Each line spent leaves less elsewhere.
Players guess where a rival will put theirs.
cons: One neglected grid can be lost at once.
The split can be hard to compare across grids.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws lines until a signal comes, such as the music stopping, and then the squares closed so far are counted and the slowest player is caught.
pros: A signal makes players hurry.
A rush gives surprising runs of squares.
cons: Fast drawing leads to sloppy lines.
Players caught early sit out the next round.

pairs.tendency: You may put cards back and take new ones before drawing, so you can look for the card that lets you close a square on this turn.
pros: A swap gives a second chance.
Players aim for the line that closes a square.
cons: A rival can see which cards you throw back.
Swapping slows a quick game.

pairs.tendency: You may pick up the whole discard pile if you can use the top card at once, so a card that closes a square can bring a large hand along.
pros: A square can win a whole pile.
Players watch what others throw away.
cons: A big pile can bury you in cards.
A rival can wait to take the pile.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named for the hand and its cards beat the rest, so a player holding trumps can draw a line that others cannot answer.
pros: A trump gives a sure line.
Players plan around one named suit.
cons: A hand without trumps closes few squares.
The chosen suit can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: You play two grids at once, so a line that gives away a square on one grid might win a square on the other.
pros: One grid's sacrifice can pay off on the other.
Players attack and defend together.
cons: Two grids are hard to follow.
A slip on one can lose both.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand in for any line you need, so it can close a square that would otherwise stay open.
pros: A wild card can finish a run.
Players save it for a square they need.
cons: Rivals can wait for you to spend it.
A single wild card can swing too much.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the grid join up, so a line off the right side carries on from the left, and squares can close across the join.
pros: The grid has no safe edge.
Players find squares in new places.
cons: Players can miss a square across the join.
Counting the open sides gets harder.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a hidden square, and the others ask yes or no questions before drawing a line, so each answer shrinks where a closed square could be.
pros: Each answer narrows the squares left to close.
Players ask before they draw.
cons: The questions can slow the lines.
A weak question can waste a whole turn.

pairs.tendency: A hidden square is guessed with a line, and each guess is answered with how many sides are right and where, so a guess is also a move.
pros: Every guess gives a clue about the square.
Players learn from the rival's guesses too.
cons: A wild guess wastes a line.
Each answer needs to be worked out.

pairs.tendency: Players race to fill their own row of squares, and the first to close the last one wins, so every square is a step towards the end.
pros: The target is easy to see.
Every square is a step forward.
cons: A leader can pull far ahead.
Players behind may give up on the race.

pairs.tendency: The player with the most closed squares at the end wins, so the count is the aim, and a run of squares near the end can change who is ahead.
pros: Scoring is easy to follow.
Players compare how many squares each holds.
cons: A late run can undo a long lead.
Counting at the end takes time.

pairs.tendency: A player whose last square is closed by a rival is out, and the last player with a square still open wins, so closing squares removes rivals.
pros: A closed square knocks a player out.
Each closed square takes someone out.
cons: Players knocked out early sit and wait.
The game feels harsh for the weakest.

pairs.tendency: The team draws lines together while the game closes squares of its own, and the team survives if the game has not closed too many by the end.
pros: Players share the aim of keeping squares open.
The game takes the part of a rival.
cons: One player can tell the others what to draw.
Losing together can feel heavy.

pairs.tendency: The group draws lines to reach a shared target number of squares, so each closed square is a step they all take together.
pros: Everyone sees the shared goal.
Players help each other plan a run.
cons: There is little tension between players.
One player can take every square.

pairs.tendency: Each player secretly wants a different set of squares, such as the corners, so a closed square tells nobody whose goal it served.
pros: A square can serve a secret aim.
Players watch lines for clues about goals.
cons: One line can give a goal away.
Secret aims hide how close the game is.

pairs.tendency: Each closed square is a scene in a story, and the game ends when the story does, so players close squares to move the story along.
pros: A square becomes a scene.
The grid fills as the story goes.
cons: The story can end before the squares do.
Story and counting pull against each other.

pairs.tendency: The grid fills with lines and squares, but nobody wins, so players stop at the end and look at what they made.
pros: Players draw without a score to chase.
The finished grid is something to talk about.
cons: Without a prize, the longest runs lose their pull.
Some players may drift away.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means, such as closing one square or closing every square, so the same grid can feel very different to each.
pros: Goals fit each player.
Players learn what others value.
cons: A goal that is too easy ends interest.
Two players may not know who has won.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player has the fewest squares and loses, so everyone else is simply safe, and a run of squares moves you away from last place.
pros: The danger of being last sharpens play.
The leader can relax once safe.
cons: One player is left with the loss.
Players who are safe can stop trying.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep the grid open as long as possible, so players draw lines that avoid closing the last squares and keep the game alive.
pros: Players work together to keep drawing.
The game can run for a long time.
cons: Closing a square can end the fun.
The score stops meaning much.

pairs.tendency: The game is made so that nobody can win, yet closing a square still lets you draw again, which tempts players to chase a score that is not there.
pros: Chasing squares shows what the game takes away.
Players talk about why they kept going.
cons: Players may feel the game is broken.
The point can be missed.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a grid with some lines already drawn, and you win if you close every square before you run out of lines.
pros: The grid is a puzzle to solve.
Each run of squares feels like progress.
cons: A poor opening can leave no way through.
Players alone have no one to learn from.

pairs.tendency: Several short grids are played in a row, and whoever wins the most grids wins, so a lost grid can still be made up for.
pros: A loss is not the end of the match.
A short grid is quick to learn from.
cons: The match can end before everyone has played.
Closing squares on one grid can feel small.

pairs.tendency: Every square you close counts against you, so players draw lines that make a rival close squares, and the player with the fewest squares wins.
pros: Closing a square becomes a risk.
Players draw to hand squares to a rival.
cons: Going again after a square is a penalty.
Players can stall by avoiding every square.

pairs.tendency: Squares add up to a target number, and you have to land on it exactly, so a long run of squares can carry you past the total.
pros: A run can overshoot and cost the win.
Players count squares carefully.
cons: Players can stop a run early on purpose.
Counting slows play near the end.

pairs.tendency: The player who closes the most squares loses, so every line is drawn to avoid the third side of a square, and the last safe line becomes the prize.
pros: Players hunt for the last safe line.
Each line needs careful thought.
cons: The rule of going again turns into a penalty.
Players can stall for a long time.

pairs.tendency: Each player draws on their own grid at the same time, closing squares without touching each other's lines, and compare totals at the end.
pros: Players work at their own pace.
Squares are counted the same way for all.
cons: Rivals have little to do with each other.
Players only compare at the end.

pairs.tendency: Players draw lines on purpose to cut each other's chains and force a rival to close squares, so each turn is aimed at someone.
pros: Each line has a clear target.
Players feel the cost of a rival's line.
cons: Lines aimed at one player can feel unkind.
A trailing player is hit again and again.

pairs.tendency: Players never attack each other directly, but each line changes which squares stay open, so a rival feels it through the shape of the grid.
pros: The grid carries every effect.
Players read each other by the lines.
cons: The cause of a loss is hard to see.
One line can matter for several turns.

pairs.tendency: The whole team draws together against the grid, which closes squares on its own turns, and they win or lose together.
pros: Everyone shares the plan.
Players talk through each line.
cons: One player can lead every move.
There is little between players to argue.

pairs.tendency: Players draw on one grid and help close squares, but each keeps a private count, so each wants a few more squares than the rest.
pros: Players have to weigh sharing against taking.
Helping and taking both feel natural.
cons: A player can take squares others set up.
The private count can be hard to keep.

pairs.tendency: Two teams draw on one grid, and each team's total counts together, so teammates plan lines that give away few squares.
pros: Teammates plan a run together.
The grid becomes a team contest.
cons: One strong player can lead their team.
Teammates can disagree about a safe line.

pairs.tendency: Most players close squares for the team, but one secretly leaves squares open for the other side, so an odd line may be a mistake or a betrayal.
pros: Players study lines for signs of a traitor.
A single odd line can start a long debate.
cons: A fair player can be blamed for a slip.
Accusations can upset players.

pairs.tendency: Players send a letter naming their next line, and each draws it on their own copy, so a run of squares is closed one letter at a time.
pros: Waiting for a reply is part of the game.
Each line is thought over with care.
cons: A lost letter can leave the grids different.
A game can last weeks.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and their lines follow a fixed rule or come from an earlier game, so squares are closed against a rival who cannot answer.
pros: The absent player's lines can be studied.
The table plays against a known pattern.
cons: A fixed rule may become easy to beat.
The absent side cannot adapt.

pairs.tendency: One player draws the dots and describes what the squares stand for, such as rooms of a house, while the others draw lines as their characters.
pros: A square becomes a room or a field.
The grid is an open world.
cons: The game master has to follow every line.
The others rely on one person's pace.

pairs.tendency: The grid is chalked on a pavement and passers-by can join in with a line, so squares are closed by people who have never met.
pros: Anyone can add a line.
Squares are closed by many hands.
cons: Passers-by may not know the rules.
A big grid can be rubbed out by rain.

pairs.tendency: All the players but one team up against a lone player, and the lone player draws extra lines to close squares for more points if they win.
pros: The lone player gets a stronger turn.
A team has to plan together.
cons: The lone player is outnumbered at every turn.
The team can give away squares by arguing.

pairs.tendency: You draw both sides of the grid yourself, closing squares as well as you can, and compare your total with a friend's later.
pros: The game can be played anywhere.
You can try one run again and again.
cons: There is nobody to outwit.
A quiet grid can feel dull.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards pick the line to draw, so closing a square is mostly luck, and a long run follows a lucky streak.
pros: The game is quick and light.
Anyone can win a grid.
cons: Planning a safe line hardly matters.
Players may stop caring about the grid.

pairs.tendency: Dice give a line to draw, but a player can spend a card to move it, so an unlucky throw need not hand a square to a rival.
pros: An unlucky throw can be softened.
Players still plan their lines.
cons: Cards for softening can run out.
The cards add more rules to keep in mind.

pairs.tendency: Players choose their lines carefully, and a few random cards alter which lines are open, so a closed square is mostly earned but sometimes lucky.
pros: Planning is mostly rewarded.
A random card keeps an expert guessing.
cons: An expert tends to win most grids.
Luck can spoil a careful chain.

pairs.tendency: Nothing is left to chance, so every closed square comes from counting open sides, and the player who counts chains more cleverly tends to win the endgame.
pros: Every result has a reason.
Players can learn how to count chains.
cons: An expert beats a newcomer every time.
Long thinking can slow the table.

pairs.tendency: A throw of dice is read as a sign about where to draw, so a line is chosen by what it might mean, not by the squares it closes.
pros: A throw gives a reason to draw.
Players talk about what a sign means.
cons: A sign can lead to giving a square away.
Squares and signs rarely agree.

pairs.tendency: Players try to sense when a rival will draw the line that closes a square, and draw the same line together, with no rule to fix the order.
pros: Players learn to read each other.
A shared line feels like a small win.
cons: Two players can draw the same line by mistake.
It is hard to say who closed the square.

pairs.tendency: A roll of the dice is looked up on a table that says what happens next, and the result may give a line, a square or an event.
pros: The dice write part of the story.
A surprising result gets players talking.
cons: The table can hide how many squares were won.
Looking up results slows the turns.

pairs.tendency: Every line and every square is visible to both players, so a player who can see where a chain will end can plan a sacrifice.
pros: Nothing on the grid is hidden.
Mistakes are plain for all to see.
cons: A strong player can plan many lines ahead.
Slow thinkers hold up the game.

pairs.tendency: Players hold cards no one else can see, and each card lets them draw a certain line, so a rival cannot tell which square you are ready to close.
pros: Players can hide a plan for a run.
Bluffing brings life to a grid.
cons: A hidden hand can leave a player stuck.
Players cannot plan together.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles, and a closed square may help your side or a rival's, so nobody is sure whom a line is helping.
pros: A closed square can be read two ways.
Players watch lines for signs of a role.
cons: A mistake is hard to tell from a lie.
Some players can feel left out.

pairs.tendency: Players work out from the lines drawn which squares are hidden or safe, so each line is both a move and a clue to a pattern.
pros: Lines work as clues.
Working out a hidden square is satisfying.
cons: The deduction can take over from the squares.
Slow solvers hold up the turn.

pairs.tendency: You draw a line that looks like a trap, or a safe one that is a trap, so a rival has to guess whether to close the square you offer.
pros: A safe-looking line may hide a sacrifice.
Players try to read a rival's nerve.
cons: A bluff on a small grid shows.
Lies about a line can upset players.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about which lines count, and the others find it only by drawing a line and being told no.
pros: Players learn the rule by drawing.
A closed square feels like finding a key.
cons: Players told no often can feel unfairly stopped.
The game slows while rules are being found.

pairs.tendency: One player can see which squares will close, but may only hint with pictures, so the others draw lines guided by hints.
pros: A hint can lead to a run of squares.
The hinter has a clear job.
cons: A hint can be read the wrong way.
The hinter has to wait while others draw.

pairs.tendency: The grid starts hidden, and squares are turned over only when someone draws a line beside them, so nobody knows which squares are worth closing.
pros: Each new line shows more of the grid.
The first lines are an open gamble.
cons: A line can open a square for a rival.
Players cannot plan a chain at the start.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up for all to see, and a player may draw the lines it allows as well as their own, so its lines are known.
pros: An open hand gives a clear chance.
Players can plan around it.
cons: Rivals can also plan around it.
Playing two hands is hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Some of your closed squares are kept secret, so nobody can add up the totals for certain and each player has to guess who is ahead.
pros: Nobody knows who is winning.
Players have to guess at the totals.
cons: The grid shows squares, so secrets leak.
A player may go quiet and wait.

pairs.tendency: One player draws at a time, and closing a square gives them another line, so a single turn can run long while the others wait.
pros: Players have time to think about each line.
A long run of squares is a thrill.
cons: A player waits while a rival finishes a chain.
One run can end the game.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses a line in secret and all reveal together, so two players who pick the same line close a square at the same time.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn.
The reveal brings a burst of surprise.
cons: Two players can close the same square.
The rule of drawing again does not work.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may draw a line at any moment, so players race to close a square before another player draws its last side.
pros: The grid fills fast.
Quick eyes win squares.
cons: Players can grab the same line.
Slow players can be left out.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a run of squares has to be finished before time runs out, so a long chain is drawn in a hurry.
pros: The clock keeps the game moving.
A long run is a thrill.
cons: A hurried line can hand over a square.
A rushed run can end a turn too soon.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over real days, with one line drawn each morning, so a closed square is something you wait to see.
pros: Waiting makes each line feel weighty.
Players think about a line for hours.
cons: A grid left open can be forgotten.
A run of squares can take days.

pairs.tendency: Players pause and breathe before each line, so a run of squares is drawn slowly, and the waiting is part of the game.
pros: Each line is thought over with care.
The slowness lowers the pressure.
cons: A long run feels very long.
Players can lose track of the grid.

pairs.tendency: The turns get shorter as the game goes on, so the first lines are drawn with time to think and the last squares in a rush.
pros: The ending comes with a burst of speed.
Players learn to plan before the rush.
cons: Late squares are closed by chance.
A fast ending can undo a careful lead.

pairs.tendency: Closing a square gives you an extra turn straight away, so one move can lead to another, and a lucky player can run a long chain.
pros: The rule fits the game's own pace.
A long run of squares is a thrill.
cons: A rival may be left watching for many lines.
An extra turn can come on top of another.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is drawing lines without closing squares, and the second is closing them, so the way you draw in stage one sets up the chains of stage two.
pros: The first stage sets up the second.
Players plan before they close squares.
cons: A poor first stage can lose the game.
Stage two can feel decided by stage one.

pairs.tendency: Each square stands for a part of a real system, such as a field and its well, so closing one shows what that part does to the others.
pros: A closed square has a real meaning.
Players see how parts of a system link.
cons: Players can close squares and forget the system.
The grid can look too tidy for reality.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a real group, such as farmers or a village council, and each draws lines for what that group needs, closing squares as its own.
pros: Each group draws in its own way.
The grid shows competing needs.
cons: One group can close most squares.
Players may play the score and not the group.

pairs.tendency: Squares are drawn from one limited stock of lines, so a run of squares for one player leaves fewer for everyone else.
pros: Players see how fast a stock runs out.
Taking a run is a real temptation.
cons: The last lines may go to a few players.
A greedy run can end the game.

pairs.tendency: A line drawn now shows its effect a few rounds later, so a square closes only after a delay and players have to plan ahead for it.
pros: A line is a choice for later.
Players see a cause in a late result.
cons: A delay can make the cause hard to find.
A player can forget what they set up.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule, such as needing three sides to count as a square, then play on to see how it changes the runs of squares.
pros: A rule can be tested in one grid.
Players see what a small change does.
cons: A rule can break the game's pace.
Players may argue about what changed.

pairs.tendency: After the grid is full, players talk about why chains went to one player, and which lines handed over squares, and what they would draw differently.
pros: Players name the lines that mattered.
The grid is a record to look back on.
cons: A short game leaves little to discuss.
Talk can turn into blame.

pairs.tendency: Lines drawn stay on the paper and the next game starts on the same sheet, so squares closed earlier shape every grid after it.
pros: Every line has lasting weight.
Players see a history on the sheet.
cons: A poor early game can ruin the next.
The sheet fills up and becomes hard to use.

pairs.tendency: The rule of drawing again after a square says that success earns more success, so the game itself argues that winners tend to pull ahead.
pros: The rule makes a point without words.
Players can discuss what the rule says.
cons: Players may find the point too blunt.
A game of chance can lose the point.

pairs.tendency: The squares players close are worth something real, such as who washes the cups, so a run of squares carries a weight beyond the table.
pros: Closing a square feels like it counts.
Players think hard before a line.
cons: A lost square can cause real annoyance.
Some players feel pressure to avoid risk.

pairs.tendency: Each square is a point for something that matters, such as kindness, and players chase the squares and forget what they stood for.
pros: Players see how a number replaces a value.
The grid shows what gets chased.
cons: Players may get the point only when told.
Players can feel scolded for playing to win.

pairs.tendency: Players draw squares as parts of a future they would like, such as shared fields, and see how it might feel before it is tried.
pros: Squares become parts of a new plan.
Players talk about how a future works.
cons: A neat grid can hide the hard parts.
Players may close squares to win, not to learn.

pairs.tendency: A closed square gives you another line, which can close another, so success makes the next success easier, and a lead can grow on itself.
pros: A small lead is felt and grows.
The loop shows how gains pile up.
cons: A winner can be impossible to catch.
A trailing player may feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: A grid stays quiet while lines are drawn without closing squares, and then one line sets off a long run, so everything changes at once.
pros: A long quiet stretch ends with a burst.
The sudden run is a vivid example.
cons: The quiet stretch can feel slow.
Players can miss the line that tipped it.

pairs.tendency: Open squares with three sides done pile up on the grid, and the size of the pile matters more than any single line.
pros: The pile is easy to see.
Players learn to judge its size.
cons: A big pile can be taken in one turn.
Waiting for a big pile can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: Between the players' turns, a fixed rule draws a line by itself, so squares can close or be given away without any player choosing.
pros: The board feels as if it moves alone.
Players plan around a known rule.
cons: A rule's line can hand over a square.
Players may feel they are not in control.

pairs.tendency: Event cards add or remove lines on the grid, such as a flood wiping out a row, so a player has to respond to a change nobody chose.
pros: A shock tests each player's plan.
Players have to respond to the same event.
cons: An event can undo a run of squares.
A harsh event can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: Each round of drawing stands for a year, so a grid that fills over many rounds shows a place growing slowly.
pros: A long span fits in an afternoon.
Closed squares show growth over time.
cons: Players may not feel a year pass.
A year can be spent on a single line.

pairs.tendency: A gauge beside the grid moves with every square closed, so players see what each run does to the whole system, not only to the score.
pros: One look shows how the system is doing.
A closed square has a visible effect.
cons: Players watch the gauge, not the grid.
A gauge can hide who is ahead.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with different numbers of lines already drawn, so one player starts nearer to closing squares and the game does not even it out.
pros: The grid shows an unfair start.
Players see how a head start grows.
cons: A player far behind can lose hope.
A big gap ends the game early.

pairs.tendency: Whoever has closed the most squares writes a rule for the rest, such as cutting the others' turns, so a lead grows into power.
pros: Players see how a lead can become power.
A rule written by the leader is felt.
cons: A leader's rule can end the game.
The others may feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: Each role wants a different kind of square, such as fields or wells, and a line that closes one kind can give away another.
pros: One line can help one role and hurt another.
Players know what others want.
cons: A weak kind of square can lose.
Players may argue over squares.

pairs.tendency: The game opens on a described situation, such as a village with a few fences already up, and the first lines are drawn from it.
pros: The opening gives lines a reason.
Players share the same picture.
cons: A long description delays the first line.
A set start can narrow the options.

pairs.tendency: A player may try a line the rules do not allow and explain why it ought to count, and the table decides if the square closes.
pros: Players practise giving reasons.
A new kind of line can be tried.
cons: Arguments can run longer than the drawing.
Loud players can win a disputed square.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points, such as after every few squares, so players say what they notice on the grid before going on.
pros: Players see patterns while they play.
A pause breaks a long run into parts.
cons: A pause can cool a game that was hot.
Pausing too often slows the game.

pairs.tendency: The same grid is drawn more than once with one change, such as who goes first, and players compare how the squares closed each time.
pros: Players learn what a small change does.
Each grid becomes a result to compare.
cons: Repeating the grid can feel dull.
Players learn the grid and stop exploring.

pairs.tendency: The game says what it leaves out of the real situation, such as weather or prices, so players know where a closed square stops being true.
pros: Players know where the model stops.
The grid is not mistaken for the world.
cons: A long list of gaps can feel heavy.
Players may care more about the squares.

pairs.tendency: The people whose situation the grid shows help design it and check that the squares stand for something true.
pros: The grid reflects real lives.
Players trust what the squares mean.
cons: Design takes more talk than drawing.
People may disagree about what a square means.

pairs.tendency: Each player is one link in a chain, and drawing a line passes an order down the chain, so a square may close only when the whole chain has acted.
pros: One line reaches every link.
Players see how a delay passes along.
cons: A late link holds back the whole chain.
Players can lose sight of the squares.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own corner of the grid, and has to guess whether a line will close a square in the part they cannot see.
pros: Players learn how little they can see.
Guessing about the rest is part of play.
cons: A closed square can come as a surprise.
Players may blame each other for hidden parts.

pairs.tendency: The slowest player draws the lines everyone waits on, so the pace of every square is set by the narrowest step.
pros: The slowest step is easy to spot.
Speeding up one step changes little.
cons: One player can hold up the whole table.
Players may blame the slow step, not the system.

pairs.tendency: Lines are drawn ahead to a guess and pushed along, or drawn only when a square calls for them, so players feel the difference in waste.
pros: Players feel two ways of working.
Waste and shortage show on the grid.
cons: A guess can leave stray lines nobody uses.
Waiting for a pull can leave a square unclosed.

pairs.tendency: Players choose how many lines to draw in one go, a long run now or one line at a time, and pay for it in waiting or setup.
pros: The choice of how many is clear.
Players see waiting cost against setup cost.
cons: A big batch can give a rival a run.
A tiny batch can slow the whole table.

pairs.tendency: A pen can fail at random and has to be repaired, so a plan to draw a long run of squares may be stopped partway.
pros: Plans have to allow for a pen failing.
Repairs add a reason to wait.
cons: One failure can ruin a run.
A failure can feel like plain misfortune.

pairs.tendency: Open squares left unclaimed cost something each round, and running out of lines costs more, so players keep balancing between the two.
pros: Players feel both kinds of cost.
The balance is easy to see on the grid.
cons: Players may watch costs and not squares.
Balancing slows a quick game.

pairs.tendency: The dice say how far you walk, but the piles only shrink when you take from them, so the throw and the taking are two separate parts of a turn.
pros: Luck softens a cold game of counting.
Beginners can win by a lucky throw.
cons: The two parts feel stuck together.
A low throw wastes a clever pile move.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round the table and each player keeps one, and a kept card lets you take from a pile, so every pick also shrinks the pile that is left.
pros: Picks have a clear reason.
Players watch the pile drop.
cons: Passing a card shows what you want.
Long waits sit between turns.

pairs.tendency: Players offer a price for the right to take from the pile first, and whoever pays most takes first and leaves the rest smaller.
pros: Going first has a price.
Players learn what a turn is worth.
cons: Taking first is rarely worth the highest price.
Bids that are too high lose the pile.

pairs.tendency: You take more and more from the pile for points, and if you take past a hidden limit you lose the lot you took.
pros: Every extra piece is a small bet.
The pile gives a clear sense of danger.
cons: One greedy take wipes out a turn.
Careful players take very little each time.

pairs.tendency: Each region holds a pile of pieces and you take from the region you want to win, so a region shrinks as players fight over it.
pros: Regions become cheaper to win as they empty.
Players choose which region to give up.
cons: A small region is easy to take but worth little.
Empty regions leave nothing to fight for.

pairs.tendency: A worker on a board spot lets you take from one pile, and a spot that is taken stops others taking from that pile this turn.
pros: Spots decide who takes from which pile.
The piles shrink round after round.
cons: Late workers find an empty pile.
A blocked spot means a wasted turn.

pairs.tendency: You remove pieces to leave a pattern on the board, but nothing is added back, so each take can break a shape you were making.
pros: Every removal changes the pattern.
Players plan shapes many moves ahead.
cons: A needed piece can be taken by a rival.
Patterns get harder to finish as pieces go.

pairs.tendency: Your hand holds cards that say how many pieces you may take, so you save the big cards for when the pile is small enough to finish.
pros: Cards make a plain game of counting less rigid.
Players plan the last few takes.
cons: A hand can sit unused as the pile ends.
Hidden cards hide the count from others.

pairs.tendency: Each trick won lets that player take from the pile, so winning a trick means making the pile smaller for everyone.
pros: Tricks have a plain prize.
Players count how many takes are left.
cons: Winning a trick can help the player behind you.
A weak hand wins no takes.

pairs.tendency: Players can talk before a take, such as asking someone to leave a pile alone, but there is only one pile and the last piece wins.
pros: Players can plan a take together.
Deals tell you who is close to winning.
cons: A deal can be broken by the last move.
Talking does not change the count.

pairs.tendency: The pieces you take are sets you are collecting, so a pile holds what everyone wants and every take leaves fewer sets to finish.
pros: Each take has a clear purpose.
Players can see which sets are running out.
cons: A set can be stranded when the pile is gone.
Players start taking only to block others.

pairs.tendency: You take tiles from a pile to lay on a shared map, so the map grows while the pile empties and the last tile ends the game.
pros: Map and pile run out together.
The end of the game is visible.
cons: The last tiles may not fit anywhere.
The final tile decides the map.

pairs.tendency: One player takes from the pile and calls out how many, and the next answers with a take of their own, so the pile is passed down like a chain.
pros: Each take answers the last.
Players read the count aloud.
cons: A small slip in counting breaks the chain.
A fast chain is hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so you show how many pieces you take only by lifting them, and the others have to read your move from the pile.
pros: Players watch the pile closely.
Counting is done by eye.
cons: A quick take can be misread.
A quiet game of counting can feel flat.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may change the rule for how many you can take, so the count that was safe a turn ago may not be safe now.
pros: The same pile can feel new each round.
Players can write rules that help their count.
cons: Old plans in counting stop working.
Arguments start about which rule is on the table.

pairs.tendency: You speak as a character and describe each take in their voice, such as a villager drawing from a well, while the count itself stays plain.
pros: A bare count gets a story.
Characters give a reason for each take.
cons: The acting is longer than the move.
A quiet player may speak little.

pairs.tendency: Taking a piece needs a steady hand, such as lifting a stick from a pile without moving the rest, and a shaky take can cost the game.
pros: Hands and counting both matter.
A tense take is easy to watch.
cons: A shaky hand can beat a sound count.
The turns slow while hands steady.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and each piece taken from a pile crosses a place off the drawing, so the map empties as it is made.
pros: The drawing shows what has gone.
The map is made together.
cons: Crossed-off places cannot be used again.
Drawing takes more time than taking.

pairs.tendency: You ask another player for a card, and a card you get lets you take from the pile, so the pile shrinks only on turns where you were told yes.
pros: Cards give each take a reason.
Players listen to each question.
cons: A no leaves you with nothing to take.
The pile may stand still for rounds.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on how many pieces the bank will take from the pile, and the bank takes at fixed odds, so the count decides who is paid.
pros: Odds are known before the take.
The pile gives each bet a clear limit.
cons: The bank sees many bets before it takes.
Winning bets can come to an end with the pile.

pairs.tendency: Players put coins down before a throw, and the throw says how many pieces come off the pile, so luck now sets the pace of the game.
pros: Bets add a stake to each take.
The throw can end the pile suddenly.
cons: Skill in counting no longer matters much.
A big pot can finish in one throw.

pairs.tendency: You keep putting chips in while you think your cards can take the last piece, and others raise or drop out as the pile gets smaller.
pros: Chips show how sure each player is.
The shrinking pile raises the stakes.
cons: A raise can give away a close finish.
Players who drop out lose their chips.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a side before play, and each side takes from the pile in its own way, so the sides count differently.
pros: Sides give different ways to take.
A plain game can be made even or uneven.
cons: A side that takes more can end the game fast.
Players need to learn two sets of rules.

pairs.tendency: Before play you say how many pieces you will take, then you try to take exactly that, while the pile runs down.
pros: The aim is spoken aloud at the start.
Each take serves a stated plan.
cons: A big promise may fail when the pile runs out.
Rivals may take pieces to stop you.

pairs.tendency: When you take an enemy piece it joins your side, so taking a piece is both removing it from them and adding it to you.
pros: One move changes both sides.
A lead can swing in a single take.
cons: Pieces are no longer only taken away.
Counting becomes harder than a plain pile.

pairs.tendency: A caught player waits in jail, and rescuing them returns a piece to the board, so nothing taken away stays gone for long.
pros: Players have a reason to go back for friends.
A lost piece is not always lost.
cons: The last move can be undone by a rescue.
The count stops running down.

pairs.tendency: You take stones by ringing them in, and the board only gets emptier, so each capture leaves more open space and fewer stones.
pros: Every capture clears the board.
Players plan a ring before they close it.
cons: A ring gives away which pieces you want.
Empty boards leave little to take.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind may take more pieces from the pile at a go, but a bigger take ends the game sooner for everyone.
pros: A lead can be cut in a turn.
The last player still has a plan.
cons: The leader waits while others catch up.
Help can finish the pile too soon.

pairs.tendency: The dice or cards say how many pieces come off the pile, and players make no choice at all, so the last piece goes to whoever the luck favours.
pros: The game moves fast.
Anyone can win.
cons: Counting no longer helps.
Players have nothing to decide.

pairs.tendency: The player who is It runs after the rest, and a touch lets It take a piece from the runner, so every touch leaves the runner with less.
pros: A touch has a clear prize.
Runners keep moving with pieces in their hands.
cons: A runner who is touched often loses nearly everything.
Running while carrying pieces is awkward.

pairs.tendency: You pick which player to take from, so the take is a hit on one of them, and the pile that is left is smaller for the one you picked.
pros: Who you pick is a choice of its own.
Players watch who was hit before.
cons: A player hit often can feel picked on.
With many players the choice slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: You take away your rival's stones to cut a chain from one side to the other, so every capture opens a gap and no piece is put back.
pros: Each take can cut a chain.
The board gets easier to cross.
cons: Taking pieces may not help to connect.
A chain with few stones is easy to cut.

pairs.tendency: Each take type beats one other and loses to a third, so players pick between a small, a middle and a large take, and the pile is always shrinking.
pros: No take always wins.
Players guess what the other will take.
cons: A pile with a count has one winning move, so the cycle may be ignored.
Guessing is more than counting.

pairs.tendency: You show a pair or a run in your hand to score, and the combination you declare lets you take from the pile, while the cards stay in your hand.
pros: Showing a combination scores something.
Players track how many takes are left.
cons: A declared pair tells others what you hold.
Declaring can end with the pile gone.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that changes how many pieces they can take, so a pile that is safe for one player is not safe for another.
pros: Every player counts differently.
Powers give each player a plan.
cons: A strong power can end the game early.
Players have to learn each other's powers.

pairs.tendency: Part-way through, a player offers to double the game and the other takes it or gives up, so the shrinking pile makes the offer more tempting each round.
pros: The offer grows as the pile shrinks.
Players read their own position closely.
cons: A late double can end the game at once.
Refusing costs the points already at stake.

pairs.tendency: If you can take, you have to, so a player can be made to empty a pile at the wrong moment by leaving them one take.
pros: Moves can be forced several turns ahead.
Traps are easy to set.
cons: A forced take may lose the game.
Players with only one move cannot plan.

pairs.tendency: Your character grows stronger as the game goes on, but the pile only shrinks, so later takes are bigger while the pile has less in it.
pros: Late takes feel more powerful.
Players plan when to grow.
cons: The pile may be gone before a character is strong.
Strength in a count adds little.

pairs.tendency: Players say the list so far and add an item, while the pile of pieces goes down by one each time, so memory and the count run together.
pros: Memory and counting share each turn.
The game grows longer as it ends.
cons: A lost item can end the game for a player.
Both counts are hard to keep.

pairs.tendency: The weaker player may take more pieces at once, or start with a bigger share, so the count is tilted to even out skill.
pros: A weaker player has a fair chance.
Players see what the tilt is worth.
cons: The handicap can be seen as unfair by the stronger.
An uneven count can end in a draw.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are hidden among the piles and the hunters take pieces away until the one that was hidden is found, so every take shrinks the places left to look.
pros: Every take narrows the search.
Players need to remember where they looked.
cons: The hidden piece may be taken by accident.
Searching long takes time.

pairs.tendency: Your piece hops over another and takes it, so the board empties by jumps, and a jump also moves your piece to a new place.
pros: Taking and moving happen in one step.
Chains of jumps are possible.
cons: A jump can leave your piece open.
Pieces left near the end have little to take.

pairs.tendency: You roll dice, keep some and roll the rest, and the total of your dice says how many pieces you take from the pile.
pros: Dice give each take a size.
Players choose which dice to keep.
cons: A low roll takes few pieces.
Rolling and taking make a turn longer.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a piece sends it back to the start, so a piece can be taken from the board and the count comes back up when it restarts.
pros: A taken piece returns to play.
Safe spaces protect pieces.
cons: The count does not run down in a plain way.
A long game may never end.

pairs.tendency: A row of three lets you take one of your rival's pieces, so the board gets emptier with every row, and the rival with fewer pieces is nearer to losing.
pros: A row has a clear prize.
Players plan how to block rows.
cons: Taking a piece may break a row of your own.
A player with few pieces cannot build rows.

pairs.tendency: The pieces are letters, and each word you make takes its letters off the table, so the words get shorter as the pile gets smaller.
pros: Words have to be made from what is left.
A dictionary settles arguments.
cons: Late turns have few letters to work with.
A long word can leave a poor pile for you.

pairs.tendency: You add a tile to a line only if the numbers match, and the tiles in your hand are taken out one by one, so a player who runs out of tiles first wins.
pros: Every tile played brings you nearer the end.
Hands get smaller round after round.
cons: A missing number can stop you.
Blocked games end with no winner.

pairs.tendency: You lay a finished set face up and take cards from your hand to add to it, so your hand shrinks as the table fills.
pros: Hands shrink as sets grow.
Others can add to a set.
cons: A laid set shows what you had.
Cards on the table cannot be taken back.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that works once, and using it removes its marker, so you spend the power when the pile is at the right size.
pros: Players choose when to spend a power.
A power can change who takes the last piece.
cons: A power spent too early is gone.
A player who saves it may never use it.

pairs.tendency: You offer a take and the other player may turn it down or choose between two takes you offer, so you have to offer a take you can live with.
pros: Each offer has to work for both players.
Players think about the other's choice.
cons: A weak offer is turned down.
A turn can end without a take.

pairs.tendency: A message goes from player to player and may change on the way, while players take from the pile, so a wrong count can get passed on.
pros: A message may carry the count.
Small changes can have big effects.
cons: Nobody can check the count until the end.
A wrong message can lose the game.

pairs.tendency: You hand some cards to another player before play, and the cards you get say how many pieces you may take from the pile.
pros: Passing shapes who can take what.
Players have to plan before they see their hand.
cons: A card you pass may help your rival.
The pile may favour one hand.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the piles and the other picks which side to play, so the first player has to make the piles fair, or the second picks the side that takes last.
pros: The setter wants a fair start.
The chooser has a say.
cons: A skilled chooser can see who wins at once.
Counting the piles takes a long time.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end can turn into a stronger piece, but taking pieces away leaves fewer to push forward.
pros: Pieces have a reason to go forward.
A promoted piece can take more.
cons: A player with few pieces cannot reach the end.
The count of pieces matters more than the move.

pairs.tendency: Your team runs in legs, and each runner takes a piece from the pile before passing on, so the team that takes the last piece is the one that finishes.
pros: Teams share the taking.
Each leg has a clear job.
cons: A slow runner loses the pile.
A leg can end with the pile gone.

pairs.tendency: Stones in a safe shape cannot be taken, so players build shapes to protect them while the other stones are taken away.
pros: Safe shapes give a goal.
A safe stone is a stone that stays.
cons: Safe shapes cannot be taken, so the last move may be impossible.
A board full of safe shapes cannot end.

pairs.tendency: Winning tricks lets you take pieces, and the named cards are the prizes, so the pile shrinks as the prizes are claimed.
pros: Named cards give each trick a reason.
Players track which prizes are left.
cons: A card can win more than one prize.
The last prize may be decided by one card.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle can be used by everyone, and taking one removes it for the others, so the middle gets thinner each turn.
pros: Everyone sees the same cards.
A card taken is gone for others.
cons: A shared card tells rivals what you want.
The middle can empty before it is useful.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the pot and a winner takes it all, so the pot is a pile that is taken away at once, or grows if nobody wins.
pros: The pot gives a clear prize.
A pot that grows makes the next round matter more.
cons: Taking it all ends the round at once.
Losers lose what they put in.

pairs.tendency: You scoop up the seeds from a pit and drop them along the row, so the pile is spread out rather than taken away, and the last seed decides what you take.
pros: Taking and moving happen together.
The count is part of the move.
cons: Seeds are not removed in a plain way.
Counting the last seed takes some practice.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and one player takes it or swaps it, so a pile of cards is taken away before play begins.
pros: The first take is a surprise.
A weak hand can be swapped.
cons: A swap hides which hand was taken.
The first take is nearly luck.

pairs.tendency: Some squares on the track have their own rule, and a square can make you take pieces or give them back, so the pile does not only run down.
pros: Squares add small surprises.
Players choose which square to aim for.
cons: A square that sends you back adds pieces.
The rules of the squares take time to learn.

pairs.tendency: Every card or piece has a price, so a take costs something, and a player has to choose between a big take and keeping what they have.
pros: A take has a price.
Players choose how much to spend.
cons: Spending too much leaves nothing for the end.
A cheap take may leave the pile too large.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed number of pieces between several piles, so you can take from only one at a time and leave the others for later.
pros: Each pile is a different choice.
Players can plan two piles at once.
cons: A pile left alone can be emptied by a rival.
Sharing out takes a long time.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until a signal sounds, then players take a piece from the pile, and the slowest player is caught with nothing.
pros: A signal makes the take sudden.
Players stay alert.
cons: Fast players empty the pile.
Slow players cannot take at all.

pairs.tendency: You put cards back and take new ones from the table, and a swapped card changes how many pieces you may take from the pile.
pros: A swap changes your take.
Players can fix a weak hand.
cons: Swapping can slow the game.
A swap can give away what you want.

pairs.tendency: Every discarded card goes in one pile and you may take the whole pile, so a take can be very large and leave nothing behind.
pros: A big pile makes a big take.
Players weigh when to take.
cons: A big take leaves the table empty.
Taking the pile can end the game in one move.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the others, so a trump lets you take from the pile when a lower card would not, and the trump suit changes who may take.
pros: A trump gives a clear way to win.
Players count the trumps left.
cons: A low trump can beat a high card.
A hand with no trump cannot take.

pairs.tendency: You play one side on one board and the other side on the other, so you take pieces on both boards and the last move on either board can decide the game.
pros: Two counts run together.
A take on one board can help the other.
cons: Players have to track two piles.
Last moves on two boards are hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any take, so it can finish a pile at the right moment or break a count you were planning against.
pros: One card can settle a close count.
Players hold a wild card for the end.
cons: A wild card can undo a long plan.
A wild card turns up by luck.

pairs.tendency: The board edges are joined, so a take from the right edge can continue on the left, and a pile can be reached from both sides.
pros: A pile has no far edge.
Takes can run around the board.
cons: Edge pieces are no longer safe.
Counting round the edge takes practice.

pairs.tendency: One player has a secret and the others ask yes or no questions, and each answer takes away some of the things it could be.
pros: Every question cuts the list.
Players can see the list shrink.
cons: A poor question leaves most things in.
A list of only two items ends the game quickly.

pairs.tendency: A move that closes a square lets you go again, so one player can take many lines in a row, and the last lines in the game go to whoever is left.
pros: A closing move earns another.
Players plan chains of squares.
cons: One player can take all the last squares.
Players avoid giving the opponent a square.

pairs.tendency: The codemaker says how many parts of a guess are right, and each answer takes away codes that cannot be the answer.
pros: Each reply shrinks the list.
Players can count what is left.
cons: A weak guess tells little.
A short list ends the game very fast.

pairs.tendency: Each take moves the pile nearer to empty, and the race is to make the last take, so the game ends when the count reaches nothing.
pros: The end is easy to see.
Every take is a step forward.
cons: A race is only a count.
The leader at the start may be the one who loses.

pairs.tendency: Each piece taken is worth points, and the player with most points wins, so taking the last piece does not always win the game.
pros: Each take has a score.
Players weigh a big take against a small one.
cons: The last move may not decide the game.
A big take early can leave points behind.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one and the last one left wins, so each take removes a rival, and the last move decides who stays.
pros: The end is clear.
Knocked-out players stay out.
cons: Early players wait a long time.
A player can be picked on.

pairs.tendency: Players share one pile and win together if it lasts, but each take makes it smaller, so every player is taking from the same thing.
pros: Players plan a shared take.
The game shows how a pile runs out.
cons: A greedy take hurts everyone.
The last move gives one player all the blame.

pairs.tendency: Players work towards a shared goal and each take uses up part of the pile that the goal needs, so everyone has to plan how much to take.
pros: A goal gives each take a reason.
Players talk about the count.
cons: One player can take too much.
The pile can run out before the goal.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret aim and takes pieces to suit it, while the shared pile gets smaller, so a take may or may not give your goal away.
pros: Each take can hide an aim.
Players guess at others' goals.
cons: A big take shows what you want.
A goal can be lost when a pile is gone.

pairs.tendency: The story ends when the pile is gone, and each take moves it forward, so the last piece taken is the last scene.
pros: The pile gives the story an end.
Each take is a step in the tale.
cons: The story can feel rushed.
The last take may not suit the ending.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, but pieces are still taken until the pile is gone, so players watch the pile shrink and then talk about what happened.
pros: Players can watch the pile disappear.
Taking has no pressure.
cons: The count has little point without a winner.
Players may stop taking early.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means, such as taking only a few pieces or leaving a pile alone, and takes from the pile to match.
pros: Goals can be small or large.
Players take in different ways.
cons: The last move may not matter to everyone.
Players may disagree about who did well.

pairs.tendency: The player forced to take the last piece loses and everyone else is safe, so each player tries to leave the pile small for the next player.
pros: The game has one clear loser.
Players count carefully near the end.
cons: The loser knows it several moves ahead.
A player can be set up by the others.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, but every take makes the pile smaller, so the game works against its own aim and the pile has to be refilled.
pros: Players take as little as they can.
The count is read as a way to slow play.
cons: The game cannot go on once the pile is empty.
Players may refill the pile.

pairs.tendency: The pile runs down whatever players do, so the last move happens anyway and the game gives no win, which turns the count into a plain fact.
pros: The pile shows what players cannot stop.
The game ends in a certain way.
cons: A last move with no win can feel empty.
Players may stop caring about the count.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a layout of cards and take cards away until the table is clear, and you lose if you get stuck with cards left.
pros: A clear table is a plain aim.
Players can try again at once.
cons: A stuck layout cannot be fixed.
Nobody else takes a turn.

pairs.tendency: Several short games of taking are played and the player with most wins takes the match, so a short pile is played again and again.
pros: Each game is quick.
Players can learn from the last game.
cons: A player who sees the count wins every time.
Games can end early if one player leads.

pairs.tendency: Each piece you take counts against you, so the player who takes the fewest wins, and players try not to take from the pile at all.
pros: Taking is a cost.
Players try to leave pieces for others.
cons: A pile cannot be left alone.
The last player to take loses most.

pairs.tendency: You have to reach the target exactly, so a take that goes past it costs you the game, and a pile that is almost gone leaves few choices.
pros: The last take needs care.
Players count to the end.
cons: A big take can end in a loss.
A player can be stuck with no exact take.

pairs.tendency: The player who takes the last piece loses, so each player tries to leave the pile for the other, and the count is worked in reverse.
pros: The usual aim is turned round.
Players find the safe counts again.
cons: Beginners often take the last piece.
The play rule has to be said clearly.

pairs.tendency: Everyone takes from their own pile at the same time, so players do not affect each other, and each one watches only their own count.
pros: Players do not wait for others.
Each pile is a small puzzle.
cons: Nothing a rival does changes your pile.
The game has little to say between players.

pairs.tendency: You take from the pile that a rival needs, so each take is a move against them, and the pile that is left is smaller for them.
pros: Each take hurts a rival.
Players learn to read each other's piles.
cons: A player can be targeted all game.
Takes can feel like attacks.

pairs.tendency: Players take pieces from the board, and the board shows what each take has done, so a rival feels your take only through what is left.
pros: A take is felt without a hit.
The board shows what each player did.
cons: A player may not see who took.
Players have to read the board often.

pairs.tendency: Players share one pile and win together by taking the last piece, so they plan each take as a team and talk through the count.
pros: Players can plan together.
The count is shared by all.
cons: A player who knows the count can lead.
Quiet players may take no part.

pairs.tendency: Players take from a shared pile towards a shared aim, but each wants to take the last piece for themselves, so the end is a quiet race.
pros: Players work together for most of the game.
The last move is a private aim.
cons: A player can hold back to take the last piece.
Trust runs down as the pile does.

pairs.tendency: Two teams take from the same pile in turn, and the team that takes the last piece wins, so teammates plan each take together.
pros: Teams plan the count together.
Teammates can warn each other.
cons: Talk can show your plan to the other team.
One player can lose it for the team.

pairs.tendency: Most players take to keep the pile fair, but one secretly takes to end the game for them, so a take that looks wrong may be a clue.
pros: Odd takes become clues.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: A careful player may be wrongly blamed.
Counting makes lies easy to spot.

pairs.tendency: Players post their takes by letter, so a game of one pile may last weeks, and each reply says what was taken.
pros: Each take can be thought out.
Waiting becomes part of the game.
cons: A lost letter can break the count.
The game may end before the pile.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and their takes are set out in advance or made by someone else, so the count goes on without them.
pros: The pile has one fewer player.
A missing player can be played by a plan.
cons: Takes made for them can feel wrong.
The last move may fall to the absent player.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and decides how much each take removes, so the pile is whatever the game master says it is.
pros: The game master can set the count.
Players meet piles that are made to be met.
cons: The game master can end the game at will.
The count loses its plain rules.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by join in and take from a pile in the street, such as stones in the dust, so the group is always changing and the last take falls to whoever is there.
pros: Anyone can join at any time.
The pile is easy to make.
cons: The player who takes last may be new to the game.
Players arriving late can break the count.

pairs.tendency: One player plays alone and all the others share a pile against them, so the lone player takes in a different way from the group.
pros: The lone player has a clear aim.
The group has to agree each take.
cons: The group may take too many at once.
The lone player waits while the group talks.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a pile and take pieces until it is gone, so the game is a puzzle where nobody takes a turn after you.
pros: A pile is a plain puzzle.
Players can try again at once.
cons: Nobody else changes the count.
A solved pile is the same each time.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide how many pieces come off the pile, so a clever take matters little, and the last piece falls by luck.
pros: The game moves fast.
Anyone can win.
cons: Skill in counting does not help.
Players have little to decide.

pairs.tendency: Dice set how much you may take, but you can change it with a card or a re-roll, so luck is softened and the count still matters.
pros: Players can soften a poor roll.
The count still has a plan.
cons: A re-roll can slow the turn.
The plan is spoilt by a low throw.

pairs.tendency: The count is mostly skill, but a little luck such as a drawn card adds a surprise, so a clear plan can still be broken.
pros: A plain count gets some surprise.
Skilled players still tend to win.
cons: A lucky draw can beat a sound count.
Surprise can cut across a plan.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice and no hidden cards, so a player who has worked out the count wins every time, and the game is only a puzzle of numbers.
pros: The game is fair to all.
Players can learn the count.
cons: A player who knows it always wins.
A solved pile has no surprises.

pairs.tendency: Players throw the dice to see what a take means, such as a hint about how many to take, but the pile still runs down, so a sign is read before a take.
pros: A throw gives each take a meaning.
Players think about what the throw says.
cons: A sign can be read in many ways.
A count has one plain answer.

pairs.tendency: Players try to take together without a signal, such as each lifting a piece at the same moment, so the pile shrinks when the group is in step.
pros: Players watch one another closely.
A take can feel shared.
cons: Two takes at once can break the count.
Players cannot plan the last move.

pairs.tendency: The dice are looked up on a table, and the table says how many pieces are taken, so each roll tells what happened and the pile runs down.
pros: Each roll gives the take a story.
The pile shows what the story has used up.
cons: The table can empty the pile too fast.
The story ends when the pile does.

pairs.tendency: Everyone can see the whole pile and every take, so a player who has worked out the count knows who will win from the start.
pros: Players see all the facts.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: A player who counts well always wins.
The game may be solved in minutes.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards that no one else can see, and the cards say how many pieces may be taken, so the count is not clear to others.
pros: A hidden card hides the count.
Players guess what is held.
cons: A player who bluffs can take more.
Players can only guess what is in each hand.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles, and the pile is taken down by players with different aims, so a take can show or hide which side you are on.
pros: Takes can be clues.
Roles give each take a hidden aim.
cons: A take can give away a role.
A careful player may be wrongly blamed.

pairs.tendency: Players use clues to work out what is hidden, and each take shows a little more, so the pile gets smaller and the answer gets easier.
pros: Each take gives a clue.
The answer is easier near the end.
cons: A wrong take hides the clue.
A small pile gives the answer away.

pairs.tendency: You say you will take only a few pieces and then take more, or the other way round, while the others guess if you told the truth.
pros: A count can be lied about.
Players read each other's faces.
cons: Pieces taken need checking.
A caught lie ends the turn.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about how much can be taken, and the others find it by breaking it, so the count is learnt in the first moves.
pros: The count is learnt in play.
A new player learns by trying.
cons: The first takes are only guesses.
Players can lose before they learn the rule.

pairs.tendency: One player can see the safe count but cannot say it, so they can only give hints about how much to take, and the others have to work it out.
pros: A hint is a small gift.
The group has to think together.
cons: A poor hint is lost on the others.
The player who knows can be asked too often.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden, and each piece you take shows a new area, so every take uncovers something that cannot be covered again.
pros: A take is also a look.
The map grows as the pile shrinks.
cons: Nobody knows what is left.
A hidden pile cannot be counted.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up and may be played by anyone, so the pieces that hand takes from the pile are known and the other hands are not.
pros: One hand is known to all.
Players can plan a take with it.
cons: The open hand tells what is left.
The shared hand is used by one player.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, so players take from the pile without being sure who is ahead and have to guess when to take the last piece.
pros: Takes hide the score.
Players guess who leads.
cons: A take made on a guess can lose.
The last move may not be the winning one.

pairs.tendency: One player takes at a time, going round the table, so the pile goes down turn by turn and everyone sees each take before their own.
pros: Each take can be planned.
The count is clear to all.
cons: Players wait for their go.
A player who counts well waits to win.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses how many to take in secret and all reveal together, so the pile may drop by many takes in one go and nobody can answer.
pros: Nobody waits.
Players guess at one another.
cons: The pile can drop too far in one round.
The last move may go to no one.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so anyone can take at any moment and the fastest hand empties the pile, so the count counts for little.
pros: The game is fast.
Quick players have a chance.
cons: Slow players are left out.
Nobody can plan the last move.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so you have to choose how many to take before time runs out, and a rushed take can leave the pile in a poor count.
pros: A clock keeps the game moving.
Players have to count fast.
cons: A rushed take leaves a poor count.
A slow counter loses the turn.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days, and you take from the pile once a day, so the pile shrinks over weeks and waiting is part of the game.
pros: The pile is slow to go.
Players can think a long time.
cons: A missed day can lose a turn.
The game may not be finished by all.

pairs.tendency: The game slows down by design, such as a pause before each take, so players spend time looking at a pile that is getting smaller.
pros: Players think about each take.
The pile feels heavier.
cons: The slow pace can feel flat.
A solved pile makes a slow game dull.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so takes come faster, the pile drops quickly, and the end comes in a rush.
pros: The game ends with excitement.
Players take larger piles in the last rounds.
cons: A rush leaves little time to count.
The last moves may be mistakes.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw or a capture gives you another go at once, so one player can take several times in a row and may empty the pile alone.
pros: A lucky streak is possible.
An extra go has a clear prize.
cons: One player can take the last piece alone.
Other players wait for a long time.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, and the first stage sets up the piles for the second, so the takes in stage one decide what is left to count in stage two.
pros: Early takes shape the end.
Each stage has its own rules.
cons: A poor first stage leaves a hard second.
Players have to learn two sets of rules.

pairs.tendency: The piles stand for real things, such as water in a village's wells, and every take removes some of the supply, so a move has the effect it would have in life.
pros: A pile shows what a take costs.
The count has a real meaning.
cons: A plain pile leaves out much of real life.
Nothing is added back, as it would be in life.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group, such as farmers or a village council, and takes from the pile for the group's needs, so each take shows whose needs are met.
pros: Takes show different needs.
Players see the pile from each side.
