cons: One group can empty the pile for all.
A role may force a take that its player dislikes.

pairs.tendency: Everyone takes from one limited pile, such as the water under a village, and if players take too much it runs out for all of them.
pros: Takes show what is shared.
Players learn how a pile runs out.
cons: A greedy take hurts everyone.
Nothing is added back, so the loss is permanent.

pairs.tendency: A take shows its effect only a few rounds later, so a player may empty a pile before they see what it costs.
pros: Takes have long-term effects.
Players learn to look ahead.
cons: A late effect is hard to trace back.
The last move may come before the effect.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule about how much may be taken and then play on to see what changes, so the count shows what the rule does.
pros: A rule can be tested safely.
The count shows the effect at once.
cons: A simple pile may not show a real rule's effect.
Players may argue about the rule.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about the takes: what was taken, when, and what it meant, using the empty pile as the starting point.
pros: The empty pile starts the talk.
Players can name the moves that mattered.
cons: The count can be too plain to talk about.
The talk may stay on who won.

pairs.tendency: Nothing taken is ever put back, and the next game starts from the pile that is left, so what you take stays taken for ever.
pros: A take is a lasting choice.
The next game starts from what is left.
cons: A small pile may leave no game.
A poor take cannot be undone.

pairs.tendency: The rule that nothing returns makes a point about the world, such as that a use is final, and the players feel it with every take.
pros: The rule says something plain.
The pile shows the argument.
cons: A plain count may say too little.
Players may not notice the point.

pairs.tendency: The last piece taken carries a real stake, such as a chore, so the count feels serious and players avoid the take that loses.
pros: A plain count feels serious.
Players think hard about each take.
cons: A real loss can upset players.
Some players refuse to take.

pairs.tendency: Pieces stand for something that matters, such as time or kindness, and taking them turns that into a count, so players chase the pieces and forget the value.
pros: A pile shows what a count does.
Players see how a number replaces a value.
cons: The pieces become only a count.
A real value is lost in the take.

pairs.tendency: Players try a way of sharing a pile that does not exist yet, such as a village that takes only what it needs, to see how it feels.
pros: A new way can be tried in minutes.
A shared pile shows how a rule feels.
cons: The count is too plain for a real future.
A rule is tested only once.

pairs.tendency: A take makes the next take easier, such as a bigger pile in hand giving a bigger take, so a lead grows with each move.
pros: A lead gets larger by itself.
Players see a loop at work.
cons: A leader can run away with the game.
The player who is behind has no way back.

pairs.tendency: The pile shrinks slowly with little effect until a line is crossed, and then one take ends the game, so the last few takes matter most.
pros: The last takes matter most.
A small pile can end the game.
cons: The line is easy to cross by mistake.
Early takes seem to matter little.

pairs.tendency: What is taken piles up in a player's store, such as debt, and the pile on the table shrinks, so the size of each pile matters more than one take.
pros: Two piles tell one story.
A big store is easy to see.
cons: Players count two piles at once.
A store can grow without the owner noticing.

pairs.tendency: Between turns the world takes from the pile by a fixed rule, such as the river rising, so the pile shrinks even when no player takes.
pros: The pile shrinks by itself.
Players plan around the world's take.
cons: A pile may be gone before a player acts.
The world takes the last piece.

pairs.tendency: A flood or a price crash removes part of the pile with no player choosing it, and every player has to answer by taking less or more.
pros: A shock changes the count.
Players have to think fast.
cons: A shock can end the game by chance.
A plan made on the count is spoilt.

pairs.tendency: Each round stands for a year, so a take removes a year's use of the pile, and a long life fits into a short game.
pros: Years pass in a few takes.
The pile shows long use.
cons: A year of takes is hard to feel.
A short game leaves little time to learn.

pairs.tendency: A gauge on the board shows how much is left in the pile, so every take moves the gauge and everyone can see the world getting smaller.
pros: Takes move a gauge.
The pile is easy to read.
cons: A gauge shows the count, not who leads.
Players watch the gauge and miss other moves.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with piles of different sizes, and the game does not even them out, so a player with a large pile can take for longer.
pros: The start is unequal on purpose.
Players learn what a head start is worth.
cons: A small pile can run out at once.
A player with the small pile may stop trying.

pairs.tendency: The player who is ahead writes the rule for how much may be taken, so the others take by that rule and the pile runs down by it.
pros: The leader's rule can be felt.
Players see what a rule does.
cons: Others have no say in the count.
A rule can be written so that the leader always wins.

pairs.tendency: Each role wants something different from the pile, such as the catch or the fish left in the lake, so every take helps one role and hurts another.
pros: Each take takes a side.
Players know what each role wants.
cons: One role can empty the pile for all.
A last take may please nobody.

pairs.tendency: Play opens on a described pile, who holds what and what is at stake, and every player reads it before the first take.
pros: Players see the pile first.
The first take has a reason.
cons: A long start can slow the game.
A plain pile gives the situation little to describe.

pairs.tendency: A player says how many they take and why it would work, and the table decides, so the count is a matter of argument and not a plain rule.
pros: A take can be argued.
Players explain their count.
cons: An argument can run longer than the take.
The last move may be unclear.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points so players say how much is left and what they have noticed, before taking on.
pros: Players look at the pile together.
A pause can show a lost count.
cons: A stop breaks the pace of the count.
Players may only repeat what is clear.

pairs.tendency: The same pile is played again with one thing changed, such as who takes first, and players compare how it ended each time.
pros: One change can be seen clearly.
Players learn the count by comparing.
cons: A solved pile ends the same each time.
Players tire of the same pile.

pairs.tendency: The game tells players what it leaves out, such as that real piles can be refilled, so they know where the count stops being true.
pros: Players know where the count ends.
A plain pile is shown as a simple one.
cons: The note can feel longer than the game.
A reader may skip the note.

pairs.tendency: The people whose situation the pile stands for help design it, and play it to check that the takes ring true, so the count is theirs.
pros: The pile matches real life.
Players correct each other's count.
cons: A true pile may not give a plain game.
Designing it with others takes much longer.

pairs.tendency: Each player is one link in a chain, and every take from a pile cuts the supply for the next link, so one player's take reaches all the others.
pros: A take reaches every link.
Players feel the next link's need.
cons: A big take can leave the next link with nothing.
The last link has the least to take.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own pile, so the takes are made from a guess about the whole, and nobody knows how much is left in total.
pros: Takes are made on a guess.
Players learn the limits of what they see.
cons: A guess can end in an empty pile.
A count with hidden piles is hard to plan.

pairs.tendency: The slowest pile sets the pace, so a take from any other pile changes nothing until the slow one is cleared.
pros: The slow pile is easy to find.
A take on the right pile matters.
cons: Taking from other piles gains nothing.
Players can waste moves on the wrong pile.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are taken ahead of need, which pushes them down the line, or only when an order pulls them, so the pile is taken early or late.
pros: Players feel both ways of taking.
The pile shows what waiting costs.
cons: Taking ahead can leave a pile too small.
Waiting for an order slows the game.

pairs.tendency: Players choose how many to take at once, one at a time or a large batch, and each choice costs waiting or setting up.
pros: Batch size is a plain choice.
Players feel the cost of each take.
cons: A large batch leaves little for others.
A small batch takes many turns.

pairs.tendency: A machine breaks at random and the take it was to make is lost, so a plan that counted on every take will not hold.
pros: A plan has to allow for breaks.
Players learn to keep a spare take.
cons: A break can end a count.
A broken machine leaves a pile unchanged.

pairs.tendency: Holding pieces costs something every round and running out costs more, so players keep balancing how much to take from the pile.
pros: A take has a price on both sides.
Players weigh a big take against a small one.
cons: A take that is too big costs each round.
A take that is too small leaves the pile for others.

pairs.tendency: A throw of the dice moves your piece, and the space you land on lets you make one guess at the hidden code.
pros: Each guess is earned on the track.
Players see progress in two ways at once.
cons: A low throw means a late guess.
The track and the code feel separate.

pairs.tendency: Players pick and pass cards, and the cards they keep become the parts they use to build their next guess at the code.
pros: Each pick shapes what you can guess.
Passed cards reveal what others lack.
cons: Players may guess with whatever is left.
A late guess waits on a slow pass.

pairs.tendency: Players offer to pay for the right to guess next, so a player who thinks the code is close will pay more to get there first.
pros: A high bid shows how sure a player is.
Guesses have a price.
cons: Rich players can buy many guesses.
Bidding can cost more than a guess is worth.

pairs.tendency: The guesser keeps guessing while the answers improve, and may stop to bank the points before a poor answer wipes them out.
pros: Each answer adds to the temptation.
Players weigh a clue against a risk.
cons: One poor answer can lose the lot.
Players may stop long before the code is found.

pairs.tendency: Players guess a code that tells where a region's hidden strength lies, then place pieces on the map to hold what they have found.
pros: Clues turn into places on the map.
Guessing has a use on the board.
cons: A guess shows which region you are after.
The map and the code take turns.

pairs.tendency: A worker on a board spot lets a player make a guess, and each spot taken means one less guess for everyone else.
pros: Spots decide who gets to guess.
Workers and clues both matter.
cons: A taken spot can block a guess.
Players wait while others weigh their spots.

pairs.tendency: The hidden code is a pattern of colours or shapes, and each answer tells the guesser how near their own pattern is to it.
pros: Guessing and building share one picture.
Answers read like a fit score.
cons: A long pattern needs many guesses.
The count says little about which part is wrong.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand are the parts of each guess, so players choose which to play now and which to keep for a later try.
pros: Keeping a card shapes the next guess.
Players plan more than one guess ahead.
cons: A small hand limits what can be tried.
Hoarded cards slow the guessing.

pairs.tendency: A player guesses which cards others hold from the answers given, then uses that knowledge when the tricks are played.
pros: Answers work as scouting for the tricks.
Players plan with more knowledge.
cons: The questions slow the start of the tricks.
A clear answer tells rivals as much.

pairs.tendency: The guesser can trade for hints or promise a share, but the answer given is still only a count and nobody can fake it.
pros: Players trade information, not only goods.
Alliances form around the same code.
cons: A player can sell a hint that is wrong.
Talk can slow every guess.

pairs.tendency: The code is a set that the setter has hidden, and the guesser collects matching parts until the answers say the set is complete.
pros: A set has a clear end point.
The count shows how many are still missing.
cons: A set with many parts needs many answers.
Players may guess at random.

pairs.tendency: Tiles placed on a shared map make up the code or the guess, and the answer counts how many tiles are right and where.
pros: The map doubles as the code.
A placed tile is a fact on the board.
cons: A wrong tile cannot be taken back easily.
Answers are hard to read on a big map.

pairs.tendency: One player calls a guess and the other answers with two numbers, so the game moves in short rounds of call and reply.
pros: Each answer sets up the next call.
The turns are brisk and clear.
cons: The chain can feel the same every round.
A slow answer stops the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Nobody may talk, so the guess is shown by pieces and the answer by a count of markers, with no explaining.
pros: Markers carry all the meaning.
Players watch the table closely.
cons: An answer can be misread.
A silent table can feel tense and slow.

pairs.tendency: A player may change the rule for answers, such as how the count is made, so the guesser's old reasoning can stop working.
pros: The code game changes shape each round.
A rule can help your own guessing.
cons: Earlier answers lose their meaning.
Players can argue over which rule applies.

pairs.tendency: The setter and guesser speak as characters, so each guess is a question put in a voice and each count is an answer in character.
pros: A clue game becomes a short scene.
Characters can hint in their own way.
cons: The acting can run longer than the guessing.
Shy players may only read the counts.

pairs.tendency: Before each guess a player has to pass a test of hands, so a steady hand earns more tries at the code.
pros: Hands and reasoning both count.
Players watch each other's attempts.
cons: A shaky hand leaves few guesses.
The game stops while a try goes on.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and the hidden code is a place or feature on it, found through counts of what is right.
pros: The drawing gives the code a place.
Everyone owns a piece of the map.
cons: Drawing slows the guessing.
The counts may not suit a map.

pairs.tendency: You ask a player for a card, and the answer counts how many cards they hold that match, not only a yes or no.
pros: Each ask gives a number, not just a yes.
Players learn hands faster.
cons: A question shows which cards you hold.
A hand with many cards is asked constantly.

pairs.tendency: The bank holds the code, players bet on a guess before it is answered, and the count of right parts decides who is paid.
pros: Odds are clear before anyone guesses.
The count settles each bet.
cons: The bank sees every bet before it answers.
The bank can be asked many questions.

pairs.tendency: Players put coins down before the dice land, and the throw decides the code or the order of guesses, so the counts depend on luck.
pros: A throw gives the guessing a start.
Bets add a stake to each guess.
cons: Luck can set the code too easily.
A big pot can end a short round early.

pairs.tendency: Players raise or fold as the counts come in, so each answer tells them how much to put in the pot.
pros: Each count works as a signal for the bet.
Chips show how sure each player is.
cons: An answer can give your hand away.
Players who drop out stop guessing.

pairs.tendency: Each player arrives with a different side, and the hidden code is built from what that side has, so counts read differently for each.
pros: Players guess with different pieces.
Each side keeps its own style.
cons: One side can have a much easier code.
Sides needing rare parts can wait long.

pairs.tendency: You say up front how many guesses you will need, and the counts either keep your promise on track or break it.
pros: The aim is spoken at the start.
Every count measures the promise.
cons: A small contract may be too easy.
A promise that is too big can fail early.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece changes sides, and the code can be made from pieces that have changed hands, so counts of right parts can swing at once.
pros: A catch brings more than one gain.
Players track which side owns each part.
cons: A lead in counts can vanish in a move.
Players lose track of who holds what.

pairs.tendency: A caught player waits in jail, and a teammate who reaches the jail may use a count of right parts to open it.
pros: Teammates have a reason to go back.
The counts work as a key.
cons: A player in jail can only watch.
A rescuer who guesses badly gets caught too.

pairs.tendency: You trap pieces by placing yours around them, and the counts of right parts show where your ring is close to closing.
pros: Counts help plan the ring.
Players aim at a clear target.
cons: A guess shows which piece you are circling.
The target can slip out while you guess.

pairs.tendency: Players who are behind get extra guesses or a clearer count, so a lead can be cut down while the code is still hidden.
pros: A trailing player still has something to try.
A lead is never fully safe.
cons: The leader may wait while others catch up.
An extra guess can solve the code too fast.

pairs.tendency: The code is set by dice or cards and nobody chooses it, so the guesser can only read the counts and cannot affect the secret.
pros: The setter has no hidden advantage.
The game runs briskly.
cons: Players only read answers, not plan.
A lucky code can fall in one guess.

pairs.tendency: The runners hold parts of the code, and It chases them, with each touch giving a count of how many parts are right.
pros: A touch gives a clue.
Runners keep moving while others guess.
cons: Running and counting are hard to do together.
A player who is tagged often loses the most.

pairs.tendency: You choose which player to guess about, and the count that comes back is about that player's hidden code alone.
pros: Who you pick is a decision of its own.
Players learn which rivals are open.
cons: A player picked often can feel singled out.
The choice slows a table of many players.

pairs.tendency: Stones making a chain are the guess, and the answer counts how many stones sit in the right places along the hidden route.
pros: The route is a clear target.
Counts show which stones to keep.
cons: The other player can cut the chain meanwhile.
Counts say little about the missing link.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, and the counts tell the guesser which of the three the setter used.
pros: Counts stop a pattern from staying secret.
No single guess works every time.
cons: A guesser can loop through the same three.
Only three choices make the code short.

pairs.tendency: You show a pair or a run you hold, and the counts tell rivals how many of the other cards in your hand match it.
pros: Declaring shows part of your hand.
Counts give rivals something to guess from.
cons: A declared pair can be read too easily.
Hiding a pair can cost you points.

pairs.tendency: Each player has one power that changes the rule, so the count for each guesser may be read or worked out differently.
pros: Each player guesses in their own way.
Powers give every table a different feel.
cons: One power can make the code too easy.
The rules are harder to keep in mind.

pairs.tendency: Part-way through the guessing, a player may double the stakes, and the other has to accept or give up what is already at stake.
pros: A doubled stake adds a hard choice.
Players show how close they think they are.
cons: A double can bluff a rival out.
Giving up early ends a long round.

pairs.tendency: A capture is forced when it is open, so a guesser can use counts to set a trap that makes the other player take a losing move.
pros: Counts help set a trap.
A forced move is easy to predict.
cons: The forced capture can steer the guess too much.
A player can be walked into a loss.

pairs.tendency: Each guess builds the character's power, so a player who found part of the code gets stronger for the next guess.
pros: Progress carries into the next try.
A hard code feels fairer later on.
cons: A strong player gets stronger still.
A weak start is slow to recover.

pairs.tendency: Each player says the whole list so far and adds one more item, and the guesser has to find which items in the hidden list are right and where.
pros: The list gets harder to hold in the head.
Counts help check the list.
cons: A long list tires the memory.
One slip can spoil the whole list.

pairs.tendency: The more skilled player hides a harder code or guesses with fewer tries, so a weaker player has a real chance of finding it.
pros: The two players are closer in their results.
The code can be set to suit each player.
cons: A strong player may feel held back.
Setting the handicap takes some time.

pairs.tendency: Someone hides a code or an object, and the others guess where it is from counts, so each answer says how near they are.
pros: Each answer narrows the hunt.
The hider has a clear job.
cons: A hiding place can be too easy to guess.
The hunt stops when the thing is found.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another into a space behind it, and the counts tell how many pieces are in the right squares for a jump.
pros: Counts help plan the next hop.
A hop can change many counts at once.
cons: One jump can undo many guesses.
Pieces are hard to track after a long chain.

pairs.tendency: You keep some dice and roll the rest, and the counts tell you how many are right and in the right place before you roll again.
pros: The counts tell which dice to keep.
A short run of rolls gives quick feedback.
cons: Luck can still undo a careful keep.
A limit on rolls can cut the guess short.

pairs.tendency: A piece landing on another sends it back, so a guesser who is sent back loses the parts of the code they had found.
pros: A hit has a clear cost.
Safe spaces protect what you have found.
cons: A player sent back can lose all progress.
The count is hard to use after a hit.

pairs.tendency: Making a row lets you take a piece, and the counts tell how many of your pieces are in the right squares for that row.
pros: Counts point towards a row.
A row has a reward.
cons: A rival can break the row while you count.
The counts can hide which piece to move.

pairs.tendency: The code is a word, each guess is a word, and the count tells how many letters are right and in the right place.
pros: Players use what they know of words.
Counts steer the next guess.
cons: A word with repeated letters is hard to count.
A dictionary may be needed to settle things.

pairs.tendency: You add a tile whose number matches the open end, and the counts tell the guesser how many tiles match and sit in the right place.
pros: Tiles have a clear fit.
The counts tell which end is open.
cons: A player with no match misses a turn.
A hard code can leave many tiles unplayed.

pairs.tendency: You lay down a set of cards face up, and the counts say how many of the hidden cards match what you laid.
pros: A laid set shows part of the answer.
Others can add to what you laid.
cons: Laying early shows your hand.
The counts can get lost in the laid cards.

pairs.tendency: Each piece or player has a power that works once, so the question is when to spend it, such as a clearer count on a hard guess.
pros: A single use makes the timing matter.
A spent power is easy to see.
cons: Players can waste a power early.
A player with no power left can only guess.

pairs.tendency: You offer a guess, and the other player can refuse it or choose between two, so the count that comes back is partly their choice.
pros: The answerer has a real choice.
Guessing becomes a small bargain.
cons: A refusal can waste a turn.
A rival can steer you to a weaker guess.

pairs.tendency: A message goes along the line and may change, and the guesser's count shows how much of it arrived right and in the right place.
pros: The count shows how far a message drifted.
Players see where it went wrong.
cons: The message can fail before the guesser sees it.
A long chain can lose everything.

pairs.tendency: Before play you hand cards to another player, and the counts later tell you how many of the passed cards were right for your hidden hand.
pros: A pass shapes the later guessing.
Players guess what others will give.
cons: You cannot see what you will get.
A poor pass can spoil a code.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the code and the other picks a side, so the setter aims for a code as easy to guess as to hide.
pros: The setter has to be fair to both sides.
The pick shows how hard players think it is.
cons: The first player may take long setting up.
A close split can end in a draw.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a stronger one, and counts guide you towards the squares that lead there.
pros: Counts point the way forward.
A stronger piece gives a reason to push on.
cons: A promotion can end the guessing early.
The race for the end can ignore the code.

pairs.tendency: A team runs the code game in legs, and each runner hands the count to the next, so one runner's guess shapes the next.
pros: Teammates depend on each other's counts.
Each leg is short and clear.
cons: One slow runner holds up the team.
A wrong count passes along the line.

pairs.tendency: A shape that cannot be taken is the hidden code, and counts tell the guesser how many stones already sit in the right places for it.
pros: The shape gives a clear goal.
Counts show how near it is.
cons: The other player can surround you.
A near shape can be broken by one move.

pairs.tendency: Named cards give the prizes, and the counts tell a guesser how many of those cards a rival holds and where.
pros: Counts show where the prizes lie.
One card can win more than one prize.
cons: A guess about a prize card shows your aim.
The prize cards can get lost among the others.

pairs.tendency: Some cards sit face up in the middle, and the counts tell a guesser how many of the hidden cards fit with them.
pros: Open cards give everyone a start.
Counts work on shared facts.
cons: Everyone can use the same counts.
Open cards can make a code too easy.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle, and whoever finds the code first takes the pot, which grows if nobody does.
pros: The pot gives every guess a reason.
A long round makes the next one worth more.
cons: A big pot can push players to guess early.
An unsolved code can drag on.

pairs.tendency: You scoop seeds from one pit and drop them in the next, and the counts tell where the last seed lands against the hidden pit.
pros: Counts guide the choice of pit.
A sow can change many pits at once.
cons: The counts are hard to work out mid-sow.
A long sow makes the pit hard to track.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand sits face down, and one player may take, swap or buy it, using counts to guess what it holds.
pros: The spare hand is a prize to guess about.
Counts help judge its value.
cons: A swap can drop a hand you worked out.
Buying a hand can cost more than it gives.

pairs.tendency: Some squares keep you safe, send you back or cost a turn, and the counts tell the guesser how many of the hidden squares they have found.
pros: Squares make the code a place on the track.
A safe square holds what you found.
cons: A send-back square can wipe a clue.
The track and the code feel separate.

pairs.tendency: Every card or item has a price, so a guesser has to pay to try, and the counts tell if the spend was worth making.
pros: Each guess has a clear cost.
Players learn what a clue is worth.
cons: Poor counts leave you with nothing to spend.
Careful spending can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed amount between several guesses, and the counts show which of them is close, so you move your forces to it.
pros: Counts guide where the forces go.
Players plan their spread.
cons: A rival can see where you put most.
Spreading thin may find nothing.

pairs.tendency: Everyone guesses until a signal comes, and then players stop and freeze, so the last count they had is the one they act on.
pros: The signal makes the guessing urgent.
Everyone ends together.
cons: A frozen player cannot use a late count.
The slowest guesser is caught.

pairs.tendency: You swap cards before the hand is played, and the counts tell how many of your new cards fit the hidden hand.
pros: A swap is a guess with a reason.
Counts tell if the swap helped.
cons: Swapping can give away what you want.
Another player may have to agree.

pairs.tendency: You may take the whole discard pile, and the counts tell how many cards in it match what you need and where.
pros: The pile shows what others threw away.
A big pile gives a lot to guess from.
cons: A full pile is heavy to carry.
A taken pile may hold few useful cards.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the others, so the counts tell you how many of the trumps you have found and how many sit in the right places.
pros: A trump gives guessing a clear aim.
Counts show who holds the strong suit.
cons: Finding the trump suit early can end the code.
A low trump can mislead a guesser.

pairs.tendency: You play both sides on two boards, so the counts from one board help guess the code on the other.
pros: Both boards give clues.
Attack and defence run together.
cons: Players can mix up the two boards.
A clear count on one board costs the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any card, so a count may include a part that is right only because the card was wild.
pros: A wild card can finish a set.
It gives a guesser a way out.
cons: Counts become harder to trust.
A wild card can make the code too easy.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board join, so a part of the code that runs off one side shows up on the other, and counts have to allow for that.
pros: Place counts follow the loop of the board.
A code has no edge to hide behind.
cons: The loop makes right place hard to see.
New players may miss that the edges join.

pairs.tendency: Both games shrink a list of possibilities, but here an answer is two numbers and there it is only yes or no, so players weigh which suits them.
pros: Both give a clear way to narrow things.
A number carries more than a yes or no.
cons: Two ways of answering can confuse players.
A yes or no can feel thin.

pairs.tendency: Players race to solve the code first, and each count is a step forward or a sign of being off track.
pros: Counts show who is ahead.
The race has a clear end.
cons: A lucky guess can win it at once.
A player far behind can feel out of it.

pairs.tendency: Points come from finding the code in fewer guesses, so each count is also a measure of how close a player is to scoring.
pros: Fewer guesses mean more points.
Counts work as a running score.
cons: A poor round is hard to recover from.
The points can feel small beside the guessing.

pairs.tendency: Players who fail to find a code in time are knocked out, and the counts show who is close to being the last still guessing.
pros: Each count is a risk of leaving the game.
A tense end is likely.
cons: Knocked-out players wait a long time.
A strong code can end a player at once.

pairs.tendency: Everyone works to crack a code before the game wears them down, and each count is shared with the whole table.
pros: Everyone reads the same counts.
A hard code tests the whole team.
cons: One loud player can take over the guessing.
A long code can leave the team worn out.

pairs.tendency: All players aim at one hidden code, and each count is shared, so every guess moves the whole table closer.
pros: One count helps everyone.
Players work out the code together.
cons: A quiet player can be left out.
The code can be found by one player alone.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal while a shared code is guessed, so a count may help one player more than another.
pros: The same count means different things to each player.
Players watch for who guesses oddly.
cons: A guess can give a goal away.
A secret goal can be hard to track.

pairs.tendency: The hidden code is part of a story, and each count tells the guesser how close they are to the next scene.
pros: Counts move the story along.
Players learn a story by guessing it.
cons: A tough code can stall the tale.
The ending is set by the code.

pairs.tendency: There is nobody to win, so players guess the hidden code just to see what the counts show and talk about it afterwards.
pros: Counts are enjoyed for their own sake.
Players can try odd guesses.
cons: Nothing pushes players to finish.
The code game can fade without an end.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what finding the code means, such as the fewest guesses or only part of it, and reads counts against that.
pros: Each player judges their own result.
A part-solved code can still count.
cons: Players may measure themselves unevenly.
It is hard to compare one player with another.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player fails to crack a code in time, and everyone else is simply safe.
pros: Every count lowers or raises a risk of losing.
The pressure is spread across the table.
cons: The loser can feel singled out.
The safe players may stop caring.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep the code game going, so the setter and guesser swap roles and pick new codes after each answer.
pros: Roles swap and the game carries on.
Counts become a shared habit.
cons: There is no end to the guessing.
A code that is too hard can stall everyone.

pairs.tendency: The code is made so that no count ever gets a player to the answer, which turns the guessing into a puzzle about the game itself.
pros: Players question what the counts are for.
The game shows its own limits.
cons: Players may feel the guessing is empty.
The code game can feel unfair.

pairs.tendency: You guess a layout alone, and the counts tell you how many cards are right and in the right place until you clear it or get stuck.
pros: A solo player gets clear feedback.
Each count points to the next move.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
There is no one to share the guess with.

pairs.tendency: Short code games are played in a row, and the player who cracks the most codes wins, so counts matter in every round.
pros: A poor round is followed by a fresh one.
Players learn from earlier counts.
cons: A strong early lead can end the match.
A long set can wear out the setter.

pairs.tendency: Each wrong guess adds a point against you, so each count tells you how many points you may be about to pick up.
pros: A close count saves points.
Players weigh each guess carefully.
cons: A few early errors can decide the game.
A careful player may stall to avoid points.

pairs.tendency: You have to land on the exact number, and the counts tell you how many parts are right, but a guess that overshoots costs the win.
pros: Counts show how near the exact number is.
An overshoot has a clear cost.
cons: A near guess can still lose.
A player may wait many turns for the throw.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to give away the code or lose it, so a player reads each count to see how far they are from being right.
pros: The aim turns the usual guessing upside down.
Players think about what a wrong guess looks like.
cons: Wrong guesses on purpose are hard to make.
Counts are easy to read the wrong way round.

pairs.tendency: Each player guesses their own code at the same time, and the counts affect nobody else, so the game is a quiet race.
pros: Everyone works at their own pace.
No one blocks anyone else.
cons: There is little to talk about.
Players have no reason to watch each other.

pairs.tendency: Players guess about each other's hidden codes and can strike at a rival once the count shows how close they are.
pros: A near count turns into an attack.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: A leader draws attacks from all sides.
A hard code can leave a player out.

pairs.tendency: Players build codes on the board and cannot hit each other, so a rival's changes to the board alter the counts you receive.
pros: The board carries the effect of a rival's move.
There is no direct attack to avoid.
cons: Counts can change without a clear cause.
A player may not know who caused a change.

pairs.tendency: The whole table guesses one code against the game, and everyone shares the counts and wins or loses together.
pros: The team reads every count at once.
A hard code tests how well players talk.
cons: One player can do most of the guessing.
An early find can end the fun.

pairs.tendency: Players guess a shared code together, but each has a small private reason to find it first, so counts are shared with some care.
pros: Players have to trade help against self-interest.
A shared count helps and tempts.
cons: A player can hold a count back.
Trust can break down during the round.

pairs.tendency: Two teams each hide a code from the other, and teammates share the counts while they race to crack the rival's code.
pros: Teammates talk through each count.
Each team has a clear target.
cons: One strong guesser can carry a team.
Teammates can disagree about a guess.

pairs.tendency: Most players guess the code together, while one secretly gives wrong counts, so the others have to check which answers are true.
pros: Counts can be trusted or doubted.
A traitor can spread doubt.
cons: A wrong count may be hard to prove.
Players can end up accusing one another.

pairs.tendency: Guesses and counts go back and forth by letter, so each answer arrives days later and the guesser has long to think.
pros: Waiting gives time to plan a guess.
A letter can hold a careful count.
cons: A guess can take days to answer.
A lost letter can stall the game.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so their hidden code is set before play and the counts come from rules or a record.
pros: The absent code is fixed in advance.
Players can guess from earlier games.
cons: Nobody can fix a wrong count.
The absent player cannot change the code.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and sets the hidden code, and the others guess it, with each count coming from the game master.
pros: The game master controls the pace.
Counts can be told in the world's own words.
cons: The game master can slip on a count.
The game master has no one to guess against.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or park, and passers-by can join in to guess a code chalked or hidden nearby.
pros: Anyone can join and guess.
Counts are easy to share aloud.
cons: A code can be guessed by outsiders.
A busy place can cause a miscount.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the code and the rest guess it together, and the lone setter is paid more if the code is not cracked.
pros: The setter has a clear reward.
The group has to agree on each guess.
cons: The lone setter can feel outnumbered.
A group may find a code very quickly.

pairs.tendency: One player sets and guesses a code alone, so the counts come from a rule or a book and the player compares results later.
pros: A player can try any time.
Counts are always available.
cons: There is no one to ask about a count.
The setter can be too easy to guess.

pairs.tendency: The code is mostly set by dice, so counts tell the guesser how lucky the code was more than how well they guessed.
pros: Anyone can win.
The game runs briskly.
cons: Counts say little about the guesser's skill.
Skilled players may feel the game has no pull.

pairs.tendency: The code is partly set by luck, but players can reroll or pick, so a poor count can be softened by a later try.
pros: A poor first guess is not fatal.
Choices still matter against luck.
cons: A reroll can erase a useful count.
Players may lean on the reroll too much.

pairs.tendency: The guesser's reasoning decides most of the game, with a little luck in what the code is, so the counts reward working out.
pros: Careful counting pays off.
A small piece of luck keeps it open.
cons: A lucky code can end the game early.
The luck can hide sound reasoning.

pairs.tendency: The code is set by choice, not luck, and the guesser wins by reading each count and working out what remains.
pros: Every count adds to the reasoning.
The sharpest reasoner tends to win.
cons: A new player can find it hard.
A weak setter can make the code too easy.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards give a sign, and the hidden code is the meaning of it, so counts tell how near a reading is to the sign.
pros: Counts turn a sign into a talking point.
Players discuss what they read.
cons: A count cannot say what a sign means.
Different readings may all seem right.

pairs.tendency: Players try to sense when others will act and guess a code together, and counts tell them how well they are in step.
pros: Counts show how well players are in step.
A shared sense can grow.
cons: The count cannot show why players differ.
Players can feel they are guessing at random.

pairs.tendency: The dice are looked up on a table to set the hidden code, so counts tell the guesser how close they are to what the table says.
pros: The table gives the code a story.
Counts feed back into the tale.
cons: A table roll can set a code too hard.
The story loses shape if the code is odd.

pairs.tendency: Everything is open except the code itself, so the guesser sees every move and the only unknown is the one hidden thing.
pros: The one secret stands out.
Players know what the counts rest on.
cons: Open play leaves little to bluff with.
A code can be worked out by anyone watching.

pairs.tendency: Players hold cards no one can see, and the counts tell a guesser about the cards held, so each answer gives away a little of a hand.
pros: Counts give hints about hands.
Players guess and bluff together.
cons: An answer can reveal your own hand.
A player holding many cards gives away more.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and counts about a code may be true or false depending on who gives them.
pros: Each count is checked against who gave it.
Players think about motives.
cons: A role can taint every count.
Players may stop trusting any answer.

pairs.tendency: Players use the counts as clues to work out hidden facts, and each answer rules some possibilities out.
pros: Each answer removes some options.
Reasoning is plain to see.
cons: A wrong early guess can mislead the rest.
Players may spend long on a single count.

pairs.tendency: A setter can bluff about the code, but the counts are fixed, so the bluff lies in what the setter says around them.
pros: A bluff has something real to push against.
Players read faces as well as counts.
cons: A bluff can fall flat against a plain count.
A setter has few ways to lie.

pairs.tendency: The code is a secret rule, and each count tells you how near your guess is to it, so you learn the rule by being close.
pros: Counts show how near the rule is.
Players learn by trying.
cons: A rule can be hard to guess from counts.
New players may feel lost.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the code but may only answer with counts or hints, so the others guess from what they are told.
pros: The setter has a clear limit.
Counts stand in for words.
cons: A count may be too thin to help.
The silent player may feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden and is turned over as players explore, so counts about the code are checked against what the map shows.
pros: New parts of the map give new clues.
Counts and the map can agree or not.
cons: Exploring can leave the code behind.
A hidden map can hide the answer long.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so a guesser can compare counts about the hidden hands with what the open hand shows.
pros: The open hand gives a fixed point.
Counts narrow what the other hands hold.
cons: The open hand reveals part of the code.
The open hand has less to hide.

pairs.tendency: Scores are kept secret, so players use the counts to guess who is ahead, and each answer hints at a rival's total.
pros: A count can hint at a score.
Everyone has to guess who leads.
cons: Nobody can check the guesses.
A leader can hide a long way ahead.

pairs.tendency: One player guesses at a time and gets a count back, so everyone else watches the answers and learns from each.
pros: Each count is seen by all.
Waiting players can think ahead.
cons: A slow guesser holds everyone up.
Players can copy a sharp guess.

pairs.tendency: Everyone guesses together in secret and then all reveal, so each player gets a count at once and nobody waits.
pros: Nobody sits idle.
Counts arrive for the whole table.
cons: A quick guesser has no edge.
A noisy table can make counting hard.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can guess at any moment and the fastest answer is counted first, so players race to use each count.
pros: Quick thinking is rewarded.
Counts come in a rush.
cons: A slow player can be left behind.
Counts can arrive in a muddle.

pairs.tendency: Each guess has a clock, so a guesser has to choose after a short look at the counts, and a late guess is lost.
pros: The clock keeps guessing moving.
Players act on the counts they have.
cons: A hurried guess often wastes a count.
A slow thinker can feel rushed.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over real days, with one guess and one count a day, so waiting for the answer is part of the game.
pros: Each day gives time to think.
Counts become small events.
cons: A player can forget the code in between.
A long game can lose its pull.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down with a pause before each guess, so each count is read slowly and carefully.
pros: A pause gives time to read a count.
Players guess with more care.
cons: Slow play can be dull.
A pause can break the rhythm of the guessing.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, with shorter clocks or more guesses a round, so counts are read faster each time.
pros: The pace builds as the code gets closer.
Late rounds feel tense.
cons: A fast end leaves no time to count.
Players can make mistakes in the rush.

pairs.tendency: Some throws or hits give another go at once, so a player may make two guesses and read two counts before anyone replies.
pros: A lucky player gets a quick second look.
Two counts can narrow the code fast.
cons: A lucky player can solve it before others try.
Others wait a long while.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages, such as setting a code first and then guessing it, and what is learnt in one stage carries into the next.
pros: Each stage has its own job.
Counts from one stage guide the next.
cons: Early choices can set a weak code.
A change of rules can confuse players.

pairs.tendency: The hidden code stands for the setting of a real system, and each count tells how close the model is to how it really works.
pros: Counts become a way to test a model.
Players learn what a system depends on.
cons: A count cannot show why a guess is wrong.
A simple code can oversimplify the system.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group with its own needs and guesses the code from that group's view, so counts mean different things to each.
pros: Players see the code from other standpoints.
A count can lead to talk between groups.
cons: Each role may read the count differently.
A role with little to guess can be bored.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and each guess takes some of it, so the counts have to be weighed against what is left.
pros: A guess has a visible cost to all.
Players share the cost of finding the code.
cons: A heavy guesser can use up the store.
Players may stop guessing to save it.

pairs.tendency: A guess shows its effect only a few rounds later, so counts that come back late have to be linked to the guess that caused them.
pros: Players learn to link cause and effect.
A late count rewards careful notes.
cons: A count is hard to tie to its guess.
Players can give up before the answer comes.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and then use the counts to see what it changes, so the guessing becomes a small test.
pros: A rule can be tried with little risk.
Counts give clear evidence of what changed.
cons: One round can be too short to show effects.
Players can argue over what the counts mean.

pairs.tendency: After the guessing, everyone goes through the counts and what they showed, and compares them with the real problem.
pros: Counts give the talk something to hold on to.
Players can see how they narrowed the code.
cons: The counts may seem remote from the real problem.
A short debrief can leave things unsaid.

pairs.tendency: Each guess changes the game permanently, so a count that arrives cannot be undone and the next code starts where this one ended.
pros: Every guess carries a real cost.
Players think hard before a guess.
cons: A wrong guess cannot be taken back.
Players may freeze rather than try.

pairs.tendency: The way counts are made makes a point about the world, such as rewarding near answers over exact ones.
pros: The counting rule says something.
Players can argue about what it says.
cons: Players may miss the point.
The point can feel forced.

pairs.tendency: Real money or a promise rides on the code, so each count carries more weight than a game normally gives it.
pros: Each count matters beyond the table.
Players take the guessing seriously.
cons: A real loss can sour a friendship.
A player may be pushed to guess early.

pairs.tendency: A number stands for something that matters, such as health, and the counts of right parts show how near a player is to the number.
pros: A count shows how near a value is.
Players see what a number can miss.
cons: Players chase the count, not the value.
The number can crowd out what it stands for.

pairs.tendency: Players try out a way of living that does not exist yet, and the counts show how close each guess of its rules is to working.
pros: Counts give early signs of what holds up.
Players feel a future before it comes.
cons: Counts cannot say if the future will work.
The code can feel far from a real life.

pairs.tendency: A close count makes the next guess easier, and a poor one makes it harder, so players can pull ahead or fall behind quickly.
pros: Early gains build on themselves.
Players see a loop at work.
cons: A lead grows hard to catch.
A poor start can feel hopeless.

pairs.tendency: Counts creep up slowly with little change, and then one guess crosses a line and the whole code opens at once.
pros: A sudden turn gives a clear moment.
Players feel how change can build.
cons: Long stretches can feel flat.
A player may miss the point of crossing.

pairs.tendency: Right parts pile up round by round, so the size of what you know matters more than any one count.
pros: Players watch knowledge grow.
The pile shows how much is solved.
cons: A big pile can make the last guess automatic.
A single count seems small beside the pile.

pairs.tendency: Between turns the world moves by a fixed rule and changes the code a little, so an old count may no longer hold.
pros: Players keep guessing as things change.
Nobody decides the shift.
cons: An old count can mislead.
Notes made earlier can be out of date.

pairs.tendency: A card or roll changes the hidden code without warning, so a count that was right a moment ago may now be wrong.
pros: Players adjust to a shock.
A solved code is not safe.
cons: A shock can undo a lot of work.
Players can feel their effort was wasted.

pairs.tendency: Each round stands for a year, so a count is a yearly report on how close the guess is to how things really are.
pros: Many years pass in an afternoon.
Counts show change over time.
cons: A year's count is thin as a record.
The code game can feel too fast.

pairs.tendency: Gauges on the board show how the system is doing, and the counts tell the guesser how close the code is to what the gauges show.
pros: Gauges give the counts a place to sit.
Everyone can see how things stand.
cons: Players may watch the gauges instead of guessing.
A gauge can disagree with a count.

pairs.tendency: Players start with different amounts, so some begin with more clues or tries and read the counts from a stronger place.
pros: A head start tells in the counts.
A count means more with more to go on.
cons: A poor start can feel unfair.
The leader may keep the lead throughout.

pairs.tendency: The player in front writes the rules for answers, so counts may be changed in ways that keep the leader ahead.
pros: Players feel how power shapes a game.
A leader's rule can explain a gap.
cons: Others can feel locked out.
Counts can lose meaning once the rules change.

pairs.tendency: Each role wins by its own measure, so a count that helps one role may hurt another and all can see what each wants.
pros: Roles pull against each other in the open.
Counts show where the goals clash.
cons: A player may never be able to win.
Players can argue over what a count shows.

pairs.tendency: The game opens on a described situation, and the hidden code is part of it, so players guess what is true from the counts.
pros: Everyone starts from the same facts.
Counts have a story to fit into.
cons: A long opening can slow the first guess.
Players may guess what the text hints at.

pairs.tendency: A player explains why a guess would work and the table decides what count to give, so the count is argued, not fixed.
pros: Players have to explain their guesses.
The table judges what is close.
cons: A count can turn into an argument.
A loud voice can sway the table.

pairs.tendency: Play stops at set points so players can say what the counts have told them before going on.
pros: Players can think about what they know.
Counts get talked through.
cons: A pause can break the pace.
Some players may have little to say.

pairs.tendency: The same code game is played again with one thing changed, and the counts are compared round by round.
pros: Players see what the change did.
Counts give a clear way to compare.
cons: Players may remember the first code.
A small change can hide in the noise.

pairs.tendency: The game says what the counts leave out, such as why a guess was wrong, so players know where the code stops matching reality.
pros: Players know what the game cannot say.
A count is read with its limits in mind.
cons: The note can take the fun from a count.
Players may skip it.

pairs.tendency: The people the game is about help set the code and test the counts, so the answers match what they know.
pros: The counts ring true to those who know.
The setting is checked by the people in it.
cons: Designing with them takes time.
Their view can make a code others find hard.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a link in a chain and guesses the next link's hidden order from the counts, so a wrong count spreads down the chain.
pros: One count can reach every player.
Players see how a mistake travels.
cons: A wrong count at one link spoils the rest.
Players may blame the nearest link.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own stock and the counts they are given, and have to guess the hidden rest from them.
pros: Players feel what a narrow view is like.
Counts become the only link to the whole.
cons: A thin view can lead to wild guesses.
Players can feel cut off.

pairs.tendency: The slowest step sets the pace, so the counts help a guesser find which step is the slow one and where speeding up does nothing.
pros: Counts point to the slow step.
Players see why one fix changes little.
cons: A count may not show which step is slow.
Players may fix the wrong step.

pairs.tendency: Goods are made to a guess or only when an order comes, and the counts tell how close the guess was to what was ordered.
pros: Counts show how well the guess matched.
Players feel the gap between ahead and on order.
cons: Guessing wrong leaves goods unsold.
Waiting for orders can leave shelves empty.

pairs.tendency: Players choose how many to make at once, and the counts show how many of the batch were right and in the right place.
pros: A big batch makes a count weigh more.
Players weigh waiting against setting up.
cons: A big batch of wrong goods costs a lot.
A batch of one slows the whole line.

pairs.tendency: Equipment fails at random, so a count that was right yesterday may fail today and the guesser has to plan for a gap.
pros: Players learn to plan for a break.
Counts show where a failure bit.
cons: A breakdown can wipe out a sound guess.
Players can blame luck for a poor count.

pairs.tendency: Holding stock costs something every round and running out costs more, so players use counts to guess how much to hold.
pros: Counts help set how much to keep.
Players feel both sides of the cost.
cons: A cautious guess can pile up stock.
A bold guess can leave a shortage.

themes.line: The abstract theme gives the game no story or setting, just shapes, colours and moves, so the rules are the whole experience.
The historical theme sets the game in a real time and place from the past, so the moves can stand for real events.
The fantasy theme brings dragons, magic or quests, so the same moves can feel like an adventure.
The science-fiction theme sets the game in space or the future, so the same moves can feel like exploring or inventing.
The everyday-life theme uses places players already know, like a market or a school, so the rules are easier to picture.
The absurd theme makes the setting silly on purpose, so players can laugh at their own moves.
The educational theme ties the game to something to learn, so playing also teaches a fact or a skill.
The real-world-issue theme connects the game to a problem people face today, so the moves can start a conversation.
The poetic theme makes the game short and a little strange, so the moves ask players to notice something rather than to win it.
The ritual-or-sacred theme turns the board into a path towards something holy, so each move can feel like a step in a practice.
The mortality-and-loss theme ties the game to time running out or someone being lost, so the moves can carry weight beyond the table.
The war-and-conquest theme sets the game among armies and borders, so the moves can stand for taking and holding ground.

The game is aimed at competition (agon). The pleasure of testing your ability against a rival under rules built to make the contest fair, so that whoever wins has clearly shown superiority in one quality such as speed, memory or ingenuity. (Roger Caillois; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Macklin and Sharp)

The game is aimed at chance (alea). The pleasure of leaving the result to luck: waiting, hoping and risking a stake, with no skill able to change the outcome. In the milder sense Macklin and Sharp give, the pleasure of planning around unpredictable events. (Roger Caillois; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Macklin and Sharp)

The game is aimed at make believe (mimicry). The pleasure of accepting a pretended world, or of behaving as someone other than yourself, so that you feel more than your ordinary self through fantasy, disguise or pretence. (Roger Caillois; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at vertigo (ilinx). The pleasure of deliberately unsettling your balance or perception, a short voluptuous panic in an otherwise clear mind, through spinning, falling, speed or other dizziness. (Roger Caillois; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; McKenzie Wark)

The game is aimed at exuberance (paidia). The unplanned pleasure of free, noisy, improvised play with no purpose but itself, such as a kitten with wool or a baby with a rattle, tending to run to excess. Boyd names the same ground as spontaneity (acting freely as a whole person) plus exhilaration (a lift that is more than mere excitement). (Roger Caillois; Neva Boyd)

The game is aimed at challenge (ludus). The pleasure of working against a difficulty that has been set up for its own sake, an obstacle and not an opponent, and of reaching a satisfactory solution for no other reward. (Roger Caillois; Elias; Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at skill mastery. The satisfaction of developing and using skill, whether quick bodily skill (timing, precision) or mental skill (planning, analysis), and of playing well in itself. (Macklin and Sharp; Elias)

The game is aimed at learning. The pleasure of absorbing a pattern, understanding something new or seeing yourself improve, which the brain rewards. Koster restricts the word fun to this; Burgun and Elias describe the same pleasure as mastery or self-improvement over many plays. (Raph Koster; Keith Burgun; Elias)

The game is aimed at flow. Complete absorption in an activity in which the challenge meets your skill, done for its own sake, with self-consciousness and sense of time dropping away. (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Raph Koster; Jane McGonigal)

The game is aimed at hard fun. Enjoyable hard work: choosing a demanding task so that the stress you feel is energising and optimistic, not fearful, and leaves you stronger than you started. (Jane McGonigal; Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at easy fun. Relaxing, low-effort enjoyment such as passive entertainment. McGonigal argues it leaves people feeling lower than hard fun does; Csikszentmihalyi's 'pleasure' is the same ground, contentment from needs being met, which restores order but does not make you grow. (Jane McGonigal; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at triumph (fiero). The surge of triumph after overcoming a real difficulty, often shown with arms thrown up. The harder the obstacle, the stronger it is. Elias lists the plain pleasure of winning as a reward. (Jane McGonigal; Raph Koster; Elias)
The game is aimed at hope of success. The feeling of confidence that you can succeed and are improving, and the charged moment of hope just before success when you try hardest. (Jane McGonigal)

The game is aimed at vicarious pride (naches). The bursting pride of seeing someone you taught or helped succeed, for example coaching a friend through a game you have mastered. Koster adds kvell, the feeling of bragging about someone you mentor. (Jane McGonigal; Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at happy embarrassment. Playful teasing and trash-talking that stings a little and, because it is plainly not meant to hurt, confirms trust and warms the relationship. (Jane McGonigal)
The game is aimed at gloating (schadenfreude). The pleasure of seeing a rival fail, in effect a put-down. (Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at cooperation. The pleasure of working with others towards a shared goal, in step with them and doing what none of you could alone, like a pass that leads to a goal. (Macklin and Sharp)

The game is aimed at sociability. The pleasure of the company of other players: talk, give and take, belonging and the bonds that form around a game, before and after as well as during it. (Elias; Jane McGonigal; Germaine and Wake; Neva Boyd)

The game is aimed at playing well together. Satisfaction in how a group plays, judged by the manner of playing together, not by who wins; choosing and changing games to suit what all are willing to play, and competing as a loving challenge to each other. (Bernie DeKoven)
The game is aimed at negotiation. The pleasure of social give-and-take in a game: persuading, forming and breaking alliances and bargaining. (Elias)
The game is aimed at status. The satisfaction of standing, ranking or being seen as skilled within a group, including records of who won and by how much. (Raph Koster; Elias)

The game is aimed at delight. The brief pleasure of recognising a pattern and being surprised by it, such as the end of a mystery when everything falls into place. Elias uses aesthetic enjoyment for the look of the game, its graphics and well-made pieces. (Raph Koster; Elias; Johan Huizinga)

The game is aimed at elegant action. The pleasure of acting, deciding or solving well: the elegance of a clean solution or a perfectly dodged obstacle, and the fit between your abilities and the task. (C. Thi Nguyen)

The game is aimed at touch. The pleasure of handling the components: the weight of chess pieces, the feel of shuffling cards, rolling dice, punching out cardboard, a well-carved game piece. (Germaine and Wake; Elias; Raph Koster)
The game is aimed at excitement. The bodily charge of fast, physical or risky play, such as an adrenaline rush, or the physical reactions of mastering a bodily problem. (Elias; Raph Koster)
The game is aimed at escape. The relief of stepping out of everyday life and its cares for a time. (Elias; Germaine and Wake)

The game is aimed at discovery. The pleasure of exploring a world or a space of possibilities, finding out how it works and what is in it, and of the sense of discovering something new. (Macklin and Sharp; Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi; Jane McGonigal; Raph Koster)

The game is aimed at epic meaning. The satisfaction of belonging to, and contributing to, something larger and longer-lasting than yourself, felt with curiosity, awe and wonder at large scales. (Jane McGonigal)
The game is aimed at story. The pleasure of a story unfolding through your actions, whether you take on a character in a loose rule-set or move through a designed narrative. (Macklin and Sharp)
The game is aimed at performance. The pleasure of acting, improvising and putting on a show, often as much fun to watch as to play, such as charades or a physical dance of bodies. (Macklin and Sharp)
The game is aimed at expression. The pleasure of expressing a feeling or idea through a game, as the maker or as the player. (Macklin and Sharp; Neva Boyd; Raph Koster)
The game is aimed at simulation. The pleasure of playing inside a model of a real system, for example as mayor or tycoon, and seeing its workings and the point of view it takes. (Macklin and Sharp)
The game is aimed at tension. The strain of an undecided outcome: wanting something to succeed or resolve and striving to decide it, strongest in contests and gambling. (Johan Huizinga)

The game is aimed at rapture. Complete absorption and devotion in play that passes into elation and abolishes the sense of 'only' playing; frivolity and ecstasy are the poles between which play moves. (Johan Huizinga)

The game is aimed at whimsy. The pleasure of silly actions, unexpected results and absurdity, a sense of euphoria that has to be felt to be understood; for DeKoven also a shared joke, savoured between players. (Macklin and Sharp; Bernie DeKoven)
The game is aimed at fun failure. The enjoyment of failing in an entertaining way, when failure shows your agency, makes you laugh and keeps hope and learning going. (Jane McGonigal)
The game is aimed at blissful productivity. The pleasure of being immersed in clear, demanding work that gives quick, visible results. (Jane McGonigal)
The game is aimed at value clarity. The satisfaction of goals that are clear, comparable and rankable, offering relief from the muddle of real-life values. (C. Thi Nguyen)

The game is aimed at striving. Taking up a goal only for the sake of the struggle to reach it, so that the activity is the point and the winning is a device; the reverse of ordinary practical life. (C. Thi Nguyen)
The game is aimed at mirth. Plain gladness in play, tending to break out in laughter. (Neva Boyd; Johan Huizinga)

The game is aimed at subversion. Playing against the expected script: acting out the forbidden or unexpected, redressing or reskinning, or rewriting the rules, in order to question conventions. (Mary Flanagan)

The game is aimed at creative playing. The excitement of play that comes from the precarious meeting of inner reality and the real, shared world, Winnicott's account of children's playing. (D. W. Winnicott)
